title: API reference
text: Bleep Bus API reference (spec v0.1) The complete reference for plugin developers using the SDK: concepts, lifecycle, every function, type and error code, the C++ and JUCE helpers, host notes, pitfalls and the conformance checklist. The source of truth is the commented header bus/include/bleep bus.h ; CI checks that every function in it is documented here. Language: plain C99 API, usable from C, C++, Rust, Zig, Swift … Linking: one static library ( bleep bus ), no dependencies. License: MIT. Link it into closed-source plugins freely. Thread markers used below: [RT] real-time safe: no locks, no allocation, no system calls. Call it from the audio thread. [non-RT] may lock or allocate. Never call it from the audio thread.

title: Concepts
text: Concepts Term Meaning Bus One shared-memory segment per namespace ( default unless set). Open one handle per plugin instance, or share one per process. Endpoint One registered plugin instance, with a stable 64-bit UID that you save in the plugin state. Output A named signal an endpoint publishes every block. Input A named destination. It sums all cables into it. Cable (source UID, output name, amount) , stored with the receiving input. Block One audio callback (≤ 4096 samples), framed by bb begin block / bb end block . Signal conventions Type Range Notes BB SIGNAL CONTROL −1..+1 (bipolar) or 0..1 (unipolar) declare polarity per output BB SIGNAL GATE high ≥ 0.5 BB SIGNAL TRIGGER single sample of 1.0 take the max when decimating BB SIGNAL PITCH 1.0 per octave, 0 = C4 (MIDI 60) Latency A reader gets each source's block for the reader's previous block: exactly one block late, whatever order the host runs the tracks in. That keeps renders deterministic, including offline export. Don't use the bus for phase-critical audio. Applying modulation Apply an input as an offset in the parameter's normalised range, inside your DSP. Never move the host parameter. float base = knob normalised; / what the user set / uint32 t n sources = bb read input(cutoff in, mod, n); for (uint32 t i = 0; i 1.f ? 1.f : v; cutoff hz[i] = 20.f powf(1000.f, v); / exponential mapping = octaves / }

title: Lifecycle
text: Lifecycle constructor bb bus open → bb register instance → bb add output / bb add input restore state bb set instance uid(saved uid) → bb load connections(saved text) audio callback bb begin block → bb read input … bb write output → bb end block save state bb endpoint uid → bb save connections UI / timer bb list outputs (source menus), bb connect / bb disconnect, bb endpoint patch version (mark the set dirty) destructor bb unregister instance → bb bus close Rules: Register in the constructor with UID 0 (a fresh UID), so the instance is on the bus before the host restores its state. When the host restores state, call bb set instance uid with the saved UID. If it returns BB ERR UID IN USE , the user duplicated the device: keep the fresh UID, and still load the saved cables. Add all inputs before bb load connections . Save bb endpoint uid (not the UID you asked for) and the bb save connections text in your plugin state. Poll bb endpoint patch version on the message thread a few times per second. When it changes, tell the host your state changed. In JUCE: updateHostDisplay(ChangeDetails().withNonParameterStateChanged(true)) . Unregister before closing the bus.

title: Bus functions
text: Bus functions bb bus open bb bus bb bus open(uint32 t spec version, const char bus namespace, bb error err); Opens the bus segment, creating it if needed. [non-RT] spec version : pass BB SPEC VERSION . bus namespace : NULL for the environment variable BLEEP BUS NAMESPACE , else "default" . Otherwise 1–16 characters from [a-z0-9 -] . err : optional. Returns a handle, or NULL . Errors: BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH (you or the existing segment speak another version), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR SHARED MEMORY , BB ERR CORRUPT , BB ERR TIMEOUT . bb error err; bb bus bus = bb bus open(BB SPEC VERSION, NULL, &err); if (!bus) log("bus offline: %s", bb error string(err)); / keep working without it / bb bus close void bb bus close(bb bus bus); Unmaps the bus. Unregister all endpoints opened through it first. NULL is ignored. [non-RT] bb bus unlink bb error bb bus unlink(const char bus namespace); Removes the named segment from the operating system. For tools and tests only. Processes that still map it keep using the old segment. On Windows this is a no-op; the mapping disappears with its last handle. [non-RT] bb generate uid uint64 t bb generate uid(void); Returns a random, non-zero 64-bit UID. [non-RT] bb error string const char bb error string(bb error err); Static English text for an error code. [RT]

title: Endpoint functions
text: Endpoint functions bb register instance bb endpoint bb register instance(bb bus bus, const bb instance info info, bb error err); Registers a plugin instance. [non-RT] bb instance info info = BB INSTANCE INFO INIT; / sets struct size / info.uid = 0; / 0 = generate / info.display name = "Function"; / user-facing; may be NULL / info.track name = NULL; / if known / info.vendor = "Brilliant Bleep"; info.product = "Function"; bb endpoint ep = bb register instance(bus, &info, &err); If info.uid is already live, a fresh UID is used. The endpoint is still returned, and err is BB ERR UID IN USE . Endpoints of crashed processes are reclaimed here. Names are truncated at a UTF-8 boundary. Errors: BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR FULL (64 endpoints), BB ERR TIMEOUT . bb unregister instance void bb unregister instance(bb endpoint ep); Removes the instance, its ports and the cables into its inputs. Cables from its outputs stay with their receivers and read silence until the UID returns. Frees ep . [non-RT] bb endpoint uid uint64 t bb endpoint uid(const bb endpoint ep); The current UID. Save this one. [RT] bb endpoint bus bb bus bb endpoint bus(const bb endpoint ep); The bus the endpoint belongs to. [RT] bb set instance uid bb error bb set instance uid(bb endpoint ep, uint64 t uid); Switches to a saved UID after state restore. [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR UID IN USE (another live endpoint owns it; nothing changes), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT (0), BB ERR NOT FOUND . bb set instance name bb error bb set instance name(bb endpoint ep, const char display name); Sets the user-facing name shown in other plugins' source menus. [non-RT] bb set track name bb error bb set track name(bb endpoint ep, const char track name); Sets the host track name if your plugin learns it (JUCE: updateTrackProperties ). That callback may come on any thread, so store the name and apply it from your message thread. [non-RT] bb endpoint patch version uint32 t bb endpoint patch version(const bb endpoint ep); Increases whenever any process changes a cable into this endpoint. Poll it and mark your state as changed when it moves. [RT]

title: Port functions
text: Port functions bb add output bb output bb add output(bb endpoint ep, const char name, bb signal type type, bb polarity polarity, bb error err); Adds an output. [non-RT] name : 1–31 bytes UTF-8, no control characters, no / , unique among this endpoint's outputs. Keep it short and stable ( "A" , "EOC" , "Env" ), because cables refer to it by name. type : BB SIGNAL CONTROL , GATE , TRIGGER or PITCH . AUDIO is reserved. Errors: BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR ALREADY EXISTS , BB ERR FULL . Outputs live until the endpoint is unregistered. bb add input bb input bb add input(bb endpoint ep, const char name, bb signal type type, bb error err); Adds an input, with the same naming rules. Name a parameter's modulation input after the parameter ( "Cutoff" ). [non-RT]

title: Audio-thread functions
text: Audio-thread functions typedef struct bb block info { uint32 t struct size; / BB BLOCK INFO INIT / uint32 t num samples; / 1..4096 / int64 t transport sample pos; / host position of the first sample / double sample rate; uint32 t flags; / BB BLOCK PLAYING / uint64 t host time ns; / 0 = library clock / } bb block info; bb begin block void bb begin block(bb endpoint ep, const bb block info info); Starts a block. [RT] Split host blocks larger than BB MAX BLOCK SAMPLES into sub-blocks and advance transport sample pos for each. Set BB BLOCK PLAYING whenever the transport runs, offline export included. The deterministic timing rule depends on it. bb write output void bb write output(bb output out, const float samples, uint32 t num samples); Publishes this block's samples. [RT] A shorter write holds its last sample to the end of the block. A second call in the same block overwrites. Outputs you don't write publish zeros. bb read input uint32 t bb read input(bb input in, float dest, uint32 t num samples); Fills dest with Σ (source × amount) over all cables. [RT] Returns the number of cables whose source is present. Use it to tell "unpatched" from "patched but zero". Each source arrives one block late (see Concepts). If the source has no suitable block, its last value is held. bb end block void bb end block(bb endpoint ep); Ends the block. [RT] bb block info b = BB BLOCK INFO INIT; b.num samples = n; b.sample rate = sr; b.transport sample pos = pos; b.flags = playing ? BB BLOCK PLAYING : 0; bb begin block(ep, &b); bb read input(rate in, rate mod, n); render lfo(lfo, rate mod, n); bb write output(lfo out, lfo, n); bb end block(ep);

title: Connection functions
text: Connection functions Cables are stored with the receiving input in shared memory, so any process can edit them. The receiver saves them with its state. bb connect bb error bb connect(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name, uint64 t src uid, const char output name, float amount); Adds a cable, or updates the amount if the cable already exists. [non-RT] The destination must be registered. The source doesn't need to be: the cable reads silence until it appears. The amount is clamped to ±1000. Errors: BB ERR NOT FOUND (no such destination input), BB ERR FULL (8 cables per input), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT . bb connect(bus, filter uid, "Cutoff", lfo uid, "A", -0.3f); bb disconnect bb error bb disconnect(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name, uint64 t src uid, const char output name); Removes one cable. [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR NOT FOUND . bb disconnect all bb error bb disconnect all(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name); Removes every cable into an input. [non-RT]

title: Discovery functions
text: Discovery functions Each list function copies up to capacity records and returns the total available. Call it with capacity = 0 to size a buffer. Records are ordered by table slot, which is stable while the bus runs. All are [non-RT] . bb list endpoints uint32 t bb list endpoints(bb bus bus, bb endpoint info dest, uint32 t capacity); bb endpoint info : uid , pid , num outputs , num inputs , display name , track name , vendor , product . bb list outputs uint32 t bb list outputs(bb bus bus, bb output info dest, uint32 t capacity); Every output on the bus with its owner's names. This is what a source menu shows. bb output info : endpoint uid , type , polarity , name , endpoint name , track name . bb list inputs uint32 t bb list inputs(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, bb input info dest, uint32 t capacity); The inputs of one endpoint, with num connections . bb list connections uint32 t bb list connections(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, const char input name, bb connection info dest, uint32 t capacity); The cables into one input. bb connection info : source uid , amount , output name , source present (0 for a ghost source). bb registry generation uint32 t bb registry generation(const bb bus bus); Changes whenever an endpoint or port appears, disappears or is renamed. Cache your lists and refresh them when it changes. [RT] bb connection generation uint32 t bb connection generation(const bb bus bus); Changes whenever any cable on the bus changes. [RT] bb peek output uint32 t bb peek output(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, const char output name, float dest, uint32 t capacity); Copies the newest completed block of any output, e.g. for a scope. Returns the number of samples copied (0 if the output doesn't exist).

title: State functions
text: State functions bb save connections size t bb save connections(bb endpoint ep, void buf, size t cap); Writes all cables into this endpoint's inputs as NUL-terminated UTF-8 text. Returns the bytes needed, including the NUL. If that exceeds cap , nothing is written. [non-RT] size t n = bb save connections(ep, NULL, 0); char text = malloc(n); bb save connections(ep, text, n); / store text next to your parameters / Format (tab-separated, locale-independent): bleep-bus-connections 1 Cutoff 0123456789abcdef A -0.300000 bb load connections bb error bb load connections(bb endpoint ep, const void buf, size t len); Replaces all cables into this endpoint's inputs with the saved ones. Add your inputs first. Lines for unknown inputs are skipped. Loading does not change bb endpoint patch version . [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR PARSE .

title: Types, constants and errors
text: Types, constants and errors Constants Name Value Meaning BB SPEC VERSION BB MAKE SPEC VERSION(0, 1) pass to bb bus open BB MAX ENDPOINTS 64 per bus BB MAX OUTPUTS 256 per bus BB MAX INPUTS 512 per bus BB MAX CONNECTIONS PER INPUT 8 BB MAX PORTS PER ENDPOINT 64 outputs, and inputs, each BB MAX BLOCK SAMPLES 4096 split larger blocks BB NAME BYTES 64 endpoint/track name field, incl. NUL BB PORT NAME BYTES 32 port name field, incl. NUL BB BLOCK PLAYING 1 bb block info.flags Errors Code Value When BB OK 0 BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT 1 NULL, bad name or namespace, NaN amount BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH 2 incompatible spec version (yours or the segment's) BB ERR SHARED MEMORY 3 the OS refused the segment (sandbox?) BB ERR CORRUPT 4 the segment is not a Bleep Bus segment BB ERR FULL 5 a table is full BB ERR NOT FOUND 6 no such endpoint, input or cable BB ERR ALREADY EXISTS 7 port name taken BB ERR UID IN USE 8 UID owned by another live endpoint BB ERR TIMEOUT 9 registry lock or initialisation took > 2 s BB ERR PARSE 10 saved cable text is malformed A plugin MUST keep working (passing audio, using its knobs) when the bus is unavailable.

title: C++ and JUCE helpers
text: C++ and JUCE helpers bus/wrappers/cpp/bleep bus.hpp is a header-only C++17 RAII wrapper. Each method maps to one C function and has the same thread rules. #include "bleep bus.hpp" bleep::Bus bus; // bb bus open bleep::Endpoint ep(bus, "Bass Wobble", "Function", "Me"); // bb register instance bleep::Output a = ep.addOutput("A", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, BB POLARITY UNIPOLAR); bleep::Input rate = ep.addInput("Rate"); for (const bb output info& o : bus.outputs()) { / source menu / } bus.connect(ep.uid(), "Rate", otherUid, "Out", 0.5f); std::string saved = ep.saveConnections(); bus/wrappers/juce/bleep bus juce.h fills bb block info from JUCE's play head and splits large blocks: #include #include "bleep bus juce.h" void processBlock(juce::AudioBuffer & buffer, juce::MidiBuffer&) override { auto t = bleep::juce helpers::readTransport(getPlayHead(), fallbackPos); fallbackPos += buffer.getNumSamples(); bleep::juce helpers::forEachBusBlock(t, getSampleRate(), buffer.getNumSamples(), & { endpoint.beginBlock(info); rate.read(rateMod.data(), info.num samples); renderLfo(lfo.data(), rateMod.data(), info.num samples); a.write(lfo.data(), info.num samples); endpoint.endBlock(); }); } CMake: add subdirectory(path/to/bleep/bus) and link bleep bus cpp . That target brings in the C library and both wrapper folders.

title: Host notes and pitfalls
text: Host notes Ableton Live hosts plugins in one process and runs tracks on parallel threads. Each track keeps its own transport stamps, so the position rule applies. MIDI generated by a plugin is only routable from VST3 instruments: use the "MIDI From" routing of a second MIDI track. Bitwig can sandbox plugins in separate processes. The bus is shared memory, so this works. All processes must use the same namespace. Logic / AUv3 sandbox: sandboxed app extensions may not open POSIX shared memory. bb bus open then fails with BB ERR SHARED MEMORY ; keep working without the bus. Offline export runs faster than real time. Report BB BLOCK PLAYING and the true transport position, and timing stays exact. Pitfalls Calling [non-RT] functions on the audio thread. bb connect , the list functions and registration take a cross-process lock. Saving the requested UID instead of bb endpoint uid . After a device duplication they differ. Loading cables before adding inputs. Unknown inputs are skipped. Moving host parameters to show modulation. Apply modulation inside the DSP and draw it in your UI instead. Assuming zero latency. Feedback through the bus adds one block per pass. Renaming outputs between versions breaks users' cables. Treat port names as API. Forgetting BB BLOCK PLAYING . Without it, timing falls back to the wall-clock rule, which isn't deterministic during export.

title: Conformance checklist
text: Conformance checklist Before you call your plugin "Bleep Bus compatible": [ ] Opens the bus with BB SPEC VERSION and keeps working when it is unavailable. [ ] Registers one endpoint per instance and saves bb endpoint uid in its state. [ ] Restores the saved UID with bb set instance uid and handles BB ERR UID IN USE . [ ] Saves and restores cables with bb save connections / bb load connections . [ ] Frames every audio block with begin/end, ≤ 4096 samples, true transport position and BB BLOCK PLAYING . [ ] Calls only [RT] functions on the audio thread. [ ] Applies modulation as a normalised offset without moving host parameters. [ ] Watches bb endpoint patch version and marks its state as changed. [ ] Unregisters in its destructor. [ ] Uses stable, short port names; parameter inputs are named after the parameter. [ ] bb conformance run passes against the library build you ship. See Conformance for running the suite and the validator.

title: Standalone app
text: Standalone app The Bleep App is the same engine, board and modules as the plugins, without a DAW. Besides the board it adds projects, a preset browser, an audio device, system audio, its own MIDI ports, Ableton Link and the servers that connect it to Live and to the browser. Prerequisites CMake 3.22 or newer, a C++ compiler (Xcode command line tools on macOS, Visual Studio on Windows), optionally Ninja, and JUCE 8.0.9 (downloaded on the first build, or --juce / BLEEP JUCE DIR ). The first build also fetches Ableton Link 4.1. Build and run scripts/run/run-app.sh # Release build, then start with console output here scripts/run/run-app.sh my-project.bleepboard # open a project scripts/run/run-app.sh --no-build # start the last build scripts/run/run-app.sh --smoke # no audio inputs or Link; print a report and quit scripts/run/run-app.sh --ui-dev # read the board UI from patch/; ⌘R after an edit Without the script: cmake -S patch -B build/patch -DCMAKE BUILD TYPE=Release -DBLEEP JUCE DIR=… , then cmake --build build/patch --target BleepApp . The result is build/patch/BleepApp artefacts/Release/Bleep App.app (macOS) or an executable in the same folder on Windows. CMake option Default Effect BLEEP BUILD APP ON Build the standalone app BLEEP LINK ON Include Ableton Link. This makes the app binary GPL. Turn it off for a build that must stay MIT BLEEP UI DEV OFF Development only: the UI comes from the source tree. Never ship BLEEP LINK DIR unset Use a local Link checkout instead of downloading it What the app adds Projects and presets: .bleepboard projects; a preset browser with five demo boards for every advanced module and your own boards. Audio and MIDI: channel pairs of the audio device become In 1/2 , Out 1/2 … ports. The app creates its own MIDI ports ( Bleep App 1…n ), which Live can use as MIDI From and MIDI To . System audio: what the computer plays, as a System node. Core Audio tap on macOS 14.2+, WASAPI loopback on Windows, PulseAudio or PipeWire monitor on Linux (needs libpulse at build time). Ableton Link: the Link node puts tempo, beat, bar, clock and start/stop on the board. Bleep Audio Bridge: each bridge plugin in Live is a node with Send and Return ; while bridges are connected, Live's audio blocks drive the app. Web connection: off by default. File → Settings → Web listens on 127.0.0.1:47100 for Bleep Play pages and for plugins whose Board is Bleep Play . BLEEP WEB PORT= turns it on for one run; BLEEP WEB ROOT= makes the app serve Bleep Play from a folder scripts/build/build-web.sh wrote. Checks before you hand out a build scripts/build/build-patch.sh # plugins and tests; the app is built from the same tree scripts/run/run-app.sh --smoke On macOS, start the smoke run with --system-audio through LaunchServices ( open -W … --args --smoke --system-audio ), or the audio permission is not the app's and the capture stays silent. Licences and signing Link is GPLv2-or-later , so app binaries built with it are distributed under the GPL with their source. A closed-source build needs a licence from Ableton, or -DBLEEP LINK=OFF (the app then uses an internal clock). JUCE is AGPLv3 or commercial. No script here signs or notarises the app. A downloaded unsigned macOS build is blocked by Gatekeeper until it is signed with a Developer ID and notarised. The app is released to the Bleep Store like the plugins, with the store signature described in Signing. Modules in the app The app loads modules from the Bleep Store as signed .wasm files, through an embedded WebAssembly runtime. See the Module ABI and the Bleep Store.

title: Conformance
text: Conformance suite bb conformance is the open test host and validator. cmake -S bus -B build/bus && cmake --build build/bus ./build/bus/bb conformance run # all checks, TAP output, private namespace ./build/bus/bb conformance inspect # print + validate the live "default" bus ./build/bus/bb conformance peer-send # interop peer run checks: Area What Layout struct sizes and offsets match the spec; a fresh segment's header Versioning wrong requested version, foreign segment versions, corrupt magic Registry ports, names, listings, generations, UID collisions, dead-process reclamation, lock recovery Timing one block of latency in random thread order, offline export, loops, stopped transport, real threads Signals summing and amounts, ghost sources, unwritten/short/oversized blocks State save/load round trip, locale-independent amounts, malformed input IPC a second process publishes, this one reads To test another implementation of the C API, link bb conformance.c against it instead of bleep bus . To test interop between your implementation and the reference, run peer-send from one and a reader from the other. "Bleep Bus compatible" Plugins that pass the suite and the checklist may use the "Bleep Bus compatible" badge. The protocol is free to use; the names and logo are trademarks of Brilliant Bleep.

title: Module developers
text: Module developers A module is a node on the board: a folder in patch/modules/ / with a module.json , a C++ node that declares its knobs and jacks and processes audio in process() , DSP without JUCE, an optional custom view in JavaScript, tests, and a user manual. The same source is built for every host. The result is one standalone .wasm file that the engine in the plugins, the Bleep App and the browser all run, so a module you write works everywhere without per-platform code. The path Write it. Writing a module: the folder layout, BLEEP REGISTER MODULE , shared DSP in patch/common/dsp/ , engine features (stepped knobs, groups, buttons, node data, media, voices, custom views). Test it. DSP tests per module, plus bleep module harness , which runs every module with every input fed at several sample rates and checks that outputs stay finite and bounded. Document it. A manual in doc/ .md with a screenshot. The board shows it behind the view's ? button and this website shows it under Modules. Package and sign it. Publishing a module: a .bleepmod package, signed by your developer key. Release it. To the Bleep Store, where users and the apps install it. What a module must satisfy Module ABI: the exports, memory limits, determinism rules and versioning a host expects of the .wasm file. Signing: the chain of trust the apps check before they run a module. Licences: a module ported from other code keeps the original's licence and says so in module.json ; copyleft ports ship only through the store, never inside the apps. Writing a module has the rules. Modules and the Bleep Bus Modules talk to each other with cables on the board. They do not use Bleep Bus, which connects separate plugins in a DAW.

title: Writing a module
text: Writing a module A module is a folder in patch/modules/ with a module.json . The build finds it on its own and the module registers itself, so adding one touches no shared file: patch/modules/ / ├── module.json name, slug (= type id), tagline, colour, formats, doc ├── Module.cpp the node: spec (params, jacks, buttons) and process() ├── dsp/ Dsp.h the DSP, no JUCE (namespace bleep::patch) ├── doc/ .md the user documentation (the view's ? button and the website) ├── doc/ .png screenshot of the module view, shown at the top of the doc ├── ui/ .js optional custom displays for the module view └── tests/test .cpp DSP tests: each file is its own executable and ctest End Module.cpp with the registration function ( static , it is only used here) and BLEEP REGISTER MODULE(registerFooModule); The design lives in doc/specs/modules/ .md (in the repository); the module follows it, and the spec is updated where the implementation had to differ. Advanced modules also get five demo patches ( patch/presets/demos/ .mjs , whole boards for the app's preset browser, see patch/presets/demos/README.md ) and a Demo patches section in their doc. Ported code and licences A module that is ported from, or adapted from, someone else's code (an open-source plugin, firmware, a library) must say so, and keeps the original's licence terms. scripts/check/check-repo.py enforces all of it in CI. module.json gets two fields: { "license": "MIT", "origin": { "name": "PitchShifter (DaisySP)", "author": "Electrosmith, LLC", "url": "https://github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP", "license": "MIT", "copyright": "Copyright (c) 2020 Electrosmith, Corp", "changes": "Rewritten for block processing; interpolation and crossfade changed" } } license is the module's SPDX id; leave it out for MIT. Every source file of the module ( .cpp , .h , .js , tests) starts with // SPDX-License-Identifier: . origin is present exactly when code was taken from somewhere: name , author , url , license (SPDX id of the original) and copyright (its notice, verbatim) are required; changes says what we altered. Permissive originals (MIT, BSD, ISC, Apache-2.0, Zlib, ...) may be ported into an MIT module. The original copyright notice and licence text stay. Copyleft originals (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL) make the module keep that licence: license must equal origin.license . Such a module is never compiled into the apps and plugins (CMake leaves it out of them; tests and tools still build it): it ships only as an optional .wasm module from the Bleep Store, under its own licence, with its source. The store shows the licence on the module's detail view. A module with an origin , or any licence other than MIT, has a LICENSE file in its folder with the full licence text and the original copyright notice. The package carries it. The store's detail view shows the module's license and, for a port, its origin . The module's doc has an ## Origin section that names the source, links it and gives the licence. The package's store summary gets "Based on by ( )." added by the packager. Code under no clear licence, or "all rights reserved", is not ported. Algorithms described in papers or books may be reimplemented freely; say so in the Origin section, and leave out origin if none of the source's code was used. Building and testing cmake -S patch -B build/light -G Ninja -DBLEEP LIGHT TESTS=ON # juce core only, no plugins cmake --build build/light && ctest --test-dir build/light build/light/bleep module harness artefacts/Release/bleep module harness # one module, with CPU use bleep module harness runs every module type on a compiled board with every input fed (noise, control, gates, triggers, pitch, notes), knobs at defaults, at 0, at 1 and random, at three sample rates, with the transport starting, stopping and jumping. Outputs must stay finite and within ±64. After changing params or jacks, regenerate the board UI's type list ( bleep dump types --write patch/board/ui/demo-types.json ). The website reads each module's category from it. A module whose type list entry doesn't exist yet needs "category" in its module.json . Every doc starts with its screenshot ( Name in the module view under the title). With scripts/run/ui-server.py running, scripts/docs/module-screenshots.py [type ...] retakes them after a view changes. The website shows them; the plugins only embed the .md files. Shared code Before writing DSP, look in patch/common/dsp/ (namespace bleep::dsp ): Header What OscCore.h , Wavetable.h , Partials.h , Formant.h , Folder.h oscillators, tables, additive, formant bursts, wavefolding ModalBank.h , Waveguide.h , Exciter.h , Room.h , Vactrol.h physical models, small rooms, low-pass-gate cells Delay.h , Hilbert.h , Fdn.h , Grains.h , Lofi.h delays, frequency shifting, reverb, granular, degradation Chords.h , Harmony.h , Scales.h , SeqClock.h , SeqNotes.h , Tempo.h chords and voicing, the harmony bus, scales, sequencer timing and note output Waves.h , Shapes.h , Slope.h , Chaos.h , Random.h , Noise.h LFO waves, shape library, slope generators, chaos/neurons, seeded randomness Svf.h , Smoothing.h , Oversampler.h , Clip.h , Gain.h , Drums.h filters, smoothing and edges, oversampling, limiting, faders, drum parts Randomness is always seeded and counter-based ( Random.h ), so offline renders repeat. Transport-synced timing derives positions from ctx.ppqAt(i) so a module stays on the grid after loop jumps. Engine features All in patch/engine/Spec.h and Module.h . Stepped knobs. ParamSpec::stepped(id, name, choices, def) and ParamSpec::steppedInt(id, name, min, max, def) are choices and integers that can be modulated: the view shows a knob that snaps, a cable moves it through the steps. value(c, i, s) returns the rounded value. Groups. ParamSpec::percent(...).inGroup("Envelope") puts knobs under a heading in the module view. Use groups on modules with many knobs. Shown in some modes. .when("mode", 2, 3) on a param or a jack shows it only while the setting mode is 2 or 3 (in its own units). Use it for jacks beyond a Count setting ( .when("count", 5, 8) on jack 5) and for knobs that only mean something in one mode. Hidden jacks keep their cables and show dimmed; the module still receives them. Names that follow a mode. .namedBy("mode", {"Tone", "Shape", "Blend"}) renames a knob or jack with the setting's value, for modules whose knobs mean different things per model. Normalled inputs. JackSpec{"b", "Trig B", Signal::Trigger}.normalledTo("a") : while unpatched, Trig B reads Trig A 's signal. ctx.inputConnected[b] stays false, so the module can tell. Unread outputs. ctx.isOutputConnected(k) is false when nothing reads output k . Skip expensive work for it (a filter bank's band outputs), but leave the buffer finite (the node's scope shows it). Buttons and commands. s.buttons = {{"ping", "Ping", true}, {"clear", "Clear"}} adds buttons to the view (true = momentary: press sends 1, release 0). They arrive on the audio thread through the command queue: void process(const ProcessContext& c) override { pollCommands(& { if (cmd.index == Ping) ping = cmd.value > 0.5f; }); ... } Override Module::command(id, value) for commands a custom view sends with view.api.command(id, value) . Node data. s.sanitiseData (JSON in, valid JSON out) and Module::setData(json) for state beyond knobs: steps, patterns, drawn shapes, media ids. Parse on the message thread and hand the result over with RtHandoff ( Handoff.h ): publish(shared ptr) on the message thread, get() on the audio thread. Media. Audio files live in one media folder and are referenced by id ( Media.h ). A custom view makes a drop target with BleepView.mediaDrop(element, view.api, (r) => view.api.setData({...data, sample: r.id})) ; setData then calls media::load(id) and publishes the clip with RtHandoff . Modules that record override exportMedia(slot) ; the view saves with view.api.exportMedia(slot) and stores the returned id in its data. Memory. Set s.memoryHeavy = true on modules with large buffers; the board warns when one goes into a Voice Cell. Harmony bus. s.harmony = HarmonyRole::Writer (Harmony Master) or Reader (anything that follows it). Writers run before readers; the state is in ctx.harmony ( dsp/Harmony.h , kHarmonyBuses buses). Voices. Inside a Voice Cell, ctx.voice is the voice's index (−1 outside): use it as a random stream so voices vary but renders repeat. Data the module changes itself. Override takeData(json) (message thread, polled ten times a second) to store node data the module produced, e.g. a captured loop; the engine saves it in the board and calls setData . Custom views. view.api.isPatched(input) tells whether an input has a cable; hideParams: [ids] in the view hooks hides knobs the custom section edits itself. Live values for views. liveValues() for numbers (a playhead), liveArrays() for arrays (a spectrum, register bits). They arrive in the view's onState(st) as st. and st.arrays. .

title: Publishing a module
text: Publishing a module Modules are code , so the apps only run them if they are signed. The full rules are in Signing and the store's layout in Bleep Store; this page is the practical path. 1. Build the .wasm files scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker --modules-only This compiles every module with Emscripten (in Docker, so no local SDK is needed). Later builds recompile only the modules whose files changed. BLEEP WEB ONLY=oscillator,filter builds just those. 2. Package scripts/release/package-module.py One reproducible .bleepmod per module, in build/store/modules . The packager checks each .wasm against the Module ABI and adds your licence and provenance information. 3. Get a developer key and a token A publisher needs two things from the store's admin: a signing kit (your private key and a certificate issued under the store's root) and a release token for your publisher name. Module ids outside the store's own team carry your publisher namespace. Keep both private; the token is never a command-line argument. 4. Release scripts/release/release.py --modules --level patch \ --registry https:// \ --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token --kit ~/.bleep-signing-kit.json --modules releases only the modules whose package content changed since their newest published version. --dry-run checks everything, including your kit, without publishing. Versions are immutable: a fix is a new version. Compatibility Your package states the module ABI it was built for ( requires.engineAbi in module.json ). A host that does not support it refuses the module with a message instead of crashing, and the store tells the user which app version is needed.

title: Developer overview
text: Build with Beautiful Bleep Everything here is MIT-licensed. Pick the guide that matches what you want to build. I want to… Start here Make plugins talk to each other, in any DAW Bleep Bus quickstart Add a sound, effect or utility to the board Modules Work on the Bleep plugins in Ableton Live Plugins Work on the standalone Bleep App Standalone app Work on Bleep Play, the board in the browser Web Check an exact contract (ABI, signing, store) Reference How the pieces fit Bleep Bus (open protocol, shared memory) │ between any plugins ┌───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┐ │ Bleep plugins in Live │ Bleep App (standalone) │ Bleep Play (browser) │ Board, MIDI/Audio ports, │ same engine, own MIDI ports │ board UI + engine in JS, │ Instrument, FX │ Link, Audio Bridge server │ AudioWorklet └───────────────┬───────────────┴───────────────┬───────────────┴───────────┬─────── │ one engine and board per process (native) │ └──────────────── modules: one .wasm per module ────────────┘ ▲ Bleep Store: signed modules, plugins, presets Modules are the nodes on the board (oscillators, filters, sequencers). Each is a standalone WebAssembly file, so the same module runs in the plugins, the app and the browser. They are installed from the Bleep Store. Plugins are the VST3s you add in Live. A set has one engine; the first plugin loaded creates it and the others share it. Ports connect a track to the board. The app and the web build run the same board without a DAW. The three can exchange audio, MIDI and sync through bridges. Bleep Bus is separate from all of this: an open protocol for per-sample control signals between any audio plugins. Plugin or module? A module lives on the board: it has jacks, knobs and a view, and it is processed by the engine. A plugin is something a DAW loads. If your idea is a new sound or effect, write a module. If it must appear in a DAW's device chain, or exchange signals with other plugins, it is a plugin (a Bleep plugin, or any plugin using Bleep Bus). For coding assistants Every audience has single-file versions of its documentation and an llms.txt index; see "Single files" in the sidebar.

title: Plugin developers
text: Plugin developers "Plugin" means two different things here. Your own plugin, using Bleep Bus You have a plugin (any format, any DAW) and want it to send or receive per-sample control signals to other plugins. That is Bleep Bus , an open protocol over named shared memory with a small C SDK and C++/JUCE helpers. Step Page Send and receive a signal in 15 minutes Quickstart Every function, type and error API reference Implement the protocol without the SDK Specification v0.1 Prove your implementation is correct Conformance Propose a change to the protocol RFC process The Bleep plugins in Live You want to change or extend the plugins that connect Ableton Live to the board. Bleep plugins covers how they share one engine, how to build and reload them, and how they are released. If you want to add a new sound rather than a new plugin, write a module instead: it works in the plugins, the app and the browser.

title: Bleep plugins
text: Bleep plugins The Bleep plugins are VST3s for Ableton Live. Modules are not plugins: they are nodes on the board. In Live you add only: Plugin Live device On the board Bleep Board audio effect required once per set; stores and opens the board; 16 macros Bleep MIDI In instrument notes, pitch, gate, velocity and CCs from a MIDI track Bleep MIDI Out instrument (VST3 MIDI out) notes, gate/pitch, CCs and bend to another track Bleep Audio In audio effect the track's audio Bleep Audio Out instrument board audio on its own track Bleep Instrument instrument one instrument preset with its panel: MIDI in, its cell, audio out Bleep FX audio effect one effect preset with its panel: the track's audio through its cell, dry/wet Bleep Audio Bridge audio effect connects Live to the standalone Bleep App MIDI In/Out and Audio In/Out have a Board menu ( This set , Bleep App , Bleep Play ): the plugin then talks to that board instead of this set's. How they fit together One engine per process. Every plugin binary contains the engine code. The first Bleep plugin loaded creates the engine and publishes it in the process; the others use it. That binary pins itself so it is never unloaded. The rules, and how the interface may change, are in the Engine ABI: plugins share an engine when their major versions match, and a different minor is fine. Ticks. For each host block, the first plugin to run claims the block and runs the compiled board. Plugins exchange their block with the engine through small tagged rings, so a signal from an input port to an output port takes exactly two blocks whatever order Live runs the tracks in. Output ports report that latency to Live. The board is a JSON document owned by the engine and saved in Bleep Board's state. The page edits a copy and commits it; the engine sanitises it, compiles it (cells are flattened, cycles get a 32-sample feedback delay) and keeps the undo stack. Ports appear on the board on their own and cannot be deleted there. They turn into ghosts, with their cables kept, when their plugin is gone. Build scripts/build/build-patch.sh --juce /path/to/JUCE # or BLEEP JUCE DIR; otherwise JUCE 8.0.9 is downloaded scripts/build/build-patch.sh --install # also copy the VST3s to your plugin folder The script builds into build/patch/ and runs the DSP, engine and headless-host tests. VST3 and Live only for now. Without the script: cmake -S patch -B build/patch -DBLEEP JUCE DIR=… -DBLEEP FORMATS=VST3 , then cmake --build , with --target BleepMidiIn VST3 and so on to build only some plugins. Build them all when the engine major has changed. Developing in Live Live keeps a plugin's code loaded until it quits, and overwriting a loaded plugin can crash it. So: UI changes (HTML, CSS, JS): build once with --install --ui-dev . These builds read the board UI from patch/ instead of the embedded copy; press ⌘R in the board window after an edit. Never ship --ui-dev builds. DSP, bus or C++ changes: save your test set and run scripts/run/reload-live.sh . It builds first and quits Live only if the build succeeded. It never force-quits Live. Without Live: scripts/run/ui-server.py runs the board UI in a browser with a fake engine, and the engine tests simulate Live's parallel tracks ( ctest --test-dir build/patch ). Talking to other boards A plugin's Board setting chooses the board on its other side. The wire formats between Live, the app and the browser are described in the bridges design document in the repository ( doc/specs/bridges.md ); the app's side is in Standalone app and the browser's in Web. Release Plugins are signed with your developer key and released to the Bleep Store with scripts/release/release.py . The rules are in Signing. The operating-system signing (macOS Developer ID and notarisation) is separate and not automated. Licences The source is MIT. Binaries built with JUCE are also covered by JUCE's licence (AGPLv3 or a commercial one): check that before you distribute builds.

title: Bleep Bus quickstart
text: Bleep Bus quickstart A minimal sender and receiver in 15 minutes. This page is complete on its own; paste it into a coding assistant together with your plugin source. 1. Build the SDK git clone https://github.com/brilliantbleep/bleep.git cmake -S bleep/bus -B build/bus cmake --build build/bus ctest --test-dir build/bus # conformance suite 2. See it work (two terminals) ./build/bus/minimal sender # publishes a 0.5 Hz sine on output "LFO" ./build/bus/minimal receiver # patches LFO → In and prints it ./build/bus/bb conformance inspect # shows endpoints, ports and cables 3. Add it to your plugin CMake: add subdirectory(path/to/bleep/bus bleep bus) target link libraries(MyPlugin PRIVATE bleep bus cpp) # C only: bleep bus Sender (any plugin, C API): #include "bleep bus.h" / constructor / bb bus bus = bb bus open(BB SPEC VERSION, NULL, NULL); bb instance info info = BB INSTANCE INFO INIT; info.display name = "My LFO"; info.product = "My LFO"; info.vendor = "Me"; bb endpoint ep = bb register instance(bus, &info, NULL); bb output out = bb add output(ep, "LFO", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, BB POLARITY BIPOLAR, NULL); / audio callback / bb block info b = BB BLOCK INFO INIT; b.num samples = n; b.sample rate = sr; b.transport sample pos = transport pos; b.flags = playing ? BB BLOCK PLAYING : 0; bb begin block(ep, &b); bb write output(out, lfo samples, n); bb end block(ep); / destructor / bb unregister instance(ep); bb bus close(bus); Receiver: the same setup with an input, plus a cable. bb input cutoff in = bb add input(ep, "Cutoff", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, NULL); / message thread: patch the first output named "LFO" into Cutoff / bb output info outs[BB MAX OUTPUTS]; uint32 t count = bb list outputs(bus, outs, BB MAX OUTPUTS); for (uint32 t i = 0; i 1.f ? 1.f : v); set cutoff normalised(i, v); / never move the host parameter / } 4. Save the cables / getState / uint64 t uid = bb endpoint uid(ep); / save this / size t len = bb save connections(ep, NULL, 0); / + this text / / setState / bb set instance uid(ep, saved uid); / BB ERR UID IN USE: device was duplicated, fine / bb load connections(ep, saved text, saved len); 5. Load it in Live Build your plugin twice (or load two instances), put one on each of two tracks, and press play. Modulation arrives one block late, independent of track order. Next: the API reference for every function, host notes and pitfalls; the specification if you implement the bus without the SDK.

title: Engine ABI
text: The engine ABI: how Bleep plugins share one engine Every Bleep plugin is its own compiled file, but a set has one engine ( specs.md §5.3). The first plugin loaded creates it and publishes it in the process; the others find it and call it through IEngine ( patch/engine/EngineApi.h ). ABI (application binary interface) is the contract about how two compiled pieces talk: the order of the methods in the interface (a plugin calls "the 14th method", not a name), the layout of the data they pass in memory ( BlockIO , PortFrame , NoteEvent ) and the types used (plain integers, pointers and char arrays: no std::string or JUCE class crosses a binary). If both sides agree, any two builds can share an engine. If not, the result is wrong sound or a crash. Versions Changes when Builds that differ Major ( kAbiTag , bleep-engine-abi-N , plus the sizes of BlockIO , MidiEvent , Transport and a pointer) A method is inserted or removed, a shared struct changes, a type changes Refuse to share. The plugin shows "Another version of Bleep Board is loaded." Minor ( kAbiMinor , IEngine::abiMinor() ) A method is added at the end of IEngine Share. Old plugin on a new engine: fine. New plugin on an old engine: it asks engine.supports(minor) before it calls the new method, and does without it. The minor is the first method of IEngine and never moves, so a plugin can always read it. A minor starts at 0 with every major. Minors so far (of bleep-engine-abi-8 ): 1 setBridged(handle, bool) : a plugin whose Board is the app or Bleep Play (doc/specs/bridges.md) tells the engine that its node is a ghost on this set's board. A plugin checks supports(1) before calling it; without it the node stays live and receives nothing. Rules for changing IEngine Add a method: put it below the destructor, after a public: , with [minor N] in its comment; raise kAbiMinor to N ; guard every call in the plugins with supports(N) ; add it to MismatchEngine . Anything else (insert, remove, reorder, change a signature, change a shared struct): raise the major ( kAbiTag ). Reset kAbiMinor to 0 and drop the guards of the old major. A change in what an existing method does (not its shape) is not an ABI change, but if a plugin relies on the new behaviour it needs a minor that says so. Where the engine lives The engine's code is in the first Bleep plugin loaded in the process; it pins itself so it stays until Live quits. So the engine is as old as that plugin: with a mix of builds, the oldest plugin loaded first decides what the engine can do, which is why plugins check supports rather than assume. After updating plugins, restart Live. Two contracts, two numbers plugin ──(IEngine: this document)──▶ engine ──(module ABI: module-abi.md)──▶ module A plugin never talks to a module. It talks to the engine, and the engine runs the modules. So there are two contracts, each with its own version: Contract Between Form Version Engine ABI (this document) Bleep plugins and the one engine in the process C++ virtual interface, in-process kAbiTag (major) and kAbiMinor Module ABI ( module-abi.md ) The engine and a .bleepmod (WebAssembly) C functions exported by the .wasm file engineAbi , one integer in the module's requires First-party modules compiled into the plugins are not a cross-binary case: the engine creates them from the registry of its own binary, so the engine and the module are always the same build. Store modules (wasm) are where the module ABI matters: the engine checks requires.engineAbi against the range it supports, and refuses a module outside it with a message that says which. The module host that does this is part of the engine, so it is as new as the plugin that created the engine. The two numbers move independently. A new IEngine method (engine minor) says nothing about modules; a changed module export (module ABI) does not touch the plugins' interface. The module ABI could take the same major and minor scheme (compatible additions keep the number, today they are listed as "stay version 1"); that is for module-abi.md to decide, not this document. Not the Bleep Bus The Bleep Bus is a protocol between external plugins (Grit, Cinch …) and the board, with its own version. The engine ABI is the contract among the Bleep plugins themselves; the two are numbered separately.

title: Module ABI
text: Module ABI (version 1) The contract between a host (the engine in the plugins and the app, the browser's worklet, the tests) and a module , a standalone WebAssembly file. It is what engineAbi in the store's requires (see store.md ) counts. This document describes the interface that exists today in patch/web/src/WebShim.cpp , which every one of the 80 module files in the browser build already implements, plus what a host must do around it. Items marked proposed are not in the code yet. Hosts that exist: the browser ( patch/web/js/module-host.js ). A native host for the plugins and the app is the next step. A spike that ran modules inside the plugins with Wasmtime and wasm3 (commit 70c3314 ) was removed again; its measurements are in patch/wasm-host/README.md . The conformance test in section 10 is for every host. 1. Versioning engineAbi is one integer. ABI 1 is everything in this document. A change is compatible if a host that knows version N still runs every module of version N: new optional exports, new fields in the spec JSON that hosts may ignore. It is incompatible otherwise: a changed signature or layout, a changed meaning, a removed export. Incompatible changes bump the integer; compatible ones do not, and get a note under "History" below. A module states the version it was built for in module.json ( requires.engineAbi ). Proposed: the file also exports bleep abi version() → i32 , so a host can check the file itself and a file cannot lie about its package. A module without that export is ABI 1. A host supports a range and refuses modules outside it with a message that says which (never a crash). The Store section explains it ("this module needs Bleep App 1.3"). 2. The file One module.wasm holds the node types of one module folder (usually one, the drum modules have several). It is standalone : no JS glue, no JUCE, no shared memory with other modules, no table shared with the host. Requirement Detail Memory One exported linear memory named memory , growable (1 to 2 MB at start, 64 to 256 KB of stack). A host should cap it (64 MB is a sensible limit; the largest module today starts at 2 MB) and must re-read the memory base after every call, because growing moves it. Imports Only these, and the host provides them as stubs (see section 8): env.emscripten notify memory growth(i32) , bleep media info and bleep media read (section 5a; only modules that load sample files import them), and, for modules using juce core , seven WASI preview 1 functions: fd close , fd read , fd seek , fd write , environ get , environ sizes get , clock time get . Across the 80 current files these are all the imports that occur. A module importing anything else is refused. Start Exports initialize (runs C++ static constructors); the host calls it once, first. No start , no start section that does I/O. Features Whatever the pinned Emscripten (4.0.10) emits by default: no SIMD and no threads are requested, but the files do not record their feature set (the target features section is stripped), so the exact list is to be confirmed by the package step. The modules built with juce core (26 of the 80, the same 26 that import WASI) use wasm exception handling in its standardised form ( try table : -fwasm-exceptions -sWASM LEGACY EXCEPTIONS=0 ). Emscripten's older default ( try / catch ) is not accepted : Wasmtime refuses to compile it, which a first version of the host found out. Browsers have the standard form since 2025 (Chrome 137, Firefox 131, Safari 18.4). wasm3 does not support exception handling at all , so as a fallback it only runs the modules without. Proposed: the package step reads the used features out of each file and writes them to module.json ( features ), and the host checks them at load, so a missing feature is a clear message. Determinism No clock, no randomness from the host: clock time get returns 0. Any random stream is seeded by the module. The same input and knob values produce the same output on every host (the spike matched the native build to about 1e-6 on a peak of 0.4; wasm does not fuse multiply-adds the way a native build may). 3. Life of a module instance compile + instantiate the file (once per process may be shared; one instance per node) initialize() once per instance bleep spec json() the node types the file provides (JSON) bleep chunk() must equal 32, otherwise refuse h = bleep create(typeIndex, sampleRate) 0: failed, the reason is in bleep error() ptrs = bleep params ptr(h), bleep inputs ptr(h), bleep outputs ptr(h), bleep in connected ptr(h) … once repeat: knobs, data, connections … then, per 32-sample chunk: write buffers, bleep set transport, bleep process bleep destroy(h) Threads. An instance is single-threaded : a wasm runtime's store must not be entered by two threads at once, and native modules' atomics (knobs, command queues, live values) do not exist across the boundary. bleep process and the buffer writes around it run on the audio thread. Every other call ( create , destroy , set data , perform , command , live , param text , take data , sanitise data ) must not overlap with bleep process of the same instance, and must never make the audio thread wait. The host therefore marshals them onto the audio thread through queues (knobs: the host keeps the latest value and calls bleep set knob between chunks; buttons and gestures: a queue drained before the chunk; live , take data : answered from a snapshot the audio thread refreshes), or it runs them only while the audio thread is not using the instance (creation, destruction, reconfiguration). The spike did the knob and button part this way. bleep spec json , bleep type count , bleep chunk and bleep note event size touch no instance and are safe at any time after initialize . Real time. bleep process must not allocate, lock, or do I/O. Modules that allocate on create , prepare or set data do it outside the audio thread, as in native. 4. Exports h is the instance handle (an i32 address; 0 means failure). All sizes and addresses are i32 ; f32 and f64 as named. Export Signature Meaning bleep error () → ptr NUL-terminated message of the last call that failed (empty: none). bleep spec json / bleep spec json length () → ptr / () → i32 The node types as a UTF-8 JSON array (section 7). The pointer stays valid for the life of the file. bleep type count () → i32 Number of node types. bleep chunk () → i32 The chunk size, 32. Buffers are sized by it. bleep create (typeIndex: i32, sampleRate: f64) → h A new instance; runs the module's prepare and reset . bleep destroy (h) bleep reset (h) Clears state (a transport jump, a cleared tail). bleep params ptr , bleep inputs ptr , bleep outputs ptr (h) → ptr The three float buffers, fixed for the life of the instance (section 5). bleep in connected ptr , bleep out connected ptr (h) → ptr One byte per input / output jack ( ni + 1 , no + 1 bytes): 1 when patched. An output nobody reads may be skipped but must still hold valid numbers. bleep set knob (h, index: i32, normalised: f32) The value a module reads with setting() : the knob without modulation. Call it when the knob changes, and once for every knob after create , so the module sees the saved state. bleep set transport (h, bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: i32, samplePos: i64) Before each chunk. ppq is the position at the chunk start in quarter notes. The module is told the transport started when playing goes from 0 to 1 between two calls (a host that restarts the transport without stopping it calls once with 0 first). bleep set voice (h, voice: i32) Optional. Inside a Voice Cell: the voice this instance plays ( ProcessContext::voice ); −1 outside. Call after create and when it changes. bleep harmony ptr , bleep harmony size (h) → ptr , () → i32 Optional. The board-wide harmony buses (section 5). bleep host ptr , bleep host size (h) → ptr , () → i32 Optional. The mailbox of a module that asks the host to change the transport (section 5). bleep process (h, numSamples: i32) → i32 Runs numSamples (1 to 32) samples. Returns 0, or non-zero when the call was refused or failed (the outputs are then unspecified and the host should bypass). bleep notes in ptr , bleep notes out ptr (h, jack: i32) → ptr The note buffer of a notes jack (section 5). bleep note event size () → i32 16. The host checks it. bleep scratch (h, size: i32) → ptr A buffer of size bytes in the module's memory for strings going in. Valid until the next bleep scratch call; any call that reads it says so. bleep text , bleep text length (h) → ptr , (h) → i32 The last string the module handed out (UTF-8, not terminated), valid until the next call that produces one. bleep set data (h, length) Node data (the board document's data , JSON) from the scratch buffer. bleep sanitise data (h, typeIndex, length) → i32 Makes node data valid, with defaults, from the scratch buffer; the result is in bleep text (its length is returned), −1: the type has no node data. Any instance of the file will do as h . bleep perform (h, argOffset: i32, numArgs: i32) A performance gesture from the module's view (a key, a pad): the action name (NUL-terminated) in the scratch buffer, then numArgs doubles at argOffset (8-byte aligned). No undo, not saved. bleep command (h, value: f32) A view button: its id (NUL-terminated) in the scratch buffer. bleep live (h) → i32 {"values":{name:number},"arrays":{name:[number]}} for the view, in bleep text ; its length is returned. Polled about ten times a second. bleep param text (h, index, normalised: f32) → i32 How the board shows a knob at that value ("2.5 s"), in bleep text . bleep output display (h, index) → f32 The value of an output's meter. bleep take data (h) → i32 Node data the module changed itself (a captured loop): its JSON in bleep text , −1 if none. Polled. A call that throws inside a module (only the modules built with exceptions) is caught inside the file: bleep create returns 0 or the call returns its failure value, and bleep error has the message. An exception never crosses the boundary. 5. Buffers Chunks. The host cuts every block into chunks of at most 32 samples and calls bleep process once per chunk. A block of 128 samples is four calls. (Native modules see whole blocks; modules must not depend on the block size, and the harness checks this.) Layout. Jack-major, float32 , little endian, one row of 32 per jack: params : [paramIndex × 32] the effective normalised value (0 … 1) at every sample, knob plus modulation inputs : [inputJack × 32] the summed signal; a notes jack's row is unused outputs : [outputJack × 32] written by the module Rows have 32 floats even for the last, shorter chunk; the first numSamples are valid. A buffer for zero jacks still has one row. The pointers do not change for the life of the instance, so the host fetches them once; the base of the memory may change, so it adds them to the current base every call. Normalised values. A param is always 0 … 1 on the boundary. Its units (Hz, seconds, choices) come from the spec JSON and the module's own mapping ( ParamSpec ). bleep set knob and params use the same scale. Signal types (the type of a jack): audio , control , pitch (virtual volts, 1.0 = one octave, 0 = C4), gate , trigger (≥ 0.5 is high), notes . All but notes are floats in the rows above. Notes. A notes jack is a NoteBuffer in the module's memory: 64 events of 16 bytes, then an i32 count (1028 bytes). Per event: u8 type (0 on, 1 off, 2 pressure, 3 control change, 4 program change, 5 pitch bend, 6 channel pressure, 7 system realtime), u8 channel (0 to 15), i16 offset (sample inside the chunk), i32 note (MIDI number, identifies the note; for types 3 to 7 the controller number, the program number, 0, 0, or the status byte of the realtime message), f32 pitch , f32 value (velocity or pressure, 0 … 1; for a control change data ÷ 127, for a bend −1 … +1). A module handles the types it knows and ignores every other type : older modules never see types 3 to 7 do anything, because they test for 0, 1 and 2 by name. The host keeps the last 16 slots of a buffer for notes: control changes and the other new types are dropped first when a chunk is crowded. The host writes the events of an input jack and the count before each chunk; it reads an output jack's events and count after it. More than 64 per chunk are dropped. Harmony buses (modules whose spec says "harmony": "writer" or "reader" ). bleep harmony ptr(h) is the address of dsp::kHarmonyBuses (4) HarmonyState records in the module's memory, bleep harmony size() their total size ( HarmonyState is plain data, 16 bytes: valid , key , chordRoot , bass , scale , chord , quality , degree , serial , laid out as the C++ struct). The host copies the board's buses in before every chunk and, for a writer , copies them back out after it; every writer runs before every reader on the board, as natively. Host mailbox (the Transport module). A module cannot change the transport: it reads it. A module that must ask for a change (a new tempo, play and stop, Ableton Link on or off) writes the request into a record in its own memory, and bleep host ptr(h) is the address of that record, bleep host size() its size (40 bytes, little endian, no padding): Offset Type Field Direction Meaning 0 f64 tempo module → host A requested tempo in BPM; 0 = no request. 8 i32 play module → host 0 stop, 1 start from the beginning, 2 continue; −1 = no request. 12 i32 link module → host 1 Link on, 0 off; −1 = no request. 16 i32 startStopSync module → host 1 Link start/stop sync on, 0 off; −1 = no request. 20 i32 hosted host → module 1 when the host acts on requests (the standalone app); 0 in plugins and the browser. 24 i32 linkAvailable host → module 1 when the host has Ableton Link. 28 i32 linkEnabled host → module 1 when Link is on. 32 i32 linkPeers host → module The number of Link peers. A host that answers requests writes the four status fields before each block and, after the block, takes the requests and sets them back to "no request" (0 and −1). A host that does not know the export, or does not act on requests, leaves the record alone and the module still runs: its requests go nowhere. A request that is not yet taken is replaced by a newer one. Strings are UTF-8. Numbers crossing through the scratch buffer are little endian and aligned as stated. 5a. Media Four modules (Grains, Sampler, Splice, Wavetable Osc) read audio files from the computer's media folder by id ( .wav ). A module file has no disk, so the host answers through two imports of the module, env : Import Signature Meaning bleep media info (id: ptr, idLength: i32, sampleRate: ptr→f64, channels: ptr→i32) → i64 Length of the clip in frames, its sample rate and channels written to the two pointers; 0 if the clip is not available . bleep media read (id: ptr, idLength: i32, channel: i32, dst: ptr, frames: i64) → i32 Copies frames samples of one channel to dst (float32); 1 on success. The host must not block to answer: these calls come from inside bleep set data on the audio thread. A clip that is not in memory is "not available"; the host reads it on another thread and, when it is there, sends the module's last node data again ( bleep set data ), which makes the module ask again and succeed. A host with no media folder (the browser, for now) answers 0 to everything. 6. Transport and time bleep set transport(bpm, ppq, playing, samplePos) is called before every chunk; the module derives its tempo-synced timing from it ( ppq and bpm give the position at every sample of the chunk). sampleRate is fixed at create ; a different rate needs a new instance. The module sees no wall clock. 7. The spec JSON bleep spec json() is the same description the board UI gets from the engine for native modules ( describeTypes() ), and complete: a host rebuilds a node type's whole ModuleSpec from it, so the engine cannot tell it from a compiled-in one. Per node type: type , name , category , colour , description , port , creatable , standaloneOnly , params[] ( id , name , kind float int bool choice, default in 0 … 1, def in units, min , max , map exp skew and centre , format , decimals , label , steps , modulatable , choices , groups , group , conditional display showIf , namesBy and names ), inputs[] and outputs[] ( id , name , type , bipolar , normal , conditional display, names), buttons[] , memoryHeavy , groupColumns and, for the harmony bus, harmony . The parity test compares it with the native description of every module. Unknown fields are ignored by hosts, so adding one is compatible. The order of params , inputs and outputs is the index order of every call above and of the buffers. 8. What a host must do Provide the imports as stubs. emscripten notify memory growth does nothing; the WASI functions give no files, no environment, no clock: fd write accepts and drops its bytes, fd read , fd seek and fd close fail, environ report none, clock time get returns 0, and proc exit is not imported by any current file; a host that is asked for it traps the instance. This makes the sandbox complete: a module can compute and nothing else. Own the memory. Instantiate with the file's own memory, cap it (64 MB suggested), and never share it between instances. Bound time. A bleep process that runs longer than a few blocks of audio is stopped (Wasmtime: epoch interruption or fuel) and the instance is bypassed (silence out, an error in the log, a mark on the node), never allowed to stall the audio thread. wasm3 has no such interruption, so it is only for trusted (first-party, signed) modules. Proposed ; the spike does not do it yet. Check the file before running it. Its signature (see signing.md ), the imports, bleep chunk() == 32 , bleep note event size() == 16 , the ABI version. Choose the runtime deliberately. Wasmtime needs executable memory. A host that forbids it (macOS hardened runtime without allow-unsigned-executable-memory , which Ableton Live 12 has) kills the process when it is asked for, so a plugin can't try and fall back: the choice is made from what the host process is entitled to, or by a setting, before any code is compiled. Measured for the Verb on an Apple M-series: about 1.2× the native cost in the standalone benchmark and 1.5 to 1.7× through the plugin (the copies around each 32-sample chunk included, Live 12: 3.2 % of a core against 1.9 % native); wasm3 ten times Wasmtime (32.5 %). See patch/wasm-host/README.md . Compile once. One compiled module per file per process, one store and instance per node. Ahead-of-time compiled code may be cached per machine, keyed by the file's hash and the runtime version; the cache is never trusted over the signature. 9. Not in ABI 1 What a native module can do today and a wasm module cannot, yet: the port nodes (audio and MIDI in and out; they are not DSP modules and stay in the engine) and the Link tempo (a module can read the tempo, and ask for changes through the host mailbox). The harmony buses, the per-voice index, the transport-start event, sample files and the host mailbox were missing from the first version of the shim and are now optional exports and imports (sections 4, 5 and 5a), added as compatible changes. 10. Conformance A host passes when, for the same inputs and knob values, a module's output equals the native build's within rounding. The spike showed how: it ran the Verb as native, in Wasmtime and in wasm3 on the same noise with random knob changes mid-run and compared the outputs; the largest difference was 7e-7 on a peak of 0.43, and the tolerance was 1e-3 relative to the peak. Every module that ships as wasm gets the same check in the module harness (the native engine's tests keep the native modules for exactly this: the reference). A new host implementation runs the same cases against the browser host ( patch/web/test/ ). History 1 (this document): the interface of the 80 browser files, written down. Proposed additions that keep it version 1: bleep abi version , a features list in module.json , per-block time limits in hosts.

title: Signing
text:
Signing modules and plugins Everything the shop distributes as code is signed: modules (WebAssembly, see module-abi.md ) and plugins (installers for the VST3 family). A signature says two things: who published it, and that not one byte has changed since. Every developer has a private key of their own and signs with it; the user's apps check the signature before loading and refuse code that is unsigned unless the user has switched that on in the settings. The reference implementation is scripts/release/signing.py with its tests in scripts/release/test signing.py . This document is the specification; where they differ, fix whichever is wrong. Section 14 has a test vector other implementations must reproduce. 1. What it protects, and what it does not Protects against How A file changed after publishing (on the CDN, in a cache, on disk) The signature covers a hash of every file in the package. Someone else publishing under another developer's or our name Only a developer's own key signs their ids; a certificate binds the key to a publisher name and namespace. A signature moved to another module, another version, another platform The signed statement contains the kind, id, version and platform. A stolen developer key Certificates expire; the store revokes a key or a single release, and clients check a signed revocation list. The store (or its storage) being hacked The attacker cannot make a developer signature. They can still withhold updates or serve old ones, which the signed index.json (section 9) limits. It does not make a module safe by itself: a signed module is the work of an identified developer, nothing more. Modules also run in a sandbox (the ABI gives them no files, no network, a memory cap and a time limit). Plugins are native code with the user's full rights; a signature only tells whose code it is. It also cannot stop Ableton from loading some other VST3 the user put in the plugin folder: enforcement for plugins happens where Bleep installs and checks them (section 11). 2. The chain of trust root key offline, held by Brilliant Bleep; its public key is built into every app and plugin └─ issuer key online, in the store; certified by the root (valid for years, revocable) └─ developer key one per developer (or per team), made on the developer's own machine; │ certified by the issuer after the developer has an account └─ signature over one package: a module, or one platform file of a plugin Why an issuer between root and developers. The root key never goes online. The store can then issue and renew developer certificates day to day with a key that can be thrown away and replaced if it leaks, and the root signs a new issuer certificate. Brilliant Bleep's own releases are signed by a developer key like any other, with the publisher bleep and the firstParty flag, which alone allows ids without a namespace ( reverb , not acme/fuzz ). The developer's private key is made by the admin today and handed over (section 10); the store keeps only its key id. Once developers outside the team publish, they make their own and send only a request. Where each key lives. Key Where Why there Root, private Offline : the owner's keystore, with a backup. Not in the repository, not in website/.env , not on the server. Needed only to certify a new issuer or to revoke one. If the root leaked, every app and plugin that has its public key would have to be updated. A server is the most likely thing to be broken into, so it must not hold the one key that cannot be replaced. Root, public BLEEP ROOT PUBLIC KEYS in website/.env (the store checks releases against it) and built into the apps and plugins It is public; two keys during a rotation. Issuer, private, and its certificate BLEEP ISSUER KEY , BLEEP ISSUER CERT in website/.env The store needs it to issue developer keys. If it leaks, the root revokes it and certifies a new one: nothing already installed has to change. Developer, private The developer's machine or CI, as the kit the admin handed over Only they can sign as them. scripts/release/signing.py init-registry DIR makes the root and the issuer in one go and writes registry.env with the three lines for website/.env ; root.key is then moved to the keystore and the copy deleted. 3. Primitives Signatures: Ed25519 (RFC 8032): 32-byte public keys, 64-byte signatures, deterministic, fast, no parameters to get wrong. Hash: SHA-256. A key id is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the 32-byte public key, as 32 hex characters. Every signed message starts with a domain string ( BLEEP-CONTENT-1
 , BLEEP-SIG-1
 , BLEEP-CERT-1
 , BLEEP-CRL-1
 ), so a signature made for one purpose can never be accepted for another. Variable-length fields in a message are length-prefixed ( lp(x) = 4-byte big-endian length, then the bytes), so two different field lists can never produce the same bytes. JSON that is signed (certificates, the revocation list) is first turned into canonical UTF-8: keys sorted, no whitespace. Why not RSA, PGP or X.509: smaller, a format we fully control, no ASN.1 parser in the audio plugin, and no trust in the operating system's certificate store (see 13). 4. The content hash A package is a set of files with relative paths: the contents of a .bleepmod zip, or the files of a plugin's installer payload. The signature is over the content, not over the zip , because zip files are not reproducible (order, compression, timestamps): repacking the same files must not break it. contentDigest = SHA-256( "BLEEP-CONTENT-1
" u32(file count) for every file, sorted by the UTF-8 bytes of its path: lp(path) ‖ SHA-256(file content) (32 bytes) ‖ executable (1 byte: 0 or 1) ) Paths use / , are relative, and contain no empty, . or .. part and no backslash or NUL; a package that has one is refused. Duplicate paths and symbolic links are refused. META/signature.json (section 6) is never part of the content. Directories are not listed; permissions other than "executable" are not signed (they are not reproducible across systems, and the host decides them). Plugins: a single installer file ( .pkg , .msi , .zip ) is a package of one file whose path is its name. A plugin release has one such file per platform, each with its own signature, so a platform added later (the release machine and the Windows build machine are different) signs its own file. 5. The signed statement message = "BLEEP-SIG-1
" ‖ lp(kind) ‖ lp(id) ‖ lp(version) ‖ lp(platform) ‖ lp(signerKeyId) ‖ lp(contentDigest) signature = Ed25519-sign(developerPrivateKey, message) kind is module or plugin , id and version are the store's (for example acme/fuzz , 1.0.0 ), platform is any or the platform id ( macos-arm64 ). The verifier takes all of these from the artifact and its store entry, never from the signature document : a signature that is valid for something else is not valid here. 6. Certificates and the signature document A certificate is {"tbs": {...}, "issuer": , "signature": } ; the signature is the parent's Ed25519 over "BLEEP-CERT-1
" ‖ canonical(tbs) . The tbs ("to be signed") object: Field Meaning format 1 type issuer or developer keyId , publicKey The certified key (base64 of the 32 bytes) and its id. publisher The developer's namespace slug ( acme ), lower case letters, digits and - . Unique in the store; a name belongs to the first account that gets it and is not reassigned. name Display name. scopes ["module"] , ["module","plugin"] , … what the key may sign. Issuer certificates have ["issue"] . Plugins are a separate scope the store grants after a review, because they are native code. firstParty true for Brilliant Bleep's own key: may sign ids without a namespace. notBefore , notAfter Unix seconds. Developer certificates last at most 365 days and are renewed (a new certificate for the same key, or a new key). serial An integer, for the store's records. The signature document is stored as META/signature.json inside every package, and the store's entry.json repeats it per file ( files[].signature ), so a client can check a download against the entry: { "format": 1, "algorithm": "ed25519", "keyId": " ", "chain": [ , ], "signature": " " } The chain is carried with the signature so verification needs no network : only the pinned root public key(s) and, optionally, the latest revocation list. 7. Verification verify(package, signatureDocument, kind, id, version, platform, roots, now, revocationList) returns one of: Status Meaning signed Everything below passed. Carries the publisher and key id. unsigned There is no signature document. expired Everything passed except that a certificate is outside its validity period. revoked Valid, but the key (or the issuer, or this exact release) is on the revocation list. invalid Anything else: the signature, a certificate, the namespace, the scope, a malformed document. Steps, in this order; the first failure decides: The document is format 1, algorithm ed25519 , with a chain of exactly [issuer, developer]. The issuer certificate is signed by one of the pinned root public keys (the app carries one, and the next one during a rotation) and is of type issuer with scope issue ; its key id matches its key. The developer certificate is signed by that issuer and is of type developer ; its key id matches its key and the document's keyId . Revocation (section 8): any key in the chain on the list, or this (kind, id, version, contentDigest) on the list: revoked . The certificate's scopes contain kind . Namespace: id starts with / ; only a firstParty certificate may sign an id without a / . The signature verifies over the message of section 5, with the content digest recomputed from the files. Validity periods of both certificates contain now : otherwise expired . (This comes last on purpose: an old release by a developer whose certificate has since lapsed is old, not forged.) Verification never throws on bad input; malformed documents are invalid . Whether to load. The settings decide, for modules and plugins separately ( allowUnsigned.module , allowUnsigned.plugin , both off by default): Status Setting off Setting on signed load load unsigned refuse load, marked unsigned expired refuse load, marked unsigned invalid refuse refuse revoked refuse refuse invalid and revoked are not overridden by "allow unsigned": the user allowed no signature , not a broken one . (Someone who strips the signature away gets unsigned , which is exactly the situation the user chose to allow.) 8. Revocation, expiry and rotation The revocation list is v1/revocations.json , next to index.json (at a fixed address: the index does not reference it yet).
