It holds format (1), serial (rising), issued , revokedKeys ( keyId : everything signed under that key, or under any certificate it issued) and revokedArtifacts ( kind , id , version , digest ), then issuer (the issuer certificate, so verifying needs only the pinned roots) and signature : the issuer's Ed25519 over "BLEEP-CRL-1
" ‖ canonical(the five fields above) . The store writes it with the index and when a key is revoked ( developer-revoke ), and only when it changed; the serial is the time, or one more than the last, whichever is higher. The C++ client ( Client::fetchRevocations ) fetches it at start and with the index, checks the issuer certificate against the pinned roots, keeps the list with the highest serial in cache/revocations.json , and applies it offline from then on, when it verifies, installs and loads. A list with a lower or equal serial is ignored, so a mirror cannot take revocations back. A list can only take trust away, so the issuer certificate's validity dates are not checked. A client that has never fetched one still verifies; it just cannot know about revocations. A module that is already loaded stays registered until the next start; nothing revoked installs or loads after the list arrives. A stolen developer key: revoke the key. Everything signed with it stops loading; the developer gets a new key and re-signs the releases that are still good (signing is cheap, and the content did not change). A bad release: revoke that (id, version, digest) ; other versions are untouched. A leaked issuer key: the root signs a revocation for the issuer's key id and a new issuer certificate; developer certificates are reissued by the new issuer (the developers' keys do not change, so their packages do not need re-signing, only the chain inside the signature has to be replaced; the client treats a chain whose issuer is revoked as revoked and the store serves the repaired signature in entry.json ). Root rotation: apps carry up to two root public keys. A new app release adds the next root; later it drops the old one. The root key is generated and used on an offline machine only. Time comes from the device clock. A device with a wrong clock sees expired (and can allow unsigned), never signed -by-mistake for something forged. Registry-served metadata ( index.json , with generated and expires ) lets a client notice a stale clock. 9. The store's own signature Package signatures say who built a file. The store additionally signs index.json (and the revocation list) with the issuer key , to protect what the packages cannot: which release is the newest. index.json carries a rising serial , a generated time and an expires time (a week); a client rejects an index whose serial is lower than one it has seen, or that has expired, so a server or a mirror cannot hold clients on an old, vulnerable release (a rollback or freeze). The index lists each entry's contentDigest , so a client knows what to expect before downloading. 10. How a developer gets a key and signs Today: the admin issues the key and hands it over. There is no developer self-service yet. admin docker compose exec api python -m app.cli developer-create acme --scopes module [--days 365] > acme.kit.json admin docker compose exec api python -m app.cli token-create "acme CI" --publisher acme > token (hand both over privately: the kit is the developer's private key and certificate) developer scripts/release/signing.py sign fuzz.bleepmod --kit acme.kit.json --kind module --id acme/fuzz --version 1.0.0 developer scripts/release/release.py … --kit acme.kit.json --token-file token (Bleep's own plugins: the "bleep" kit and an unrestricted token) The trade-off. The admin generates the key, so the admin has seen it. That is fine for a handful of people the admin knows; the store stores only the key id, scopes and expiry (table developers ), never the key. A developer who wants a key nobody else has seen uses the request flow, which the tool already has ( keygen , request , then the admin runs issue ), and later the website will take the request directly. Account and checks (when the website does it). A website account with a confirmed e-mail address. A module scope is granted automatically for a publisher name nobody holds; the plugin scope and the bleep namespace by an admin only. Names that look like ours or like existing publishers are reserved. Revoking. python -m app.cli developer-revoke KEY ID : releases signed with that key are refused from then on. The signed revocation list (section 8) is published with it; the C++ client applies it, Bleep Play (the browser client) does not fetch it yet. Key custody. keygen writes the private key as a PKCS#8 PEM, encrypted with a passphrase when BLEEP KEY PASSPHRASE is set, mode 0600. The recommendation is a passphrase, kept in the OS keychain; a CI system holds it as a secret. A developer who loses the key requests a new one; the old certificate is revoked if there is any doubt. Hardware keys (a YubiKey with Ed25519, or a cloud KMS that offers it) work through the same interface: the tool only needs a signing function. One key per developer or team. Whoever holds the key can publish as the publisher. A team uses one key held in CI, or several keys, each with its own certificate under the same publisher. What the store enforces on every release (built; website/api/app/routers/registry.py ): Every file needs a valid signature, or the release fails. Verified under section 7 against the root keys and the revoked developer keys. With no root key configured the store refuses everything (fail closed); BLEEP REQUIRE SIGNATURES=false exists for local experiments only. A token releases for one publisher. A release token has a publisher (default bleep ); the signature's publisher must be the same, or the request is refused. One release has one publisher, and a platform added later must be signed by the same one. A signed module package must be the one that was signed. The release declares the content hash; when the file arrives, the store opens the zip and recomputes it. Who uploaded is recorded. Each file stores the token that declared it (shown by name in the admin's download details, never in the public entry.json ) and the signer's publisher and key id. Only that token may continue a draft: upload files, replace the draft or publish it. scripts/release/release.py checks first. Before building or uploading, it signs a probe with the kit and verifies it against the store's root keys ( GET /api/registry/roots ), so a wrong or expired kit fails at once instead of after a 100 MB upload. The shop publishes nothing unsigned. Packages that are not in the shop (a developer's own test builds) can still be signed locally, so the same verification path runs everywhere. 11. In the apps Where it runs. Place When What it does Module loader in the engine ( WasmModuleHost ) When a module file is first used, and again when the file's hash changes Verifies before the file is compiled, never after. Refuses per section 7. The result is cached with the file's hash, so the audio thread is never involved. Store section (module and plugin installs, updates) Before anything is written to the install folders Downloads to a temporary folder, verifies, then moves. A refusal says why in the user's words. Plugin check at startup The app and the Bleep plugins look at the Bleep plugins in the system folders Recomputes the installer's installed-file record and compares it with what the Store section recorded; a plugin that was changed afterwards, or that Bleep did not install, is shown as not verified . This is detection, not prevention: Live loads whatever is in its folder. Store upload On POST …/releases , at the file upload, and when a platform is added Verifies; refuses unsigned, invalid, revoked or for the wrong publisher (built). Website Build and download pages Shows the publisher and key id of every entry. Manual installs. Dropping a .bleepmod (or a .wasm with a module.json next to it) into the modules folder works the same as installing from the store: the folder is read at start and when it changes, each file is verified, and the node types it provides appear. A file in a folder that is not signed, or not signed by a trusted publisher, needs Allow unsigned modules . Plugins copied by hand into a system plugin folder are untouched by Live's loading, but the Store section and the startup check list them as unsigned or not verified , and the Bleep plugins refuse to install or connect to an unsigned Bleep plugin (a bridge, a bus receiver) unless Allow unsigned plugins is on. Settings → Security. Allow unsigned modules (off). Switching it on shows: "Unsigned modules run in a sandbox: they cannot read your files or use the network, but they can use a lot of CPU and make noise. Only enable this for modules you trust or have built yourself." Allow unsigned plugins (off). Switching it on shows: "Unsigned plugins are programs that run with all your rights inside your DAW. Only enable this for software you trust." Trusted developers : the developers whose keys are in the chain of what you have installed, with a way to remove one (it stops everything they signed from loading). Advanced: add a local root key , so a developer can test their own signed modules, which carry a certificate issued by their own local store or signing.py init-registry , without allowing everything that is unsigned. A status line per installed module and plugin: Signed by acme (key id on hover), Unsigned , Expired , Revoked ; refused items stay listed with the reason. On the board. A node whose module was refused becomes a placeholder with the reason ("this module is unsigned: enable it in the settings"), never a deletion, as for a missing module in store.md section 4.3. Nothing is ever downloaded or verified on the audio thread, and a plugin in Live uses only what is already installed. Choosing between copies. When several copies provide the same node type (the version bundled in the plugin, one from the store, one from the manual folder), the host takes the first that passes verification in this order: the highest compatible version , then signed over unsigned, then the manual folder over the store (so a developer's own build wins while they work on it). 12. Bundles A bundle is a store entry of kind: "bundle" with no files: a signed list of (kind, id, version, contentDigest) members, published and signed like any other entry (publisher bleep ). Installing one installs its members, each verified on its own. default-modules lists every first-party module; default-plugins lists every Bleep VST3 (Beautiful Bleep, the four port plugins, Instrument, Audio Insert), as store.md section 5a describes. 13. Decisions and alternatives Question Decision Why Own chain of trust or the OS's code signing (Apple notarisation, Authenticode)? Both, for different things. OS signing is what lets macOS and Windows run the installer and the plugin at all, and stays, done by the release pipeline. This chain says who published a module and lets Bleep check a file itself, on every OS, with no OS certificate store. For plugins, our signature is over the installer or file as released, made after OS signing. A .wasm has no OS-level signature; we need one rule for both. Sign the zip bytes or the content? The content (section 4). Zips are not reproducible. Developer keys made by the store or by the developer? By the developer. The store cannot lose or leak what it never has; proof of possession is in the request. One signature algorithm only? Yes, Ed25519; a new one means a new format . No algorithm negotiation, no downgrade. Trust on first use for developers without the store? No. A local root key (section 11) covers the legitimate case explicitly. Timestamps? Not used: no trusted time source offline. Expiry is checked against the device clock, and the index is the freshness anchor. Keeps verification offline and simple; the cost is that an expired developer needs a renewed certificate. 14. Test vector Fixed seeds (32 bytes each of 0x01 , 0x02 , 0x03 ) for the root, the issuer and the developer; notBefore 1760000000, notAfter one year later. Package acme/fuzz 1.0.0, kind module , platform any , files: path content module.json {"name":"Fuzz"} and a newline module.wasm the 8 bytes 00 61 73 6d 01 00 00 00 ui/fuzz.js // view and a newline None executable. Expected, in hex: root public key 8a88e3dd7409f195fd52db2d3cba5d72ca6709bf1d94121bf3748801b40f6f5c issuer public key 8139770ea87d175f56a35466c34c7ecccb8d8a91b4ee37a25df60f5b8fc9b394 developer public key ed4928c628d1c2c6eae90338905995612959273a5c63f93636c14614ac8737d1 developer key id b62e867fa2f33afe62d5d6b1642e1621 contentDigest 39f61d45e3115066a934dabca6cf83c346420153e85d6d58841033d62d0c1f08 signature (64 bytes) 5019b69bf480dae36510479a2c4bbeab84e94477efcdd4ec3dc1528ef6f2644471e89b42c0ac69b4ff617bac7da69e4b817717e2f99e6526d4be2c10e1a72c0b scripts/release/signing.py vector prints these and the 123-byte message; the unit test pins them. The digest and the message were also recomputed from this text alone, without the implementation. 15. Implementation Where With The store (API), release tooling, CI Python: cryptography (Ed25519, SHA-256), see scripts/release/signing.py . The website API will import the same module. Engine, plugins and app (C++) patch/store/ ( Verify , Package ): Monocypher for Ed25519 ( patch/third party/ , public domain / BSD-2) and juce::SHA256 from juce cryptography : no OpenSSL, no system dependency in an audio plugin. Built and tested; the install flow around it is not. Browser (Bleep Play) WebCrypto Ed25519 where it exists, @noble/ed25519 otherwise. All three are tested against the same packages: scripts/release/signing.py fixture writes a deterministic set ( patch/tests/store-fixtures/ : signed in several ways, tampered, expired, revoked, outside a namespace, unreadable, with the verdict each must get in cases.json ), and test signing.py (Python), patch/web/test/store-client-test.mjs (JavaScript) and patch/tests/store test.cpp (C++, ctest -R patch.store ) all check them, together with the content hash of the test vector above and the canonical JSON bytes. A change to the rules changes the generator, and the three tests tell which implementation is behind. 16. Not decided yet The root key ceremony is decided in outline: generated on an offline machine, held in the owner's keystore with a backup, used only to certify or revoke an issuer. Still open: a second person or device that can recover it, and a written rotation drill. Revocation in the browser client ( store-client.js takes a list, but does not fetch one), and revokedArtifacts : the list can carry them, the store has no command that adds one yet. Whether community (third-party, signed, not reviewed by us) is a separate release channel from stable , or all signed modules appear in one list with the publisher shown. The plugin scope review: what we check before an admin grants it. Whether the installers also carry the content-addressed file list of the installed plugin (what the startup check compares), or the Store section keeps it only locally.

title: Bleep Store
text: Bleep Store and release system Plugins, modules and presets are managed in one place, the Bleep Store . Everything that installs, updates or loads one of them (the standalone app, Bleep Play, the release pipeline) talks to the store and nothing else. Kind What it is Who loads it Form Plugin Something you load in Ableton: Bleep Board, the ports, later Bus receivers Live, the app's Store section installs it Installer per platform and format (VST3, AU, CLAP) Module A node type on the board: its DSP, view and docs The engine in the plugins, the app and the browser .bleepmod package Preset A patch (a whole board) or a cell (a subgraph, with its panel) The board .bleeppreset file (JSON) Naming: the store was first called the registry, and its technical names keep that word: the URL path /registry/v1/ , BLEEP REGISTRY URL , /api/registry , the bleep-registry bucket. In prose it is the Bleep Store, "the store" after the first mention. Plugins and modules are code : signed by their developer, immutable. Presets are data : published by anyone with an account. How code is signed and checked is in signing.md ; what a module is to the engine, in module-abi.md . Decisions Modules are WebAssembly everywhere (web and native), hosted by an embedded wasm runtime in the engine. See 4.2. The store is part of the website stack (Caddy, the FastAPI website/api and its Postgres), hosted locally for now and moved with the stack later. No separate infrastructure. Everything the shop distributes as code is signed , by its developer's own key under our root (see signing.md ). Apps refuse unsigned modules and plugins unless the user switches on Allow unsigned modules or Allow unsigned plugins in the settings. Modules and plugins reach the user three ways: from the store on demand, through two bundles the setup offers ( default modules , default plugins ), or by copying files into a folder (section 5a). Everything is free. There is no licence-key or entitlement logic anywhere. Downloading needs no login : browsing, installing plugins, modules and presets, and update checks are anonymous. Sharing a preset needs an account (the existing website/api accounts). 1. Where this stands today Modules are folders in patch/modules/ / with a module.json ; native builds compile them into the plugins through BLEEP REGISTER MODULE (static). The browser build already produces one standalone .wasm per module and a manifest.json ( patch/web/build modules.py ), loaded on demand. But website/Dockerfile runs it (emscripten, a JUCE clone) on every site build. Presets are presets/ .bleepboard plus patch/board/ui/factory-presets.json , built into the UI. The wasm-per-module work is the seed of the system: the module package is that file plus its metadata. 2. Common to every artifact Every entry in the store has the same envelope: { "kind": "module", // plugin module preset "id": "dual-filter", // slug; presets: " / " "version": "1.2.0", // semver, immutable once published "channel": "stable", // stable beta "title": "Dual Filter", "author": "brilliant-bleep", "license": "MIT", "requires": { "engineAbi": 3, "bus": ">=0.1", "modules": { "lfo": ">=1.0" } }, "files": [ { "path": "dual-filter.bleepmod", "sha256": "…", "bytes": 48213, "platform": "any", "signature": { "keyId": "…", "chain": [ … ], "signature": "…" } } ], "published": "2026-10-09T10:00:00Z" } Immutable and content-addressed. A published id@version never changes; a fix is a new version. Files are named by sha256 in storage, so caches never go stale. engineAbi is an integer bumped when the module ABI (specified in module-abi.md ; the C interface in patch/web/src/WebShim.cpp ) changes incompatibly. Hosts refuse modules they cannot run and the Store section explains why. Signing. Every file of a plugin or module entry has a developer signature ( files[].signature : a chain root > store issuer > developer, over the content hash, kind, id, version and platform), checked by the store on upload and by every host before it loads or installs. index.json and the revocation list carry the store issuer's signature, a rising serial and an expiry. Details, the settings and a test vector in signing.md . 3. The store It lives in the website stack. Published files are objects in a SeaweedFS bucket ( storage service, data on the registry-data volume; S3 API, so moving to AWS S3, R2 or similar later is a change of endpoint; MinIO was considered but no longer publishes images). The bucket is public-read and Caddy proxies /registry/ to it, so downloads are cacheable and run no app code; the API owns what is dynamic. S3 bucket bleep-registry (SeaweedFS) → Caddy proxies it read-only at /registry/v1/… /registry/v1/ ├── index.json plugins and modules per channel, signed ├── plugins/ / / installers + entry.json ├── modules/ / / .bleepmod + entry.json (+ doc, screenshot) └── presets/ / / .bleeppreset /api/… (FastAPI + Postgres, existing accounts and sessions) ├── GET /api/presets?q=&type=&tag=&sort= search (anonymous) ├── GET /api/presets/ / metadata, versions, download counts (anonymous) ├── POST /api/presets publish a version (login) ├── DELETE/PATCH /api/presets/ own presets (login); admin may unlist any ├── POST /api/presets/ /report report (anonymous or login) └── POST /api/tokens, GET /api/tokens personal access tokens for the app (login) Part Where Written by Plugins and modules (files, index.json ) S3 bucket Only the release pipeline: scripts/release/release.py uploads over the S3 API (port 8333, bound to localhost; credentials S3 ACCESS KEY / S3 SECRET KEY in website/.env ) Preset files Same bucket under presets/ The API after validation Preset metadata (title, tags, author, versions, downloads, reports, state) Postgres, new Alembic migration The API What a tile shows. Every plugin, module and preset has a title, a summary (up to 280 characters), a category and an optional screenshot, as metadata of its release: entry.json carries summary , category and image (the file name next to it, image.png , .jpg or .webp ). release.py takes them from the module package (its module.json and doc/ .png ) and, for plugins, from PLUGIN TILES and doc/store/ .png , and uploads the image with PUT /api/registry/ / /releases/ /image (PNG, JPEG or WebP up to 1 MB; display data, so not signed, and replaceable by the token that made the release). Without a screenshot the store draws a placeholder in the colour of the kind. GET /api/store returns them with image url and the categories of the matching entries, and filters by category . GET /registry/v1/index.json is the one call a client needs at start. It lists, per id, the newest version per channel, so an update check is one small request with an ETag . The API only ever sees preset search and publishing, so a stopped API doesn't stop installs of plugins and modules. Login in the app. The app has no browser cookie. Sign in opens the website's login page for a one-time device code (like gh auth login ): the app shows a code, the user confirms it on the site, and the app stores a personal access token in the OS keychain. The token only allows publishing and managing the user's own presets. Not signed in, the app works fully except Share… . Moving later. Everything is addressed by one base URL ( registry in the app's settings and the site's config), so moving the stack into the Brilliant Bleep Compose stack or behind a CDN changes configuration, not code. 4. Modules 4.1 Package A .bleepmod is a zip: module.json existing fields (name, slug, tagline, colour, category, doc) + version, requires, types[] module.wasm the DSP, standalone, C ABI (no JUCE, no JS glue) ui/ .js the module's custom view (optional) doc/ .md, .png user documentation and screenshot summary (one or two sentences, from the module's tagline , else its first node type's description) and category ("Sources", "Modulation", …, from the module's node types) are filled in by the package step. The store shows them, with the screenshot, on the module's tile. types[] replaces the generated manifest.json "types → module" map: one package can provide several node types (the drum modules do). The source layout in patch/modules/ / does not change; a package step ( scripts/package-module.py , built on build modules.py ) turns a folder into a package. Adding a module still touches no shared file. 4.2 Native modules: wasm everywhere (decided) Modules are statically linked into the plugins today. For the app to install, update and uninstall modules, the plugins need to load them at run time. Options: Native shared library per OS/arch WebAssembly everywhere Keep static, ship everything with the plugin One artifact for web, macOS, Windows, Linux no (6 builds each, code signing and notarisation per file) yes n/a Speed best AOT-compiled wasm: close to native; interpreted: too slow best Sandbox: safe to run modules from other people no yes (no syscalls, own memory) n/a Updating a module without updating the plugin yes yes no Decision: wasm everywhere. The engine gets a WasmModuleHost (embedded WAMR or wasmtime, AOT-compiled at install time and cached per machine) that implements the same Module interface the static modules do. The apps and plugins ship without modules (decided): every module, first-party or not, is installed from the store, so there is one path and one set of rules. Offline, the installer carries the default module bundle. The native sources stay in the repository: the tests run them as the reference the wasm builds are compared with, and a module that turns out too heavy as wasm may later get a native package for its platform. Gate, first answer (Verb, Apple M-series, Live 12; patch/wasm-host/ ). Wasmtime (Cranelift JIT) costs about 1.2× the native module in a standalone benchmark and 1.5 to 1.7× through the plugin, copies around each 32-sample chunk included (3.2 % of a core against 1.9 %), and loads in 44 ms; the output matches the native build to about 1e-6. The wasm3 interpreter costs ten times Wasmtime (32.5 % of a core), so it is only a fallback for very light modules. Both run in Live, which allows the executable memory Wasmtime needs. Consequences: Wasmtime is the runtime ; wasm3 stays an option for trusted, cheap modules; a host without executable memory runs only what wasm3 can carry (cheap modules; the rest show as unavailable: open , section 12) (a plugin cannot "try and fall back": Wasmtime is killed, not refused, so the runtime is chosen from the host's entitlements or a setting before any code is compiled). Still to run: the heaviest modules (Grains, Delay Network, Modal Voice). If one costs more than about 2× native, it stays static-only and is also offered as a native package (the platform field in files already allows per-platform files). Not yet tested: other DAWs, Windows, Linux. 4.3 Resolution on the board A board file lists the node types it uses. On load, a host resolves each type: bundled → installed → store (browser: fetch; app: offer to install; plugin in Live: use the installed set and show a placeholder node for a missing type, never download inside an audio host). 5. Plugins Plugins are installed from the Store section of the app, not hot-loaded: Artifacts: a signed and notarised installer per OS ( .pkg , .msi , .zip for Linux) containing all formats of one plugin, or the whole bundle. Install paths are the system's ( /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 , …). Live must not be running while a loaded plugin is replaced (the README warns of crashes); the app checks for Live and asks the user to quit it first. The store entry says which formats and OS versions each file supports. Third-party Bus receiver plugins can be listed with a download link (not hosted by us) so the Store section is one place for everything that works with the Bus. A plugin states the module engineAbi range it can host, so the app can warn when a module needs a newer plugin. 5a. Bundles, first run, and manual installs Bundles. A bundle is an entry of kind: "bundle" : no files, a signed list of members with their versions and content hashes ( signing.md , section 12). Two exist, both published by bleep : Bundle Members Why default-modules Every first-party module (80 today, about 25 MB of wasm) What the board offers out of the box, one tick instead of 80 installs default-plugins Every Bleep VST3: Bleep Board, the port plugins (MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In, Audio Out), Bleep Instrument and Audio Insert The plugins Live needs; they must all be the same version, because they share one engine Installing a bundle installs its members, each verified on its own. A bundle update is a new bundle version; the Store section shows "Update all" and installs only the members that changed. First run. When the app is installed (the installer's last page, or the first launch for a download without an installer), a setup assistant asks, with sizes and both pre-ticked: Download the default module bundle (the modules from the store, into the store folder below). Install the default plugin bundle (all VST3 bridges into the system plugin folder). If Live is running it asks to quit it first, as in section 5. Declining either is fine: the app works, a missing module is a placeholder node with an Install button, and the Store section keeps a "Default modules are not installed" banner until it is done. Offline: an offline installer carries both bundles. The apps ship without modules (4.2), so until the module bundle is installed a board shows placeholder nodes. A plugin in Live never downloads anything on its own: modules are installed from the Store section of the app or of the plugin window, on a non-audio thread. Manual installs. Everything can also be copied by hand: What Folder Notes Modules from the store /modules/registry/ / / Written by the Store section; do not edit Modules by hand /modules/local/ A .bleepmod , or .wasm with a .json (the module.json ) beside it. Read at start and when the folder changes. Plugins The system VST3 folders Copied by hand as usual; the Store section lists them with their status is ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep (macOS), %APPDATA%\Bleep (Windows), ~/.local/share/Bleep (Linux); the settings can point at another folder. Every file in these folders goes through the same check as a download (signature, imports, ABI version); unsigned ones need Allow unsigned modules (or plugins) in Settings → Security , and the app, the plugins and the Store section all read that setting from the one settings file. When several copies provide the same node type, the choice is: highest compatible version, then signed over unsigned, then the manual folder over the store ( signing.md , section 11). Build options and the store configuration. config/store.json is the one place that says where the store is ( storeUrl , the website's address; the store lives under /registry/v1/ ) and whom it trusts ( rootKeys , hex root public keys). The apps' and plugins' build bakes it in ( BLEEP STORE CONFIG names another file, BLEEP STORE URL and BLEEP STORE ROOTS override it for one build) and scripts/release/release.py uses storeUrl when no --registry or $BLEEP REGISTRY URL is given; the user can still change the address in settings.json . With -DBLEEP WASMTIME DIR= the apps and plugins are built without modules ( BLEEP BUNDLE MODULES=ON puts them back). BLEEP DATA DIR moves the data folder (tests, development); a developer's own root goes into settings.json as extraRoots . The first-run assistant answers once ( firstRunDone in settings.json ). The plugin download: the app reads the plugin entries of the index, takes the build for its platform ( macos-arm64 , ...), checks the sha256 and the signature (kind plugin , the file as a one-file package) and the Allow unsigned plugins setting, and unpacks the .vst3 bundles into the user's VST3 folder, with Live closed; an offline installer's Plugins folder (macOS: Contents/Resources/Plugins in the app) is copied instead. The pretend Store for working on the UI is the board dev server with ?store in the address. 6. Presets Two kinds, one file format ( .bleeppreset , JSON, same schema as board persistence plus the envelope in section 2): preset.type Contains Loaded as patch A whole board: nodes, cables, panels, settings Opens as a project, or merges into the current board cell One cell: its inner graph, jack names, its panel Dropped onto the board as a cell Dependencies. A preset, cell or patch, may carry needs : the modules it requires, by module slug, each with an optional inclusive min and max version: "needs": { "lfo": { "min": "1.2.0" }, "reverb": { "min": "2.0.0", "max": "2.9.9" } } Saving a preset from the board writes needs for every module its node types come from, with min set to the version installed at that moment; an author adds max by hand. Before a preset is loaded or placed (the preset browser, Add → Cell ), the board checks needs and, without a version, every module that provides one of its node types. If something is missing or too old, a dialog lists it and offers Download n from the Bleep Store , then loads; Load anyway keeps placeholder nodes, Cancel loads nothing. Versions the store cannot supply are listed with the reason and cannot be fixed by the dialog: the store offers only the newest version of a module, so a max below it, a local copy of a module, or a module the store does not have can only be loaded anyway. Factory presets carry no needs (the default module bundle covers them). The check runs in the app and in plugin windows (installing happens off the audio thread); Bleep Play installs the types a board uses by itself (section 8). Placing a preset works offline and without a store. An app built without the module store (modules compiled in; the native side's init has no store ) does not check at all. With a store, the check looks only at the modules installed here and at the store index if it is already loaded: it never waits for the network, and if the local status does not answer within 5 seconds the preset is placed anyway, with a notice. The index is cached on disk ( /cache/index.json , with the store address, the channel and the time it was fetched): every successful fetch saves it, the first look at the store reads it, and when the store cannot be reached the saved copy is used and the Store section says so. A copy saved for another address or channel is ignored. Publishing: from the board, Share… (needs an account; browsing and downloading never do), a title, tags, a licence (default CC-BY, CC0 allowed), optional audio preview. The API validates the schema, checks all referenced types exist in the store, enforces a size limit and per-user rate limit, and rejects anything that is not pure data. Versions: re-publishing creates a new version; installed copies show "update available". Local edits to an installed preset are kept as a fork. Moderation: report button, takedown by an admin (the existing admin role) sets the preset's state to unlisted; the file stays but is no longer served in search. The factory presets move out of factory-presets.json into the store's bleep author, so the app, the website and the plugins all show the same library. A small set stays bundled for offline. 7. Release process Single source: the repository. CI builds and publishes; nobody uploads by hand. Version. Every plugin and module has its own version, counted by the store: scripts/release/release.py --level x 1.x 1.1.x major minor patch takes the newest published version and counts up at that level (built for plugins; see doc/release.md ). A module's module.json carries the version once modules are released. Detect what changed. Hash the module's folder plus the patch/common/dsp/ headers it includes (and engine/ ABI). If the hash differs from the last release, the module needs a new version, and CI fails if its version was not bumped. Build and test (existing CI): the DSP tests, the module harness, the wasm build, then the harness against the wasm. Plugins: the macOS/Windows/Linux matrix, signing and notarisation. Package and sign ( scripts/package-module.py , scripts/package-plugin.sh , scripts/release/signing.py sign ): produce the artifacts and the entry.json files, each file signed with the publisher's key. Stage. Upload to …/staging/ / . A smoke job loads every staged module in the node host test and in a headless browser. Publish. Copy staged files into the immutable paths, then write index.json last, signed, in one atomic replace. A release is visible only when the index changes; rollback is putting the previous index back. Channels. beta index first for testers; promoting to stable is a new index, not a rebuild. scripts/release/release.py is built for plugins (steps 4 to 6 in a simpler form: a draft release, size- and hash-checked uploads, publish, index regenerated). It authenticates with an admin-created release token ( python -m app.cli token-create ), not with the storage credentials, so the machine that releases never holds S3 keys. Built since: adding the build of another platform to a published release ( --add-platform ), and signing : release.py signs every file with the developer's kit and checks it against the store's root keys before uploading; the store verifies every signature, binds a token to a publisher, records who uploaded and refuses a release without a valid key ( signing.md , section 10). Not built yet: change detection, staging, a signed index and revocation list, modules. 8. Website Docker no longer builds wasm. The web stage of website/Dockerfile is removed. The site image contains only the Next.js static export and the board UI. Modules load from the registry. bleep-web.js fetches index.json (cached) and then modules/ / / .bleepmod on demand, from the CDN, exactly as it loads .wasm today. Pinned for reproducibility. The site build commits a web-lock.json (module id → version → sha256) so a given site release always runs the module set it was tested with; updating it is a normal commit ( scripts/release/release.py --update-web-lock ). A newer module reaches the website when the lock is bumped, never silently. The board UI and patch/web/js/ (graph runner, worklet) are versioned with the site and declare the engineAbi they implement. The site's module catalog and docs pages read the store entries at build time instead of patch/modules/ /module.json from the repo, with the repo as a fallback in development. Preset browser on the site: read-only listing from presets/index.json , Open in Bleep Play and Open in the app ( bleep://preset/ / ). 9. The two sections: Store and Board The standalone app and the window of every Bleep plugin have the same two sections, switched at the top: Section For What is in it Board Creating patches The board (nodes, cables, cells, panels, module views, undo), loading and saving projects and presets, the transport. What the app and the plugin show today Store Managing what is on this machine Modules , Plugins and Presets tabs: installed, available and updates; Install, Update, Remove; the two default bundles; the release channel; disk use. Security : Allow unsigned modules , Allow unsigned plugins , trusted developers. In the app also Devices (audio device, MIDI ports, Link, connected plugins), and the account for sharing presets and the store URL (for self-hosting) A missing module on the board is a placeholder node with an Install button that opens the Store section at that module. In a plugin window , the Store installs modules and presets (outside the audio thread); Plugins only lists what is installed and what is newer, and says "close Live, then update with the Bleep App", because replacing a plugin Live has loaded can crash it. Bleep Play has no Store section: it installs the modules a board needs by itself, checks them, and keeps them in the browser's cache. It has no plugins to manage and presets come from the site. Docs: module manuals are read from the installed packages (each carries its docs) and open from a module's node or from its card in the Store. Not planned: a built-in shop, a patch store with payments. Local state in ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep/ (and equivalents), read by the app and by every plugin: settings.json (the Security settings, channel, store URL), installed.json (id, version, sha256, channel, source, signer), modules/ / / / , presets/ , a cache of index.json . Remove deletes the version folder; the board's nodes of a removed type show as missing, a board is never changed by it. 10. Repository layout registry/ ├── schema/ JSON Schemas: entry, index, module.json, preset └── README.md scripts/ ├── package-module.py folder → .bleepmod ├── package-plugin.sh built plugin → installer ├── release.py detect, package, stage, publish (dry run by default) └── registry-client.py fetch/verify, used by the website build and tests patch/engine/WasmModuleHost. native host for .bleepmod patch/app/SoftwareCenter. the installer logic (UI is board-style web UI like the rest) check-repo.py gets rules: registry/ depends on nothing else; the schemas are the contract the others validate against. 11. Order of work Schemas and package format. module.json gets version , requires , types . package-module.py produces .bleepmod from the existing wasm output. Validate all current modules. Store v0. The SeaweedFS service and the Caddy route (done in the compose file); release.py publishes into the bucket. The website reads from it; remove the web stage from the Dockerfile; add web-lock.json . Wasm host in the engine and the CPU gate from 4.2. Decide per module: static-only or installable. The Store section in the app and the plugin window, with Modules, Plugins and Presets; the update check at start (13 has the steps). Plugin release pipeline : signing, notarisation, installers. Presets : the schema with needs , local Library, then the /api/presets endpoints, the Postgres migration, device-code login and Share… . 12. Open questions Hosts that forbid executable memory (4.2, 13): with every module a wasm package, such a DAW can only run what wasm3 carries. Options: accept it (a message that names the DAW and the missing entitlement), keep a native build of the cheap-to-port modules as packages for that platform, or ship a second plugin build with the modules compiled in. Needs a decision before M6. Release credentials. release.py uses a release token (revocable, expiring, listed with last use), so S3 credentials stay on the server. Third-party modules. Opened by the signing design: any developer with an account can get a key and publish modules under their own namespace ( acme/fuzz ); modules are sandboxed, plugins are reviewed before the plugin scope is granted. Open: whether signed third-party modules sit in a separate community channel or in one list with the publisher shown. Signing keys. The chain, key custody for the offline root and the online issuer, and the settings are in signing.md (sections 2, 10 and 16). The root key ceremony is still to be decided. Naming: the product name, package extensions and the bleep:// scheme are placeholders like the rest of the project's names. 13. Moving the apps and plugins to store modules: work plan Done: the module packages ( package-module.py ), their release and signing, the store reading each module's node types, and the Bleep Play , which installs and verifies its modules from the store ( patch/web/js/store-client.js , tested against the Python tools). Left: the standalone app and the plugins, which today compile the modules in. What is known about the 80 modules, from their sources and the browser build: all 80 build to standalone wasm and pass the ABI check. 26 use juce core and wasm exceptions (Wasmtime only; wasm3 cannot run them). 4 read the harmony bus (chord-quantizer, harmony-master, quantizer-suite, step-sequencer), 6 use the per-voice index (beat-oscillator, chart-recorder, macro-osc, pulse-generator, test-oscillator, wave-analyzer), 4 load sample files (grains, sampler, splice, wavetable-osc). Those 14 need an ABI addition before they can leave the apps ( module-abi.md , section 9). Cells, Voice Cells and the port nodes stay in the engine: only the DSP nodes become wasm. Step What Done when M1 The gate A WasmModuleHost (Wasmtime) in the engine, used first by bleep module harness : every module runs natively and as wasm on the same inputs and knob changes. ABI additions for harmony bus, voice index and media Per module: maximum difference within rounding and CPU relative to native. All 80 pass, or the list of those that do not and why. The heaviest (Grains, Delay Network, Modal Voice; a 16-voice Voice Cell) are within about 2× native M2 Store client in C++ HTTP with juce::URL , Ed25519 and SHA-256 (Monocypher, vendored), the same checks as signing.py and store-client.js , the install folders and installed.json , the shared settings.json The test vector and a package signed by the Python tools give the same verdicts; an install from a store on another port works end to end M3 Dynamic registry Registry becomes append-only and thread-safe (modules keep references to their specs, so a spec never moves or goes away); the type list the UI shows refreshes after an install; installed modules load at start Installing a module while a board is open adds its node type without a restart M4 Store and Board The two sections in the board UI, shared by the app and the plugins, with native functions for install, update, remove, progress and the Security settings Section 9 works in the app and in a plugin window in Live M5 First run The setup assistant with the two default bundles, the installers, the plugin bundle install (app only, Live closed) A clean machine reaches a working board with one click per bundle M6 Remove the modules from the apps The CMake option that compiles modules in is off for shipped builds; the plugins lose the module code; the tests keep it as the reference The plugins are small, load no module code, and the same boards sound the same Risks, in the order they bite: a wasm instance per voice (a 16-voice cell with five modules is 80 instances of 1 to 2 MB each); hosts that forbid executable memory (Wasmtime would be killed; the choice of runtime must be made before any code is compiled); the 26 exception-using modules cannot fall back to wasm3; start-up time (compile lazily on first use, cache compiled code per machine, keyed by the package hash); first run offline . M1 decides most of these, which is why nothing is removed from the apps before it passes.

title: RFC process
text: Changing the standard: RFCs Bleep Bus is maintained by Brilliant Bleep in public. Anyone can propose a change. Issue. Open a GitHub issue labelled rfc describing the problem, not the solution. Design doc. If maintainers agree it is worth solving, open a pull request adding website/content/rfcs/NNNN-title.md : motivation, design, layout changes, compatibility, alternatives. Discussion. At least two weeks in the open. Decision. Maintainers accept, postpone or reject, and record the reasoning in the RFC. Implementation. Spec text, SDK, conformance checks and docs change in the same pull request. Version rules: 0.x minors may break the layout; after 1.0, minor versions only add fields in reserved space and new majors use a new segment name.

title: Bleep Bus specification v0.1
text: Bleep Bus specification, version 0.1 (experimental) Bleep Bus lets audio plugins exchange per-sample control signals through named operating-system shared memory. This document specifies the bus exactly enough to implement it without the reference SDK. If you only want to use the bus, read the Quickstart and the API reference instead. Status: 0.x is experimental. Every minor version MAY change the layout; implementations MUST refuse to share a segment with a different 0.x minor version. From 1.0 on, compatibility is guaranteed within a major version. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Model A bus is one shared-memory segment, identified by a namespace . An endpoint is one plugin instance. It has a stable 64-bit UID . An endpoint owns outputs and inputs (together: ports), each with a name unique per endpoint and direction. A connection (cable) links an input to a source (endpoint UID, output name) with an amount . Connections are stored with the input, i.e. with the receiving endpoint. Audio threads exchange blocks : an output publishes one block of samples per processing cycle; an input reads, for each connection, the block the source wrote for the reader's previous block (one block of latency). Contents Naming — segment names and namespaces Layout — every byte of the segment Memory ordering — atomics, seqlocks and the registry lock Registry — endpoints, ports, reclamation of dead processes Timing — block stamps and the block selection rules Signals — value conventions ("virtual volts") Connections and state — cables, amounts and the saved-state format Versioning and extensions

title: Naming
text: 1. Naming A namespace is 1 to 16 characters from [a-z0-9 -] . The default namespace is default . An implementation SHOULD use the value of the environment variable BLEEP BUS NAMESPACE when the plugin does not choose one; this lets users and test hosts separate buses (for example two DAWs running at once). The segment name is built from the major spec version and the namespace: Platform Name API macOS, Linux, other POSIX /bleepbus-v0- shm open , mmap Windows Local\bleepbus-v0- CreateFileMappingA on the paging file, MapViewOfFile macOS limits POSIX shared-memory names to 31 characters, which is why the namespace is limited to 16. The segment MUST be created with permissions for the current user only (POSIX mode 0600 ). It is never unlinked during normal operation: plugins come and go, the segment stays. Tools MAY unlink it when no host is running. Creating and opening Open the object with create permission ( O RDWR O CREAT ). If its size is 0, set it to the v0.1 total size (17 187 072 bytes). The operating system MAY round the size up to whole pages; a size at least the total size is valid. If two processes race, one resize fails harmlessly; re-read the size. Map the first 17 187 072 bytes read/write. Initialise: compare-and-swap header.init state from 0 to 1. The winner writes the header (section 2) and then stores 2 with release semantics. Everyone else waits (up to 2 s) until init state reads 2. Validate the header (magic, version, sizes, offsets). On a mismatch the implementation MUST NOT touch the segment and reports a version error.

title: Layout
text: 2. Layout All integers are little-endian with natural alignment and no packing. Strings are NUL-terminated UTF-8 within fixed-size fields. Reserved bytes MUST be zero when written and MUST be ignored when read. The reference header bus/include/bleep bus layout.h declares the same structures in C with static size checks.
