Hash name hash and output hash are 64-bit FNV-1a over the UTF-8 bytes (offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325 , prime 0x100000001b3 ). Hashes speed up lookups; equality of names is decided by the hash on the audio thread and by the full string elsewhere.

title: Memory ordering
text: 3. Memory ordering Fields marked atomic MUST be read and written with atomic operations of their full width: loads with acquire, stores with release semantics, unless stated otherwise. All other fields are plain memory protected by one of the three mechanisms below. 3.1 Registry lock (non-real-time only) Every change to the endpoint, input or output tables, and every change to a connection, happens while holding header.registry lock : Acquire: compare-and-swap 0 → own PID. While it fails, yield; after a few attempts, sleep 1 ms between attempts. If the holder's process no longer exists, a waiter MAY take the lock over with compare-and-swap holder PID → own PID. Give up after 2 s ( BB ERR TIMEOUT ). Release: store 0. The lock MUST NOT be taken on an audio thread. Readers that need consistent strings (names in listings) SHOULD take it too. 3.2 Seqlocks (audio thread readers) Output slots and the connection list of an input use sequence locks. Writer (holding the slot exclusively; for inputs, holding the registry lock): s = load relaxed(seq); store relaxed(seq, s + 1); / odd: writing / fence release(); / write the protected fields / store release(seq, s + 2); / even: consistent / Reader: s1 = load acquire(seq); if (s1 & 1) retry or skip; / copy the protected fields / fence acquire(); s2 = load relaxed(seq); if (s1 != s2) retry or skip; A reader on an audio thread MUST NOT spin on a seqlock; it skips the candidate and uses another block or its held value (section 5). 3.3 Publication order To activate a record, fill every field first, then store state = 1 with release. To change an output owner's UID, store endpoint uid (atomic) and then increment registry generation . Readers on the audio thread cache the mapping of a cable to an output index and recompute it only when registry generation or the input's seq changes. Before using a cached output they re-check state , incarnation and endpoint uid .

title: Registry
text: 4. Registry 4.1 Endpoints To register, under the registry lock: Reclaim dead endpoints (4.3). If the requested UID is 0, or already owned by an active endpoint, generate random non-zero UIDs until one is free. A plugin whose saved UID was taken (the user duplicated the device) MUST save the new UID. Take the first free endpoint record, fill it, store state = 1 . Increment registry generation . UIDs are chosen by plugins and saved in their state, so cables survive closing and reopening a set. A plugin SHOULD register immediately (with a random UID) and switch to its saved UID when the host restores its state ( bb set instance uid ); the switch fails with BB ERR UID IN USE if that UID is live elsewhere. 4.2 Ports Outputs and inputs are records in their own tables with the owner's endpoint index. Names: 1..31 bytes of UTF-8, no control characters, no / . Unique per endpoint and direction (an input and an output MAY share a name). Stable: cables refer to outputs by name. Renaming an output breaks existing cables to it. Convention: the bus input for modulating a parameter carries the parameter's display name, e.g. Cutoff . To allocate an output: set blocks written = 0 , increment incarnation , fill the remaining fields, store state = 1 , increment registry generation . An input is reset with its seqlock held odd and its connections zeroed. Limits per bus: 64 endpoints, 256 outputs, 512 inputs; per endpoint the reference SDK allows 64 outputs and 64 inputs. 4.3 Reclamation An active endpoint whose pid is not a live process (POSIX: kill(pid, 0) fails with ESRCH ; Windows: the process cannot be opened or has exited) is dead. On registration (and MAY on other occasions) implementations free it: its outputs and inputs (with their connections) are freed, the endpoint record is freed, and both generations are incremented. Unregistering frees an endpoint the same way. Cables from a removed endpoint stay stored at their receivers and read silence ("ghost source") until an endpoint with that UID and output name appears again. 4.4 Addressing Bridges (OSC, network) address ports as / / / , where each segment is the corresponding name lower-cased, with runs of characters outside [a-z0-9] replaced by - . Example: track "Bass", instance "Function 1", output "A" → /bass/function-1/a . Inside the bus, ports are addressed by (endpoint UID, port name) .

title: Timing
text: 5. Timing Hosts such as Ableton Live process tracks on parallel threads in no guaranteed order. The bus therefore has a fixed latency of one block : a reader sees what a writer produced for the reader's previous block. The result does not depend on which thread ran first, so a set renders the same way every time, including offline export. 5.1 Blocks Every block of every endpoint is framed by begin/end and carries: num samples (1..4096). Hosts with larger blocks MUST split them; peers then split the same way. transport sample pos : the host's transport position of the first sample. playing : the transport runs (also during offline export). time ns : a monotonic, system-wide clock (macOS CLOCK UPTIME RAW , Linux CLOCK MONOTONIC , Windows QueryPerformanceCounter ) or a host supplied equivalent. 5.2 Writing For each output, once per block, the writer fills slot blocks written mod 4 under its seqlock with the block's stamps and samples, sets block index = blocks written , then increments blocks written (release). Writing again within the same block rewrites the same slot. Outputs not written during a block publish zeros at block end. 5.3 Selecting the block to read Let W be blocks written of the source output and prev the reader's previous block. Candidates are blocks W−1 , W−2 , W−3 (newest first); a candidate is only valid if its seqlock reads consistently and its block index equals its number. Position rule. If the reader's previous and current blocks are both playing, choose the newest playing candidate whose transport sample pos == prev.transport sample pos . Time rule. Otherwise, or if rule 1 finds nothing, choose the newest candidate with time ns + guard <= current.time ns , where guard = 0.5 × num samples / sample rate (1 ms if the rate is unknown). This picks a block from an earlier processing cycle. Hold. If neither rule finds a block, the reader repeats the last sample it read from that connection (0 at first). Rule 1 is exact and deterministic, also when loops repeat positions and when export runs faster than real time. Rule 2 covers a stopped transport and peers that just appeared. If the chosen block is shorter than the reader's block, the remainder holds the block's last sample. 5.4 Consequences Modulation arrives one block late. At 256 samples and 48 kHz that is 5.3 ms: inaudible for modulation, unsuitable for phase-critical audio. A self-patched endpoint (output into its own input) works and also has one block of latency. Live's delay compensation does not know about the bus. These rules are what Phase 0 of the project measures in real hosts; they may be refined before 1.0.

title: Signals
text: 6. Signals All signals are 32-bit floats, one per sample, in virtual volts , chosen so that bridges to CV hardware and VCV Rack map directly. Type Value Rule Virtual volts control (0) bipolar −1..+1 or unipolar 0..1 Polarity declared per output ±1 ≈ ±5 V gate (1) high ≥ 0.5 high ≈ +5 V trigger (2) one sample of 1.0, otherwise 0.0 Readers that decimate MUST take the maximum of the span pitch (3) 1.0 per octave 0.0 = C4 = MIDI note 60 1 V/oct audio (4) reserved MUST NOT be used in v0.1 Types and polarity are advisory: any output may be connected to any input. Values outside the nominal range are allowed (a sum of cables may exceed it); receivers clamp where it matters. 6.1 Applying modulation to a parameter A receiving plugin SHOULD apply an input to a parameter as an offset in the parameter's normalised range (0..1), inside its DSP: effective = clamp(knob normalised + Σ source i × amount i, 0, 1) It MUST NOT move the host-visible parameter (no automation writes, no undo entries). Parameters with exponential mappings (cutoff, rates) are thus modulated in octaves.

title: Connections and state
text: 7. Connections and state 7.1 Cables An input holds up to 8 connections. Each is (source UID, output name, amount) . Its value is the sum over connections whose source exists of sample × amount . The amount is a finite float, clamped to ±1000. Any process MAY add, change or remove a cable into any registered input (this is how a patchbay in one plugin window edits another plugin), under the registry lock: Add : seqlock odd, fill a free connection, state = 1 , seqlock even. Change amount of an existing cable: atomic store of amount bits only; no seqlock. Remove : seqlock odd, zero the connection, seqlock even. After any of these: increment the owner's patch version and connection generation . A receiving plugin watches its patch version and tells its host that its state changed, so the set is marked as modified. 7.2 Saved state Cables belong to the receiving instance and are saved in its plugin state. The reference format is UTF-8 text, one cable per line, fields separated by a tab: bleep-bus-connections 1 The amount is written as [-]digits.digits (six fraction digits) and parsed without the C locale, so it is stable across user locales. Readers accept CRLF line ends, a missing final newline and + / - signs; lines naming inputs the endpoint does not have are ignored. Loading replaces all cables of the endpoint's inputs and increments connection generation , but not patch version (loading is not an edit).

title: Versioning and extensions
text: 8. Versioning and extensions The segment name carries the major version. The header carries major and minor. 0.x : implementations MUST match major and minor exactly and report BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH otherwise. From 1.0 : a minor version MAY only use reserved bytes and MUST keep every existing field's meaning; peers with the same major are compatible. A new major version uses a new segment name, so old and new plugins run side by side without seeing each other. Extensions (planned): string-identified, versioned capabilities, in the style of CLAP extensions ( "com.example.osc-bridge/1" ), declared per endpoint in a table that a future minor version adds in reserved space. Changes Version Date Changes 0.1 2026-10 First draft: layout, timing rules, cables, saved state. Open questions for 0.2 Pitch convention: keep 1 V/oct with 0 = C4, or switch to semitones? Namespace defaults per host process, to separate two running DAWs without configuration. A held "cable in hand" field for pick-up-and-drop patching across windows. Audio signals (stage 2): per-endpoint audio buffers allocated on demand.

title: Web developers
text: Web developers Bleep Play is the board running completely in the visitor's browser: no server and no plugin. The website serves it at /play/ and embeds it on /board/ . main thread AudioWorklet (real time) board UI (patch/board/ui, unchanged) worklet.js board-demo.js — the document, undo, graph.js — the graph runner presets module-host.js — one instance per node, bleep-web.js — loads module .wasm each its own .wasm on demand, keyboard, MIDI The UI is the same as in the plugins and the app. The engine is a JavaScript port of the native one ( graph.js : cell flattening, normalled jacks, topological order, feedback through the previous chunk, 32-sample chunks inside the 128-sample render quantum). Port nodes are built in; the computer keyboard and Web MIDI play MIDI In . Modules in the browser Each module folder is compiled, with a small shim, to one standalone .wasm : no JUCE glue, no Emscripten JS loader, no shared memory. module-host.js instantiates it with plain WebAssembly.Module and Instance , so the same code runs in an AudioWorklet and in Node (the tests). The file's contract is the Module ABI. build modules.py builds every folder, reads each file's node types back out, and writes manifest.json . The page loads a module the first time a board contains one of its types, from the Bleep Store of the site, and checks its signature in the browser before running it (Signing). Build scripts/build/build-web.sh # needs the Emscripten SDK scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules # UI and engine only scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only # modules only scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker # Emscripten in Docker About a third of the modules use juce core for node data; build modules.py --juce compiles it once for WebAssembly and links it into those modules (about +200 KB each). Test node patch/web/test/graph-test.mjs build/web/site The bridge tests ( bridge-protocol-test.mjs , bridge-ring-test.mjs , bridge-client-test.mjs , bridge-engine-test.mjs ) run in plain Node with no build and no network. Hosting Static files, plus the store the page installs its modules from ( /registry/v1/index.json ). manifest.base can point at another origin to ship modules separately from the site. The whole website stack runs with scripts/run/run-website.sh (Caddy, the API, PostgreSQL and the object storage). Connecting to the app The page can join the Bleep App, and through it Live, over a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1 : audio and MIDI both ways, plus the app's tempo and beat. Nothing connects until the page calls BleepWeb.connectBridge() . const bridge = await BleepWeb.connectBridge({ name: "Chrome", mode: "low" }); bridge.on("channels", (list) => { / Live ports the hub announces / }); bridge.on("status", ({ state }) => { / idle connecting handshake open retrying failed denied closed / }); bridge.sendMidi("node-7", [[null, 0x90, 60, 100]], { lookaheadBeats: 0.1 }); bridge.requestTempo(128); Two paths, one API. When the page is cross-origin isolated (the app serves it with COOP and COEP), the Worker and the worklet share a SharedArrayBuffer ring: mode low , 16 ms target fill. Otherwise the client falls back to safe with MessagePort chunks and 64 ms. Browser limits. Safari blocks ws://127.0.0.1 from a secure page and Chrome may ask for local-network access. connectToApp() explains the failure and points at the app's own page, http://127.0.0.1:47100/ . Remote nodes. A board node bound to a channel carries what the hub sends and sends what is patched into it. Remote Audio and Remote MIDI nodes let two boards exchange audio and MIDI without Live. Not yet in the browser Voice Cells, the Harmony bus, Link, Macros, audio input, host MIDI out and the media folder (Splice, Grains and Wavetable Osc import find no files) are not ported yet.

title: The board
text: The board One canvas per Live set with every module, port and cable. Open it from any Bleep plugin's window (it opens with the window, or comes to the front). Adding things Add (top left, or right-click on empty space) opens the Add menu: Module › one submenu per category: Sources , Modulation , Audio , Effects , Utility , Controllers , Sequencing and Drums . Each has subcategories, e.g. Sequencing › Melodic and Sequencing › Drum . Cell › New Cell , New Voice Cell , and your cell presets by category ( Synthesizers › Basic Poly comes with Beautiful Bleep). Tab (or a double-click on empty space) opens a search at the cursor instead. See Voice Cells for polyphonic synths. Patching Drag from an output (the dots on the right of a node) to an input on the left of another node. Inputs that can't take the signal fade out. Drop on a knob in an open module view to modulate it. Every knob is a destination. The modulation is an offset: the knob stays where you put it, and a ring shows the value really used. The chip under the knob sets the cable's amount (drag up or down, double-click for 100 %). Drop on a node to pick one of its knobs from a list. Drop on empty space to add a module that is connected right away. Click a cable to set its amount or delete it. Drag a cable's end at an input to move it; drop it on empty space to remove it. Several cables into one input are added up. Cable colours: yellow control, green gate and trigger (dashed), blue pitch, red audio, purple notes. Notes only connect to notes. Module views Click a node to open its view: knobs, settings and its own displays. Views float over the board; open as many as you like, drag them by the title, pin them (📌) to keep them open when you enter or leave cells. Module presets Most modules with sound-shaping knobs (oscillators, filters, effects, envelopes, drums, …) have a preset bar at the top of their view. It looks the same in every module: ‹ › step to the previous or next preset. The name in the middle opens the list, which has two parts: Factory presets that ship with Beautiful Bleep, and User presets that you saved yourself. A dot (●) next to the name means you changed a knob after loading the preset. Save keeps the current settings as a preset of your own: type a name and press Enter. If the loaded preset is one of yours and you changed it, Save overwrites it. In the menu, × (click twice) deletes one of your presets. Factory presets can't be changed or deleted. To build on one, load it, change it and save it under a new name. Reset to defaults (at the bottom of the list) puts every knob back. A preset sets the module's own knobs and settings, never its cables. Modules that keep a pattern or other content in their view (sequencers, for example) save that content in your own presets too. Modules like the Patch Bay, meters and mixers have no presets. Your presets are shared by all your boards and live next to your cell presets (in the folder Module Presets ). Cells Add → Cell → New Cell or New Voice Cell places an empty cell. Select nodes, right-click and choose Create cell ( ⌘G ) or Create voice cell . Cables that cross the new border become the cell's jacks. Drag nodes onto a cell to move them into it; the cell lights up when it takes them. Cables to the rest of the board become cell jacks (an input that already carries the same signal is reused). Inside a cell, right-click a node → Remove from cell moves it out next to the cell; its cables are rerouted over cell jacks. Cables to Voice In and Voice Out can't be kept. Double-click a cell to enter it; Esc or the path at the top leads back out. Inside, Cell In and Cell Out are the cell's jacks: drop a cable on their new input / new output row to add one. ⌘⇧G ungroups a cell again. Right-click a cell → Save as preset to keep it in the Add menu for every set: Add → Cell → . Your own presets can be deleted there under Delete preset . Shortcuts Key Action Tab, double-click Add a module ⌘G / ⌘⇧G Create a cell from the selection / ungroup ⌘D / ⌘⇧D Duplicate / duplicate with incoming cables Delete Remove the selection (not ports) Esc Close a view, leave a cell, clear the selection F Fit the board to the window T Trace: highlight what feeds and is fed by the selection M Mute: the node's outputs fall silent ⌘Z / ⌘⇧Z Undo / redo Scroll, ⌘-scroll or pinch Pan, zoom Space-drag or Alt-drag Pan

title: Getting started
text: Getting started with Beautiful Bleep This page is for Ableton Live. Bleep also runs as a standalone app and in your browser. Beautiful Bleep makes Ableton Live feel modular. All modules live on one canvas per set, the board . You connect them with cables, and small plugins called ports connect the board to your tracks. Just want a sound? Put Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track or Bleep FX on an audio track and pick a preset. No patching needed; see ways to use Bleep. Install Copy the .vst3 files to your plugin folder, then rescan plugins in Live (Settings → Plug-Ins, with "Use VST3 Plug-In System Folders" on). The plugins appear in Live's browser under Plug-Ins → Beautiful Bleep . VST3 folder macOS ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 Windows C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 Your first board (5 minutes) Put Bleep Board on any track (the master track is a good place). Every set that uses Bleep Board needs exactly one. Its window opens the board. Put Bleep FX on a synth track, after the synth. It appears on the board by itself, named after the track. On the board, press Tab , type filter and press Enter. Drag from the Insert's Send L to the Filter's In L , and from the Filter's Out L and Out R to the Insert's Return L and Return R . Press Tab again and add a Function . Click the Filter to open its view, then drag Function's A onto the Cutoff knob. The yellow ring shows the cutoff the filter really uses; drag the amount chip under the knob to set how much. Now modulate the modulator: add a Random and drag its Out onto Function's Rise knob. How the board works See the board for patching, cells and shortcuts, and ports for every plugin you can add in Live. Ports (MIDI In, Audio Out, …) appear on the board when you add them in Live. You can't delete them on the board; when a track is deactivated or the plugin is removed, its node turns into a grey ghost and keeps its cables. The board is saved in Bleep Board. A second Bleep Board in the same set stays inactive and shows a warning. Latency. Audio that goes from Live into the board and back is two audio buffers late. The output ports report this to Live, so Live's delay compensation lines it up with the rest of the set. Undo. The board has its own undo (⌘Z in the board window). Live's undo doesn't include board edits.

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Beautiful Bleep is the whole technology: the engine, the board, the modules, the plugins for your DAW, the app, the browser version, the store and the open protocol. The names below are the ones used everywhere in the docs and in the programs. Ways to run it The same board runs in three places. Patches, presets and modules work in all of them. Term What it is Bleep plugin Everything you add in your DAW (Ableton Live today): the main plugin, which stores and opens the board, and the ports. VST3. Bleep App The standalone app: the board without a DAW, with its own MIDI ports and Ableton Link. Bleep Play The board in your browser, with no install. Modules load from the Bleep Store on demand. The board and what is on it Term What it is Board The patching canvas. One per Live set, or per project in the app. It shows every node, cable and cell. Node Anything on the board that has jacks: a module, a port, a cell, an external plugin. Module A node type that processes signals: Function, Random, Filter and so on. Modules exist only on the board, never as plugins in Live. Shipped as .bleepmod packages. Cable A directed connection from an output jack to an input jack. Jack An input or output on a node. Cell A named group of nodes with its own jacks. Cells nest, can be copied and saved as cell presets. Voice Cell A cell that runs the voice you patch inside it once per note, so one voice becomes a polyphonic instrument. Panel A front panel of controls (dials, sliders, buttons, keys) for a cell or the board. Module view A module's full interface: knobs, switches, scopes. It opens as a window inside the board. Engine The shared code that runs the board. One engine runs per process, shared by every Bleep plugin loaded. Bleep plugins in Live Term What it is Bleep Board plugin The main plugin. Every Live set that uses Beautiful Bleep needs exactly one, on any track. It stores the board and opens it. Port A Bleep plugin on a track that connects that track to the board: Bleep MIDI In , MIDI Out , Audio In , Audio Out , Instrument , FX . Each port is one node on the board. Ableton bridge The ports together. Later bridges connect the board to other worlds the same way. Ghost A node whose port is not available right now (deleted, deactivated, not loaded yet). It is greyed out and keeps its cables. Bleep Audio Bridge A plugin in Live that connects a track's audio to a running Bleep App. Saving and sharing Term What it is Project Your own saved board ( .bleepboard ). Preset Something you can share, as a .bleeppreset file. A board preset is a whole board; a cell preset is one cell with its panel. Bleep Store Where plugins, modules and presets are installed from. Downloading needs no login; sharing a preset needs an account. "Patch" and "patching" stay everyday words for connecting cables. They are not names of a file or a product. For developers Term What it is Bleep Bus The open protocol and SDK that lets other plugins (Grit, Cinch, third-party) send and receive per-sample control signals through shared memory and join the board. Registry The technical name of the Bleep Store's interface ( /registry/v1/ , BLEEP REGISTRY URL ). In prose it is always the Bleep Store.

title: Connecting plugin, app and web
text: Connecting plugin, app and web Bleep runs in three places: the plugins in Live, the app and a board in your browser. Each has its own board. This page is about making them work together: a synth built in the browser and played from Live, an effect in the browser on a Live track, a sequencer in the browser that plays an instrument in Live, a patch in the app whose sound lands on a Live track. The idea is one setting, the Board menu on the plugins, plus one switch in the app and one button in the browser. Live plugins connect to the app through shared memory; Bleep Play in the browser connects to the app over a WebSocket. The app is the hub in the middle. The app sits in the middle. Live and the browser both talk to it, never to each other directly. That is why the app has to be running for any of this. Everything stays on your computer: the app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. What delay to expect Audio cannot travel for free. Each hop adds a little time, and it is better to know the numbers than to be surprised. Connection Delay Good for Live ⇄ app 2 audio buffers (about 5 ms at 256 samples) Almost anything, including playing Live → browser → Live About 45 ms for the whole round trip with the page from the app ( Low latency , 256-sample buffer, measured on a laptop with a Chrome-based browser); more with a bigger buffer or the Safe mode Sound design, effects you hear, sequences Browser page from the website Safe mode: about 64 ms of buffering in each direction, on top The same, with more headroom The browser's share is its jitter buffer (16 ms in Low latency , at least 1.5 audio buffers of the app or of Live) and the browser's own audio output. The plugin that brings the sound back reports the total to Live. Two things make the delay mostly invisible in a song: Sources that follow the transport are lined up for you. When Live's own MIDI plays a browser synth, or a browser sequencer plays a Live instrument, the plugin tells Live how late the sound will be, and Live's delay compensation moves everything else to match. On the timeline it is on the beat. Sources that answer you live are not. Playing the browser synth with a keyboard, or running a live input through a browser effect, you hear the full delay. For playing, run the instrument in the app or in a plugin instead, and use the browser for sequencing, effects and sound design. Turning it on In the app: File → Settings → Web , then Let Bleep Play pages connect to this app . It is off until you do this. The port is 47100 ; change it only if something else uses it. In a plugin: open a port plugin's window (Bleep MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In or Audio Out) and choose its Board : Board The plugin talks to This set The board of this Live set, as always Bleep App The board in the running app Bleep Play Bleep Play that has joined (through the app) In the browser: open the board and press ⇄ Connect to app (next to Start audio ). The button is in the current web build only: a copy of the board built earlier does not have it. Rebuild with scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules . For the lowest delay, open the board from the app instead of the website: the Web section of the app's Settings shows the address ( http://127.0.0.1:47100/ ). The app serves the board page from the folder named by the BLEEP WEB ROOT environment variable (the folder build-web.sh wrote, build/web/site ), for example BLEEP WEB ROOT=build/web/site "Bleep Patch.app/Contents/MacOS/Bleep Patch" . Without it the app shows only a placeholder page at that address. That page can use a faster path between the browser and its audio engine, which is what Low latency means. The website's page works too, in Safe mode, with more delay and a little more headroom. Safari does not let a website talk to an app on your computer, so use the app's page there. The first time a page from anywhere else connects, the app asks whether to allow it. Allow only pages you opened yourself. You can forget them again in Settings → Web. Which plugins do I need? Only four of the port plugins can talk to the app or Bleep Play: Bleep MIDI In , MIDI Out , Audio In and Audio Out . They are the ones with a Board menu. Pick the plugin for what should travel, then set its Board to Bleep App (a patch in the app) or Bleep Play (the browser). You want Put this on a track Board MIDI from Live to the board (Live's notes play a synth in the app or browser) Bleep MIDI In on a MIDI track Bleep App or Bleep Play MIDI from the board to Live (a board sequencer plays an instrument in Live) Bleep MIDI Out on a MIDI track, routed to your instrument (how) Bleep App or Bleep Play Audio from a Live track to the board (an effect, a sampler or analysis) Bleep Audio In on that track Bleep App or Bleep Play Audio from the board back into Live (the sound of a synth or an effect) Bleep Audio Out on its own MIDI track Bleep App or Bleep Play Sync (tempo, beat, play and stop) Nothing extra: any one of the four plugins above carries it A few things follow from that: Audio and MIDI are separate. A browser synth played from Live needs two plugins: MIDI In for the notes and Audio Out for the sound. A browser effect needs Audio In and Audio Out. Sync has no plugin of its own. As soon as one plugin with a Board other than This set is connected, Live leads the tempo and transport, and the app and Bleep Play follow it (see Tempo and transport). The other port plugins stay in Live. Bleep Board , Bleep Instrument and Bleep FX have no Board menu: they always use the board of this set. Put Bleep Board once per set if you want macros as usual. The recipes below walk through the common combinations. What you see On the app's board , a plugin with Board = Bleep App appears as the same node it would be in Live (a MIDI In , an Audio Out …), named after its track. When you set it back, or delete the plugin, the node turns grey and its cables stay. On the browser's board , a plugin with Board = Bleep Play appears as a node named Live: track name , in the same colour as the app's remote nodes. Pressing Connect again after a break reconnects them. Nodes you add yourself from the Add menu, Remote Audio and Remote MIDI , appear on the app's board as Web: name nodes. A plugin with a Board other than This set has no node on Live's own board: Bleep App there shows it as a grey ghost until you switch it back. Recipes Play a browser synth from Live In Live, make a MIDI track with Bleep MIDI In , Board = Bleep Play . Play or draw notes on it. Make another MIDI track with Bleep Audio Out , Board = Bleep Play . This is where the sound comes back. In Bleep Play, connect to the app. Live: your MIDI track and Live: your audio track appear. Cable the MIDI node's Notes into an oscillator or a synth cell, and the synth's output into the audio node's L and R . Audio Out reports the way there and back to Live, so a clip's notes sound on their beat. If you play the MIDI track live with a keyboard, expect the delay from the table above. Put a browser effect on a Live track Put Bleep Audio In ( Board = Bleep Play ) on the track to send its audio to the browser, and Bleep Audio Out ( Board = Bleep Play ) on its own track to get the result back. Mute the original track if you want only the effect. Audio travels there and back, so the delay is twice that of the table. Live lines it up with the rest of your set when the clips play. Play an instrument in Live from a browser sequencer Put Bleep MIDI Out ( Board = Bleep Play ) on a MIDI track in Live and route that track's output to the track with your instrument (see MIDI Out routing). In Bleep Play a node Live: track name appears with a Notes input: cable your sequencer's notes into it. The sequencer follows Live's tempo and position, and sends notes a short time ahead, each with the beat it belongs to. The plugin plays every note at its place in the right buffer, so it is on the beat, not just about on the beat. When you change the tempo or jump the playhead, the sequencer drops what it had queued and starts again from the new place, so nothing plays in the wrong spot. To use the browser's MIDI in the app instead, add a Remote MIDI node from the Add menu: in the app it appears as a Web: Remote MIDI node you can patch like any other MIDI source. A patch in the app, as a sound source in Live In Live, put Bleep Audio Out with Board = Bleep App on a track: the app's board now plays on that track, with its own mixer channel. The app follows Live's tempo and position while it is connected. The delay is two buffers, and Live compensates it. Do the same with Bleep MIDI In ( Board = Bleep App ) to play the app's patch from a Live MIDI track. MIDI and audio then travel in the same way, so they stay together. While Live is connected to the app, the app's own audio interface stays silent : Live's audio buffers drive the app, and its sound goes back through Live. Disconnect the plugins, or close the set, to use the app on its own. Tempo and transport One of them leads at a time: Live , as long as one of its plugins talks to the app or Bleep Play. Ableton Link in the app, if it is on. The app's own clock. Bleep Play follows whoever leads: tempo, beat and play/stop. It can ask for a new tempo or for play, and only the leader decides. If Live leads, a request from the browser changes nothing. Export and freeze A browser works on the clock of its own sound card and cannot go faster than real time. When Live exports , freezes or flattens a track faster than real time, a Bleep plugin with Board = Bleep App waits for the app and everything is in the file. With Board = Bleep Play the browser's share is silent. To get it into a file: record the web part to an audio track in real time (a track with Audio In/Out is enough), then export. When it does not work The plugin window says what it sees: It says What to do The Bleep App is not running Start the app. Until then the plugin passes its track through untouched The app is connected to another host Only one Live at a time can drive the app The app has no free bridge slot 32 plugins at most can talk to the app. Remove some The app is another version Update the plugins and the app, then restart Live Late blocks counting up The computer is busy or the buffer is small. Raise Live's buffer size In the browser, the Connect button says why it could not connect (the app is not running, the Web setting is off, the browser blocks the connection, you declined the question). In the app, Settings → Web shows who is connected and how many channels each has, and counts MIDI that arrived late or after a tempo change. What is not there yet Another computer. Everything is on one machine. A shared session (a web board on your phone, a friend playing your synth) needs a server between the computers and is planned. Playing notes across the internet is easy; sending audio live is limited by the network's delay, which no setting hides. A browser sound in a file, automatically. See Export and freeze . The page from the website in Safari. Use the page from the app. Live without the app. The app has to be running. A plugin that can take its place is a possibility later. The formats and numbers behind all this are in the design notes for developers, doc/specs/bridges.md in the source.

title: Modulating any Live parameter (loopback workaround)
text: Modulating any Live parameter (v1 workaround) Until the Max for Live bridge exists, a virtual MIDI port lets you map signals from the board to any parameter in Live: macOS: open Audio MIDI Setup → MIDI Studio → IAC Driver , tick Device is online . Windows: install loopMIDI and create a port. In Live's MIDI preferences, enable Remote for the IAC/loopMIDI input. Route the Bleep MIDI Out track's MIDI To to that port. Enter MIDI Map mode, click the target parameter, then patch a moving signal into MIDI Out's CC 1 input on the board. Live learns the mapping. Limits: 7-bit resolution, updates at Live's control rate, and the mapping overrides automation on that parameter.

title: Routing MIDI Out in Live
text: Routing MIDI Out in Live Create a MIDI track ("Mod MIDI") and load Bleep MIDI Out (VST3) as its instrument. Create a second MIDI track with the instrument you want to play. On the second track set MIDI From to Mod MIDI , choose Bleep MIDI Out in the second menu, and set Monitor to In . On the board, patch a gate (e.g. Function's EOC through Utility, or Random's Trig ) into MIDI Out's Gate , and a pitch (e.g. Random with Semitones on) into Pitch . Or patch a Notes output (from MIDI In) into its Notes input. CC numbers, channel and transpose are in its view. Live merges MIDI channels on internal routes, so one MIDI Out instance carries one stream. Use more instances for more streams.

title: Process what your computer plays
text: Process what your computer plays The System node puts everything your computer plays onto the board: a music player, a browser tab, a video call, a game. Patch it into a filter, a reverb or a delay network, and listen to the result. Or record it. It is a feature of the Bleep App. The plugins have your DAW for this, and Bleep Play cannot see other programs. You don't need a virtual audio driver (BlackHole, Loopback, VB-Cable). Bleep App asks your operating system for the sound directly. Turn it on Open File → Settings → Audio . Under System audio , tick Capture what this computer plays . Allow the permission if your system asks (macOS does, once). On the board, choose Add → Port → System . The node has two outputs, L and R , and a Gain dial, like the other Audio In nodes. It stays off until you tick the box: nothing is captured before that. The settings show what is going on: the sample rate, whether your own sound is left out, and whether sound arrives ( signal ) or not ( silent ). Recipes Hear your music player through an effect. Play something in another program, then patch System L/R → Reverb → Out 1/2 . You hear the player itself and, a moment later, the effect. Play Bleep App to headphones and the player to speakers (or mute the player's output) to hear the effect alone. A filter sweep over a song. System L/R → Filter → Out 1/2 , and an LFO on the cutoff. Record what you hear. Patch System and your synth into a mixer node and on into a recorder. Because the captured sound reaches Bleep App a moment after it leaves the other program, the effect is slightly late. See Delay below. Feedback If Bleep App plays to your speakers and System captures your speakers, a cable from System to Out 1/2 would feed back: what comes out is captured, played, captured again. Bleep App prevents this by default: Leave out Bleep App's own sound is on. The capture then holds everything except Bleep App. System Own sound left out? macOS 14.2 or later Yes Windows 10 build 20348 or later, Windows 11 Yes Older Windows No Linux No Where it can't be left out, the setting is disabled and says so. Play Bleep App to another output than the one you capture (headphones for Bleep App, speakers for everything else), or don't patch System to an output. Turn the setting off if you want to record Bleep App's own sound together with everything else. macOS You need macOS 14.2 or later . The first time you turn the capture on, macOS asks if Bleep App may record system audio. If it doesn't ask, or you said no, System stays silent. Allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording (the System Audio Recording Only list), then turn the capture off and on again. If the app is started from a terminal rather than by double-clicking it, macOS may credit the terminal instead of Bleep App, and the capture stays silent. Start the app from Finder or the Dock. Sound that is protected against copying (some streaming services) arrives as silence. That is the system's rule, not a setting. On older macOS, use a loopback driver such as BlackHole as an input device instead (File → Settings → Input). Windows Windows 10 or later. No permission prompt. With Windows 10 build 20348 or later (and Windows 11), Bleep App captures everything except itself, whichever output device you use. On older versions it captures the default output device including its own sound. If you change the default output (plug in headphones), the capture follows within a second. Linux You need PulseAudio, or PipeWire with its PulseAudio support ( pipewire-pulse , the default on most desktops), and a build of the app with libpulse (install libpulse-dev before building). Every output has a monitor , a source that carries what that output plays. The settings list them under Output to capture . Default output follows your system's default. Linux can't leave Bleep App's own sound out of a monitor: use a different output for Bleep App than for the rest, as described under Feedback . Delay The captured sound takes about 40 ms to arrive: 30 ms is a buffer that absorbs hiccups, and the system's own capture adds 10 to 20 ms. That doesn't matter for processing, mixing or recording. It does matter for playing live against the captured sound; for that, use a normal audio input (a cable or a loopback driver). Two sound cards never run at exactly the same speed. Bleep App corrects for that continuously with a tiny pitch adjustment (well below what you can hear) instead of dropping or repeating samples, so long sessions stay clean. When it doesn't work What you see What to do silent in Settings, but sound plays macOS: allow Bleep App under Privacy & Security, then turn the capture off and on. Otherwise check that the other program plays to the output that is the system default "needs macOS 14.2 or later" Update macOS, or use a loopback driver as an input device "No PulseAudio or PipeWire sound server was found" (Linux) Start your sound server; check with pactl info "This system cannot leave Bleep App out" Not an error: see Feedback The node is grey (a ghost) The capture is off or failed. Tick the box in Settings again and read the message A crackle once in a while Raise the buffer size in Settings → Audio; the capture follows it Notes for developers How it is built, the clock-drift handling and the open questions are in the specification, doc/specs/system-audio.md in the repository.

title: Ways to use Bleep
text: Ways to use Bleep Beautiful Bleep is one sound engine you can reach in three places, and in each place you can use it at three levels of effort. Three places What it is Best for Bleep plugin VST3 plugins for your DAW (Ableton Live today). See ports Making music inside a DAW project Bleep App The standalone app: the board without a DAW Playing, sound design, live use next to a DAW Bleep Play Bleep Play in your browser, no install Trying things out, sharing a project All three run the same board, the same modules and the same project files, so a project made in one place opens in the others. (Bleep Play does not have every module yet; the board page lists what is missing.) Connecting them The places work together: MIDI, audio and tempo can travel between them, and you choose where in the place you are. The plugins have a Board menu ( This set , Bleep App or Bleep Play ), the Bleep App has a Web switch in Settings, and Bleep Play has a Connect to app button. The Bleep App sits in the middle, on your computer. What works: Plugin ⇄ App App ⇄ Play Plugin ⇄ Play (through the app) MIDI Board menu on MIDI In/Out, or the app's MIDI ports Remote MIDI nodes Board menu: Bleep Play Audio Board menu on Audio In/Out, or Bleep Audio Bridge Remote Audio nodes Board menu: Bleep Play Tempo and transport Live leads; Ableton Link Bleep Play follows the app Bleep Play follows Live Audio between the plugin and the app is two buffers late; through Bleep Play it is a little more. Connecting plugin, app and Bleep Play has the numbers, the setup and some recipes. Another computer, or Bleep Play without the app, is planned, not built. Three ways to play Whichever place you are in, you choose how to start: Instrument. Pick a preset such as Warm Saws , play it with MIDI. For when you want a sound, not a board. In Live this is Bleep Instrument . Audio effect. Pick a preset such as Dub Ping-Pong , send audio through it. In Live this is Bleep FX . Full board. Every module, every cable, your own project. In Live this is the Bleep Board plugin, with ports that connect the board to your tracks. These are not three different systems. An instrument or an effect preset is a small cell on the same board as everything else. The simple modes are a shortcut: you can try presets without ever touching a cable, and when you want more, open the board, edit the preset's cell, cable it to other parts, and save it as your own. Instrument Audio effect Full board Bleep plugin Bleep Instrument Bleep FX Bleep Board and the ports Bleep App Planned Planned Yes Bleep Play Planned Planned Yes In the plugins, Instrument and FX open on the preset's panel (knobs and sliders) rather than on the board. Open Board shows the preset as a cell on the board. Cables between several plugins need the Bleep Board plugin in the set, because the board is saved there. Next: Getting started in Live, the Bleep App, or Bleep Play in your browser.

title: Ports
text: Ports: the plugins you add in Live These are the only Bleep plugins in Live's browser. Each one (except Bleep Board) appears on the board as a node, named after its track. Settings such as MIDI channels and CC numbers are in the node's view on the board. Plugin Put it on On the board Bleep Board any track, once per set Macros : 16 outputs you can automate and MIDI-map in Live Bleep MIDI In a MIDI track Notes (polyphonic), mono Pitch , Gate , Velocity , Trigger , Pressure , Bend , Mod Wheel , 8 CCs Bleep MIDI Out a MIDI track inputs Notes , Gate + Pitch (mono), 8 CCs, Bend . See routing Bleep Audio In any track, anywhere in the chain the track's audio at that point ( L , R ); the audio passes through unchanged Bleep Audio Out its own MIDI track board audio ( L , R ) on that track, with its own mixer channel Bleep Instrument a MIDI track MIDI In and Audio Out in one plugin: a board synth on one track Bleep FX any track Send (the track's audio) and Return (back to the track), with Dry/Wet. With nothing patched into Return , the audio passes through Board: Bleep MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In and Audio Out have a Board menu in their window: This set (the default), Bleep App or Web board . With the app or Bleep Play, the plugin talks to that board instead of this set's, and has no node on this set's board. See Connecting plugin, app and web. Latency: audio through the board arrives two audio buffers late. Audio Out, Instrument and Audio Insert report it to Live (Live's delay compensation then lines them up). It isn't compensated for MIDI Out, or for tracks you monitor while Reduced Latency When Monitoring is on. Ghosts: when a port's plugin is deleted, deactivated or its track is frozen, its node turns grey and its outputs fall silent. The cables stay; when the plugin comes back (for example after undo in Live), it reconnects.

title: The standalone app
text: The Bleep App The board without a DAW: for playing and sound design on its own, or next to Live. It is one of three places to use Bleep (plugin, app, web). Open the app, add modules with Tab, and patch as in Live. Projects are saved as .bleepboard files (File → Save). Audio Choose your audio interface in File → Settings . A new board starts with just In 1/2 and Out 1/2 . More pairs of your interface, the MIDI ports and the Link node are there when you need them: Add → Port . Delete the ones you don't use. What your computer plays The System node carries everything your computer plays: a music player, a browser, a video call. Patch it into effects, or into an Audio Out to process it. No virtual audio driver is needed. Turn it on in File → Settings → Audio → System audio → Capture what this computer plays . It is off until you do, because capturing sound needs your permission. Then add the node from Add → Port , like the other inputs. Your own sound is left out by default, so patching System to an output does not feed back. Where the system cannot do that (Linux, older Windows), play Bleep App to a different output than the one you capture. macOS 14.2 or later. The first time, macOS asks to allow Bleep App to record system audio. If System stays silent, allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording . Windows 10 or later. Leaving your own sound out needs Windows 10 build 20348 or later. Linux with PulseAudio or PipeWire. Settings lists the outputs you can capture. The capture adds about 40 ms of delay. It is meant for processing and recording, not for playing live against it. More, with the setup for each system and what to do when it stays silent: Process what your computer plays. A MIDI keyboard Add MIDI Device ( Add → Module → Sources ), click it and choose your controller. Patch its Notes into a Voice Cell — e.g. Basic Poly — and the cell's Out L/R into Out 1/2 . MIDI Device also has mono Pitch , Gate , Velocity , Bend , Mod Wheel and CCs. It exists only in the app. MIDI to and from Live The app has its own MIDI ports, Bleep App 1 and Bleep App 2 (more in Settings). No loopback tool needed. Add their nodes from Add → Port . Play the app from Live: on a MIDI track, set MIDI To to Bleep App 1 . On the board, the Bleep App 1 MIDI In node gets the notes. Play Live from the app: patch into the Bleep App 1 MIDI Out node; on a MIDI track in Live, set MIDI From to Bleep App 1 and Monitor to In . Audio to and from Live: Bleep Audio Bridge Put Bleep Audio Bridge on any track in Live while the app runs. In the app it appears as a node named after the track: Send L/R: the track's audio, into the board. Return L/R: audio from the board, back to the track. The plugin's Monitor setting chooses what the track plays: Send (its own audio), Return (the app's audio) or Mix . With nothing patched into the return, the track's audio passes through. While bridges are connected, Live sets the pace: the app follows Live's audio, so nothing drifts. The bridge delays audio by two audio buffers and tells Live, so Live's delay compensation keeps everything in time. Exports include the app. Tempo and transport: Ableton Link Turn on Transport → Ableton Link in the app and the Link button in Live: both share tempo, beat and (with Start/Stop Sync) play and stop. The Link node puts tempo, beat, bar, clock and play state on the board.

title: Voice Cells
text: Voice Cells: polyphonic synths A Voice Cell turns one synthesizer voice into a polyphonic instrument. Inside, you patch one voice, like a mono synth. The cell plays it once per note, up to 16 voices at a time. Make one Add → Cell → New Voice Cell gives you a cell with a starter voice inside: Oscillator → VCA, with an ADSR on the VCA's gain. It makes sound right away. Add → Cell → Synthesizers → Basic Poly is a ready-made synth: Oscillator → Multi Filter (Rough) → VCA, one ADSR for the filter and one for the VCA. Right-click an ordinary cell → Make Voice Cell turns it into one. Connect it From outside, a Voice Cell has: Jack What Notes all notes, e.g. from MIDI Device Notes Out L / Out R all voices, mixed your own inputs the same signal for every voice: an LFO, a cutoff macro, pitch bend your own outputs summed over the voices To play it from a sequencer or any pitch + gate source, put CV to Notes in between. Design the voice Double-click the cell. Inside are two fixed nodes: Voice In gives this voice its note: Pitch , Gate , Trigger , Velocity , Release , Pressure , Voice # (0, 1, 2 …) and Random (a new value per note, for a little variation between voices). Voice Out takes the voice's audio ( Out L , Out R ) and Active : patch the amp ADSR's Active here, so the voice is freed exactly when its sound has faded. A knob you turn inside changes it in every voice. Add your own shared inputs and outputs by dropping a cable on Cell In 's or Cell Out 's "new" row. Pitch bend: patch MIDI Device Bend into a shared input and, inside, into the oscillator's Pitch with amount 2/12 for ±2 semitones (that's how Basic Poly does it). Settings Click the cell to open its view: Setting What it does Voices 1–16 Allocation which free voice a new note gets: round robin, the lowest free one, or the voice that last played the same note Stealing when all voices are busy: take the oldest, quietest, lowest or highest note — or none (the new note is dropped) Mode Poly; Mono (one voice, every note restarts the envelopes); Legato (one voice, overlapping notes don't restart them) Glide time to slide from one pitch to the next; Glide Mode : always, or only when notes overlap Stereo Spread spreads the voices from left to right Output plain sum, or compensated (quieter per voice, so 8 voices don't clip) The dots on the node light up for the voices that play. Voices that don't play use no CPU. Save it Right-click → Save as preset , give it a name and a category (e.g. Synthesizers ). It then appears under Add → Cell → in every project.

title: Additive Osc
text: Additive Osc Additive Osc in the module view Introduction The Additive Osc builds its sound from up to 64 sine waves, the partials . Instead of 64 sliders it has a handful of spectral knobs: Tilt darkens or brightens, Odd/Even moves between hollow and full, Stretch and Shift bend the series into bells and metal, Comb carves moving notches and Chorus detunes the partials against each other. You can also draw your own spectrum. Partials above the top of the audio band are simply left out, so it never aliases, at any pitch. How does it work? Pitch. The fundamental is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), clamped to 1 Hz – 20 kHz and followed sample by sample. Partial n plays at the fundamental × its ratio (n, unless stretched) plus Shift . Levels. Each partial's level is the product of: Base: Saw 1/n, Square 1/n on odd partials only, Flat 1/√n (even energy per octave), or Drawn : your own bars. Tilt: dB per octave of partial number (−24 dark … +12 bright). Odd/Even: −1 odd partials only, +1 even only; the fundamental stays. Partials: how many sound; the last one fades in fractionally, so modulating it is smooth. Comb: notches every Comb Spacing partials; Comb Phase slides them along the spectrum and wraps, so an LFO sweeps them endlessly. Band limit: partials fade out between 40 % and 45 % of the sample rate and are dropped above. Levels glide over 2 ms, so all of these can be modulated without zipper noise. Normalise keeps the loudness constant (RMS 0.3) while you change the colour; off, a 64-partial saw spans about ±1. Stretch and Shift. Stretch above 0 makes upper partials go sharp (stiff strings, pianos, bells); below 0 it squeezes them together. The fundamental always stays on the note. Shift adds the same frequency (±1 × the note) to every partial: inharmonic, metallic, ring-modulated. Chorus. Each partial wanders by up to Chorus cents at about Chorus Rate , seeded, so the ensemble shimmer never repeats a pattern but every render is the same. Phases. Random starts each partial at a seeded phase (smooth, no peaky waveform); Aligned starts them all together (the sharp shape of a true saw). A Trigger restarts them. Decay. With Decay below its maximum, a Trigger strikes: every partial decays, the fundamental by 60 dB in Decay , higher partials faster by Damp (at 100 % partial 10 dies 100× faster than the fundamental). A new trigger brings the levels back up within 2 ms. At maximum (20 s) the sound sustains; without triggers it always sustains. Stereo. Width pans the odd partials left and the even partials right (up to 70 % at full width); the fundamental stays centred and the mono sum stays within 1.5 dB. How to use it? Organ / drawbars: Base Square or Drawn, Partials 8–16. Bell: Stretch +0.6, Phases Aligned, Decay 3 s, Damp 60 %, triggers from the note's gate. Pluck: Decay 0.4 s, Damp 80 %, Tilt −3 dB/oct. Moving notches: Comb 80 %, a slow LFO on Comb Phase . Ensemble pad: Chorus 20 ct, Chorus Rate 0.5 Hz, Width 70 %. Sub-bass: use the Fundamental output under the main sound. Drawing With Base on Drawn the view shows 64 bars. Drag across them to paint levels (Shift: fine, relative), double-click a bar to reset it to 1/n, or use Saw , Square , Flat , Smooth and Randomize . A drag is one undo step. The drawing is saved with the board. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Additive Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Additive Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Additive Osc: Glass Pad A saw spectrum with a gentle Tilt , slight Stretch and slow Chorus makes a wide glassy pad; an LFO drifts Tilt . Additive Osc: Hollow Reed Base Square with Odd/Even pushed to the odd side; a slow LFO sweeps it from hollow to bright. Additive Osc: Inharmonic Bells Stretch detunes the partials from each other and Decay lets them ring on a Trigger : struck bells. title: Beat Oscillator
text: Beat Oscillator Introduction Beat Oscillator is a heterodyne tone source, the way old laboratory signal generators worked. Two high carriers, A and B , run close together and are mixed, and what you hear is their difference. Turn Beat a little around zero and the tone sweeps from several kilohertz down to a slow pulse, then stops. The charm is in how imperfect it is. Pull couples the carriers so they try to lock. Inside the lock range the beat disappears; just outside it the tone stumbles along in uneven blips. Drift lets both carriers wander, and close to zero beat even a tiny wander is a big change. Warm-up starts the carriers flat, so the tone glides into tune like a cold valve instrument. How does it work? Two carriers. A runs at Carrier . B runs at Carrier plus Beat plus Fine . Pitch (1 V/oct) transposes both, so the beat tone moves with them. The Detune input adds hertz to B ( Detune Range per 1.0) without being scaled by Pitch, like a hand moved near a tuning capacitor. FM modulates B's frequency directly and can push it through zero: 1.0 is 1 kHz of deviation. Beat. The knob is cubic, so the middle is very fine: on Range ±2 kHz, 10 % is 2 Hz and 50 % is 250 Hz. Range sets the full swing (±20 Hz, ±200 Hz or ±2 kHz). Fine adds ±2 Hz for finding zero beat. The view shows the actual beat in hertz. Mixer and detector. The carriers are multiplied, and a steep low-pass (the detector ) keeps only the difference. Mixer picks the circuit: Ideal: a clean multiplier. The beat is a pure sine. Diode: a half-wave square-law mixer. The beat is brighter and slightly buzzy, with its own harmonics. Overdriven: both carriers clipped almost to squares first. The beat sounds like a triangle, with a little carrier leaking through. At 0 %, Detector passes beats up to about 2 kHz and nothing else. Open it and the sum of the carriers comes through as a whistle. You only hear it when the carriers are low: turn Carrier below about 11 kHz with the detector open. Pull. The carriers are coupled, so each one drags the other. The lock range grows with Pull (25 % → 3 Hz, 50 % → 25 Hz, 100 % → 200 Hz). Inside the lock range both carriers run at one frequency and the beat stops. Lock goes high. Just outside it the beat is much slower than the detuning (the square-root law: 30 Hz detuning with a 25 Hz lock range beats at 16.6 Hz). The phase difference crawls, then whips round once, so Out plays one-cycle blips between near-silences. Let Drift or a slow Detune move the pair across the edge and the blips lurch, bunch up and stop. Far outside it is a plain beat again. Coupling. AC removes DC from Out (below 5 Hz). Slow beats become swells, and a locked pair is silent. DC keeps slow beats as a usable modulation signal, and a locked pair holds a steady level. Drift and warm-up. With Drift up, each carrier wanders on its own smooth random curve, by up to ±25 cents at 100 %. At 10 kHz that is about ±145 Hz, enough to throw a 2 Hz beat all over the place, while a 2 kHz beat barely notices. While the transport plays, the wander follows the song position (a slow turn every 8 beats, small wobbles every beat). With Warm-up on, both carriers start up to 40 cents flat, by different amounts, and settle over the warm-up time. Warm-up starts when the transport starts. While stopped it starts when the board loads, or when you press Cold . Beat and Lock outputs. Beat measures the beat frequency by counting how often the phase difference slips a full turn, and puts it out as 1 V/oct (0 V = 261.6 Hz, i.e. C4). When the pair locks it falls smoothly to its floor of 0.1 Hz (−11.35 V). Lock is high while the carriers are locked. Repeatable. The drift curves come from Seed . A transport start resets the phases, the filters and the warm-up, so a render from the same start is always the same. Inside a Voice Cell each voice drifts on its own. The view Two dials show the actual frequencies of A and B, after drift, warm-up and pulling. Between them is the beat B − A in hertz (signed, in millihertz below 1 Hz) and the Lock lamp. The lamp is lit while locked. Outside lock it flashes once per slip, so a slow beat shows as a blinking lamp. Below them, the circle shows the phase difference ψ as a dot with a fading tail. Locked, the dot stands still. Near the edge it creeps, then flicks round. Far out it spins and blurs into a ring. How to use it? Theremin sweep: Range ±2 kHz, sweep Beat slowly from 0 % to 60 % with a slow LFO or by hand. Lurching pulse: Pull 50 %, Range ±200 Hz, Beat just past the lock edge (B − A around 27 Hz), Drift 30 %. Out into a VCA or filter. Lock as a gate: the same patch with Lock into an envelope. Drift pulls the pair in and out of lock at irregular times. Tape-warmup intro: Warm-up 30 s, Beat around 100 Hz: the tone slides into tune when the transport starts. Slow modulation: Coupling DC, Range ±20 Hz, Beat near zero: Out is a drifting sub-hertz wave for filters or panning. Whistle: Carrier 3 kHz, Detector 100 %: the sum tone joins the beat. Melodic beat: a sequencer into Pitch transposes the beat tone by octaves, and Beat (the output) gives back its pitch for a second oscillator. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Beat Oscillator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Beat Oscillator under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Beat Oscillator: Heterodyne Theremin A slow LFO sweeps Beat from a pulse to a whistle between two 10 kHz Carrier s; try the Mixer setting and Drift . Beat Oscillator: Lurching Thump Pull at 50 % and Beat just past the lock edge make single sub-bass blips that bunch up and stall as Drift moves the pair. Beat Oscillator: Locked Melody The Lock output gates a melody; a wobble on Detune drives the carriers in and out of lock. Beat Oscillator: Warm-up Whistle Low Carrier s with Detector open whistle on top of the beat, and Warm-up slides both into tune; Mixer Overdriven makes a triangle beat. Beat Oscillator: Beat Follower A sequencer on Pitch plays the beat tone, and the Beat output steers a second oscillator that follows the melody. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Carrier 500 Hz – 18 kHz 10 kHz Beat −100 … +100 % (cubic: ± Range ) +51 % (+261.6 Hz on ±2 kHz) Fine −2 … +2 Hz 0 Hz Pull 0 – 100 % 0 % Detector 0 – 100 % 0 % Drift 0 – 100 % 15 % Detune Range 0 – 200 Hz 20 Hz Range ±20 Hz, ±200 Hz, ±2 kHz ±2 kHz Mixer Ideal, Diode, Overdriven Ideal Coupling AC, DC AC Warm-up Off, 10 s, 30 s, 2 min Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Carrier: the frequency of A. Beat: B's offset from A: Range × x³. Fine: added to the offset, for dialling zero beat. Pull: coupling between the carriers; lock range 200 Hz × Pull³. Detector: the mixer's low-pass, 2.5 kHz at 0 % up to 60 kHz at 100 %. Drift: how far the carriers wander, up to ±25 cents. Detune Range: hertz added to B per 1.0 at the Detune input. Range: the full swing of Beat . Mixer: the mixing circuit (see above). Coupling: AC removes DC from Out; DC keeps it. Warm-up: how long the carriers take to come up to pitch. Seed: picks the drift curves. All knobs are modulation destinations. The Cold button restarts the warm-up while the transport is stopped. title: Dual Osc
text: Dual Osc Dual Osc in the module view Introduction The Dual Osc is two analog-style oscillators, A and B , wired together for the sounds that need two oscillators talking to each other. B can frequency-modulate A, A can sync to B, and the pair runs into a wavefolder that turns soft waves into bright, moving spectra. It is a complete complex-oscillator voice in one module, and still two ordinary oscillators when that's all you need. How does it work? Two cores. Each core reads sine, triangle, saw and pulse from one phase and morphs between them with its Shape knob (as the Oscillator). Saw, pulse, triangle and every sync jump are band-limited at their exact moment in time, so even hard-synced and frequency-modulated waves stay clean. Pitch. A plays C4 × 2^(Octave A + Tune A/12 + Fine A/1200 + Pitch). B follows the same Pitch input while B Track is on, plus its own Pitch B input; with B Track off only Pitch B moves it. B Range Low divides B by 100 (about 0.03–200 Hz), turning it into a vibrato or growl-rate modulator. FM (B → A). B's sine (whatever Shape B is), plus the FM input, modulates A's frequency by FM Depth : Linear is through-zero: A's frequency is f × (1 + 4 × depth × m). When it goes negative the phase runs backwards, so the note stays in tune at any depth. Integer ratios between A and B give harmonic, bell- and brass-like tones. Exponential is analog-style: f × 2^(4 × depth × m), ±4 octaves at 100 %. The pitch drifts upward with depth: the classic growl and siren. Sync (A → B). Each time B finishes a cycle it acts on A. Up to 50 % this is a reversing soft sync: if A is in the last part of its cycle it changes direction instead of jumping, a gentle, vocal colour. From 50 % to 100 % the reset gets harder until, at 100 %, A restarts with every cycle of B: the classic tearing sync lead when you sweep A's pitch. Folder. The A/B mix ( Balance ) is driven by Fold (gain 1 to 12) plus the Fold CV input, biased by Symmetry , and folded back into ±1 by four stages. At Fold 0 the folder is transparent; the first quarter of the knob moves it from clean to a soft sine fold, and further stages join as you turn it up. Symmetry adds even harmonics and makes the folds move. A DC blocker follows (Symmetry adds DC). Oversampled. Cores, FM, sync and folder run at 2× ( Normal ) or 4× ( High ) and every output is decimated by the same filter, so A, B, Mix, Ring, Sub and Out stay in phase with each other. Stereo. With Width above 0, Out L and Out R fold slightly different mixes (Balance ∓ Width/4) and R's Symmetry is mirrored at full width. The image collapses cleanly to mono. At Width 0 both outputs are identical. Drift. A seeded slow wander of each core's pitch, up to ±8 cents at 100 %. The same Seed gives the same drift on every render; it restarts when the transport starts. How to use it? Complex voice: Pitch from Voice In, Out L/R → VCA. Raise Fold and modulate it with an envelope for plucked, west-coast tones. FM bell: Shape A 0 % (sine), Octave B +1 or Tune B +7, FM Depth 30–60 %, Linear. Put an envelope on FM Depth . Sync lead: Sync 100 %, Octave B −1, sweep Tune A or modulate Pitch of A only (patch into Pitch with B Track off and feed B from Pitch B ). Growl: B Range Low, FM Mode Exponential, FM Depth 20 %. Two oscillators: use A and B outputs separately; Ring gives A × B. Wide pad: Width 60 %, a little Fold and Symmetry , Drift 30 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Dual Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Dual Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Dual Osc: Sync Lead B hard-syncs A ( Sync ) and a slow LFO sweeps Tune B for a tearing lead. Dual Osc: Metal Bells B frequency-modulates A ( FM Depth , FM Mode Exponential) at an odd ratio, with an envelope on the depth. Dual Osc: Folding Bass A triangle bass through the stereo wavefolder: an envelope opens Fold on every note, Symmetry drifts. Dual Osc: Drifting Pair Two saw cores a few cents apart with strong Drift and wide Width : a warm, breathing pad. Dual Osc: Ring Clang The Ring output, struck by a short envelope, plays metallic percussion over a beat. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave A, Octave B −4 … +4 (stepped) 0, −1 Tune A, Tune B −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine A, Fine B −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Shape A, Shape B 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw), 0 % (sine) Width A 5 – 95 % 50 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Sync 0 – 100 % 0 % Balance 0 – 100 % 50 % Fold 0 – 100 % 0 % Symmetry −1 … +1 0 Drift 0 – 100 % 10 % Width 0 – 100 % 0 % FM Mode Linear, Exponential Linear B Track On, Off On B Range Audio, Low (÷ 100) Audio Quality Normal (2×), High (4×) Normal Seed 0 – 999 1 Shape A / Shape B: 0 % sine, 33 % triangle, 67 % saw, 100 % pulse. Width A: pulse width of A's pulse end. FM Depth: smoothed over 5 ms, so it can be swept without clicks. Balance: 0 % only A, 100 % only B into Mix and the folder. Quality: High costs about twice the CPU and lowers aliasing of synced and folded sounds further. All knobs are modulation destinations; the settings are not.
