Unpatched outputs cost no CPU for their decimation.

title: Formant Osc
text: Formant Osc Formant Osc in the module view Introduction The Formant Osc is a pulse-formant oscillator. Every cycle of the note fires one short burst of a second, higher oscillation: the formant . The note sets the pitch; the formant sets a resonant peak in the spectrum, like the mouth shape of a voice or the body of an instrument. Sweeping Formant gives vocal, filter-like sweeps with no filter in the patch, and Narrow makes the sound brighter and buzzier. How does it work? Fundamental. The note is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch). A band-limited square and a sub (one octave down) run on the same cycle. Formant. The formant frequency comes from the Formant knob in octaves: Ratio tracking: relative to the note (+1 = twice the note, +2 = four times). The timbre is the same on every key. Fixed tracking: relative to C4. The peak stays put while the note moves, like a vowel sung on different notes. The knob goes through zero : around 0 the formant slows to 0 Hz and then runs backwards for negative values. With Start on Cosine a 0 Hz formant is the window itself, so a sweep from −1 to +1 goes formant → soft pulse → formant without a gap. Formant CV adds octaves; Formant FM modulates the formant frequency linearly (±4× at FM Depth 100 %, through zero). The burst. Each cycle the formant plays under a smooth window. Narrow shortens the window (from the whole cycle to 5 % of it) and sharpens it: fewer formant cycles per burst, a wider peak and a brighter, buzzier tone. At high notes the window is kept at least 12 samples long, so the bursts never alias; Narrow then has less range. Reset. At 100 % every burst starts identically: the spectrum is purely harmonic and the formant is a clean peak. Lower values let the formant drift against the note for inharmonic, ring-modulated and chorused colours; 0 % is a free-running formant gated by the window. Roll moves the window inside the cycle. It wraps, so turning it never cuts a burst; modulated, it gives a phasing movement against the square, best heard with Body around 50 %. Second formant. Out R plays a second formant Spread octaves away from the first, sharing the cycle and the window. At Spread 0 L and R are identical; small values give width, larger ones two peaks, one per ear. Body mixes the square (at half level) and the formant at Out . Roll and Narrow glide over 2 ms, so fast modulation doesn't click. A Sync edge restarts the cycle with a very short crossfade from the old one. How to use it? Talking bass: Octave −1, an envelope on Formant (up 2–3 octaves), Narrow 40 %. Vowel on a melody: Tracking Fixed, Formant +1.5, play notes on Pitch : the peak stays like a sung vowel. Wah: an LFO on Formant (or Formant CV ), Body 90 %. Wide pad: Spread ±0.1, Reset 80 % for slow beating. Pinging modulation: Octave −4 and below: the bursts become rhythmic pings, useful as an odd modulation source. Put Quality on High for bright patches above C6. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Formant Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Formant Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Formant Osc: Wah Lead An LFO sweeps Formant over a tune like a hand on a wah pedal. Formant Osc: Squelch Bass An envelope on Formant gives a resonant squelch with no filter; Narrow sets the bite. Formant Osc: Vowel Choir A wide Spread pad with LFOs on Formant and Narrow that seems to sing changing vowels. Formant Osc: Through Zero A low drone while Formant sweeps across zero, through a hollow ghostly moment. Formant Osc: Chatter A random generator jumps Formant on every sixteenth over a broken beat. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave −4 … +4 (stepped) 0 Coarse −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Formant −6 … +6 oct (through zero) +2 oct Narrow 0 – 100 % 30 % Body 0 – 100 % 70 % Reset 0 – 100 % 100 % Roll 0 – 100 % (wraps) 0 % Spread −1 … +1 oct 0 FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Tracking Ratio, Fixed Ratio Start Sine, Cosine Cosine Quality Normal (1×), High (2×) Normal All knobs are modulation destinations; the settings are not. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the note; 0.0 = C4 Formant CV pitch moves the formant in octaves (1.0 = one octave) Formant FM audio linear, through-zero FM of the formant, scaled by FM Depth Sync trigger restarts the cycle (and a new burst) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio square and formant mixed by Body ; R uses the second formant Formant audio the burst train alone (first formant) Square audio band-limited square at the note, ±1 Sub audio square one octave below The formant peaks at about ±1 (up to ±1.6 with very narrow bursts).

title: Macro Osc
text: Macro Osc Macro Osc in the module view Introduction The Macro Osc is sixteen synthesis models behind one Model knob. Every model is played with the same three macro knobs, Tone , Shape and Blend : they stay where they are on the panel, but change their meaning (and their label) with the model. One patch can move from a detuned analog pair to FM, a sung vowel, a plucked string or a snare by turning one knob or by sending it a cable. Each model also has a second voice on Aux : the other oscillator, the modulator, the root of a chord, the noise of a snare. And a Trigger input with a built-in decay envelope and low-pass gate turns any model into a struck, percussive sound without extra modules. It is a sketching tool and a compact voice for Voice Cells. The dedicated oscillators (Dual Osc, Wavefolder, Formant Osc, Additive Osc, Wavetable Osc, Chord Osc, Resonator, Perc Voice) go deeper into one technique each; several Macro Osc models are smaller versions of their cores. How does it work? Pitch. The frequency is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), kept between 1 Hz and 0.45 × the sample rate. The FM input is linear and through-zero, as on the Oscillator: f × (1 + 4 × FM Depth × FM), so at 100 % a ±1 signal swings the frequency by ±4×. For the noise models the pitch is the centre of their filter, for the drums the body pitch (C4 is a mid tom, Octave −2 a kick). On the models without a playable pitch (Noise Band, Dust, Kick, Snare, Metal) the FM input moves Tone instead (FM Depth 100 % and a +1 signal = the whole knob). Changing models. Model is a stepped knob: modulation snaps to the nearest model. A change crossfades over 5 ms, both models running, so a Step Sequencer or a Random can play the models like notes without clicks. A change asked for during a fade follows when the fade ends. Every model keeps its state while another one plays, so a ringing string carries on when you come back to it. Only the selected model (and, for 5 ms, the previous one) uses CPU. Trigger, envelope and gate. Trigger unpatched: the pitched and noise models sound continuously, Decay and Gate Colour do nothing and Env is 0. Pluck and Modal are excited by a quiet stream of noise instead of a strike: bowed, blown, singing. Kick , Snare and Metal are silent (the view says so). Trigger patched: each trigger lifts the envelope to Accent (unpatched: 1) in 0.5 ms, then it falls to −60 dB in Decay . Env outputs it. Out and Aux of models 1–11 go through a low-pass gate: a VCA and a 2-pole low-pass in series, both following the envelope (smoothed by 3 ms, so the gate closes with a soft tail). Gate Colour 0 % is a plain VCA (cubic), 100 % a pure filter sweep from 20 kHz down to 20 Hz, 50 % both. The struck models ( Pluck , Modal , Kick , Snare , Metal ) are hit by the trigger with strength Accent and decay with Decay themselves; the gate is not applied to them. A new hit adds energy to what is still ringing instead of restarting it, so fast rolls build up. The drums read Tone at the moment of the hit, so a moving knob doesn't smear a hit. Noise and Seed. All noise is seeded from Seed and, inside a Voice Cell, the voice number: renders repeat exactly, and every voice sounds a little different. It is reseeded when the transport starts. Quality. Eco runs everything at the sample rate and Modal with 8 modes. Normal runs Fold, FM and Phase Warp at 2× and the band-limited oscillators (VA Pair, Chord, the Vowel's glottis) at 4×, with 16 modes. High runs the oversampled models at 4× and Modal with 24 modes. At high notes Fold, FM and Phase Warp also rein in their brightness (drive, index, feedback, resonance) so the sound stays clean instead of aliasing. The models The knob names in brackets are what the panel shows for each model. Pitched 1 VA Pair. Two analog-style oscillators (band-limited saw, square and pulse, also through hard sync). Tone [Detune]: up to 70 % detunes oscillator 2 by up to a semitone on a slow curve (50 % ≈ 19 cents, a fat chorus); above, it jumps to a third, fourth, fifth and octave. Shape [Wave]: saw → square over the first half, then the pulse narrows to 5 %. Blend [Sync]: 0 free; turning up hard-syncs oscillator 2 to oscillator 1 and raises its ratio by up to three octaves: the classic sync sweep. Aux : oscillator 2 alone. 2 Fold. A sine (or triangle) folded back on itself by four stages. Tone [Fold]: drive 1…16×. Shape [Bias]: an offset before folding (50 % = none): even harmonics and movement. Blend [Source]: sine → triangle. Aux : the driven source, hard-clipped. 3 FM. Two-operator FM (phase modulation). Tone [Ratio]: the modulator's ratio: ½, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 (centre), 3.5, 4, 5, 7, 9. Each ratio owns a slice of the knob, with a short crossfade between slices. Shape [Index]: modulation index 0…8 (50 % = 2). Blend [Feedback]: the modulator modulates itself, sine → saw-like. Aux : the modulator. 4 Phase Warp. A cosine read through a bent phase, as on the Casio CZ. Tone [Warp]: from a pure sine to a sharp, saw-like wave. Shape [Resonance]: a sine at 1…16× the pitch under a falling window, restarted every cycle: a resonant filter sweep without a filter. Blend [Mix]: warp → resonance. Aux : a square one octave down. 5 Grain. One windowed sine burst per cycle (the Formant Osc's core). Tone [Formant]: the burst's frequency, ½…16× the pitch: a vocal or filter-like peak that moves without changing the note. Shape [Width]: the burst length (100 % = the whole cycle, smooth; low = short, buzzy). Blend [Pair]: adds a second burst at 1.5× the formant. Aux : a sine at the pitch. 6 Harmonic. 24 sine partials with a movable spectral peak. Tone [Centre]: the peak, from partial 1 to 24. Shape [Width]: narrow (one partial sings) → wide (a full, organ-like spectrum). Blend [Odd/Even]: all partials → odd only at 50 % (hollow, clarinet) → even only at 100 % (with the fundamental). Aux : the odd partials. Partials fade out before the Nyquist frequency, so sweeps never alias or click. 7 Table. Eight of the Wavetable Osc's factory banks. Tone [Bank]: Analog, Harmonic, Pulse, Sync, FM, Organ, Digital, Bell (in eighths of the knob; a change crossfades). Shape [X], Blend [Y]: the position on the bank's 8 × 8 grid. Aux : the same wave one octave down. 8 Chord. Four oscillators playing a chord, a few cents apart. Tone [Chord]: octaves, 5th, sus2, sus4, minor, major, m7 (50 %), maj7, 7, m9, maj9, 6/9. Shape [Voicing]: root position, 1st, 2nd and 3rd inversion, Drop 2 (50 %), Open, Wide, Spread. Blend [Wave]: sine → triangle → saw. Aux : the root alone, a bass voice that follows the chord. 9 Vowel. A glottal pulse and breath through three formant filters. Tone [Vowel]: a → e → i → o → u. Shape [Size]: the vocal tract: small (formants an octave up, a child or a chipmunk) → large (an octave down). Blend [Breath]: voiced → whispered. Aux : the breath (unvoiced) part alone. Noise 10 Noise Band. White noise through a resonant filter at the pitch. Tone [Resonance]: Q 0.5 (a wide band) … 40 (a whistling tone). Shape [Mode]: low-pass → band-pass → high-pass. Blend [Clock]: clean → sample-rate-reduced, crunchy noise. Aux : the other side: high-pass for low-pass, notch for band-pass. 11 Dust. Random clicks. Tone [Density]: 1 to 20 000 clicks per second (50 % ≈ 140): from crackle to rain to noise. Shape [Colour]: their filter, from dark (thumps an octave below the pitch) to bright (ticks). Blend [Bipolar]: all positive → half of them negative. Aux : the raw clicks. Struck 12 Pluck. A plucked string (a tuned delay-line waveguide). Tone [Bright]: the pluck: soft finger → hard pick. Shape [Damping]: bright, ringing string → dull, damped. Blend [Position]: where it is plucked: near the bridge (bright) → the middle (hollow). Decay : how long it rings. Aux : the pluck (the exciter) alone. 13 Modal. A struck object: 8 / 16 / 24 resonant modes by Quality . Tone [Material]: string → bar → plate → bell. Shape [Bright]: soft mallet and dark modes → hard mallet and bright. Blend [Stretch]: stretches the modes up to 15 % (more metallic). Decay : how long it rings. Aux : the odd modes. 14 Kick. A swept sine with a click. Patch Octave −2 for a kick drum, higher for toms. Tone [Sweep]: the pitch drop, 0…4 octaves. Shape [Punch]: how fast it drops (80 ms → 4 ms). Blend [Drive]: soft clipping. Decay : the body. Aux : the click. 15 Snare. Two drum-head resonators and noise. Tone [Snappy]: the noise (snares) level. Shape [Tone]: the balance of the two heads (low → high). Blend [Noise Colour]: the noise band, 1.5 → 12 kHz. Decay : body and snares. Aux : the noise alone. 16 Metal. Six detuned square waves, as in the 808's cymbals and hats. Tone [Colour]: the high-pass cutoff: gong → closed hat. Shape [Spread]: the detune between the six: close (a chord) → wide (clang). Blend [Ring]: a ringing band-pass resonance (a cowbell, a bell). Decay : short = hi-hat, long = cymbal. Aux : the unfiltered metal. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Macro Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Macro Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Octave, Coarse, Fine Pitch: octaves, semitones, cents. Tone, Shape, Blend The three macros (names per model, above). FM Depth Depth of the FM input (or of the Tone modulation for unpitched models). Decay The envelope and the struck models' decay, 5 ms – 10 s. Gate Colour How the gate closes: VCA (0 %) → low-pass (100 %). Level Output level of Out and Aux. Quality Eco, Normal, High (see above). Seed The noise seed. Inputs: Pitch (1 V/oct, 0 V = C4), FM , Trigger , Accent (strength of each hit, 0–1). Outputs: Out , Aux (named after what it carries), Env . Patch ideas Model sequencing. A Step Sequencer into Model (and its pitch into Pitch ): every step a different sound, from one module. Instant voice. In a Voice Cell, Voice In › Pitch to Pitch , Trigger to Trigger , Velocity to Accent : a complete polyphonic voice with its own decay and gate. Try Vowel with Gate Colour 100 % for a plucked choir. Drum kit. Three Macro Osc on Kick (Octave −2), Snare and Metal , each with a trigger from a sequencer and Accent from its velocity. Bass and chord. Chord with Aux (the root) one octave down through a filter, Out to a reverb. Talking FM. An LFO into Tone on Vowel , or into Ratio on FM , slowly; Env to a filter elsewhere. Bowed objects. Modal with Trigger unpatched and a long Decay: a singing bowl. Move Material slowly. Rhythmic noise. Dust at low density into a reverb for vinyl crackle; at high density with Clock for rain on a tin roof. Tips Decay and Gate Colour only matter while Trigger is patched. Modulating Model with audio-rate signals is possible but each change takes 5 ms; for timbre modulation use the macros. Unpatched outputs cost nothing extra: Aux is only computed while something reads it (or the view is open). Lower Quality to Eco for many voices; High for exposed high notes.

title: Oscillator
text: Oscillator Oscillator in the module view Introduction The Oscillator is the sound source of most patches. It makes a steady tone whose pitch follows the Pitch input. One knob sweeps its waveform from a pure sine to a buzzing square. It also has through-zero FM for bell-like and metallic tones, hard sync for tearing leads, and a sub-octave output for weight. How does it work? At its core is a phase that runs from 0 to 1 once per cycle. All waveforms are read from that same phase, so they are always in step: Sine , Triangle , Saw and Square , each on its own output. Saw and square are band-limited (polyBLEP), so they don't alias in the high register. Out morphs through the four with the Shape knob: sine → triangle → saw → square. Between two points you hear a crossfade of the two neighbours. Sub is a square wave one octave below. It flips every time the core completes a cycle. Pitch. The frequency is C4 (261.6 Hz) × 2^pitch, where pitch is the sum of Octave , Coarse (semitones), Fine (cents) and the Pitch input (1 V/oct: +1.0 is one octave up, 0.0 is C4). Through-zero FM. The FM input changes the frequency linearly: frequency × (1 + 4 × FM Depth × FM). With deep modulation the frequency can go negative. The phase then runs backwards instead of stopping, so the tone stays in tune even under heavy FM. Hard sync. Each rising edge at Sync (the signal crossing 0.5 upwards) resets the phase to the start of a cycle. How to use it? Basic voice: Voice In Pitch → Oscillator Pitch ; Out → VCA → Voice Out. Pick the tone with Shape (the default, 67 %, is a saw). Transpose: use Octave for whole octaves and Coarse for intervals, e.g. +7 for a fifth on a second oscillator. Detune: two oscillators with Fine at −7 and +7 cents give a wide, chorused sound. Pulse-width modulation: set Shape to 100 % (square) and patch a slow Function onto Pulse Width . FM: patch a second oscillator's Sine into FM and raise FM Depth . Integer ratios between the two ( Coarse 0, +12, +19) give harmonic tones; other ratios give bells and metal. Hard sync: patch a second oscillator's Square into Sync . Set this oscillator higher and sweep its pitch for the classic sync lead. Pitch bend and vibrato: patch a bend or LFO signal into Pitch . For ±2 semitones set the cable amount to 2/12 ≈ 17 %. Weight: mix Sub in under Out for bass. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave −3 … +3 0 Coarse −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Shape 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw) Pulse Width 5 – 95 % 50 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Octave: shifts the pitch by whole octaves. At 0 and with nothing at Pitch , the oscillator plays C4. Coarse: shifts the pitch in semitones. As a modulation destination it covers 24 semitones over the knob's full travel. Fine: shifts the pitch in cents (1/100 semitone), for detuning and tuning against other instruments. Shape: the waveform at Out : 0 % sine, 33 % triangle, 67 % saw, 100 % square, with smooth morphs between. Modulating it gives an evolving timbre. Pulse Width: the duty cycle of the square, at Square and at the square end of Out . 50 % is a hollow square; narrow pulses sound thin and nasal. It doesn't affect the other waveforms or Sub . FM Depth: how strongly the FM input moves the frequency. At 100 % an FM signal of ±1 swings the frequency by ±4 times its base value, so it passes through zero. With nothing at FM the knob does nothing. Knobs (all except Octave ) are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct added to Octave, Coarse and Fine; 0.0 = C4 FM audio linear, through-zero frequency modulation, scaled by FM Depth Sync gate each rising edge restarts the cycle (hard sync) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the waveform chosen by Shape Sine audio sine Triangle audio triangle Saw audio rising saw, band-limited Square audio pulse with the set Pulse Width , band-limited Sub audio square one octave below All outputs run between −1 and +1.

title: Test Oscillator
text: Test Oscillator Introduction Test Oscillator is modelled on the lamp-stabilised sine generators of the old electronics lab: a big calibrated dial, a range switch, and a sine that comes from a real self-oscillating loop instead of a counter. The loop's imperfections are the point. The amplitude bounces when you turn the dial or switch the range, the pitch creeps up as it warms, it hums faintly, and below a Loop Gain of 100 % it stops oscillating and becomes a ringing resonator that pings when kicked. One module is a drone, a sweep source and a drum. How does it work? The loop. A band-pass filter tuned by the dial feeds an amplifier, and the amplifier feeds the filter. When the amplifier's gain ( Loop Gain ) is above 100 %, any tiny noise grows into a sine at exactly the dial's frequency. Something has to stop it growing: The lamp. A small lamp in the loop warms up with the signal and turns the gain down when the sine gets louder than its nominal level (±0.5). It takes time to warm and cool ( Settle ), so the regulation lags behind: every disturbance makes the amplitude overshoot, undershoot and settle again over a few Settle times. That is the bounce. The Lamp output carries the lamp's heat: 0 cold, 0.5 at the nominal level, 1 at twice the power. Loop Gain decides the character: Below 100 %: no oscillation. The loop is a resonator that rings and decays: a Kick pings it, Audio In drives it like a tuned filter that saturates when pushed. The closer to 100 %, the longer the ring (at 95 % and 100 Hz it takes about 2.2 s to die away). 100 – 150 %: a clean, lamp-regulated sine of about ±0.5. Higher values start faster and bounce harder. Above 150 %: the lamp runs out of range and the amplifier clips: louder (up to ±1), harder, rich in odd harmonics; at 300 % close to a rounded square. The lamp still moves, so the bounces remain. Settle is the lamp's speed. Long values give slow, deep swells after a disturbance. Very short values let the lamp follow the waveform itself: the sine distorts, and at high loop gains it squeals and flutters in bursts. Turning the dial costs the loop some gain while it moves (up to 30 % on fast sweeps; jumps on Pitch count too). The lamp cools, and when the dial stops the amplitude surges and rings. Changing the Range breaks the loop for 4 ms, like the contacts of a real switch: a click, a dip, a surge. Drift adds the instrument's age: after power-up the pitch starts up to a semitone flat and warms up over about 30 s ( Warm-up ), it wanders by a few cents, and the mains hum ( Mains ) leaks in faintly. Tuned near 50/60 Hz (or 150/180 Hz) the oscillator gets pulled and locks to the hum. At 0 % the instrument is ideal. Square is a comparator on the sine with finite edges, and stays at 50 % duty through the bounces. Sync fires once per period at the sine's upward zero crossing. Both go quiet when the loop is silent. Power-up. With Power-up on On play the oscillator switches on when the transport starts: silent, cold and flat, then it starts up from its noise floor and warms up, the same way on every playback, so renders repeat exactly. On load switches it on when the board loads (or Seed changes) and lets it run free. How to use it? A drone with life: Loop Gain 120 %, Settle 1 s, Drift 60 %. Turn the dial slowly and let it swell. A sweep source: modulate Frequency or Pitch with a slow LFO; the amplitude dips on the fast parts and surges back. A tuned drum: Loop Gain 90–98 %, a clock into Kick , Range ×10. The Kick knob sets how hard it pings; inside a Voice Cell, Voice In › Trigger into Kick and Voice In › Pitch into Pitch give a tuned percussion voice. A resonant filter: Loop Gain 80–95 %, a drum loop or noise into Audio In ; tune the dial to taste. Wobbly tremolo: Settle 5–20 ms, Loop Gain 200 %: the lamp chases the waveform and the tone squeals and stutters. An envelope of the bounces: Lamp into a filter's cutoff. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Test Oscillator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Test Oscillator under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Test Oscillator: Living Drone Three lamp-stabilised sines with long Settle and high Drift warm up and swell against each other. Test Oscillator: Ringing Drums Loop Gain below 100 % and Kick from a Drum Grid make tuned drums on Range ×10, ×100 and ×1k. Test Oscillator: Drum Resonator A drum loop in Audio In at 99.7 % Loop Gain rings as a tuned resonator that a sequencer steers with Pitch . Test Oscillator: Squeal Tremolo A very short Settle and high Loop Gain make the lamp chase the waveform: a squealing, stuttering bass. Test Oscillator: Bouncing Bass Pitch leaps make the amplitude dip and surge, and the Lamp output sweeps a lead filter. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Frequency 1.0 – 10.0 (log) 4.4 Fine ±50 cents 0 FM 0 – 100 % 0 % Loop Gain 0 – 300 % 120 % Settle 5 ms – 2 s 250 ms Drift 0 – 100 % 40 % Kick 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Range ×1, ×10, ×100, ×1k ×100 Warm-up Off, On On Mains Off, 50 Hz, 60 Hz 50 Hz Power-up On load, On play On play Seed 0 – 999 1 Frequency: the dial; the frequency is 2 Hz × Range × Frequency (4.4 on ×100 is 880 Hz). Fine: fine tuning. FM: depth of linear frequency modulation from the FM input. Loop Gain: resonator below 100 %, regulated sine up to 150 %, clipping above. Settle: how slowly the lamp reacts; the speed of the bounces. Drift: warm-up, wander and mains hum together. Kick: how hard each Kick pulse hits (50 % pings at the nominal level). Level: the size of Sine and Square. Range: ×1 2–20 Hz, ×10 20–200 Hz, ×100 200 Hz–2 kHz, ×1k 2–20 kHz. Warm-up: the pitch starts flat after power-up and rises. Mains: the hum's frequency. Power-up: when the oscillator switches on. Seed: picks the noise and the wander. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct relative to the dial FM audio linear frequency modulation, depth set by FM Kick trigger each pulse kicks the resonator: a ping, or a bounce while oscillating Audio In audio added into the loop: excites, colours or locks it Outputs Output Signal What it does Sine audio the loop's sine, about ±0.5 when regulated, up to ±1 when clipping Square audio a band-limited square at the same frequency, 50 % duty Sync trigger one pulse per period, at the upward zero crossing Lamp control the lamp's heat, 0 … 1 (0.5 at the nominal level)

title: Wavetable Osc
text: Wavetable Osc Wavetable Osc in the module view Introduction The Wavetable Osc plays single-cycle waveforms from a bank : a grid of up to 8 × 8 cycles. X and Y pick a point on the grid and the oscillator blends the four nearest waveforms, so sweeping X and Y with envelopes and LFOs moves the timbre in two directions at once, for example brightness along X and vowel along Y. Warp bends how each cycle is read for even more motion. Eleven factory banks are built in, and you can drop in your own WAV files. Every cycle is stored band-limited at several octaves, so the sound stays clean from sub-bass to the top of the keyboard. How does it work? Pitch. C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), then the FM input: linear and through zero, ±4× at FM Depth 100 %. Banks. Bank chooses the grid (it is a stepped knob, so it can be modulated; changes crossfade over 10 ms): Bank X Y Analog sine → triangle → saw → square → 10 % pulse rounder → brighter Harmonic odd → all harmonics spectral centre low → high Vowel a → e → i → o → u small → large formant shift Pulse width 50 % → 3 % single → double pulse Sync synced saw ratio 1 → 8 saw → triangle carrier FM modulation index 0 → 6 ratio 1 … 8 Fold fold amount symmetry Organ 8 drawbar registrations third-harmonic percussion Digital bit depth 8 → 2 sample-and-hold steps 64 → 4 Spectra seeded random spectra rough → smooth Bell partials compressed → stretched bright → dark User your imported cycles Position. With Path Off, X and Y place the point directly. With a path ( Rows , Snake , Columns , Diagonal , Spiral ) Scan moves along the cells in that order instead and X and Y are hidden. Smooth blend mixes the four nearest cycles; Step plays the nearest one (a stepped, digital sound; each step is crossfaded over 2 ms). Position changes glide over 1 ms. Warp ( Warp Mode , amount by the Warp knob, which takes the mode's name): Bend: squeezes the first half of the cycle and stretches the second: brighter, resonant tones. Sync: reads the cycle up to 8 times per period, like hard sync inside the table. Mirror: folds the reading back halfway: symmetric shapes, a new even/odd balance. Squash: plays the whole cycle in the first part of the period and holds for the rest: pulse-width modulation for any wave. Steps: quantises the reading into stairs (2048 → 2 steps): lo-fi. At 0 % every warp is off. The read automatically uses fewer harmonics when a warp speeds it up, and the jumps of Sync , Steps and the Sync input are smoothed, so warping stays band-limited. Read. Cubic (smoothest), Linear , or Raw : the full table, nearest sample, no band-limiting: aliasing on purpose. Stereo. Stereo moves Out R's position along X (or along the path) from L's; both share the phase, so the sum never cancels the fundamental. At 0 % L and R are identical. Sub. A sine an octave below, in phase with the main cycle (also after Sync ). Sub Level mixes it into Out ; the Sub output is always full level. Your own tables Drop a WAV file on Import… (or click it to choose one). Choose Cycle first if you know your file's cycle length; Auto uses 2048 samples if the file is a multiple of that, else the whole file is one cycle. Up to 64 cycles are taken (the view says when a file has more); each is resampled to the table size, its DC removed and normalised. Fewer than 64 cycles fill the grid row by row and the grid shrinks to the rows used; one cycle plays everywhere. Dropping a WAV on one cell of the grid replaces just that cell (its first cycle). Silent or unreadable files are rejected and the bank stays as it was. The file is kept in the Beautiful Bleep media folder; the board stores only its id. Importing switches Bank to User . With nothing imported, User plays a sine. How to use it? Evolving pad: Analog or Harmonic , slow LFOs on X and Y, Stereo 20 %. Talking lead: Vowel , an envelope on X, Warp Bend 20 %. Scanning: Path Snake, a slow ramp on Scan . Use Pos X/Pos Y to move a filter in step. Sync sweep: Warp Mode Sync, an envelope on Warp . PWM anything: Warp Mode Squash, an LFO on Warp . Bass: Sub Level 50 %. Demo boards Five whole boards show what Wavetable Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Wavetable Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Wavetable Osc: Morphing Pad An LFO on Scan walks the Analog bank along the Snake path, with Stereo spread. Wavetable Osc: Vowel Talker The Vowel bank with X and Y moved by random generators: a tune that seems to speak. Wavetable Osc: Bell Garden The Bell bank with an envelope on Y : each note starts bright and fades to a plain tone. Wavetable Osc: Warp Bass Warp in Sync mode opened by an envelope on each note, plus Sub Level for weight. Wavetable Osc: Spiral Crawl Scan crawls the Spiral path in the Spectra bank while the X position output opens a filter. title: Chord Osc
text: Chord Osc Chord Osc in the module view Introduction The Chord Osc turns one pitch into a whole chord. Up to six oscillators play the tones of a chord built on the Pitch input: pick the quality (major, minor, sevenths, sus, add9, …), the inversion and the voicing, and morph the waveform of all voices at once. In Scale mode it builds the chords of a key instead, so a simple melody becomes a chord progression. The Root output carries the root alone, and Pitch 1–4 send the four lowest chord tones to other oscillators. How does it work? Each voice is the Oscillator's core (sine, triangle, band-limited saw and square, morphed by Shape ). The chord is built in four steps whenever the pitch or a stepped knob changes: Tones. The chord has a number of tones (C major 7 has four). With fewer Voices , tones are left out in the order fifth, extension (9th), seventh, third; the root always stays. With more Voices , tones are doubled an octave up: root first, then fifth, third, … Inversion. Positive steps move the lowest tone up an octave, negative steps move the highest tone down. The bass shows in the name ( Am7/C ). Voicing. Close keeps the chord within an octave. Drop 2 , Drop 3 and Drop 2+4 move the second, third (or second and fourth) tone from the top down an octave, as guitarists and arrangers do. Open moves the bass down an octave; Wide spreads the tones over about three octaves. Voicings that need more tones than are playing stay Close . Range guard. If the chord would reach above 8 kHz or below 16 Hz, it moves by whole octaves back into range. Every oscillator keeps "its" tone: the one playing the third plays the third of the next chord. With Glide the voices slide to their new notes (smooth voice leading); without it they jump, keeping their phase, so changes don't click. Voices that start or stop playing fade in or out over 5 ms. Scale mode. The Pitch input is snapped to the nearest note of Root and Scale (exactly between two notes, it goes down). That note's scale degree is the chord root, and the chord is stacked from scale steps: in C major a Triad on D is D minor, on G it is G major, on B it is B diminished. The view shows the chord found and its degree (ii, V, …). Latch. With a cable in Latch , the module takes the pitch and the four stepped knobs ( Chord , Inversion , Voicing , Voices ) only at each pulse and holds the chord until the next one. Tune , Shape , Detune and the others stay live. Until the first pulse it plays as if unlatched. Mixing. Out L/R is the sum of the voices divided by √(number of voices), so a four-voice chord is about as loud as two oscillators. With square waves and six voices the peaks can reach about ±2.4. Root Level sets the root voice inside the mix; the Root output is always at full level (±1). Detune gives each voice a fixed offset within ± Detune cents, drawn from Seed : the same seed always gives the same offsets. Stereo spreads the voices across the field, from the centre outwards and alternating sides, so the root stays nearest the middle. How to use it? Chord pad: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; Out L/R → Filter → VCA. A little Detune (5–10 ct) and Stereo at 60 % make it wide. Chord progression from a melody: set Mode to Scale , pick the key, and play a step sequencer into Pitch . Each note becomes the diatonic chord on it. Patch the sequencer's trigger into Latch so chords change exactly on the step. Moving chords: patch a slow LFO onto Chord (Scale mode: Triad, Seventh, Ninth, …) or Inversion for chords that keep changing colour. Voice leading: raise Glide to 100–300 ms and change chords: every voice slides to the corresponding tone of the next chord. Bass plus chords: lower Root Level and send Root through its own filter as a bass voice, or use Pitch 1 to play a separate bass oscillator. Arpeggios elsewhere: Pitch 1–4 carry the chord tones low to high; switch between them with a sequential switch for an arpeggio that follows the chord. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Chord Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Chord Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Chord Osc: Soft Minor Pads Minor 7 with the Open voicing, Detune , Stereo and Glide turns a slow bass line into melting chords. Chord Osc: Diatonic Run Mode Scale: a plain tune becomes the diatonic chord on each note, changing on the step through Latch . Chord Osc: Chord Arpeggio The Pitch 1–4 outputs feed a Switch and an oscillator: an arpeggio that follows the held chord. Chord Osc: Offbeat Stabs Short Dominant 9 stabs with the Drop 2 voicing and a squarer Shape over a four-on-the-floor beat. Chord Osc: FM Quartal Glow Sine voices in fourths with an oscillator in FM whose amount is moved by a slow LFO. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Chord Chromatic: 24 qualities; Scale: 10 stacks Major / Triad Inversion −4 … +4 0 Voicing Close, Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2+4, Open, Wide Close Voices 1 – 6 4 Shape 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw) Pulse Width 5 – 95 % 50 % Detune 0 – 50 ct 0 ct Glide 0 – 1 s 0 ms Root Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Stereo 0 – 100 % 0 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode Chromatic, Scale Chromatic Octave −3 … +3 0 Root C … B (Scale mode) C Scale Chromatic … Hirajoshi (Scale mode) Major Seed 0 – 999 1 Chord: in Chromatic mode the quality: Unison, Fifth, Major, Minor, Diminished, Augmented, Sus2, Sus4, Major 6, Minor 6, Dominant 7, Major 7, Minor 7, Half-diminished, Diminished 7, Minor-major 7, 7sus4, Add9, Minor add9, 6/9, Major 9, Minor 9, Dominant 9, Quartal. In Scale mode a stack of scale steps: Single, Fifth, Triad, Sus2, Sus4, Sixth, Seventh, Add9, Ninth, Quartal. Each mode has its own knob; both are stepped, so a cable moves them from step to step. Inversion , Voicing , Voices: stepped knobs, see How does it work? . Shape: sine → triangle → saw → square for every voice, as the Oscillator's Shape . Glide: time for a voice to reach a new note (99 %). Also glides pitch changes at the input. FM Depth: scales the FM input: at 100 % an FM signal of ±1 swings each voice's frequency by ±4× its base, through zero. Octave , Tune: transpose the whole chord. Seed: chooses the detune offsets and the voices' start phases. All knobs are modulation destinations; Mode , Octave , Root , Scale and Seed are settings. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the chord root; 0.0 = C4. Scale mode: snapped to the scale first Latch trigger when patched, the chord changes only at its pulses FM audio linear, through-zero FM for all voices, scaled by FM Depth Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio all voices, panned by Stereo , divided by √voices Root audio the chord root alone at full level, whatever the inversion and voicing Pitch 1 … 4 pitch the four lowest voices, low to high; with fewer voices the last ones repeat the highest

title: Swarm
text: Swarm Swarm in the module view Introduction The Swarm is a cloud of up to 16 oscillators played from one pitch. Their notes are spread over a chord or scale around the root, so a single Pitch signal plays anything from a thick unison to a wide, shimmering chord stack. Spread opens the cloud from unison into the chord, and every oscillator glides to its new note at its own pace, so the swarm moves like a flock instead of switching. It is a drone and pad source on its own, and a fat detuned-saw lead with Spread at 0. For a precise chord with named inversions and pitch outputs per tone, use the Chord Osc; for several independent notes, a Voice Cell. How does it work? The stack. Chord chooses a set of notes: a chord (Minor 7, Quartal, Cluster, …) or a whole scale. The stack lists those notes upward through Range octaves, e.g. Minor 7 over two octaves is C E♭ G B♭ C E♭ G B♭ C. The oscillators are spread evenly over the stack, whatever their Count , so 8 oscillators on a 9-note stack skip one note. With Stack on Centred the stack reaches down half the range and up half; on Down , all of it below the root. Spread. At 0 % every oscillator plays the root. As Spread rises, each oscillator aims at its stack note scaled by Spread and snapped to the nearest chord note, so the oscillators leave the root one after another, the highest first: the cloud blooms open. Oscillator 1 always stays on the root. Glide. Each oscillator slides to a new target with its own time, between half and one and a half times Glide (drawn from Seed ). A change of Chord or Spread therefore unfolds note by note. Changes of the root ( Pitch , Octave , Coarse , Fine ) move the whole swarm at once. Warp morphs every oscillator's waveform: sine → triangle → rounded saw (a saw with soft corners, few upper harmonics, gentle in dense chords) → bright saw. Detune offsets the oscillators by up to ± Detune cents in a Pattern : Fan spreads them evenly from flat to sharp, Alternate goes sharp, flat, less sharp, less flat, …, Random draws seeded values, Outer detunes the lowest and highest the most and the middle not at all. Drift adds a slow random walk to each detune (up to half of Detune ), each oscillator at its own pace. The root oscillator is never detuned. Cross FM connects the oscillators in a ring: each one's phase is pushed by the previous one's sine (by up to half a cycle at 100 %). A little adds grit and beating; a lot turns chords into dense, metallic noise. Level and stereo. The oscillators are summed and divided by √ Count , so Count changes the thickness, not the loudness. Width scatters them across the stereo field, alternating sides and wider the further they are from the root; the root stays centred. Oscillators that would play above 0.45 × the sample rate fade out instead of aliasing. Quality. High runs the whole swarm at twice the sample rate with a half-band decimator: cleaner high notes and deep Cross FM, at about twice the CPU. How to use it? Pad: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; Out L/R → Filter → VCA. Default settings (8 oscillators on Minor 7, Spread 30 %) already sound like a chorus of voices. Blooming chord: patch an envelope or slow LFO onto Spread and set Glide to 1–2 s: the chord opens and closes in waves. Supersaw lead: Spread 0, Warp 100 %, Count 7, Detune 15–25 ct, Pattern Fan. Shimmer: Chord on a scale (Major Pentatonic, Hirajoshi), Range 3–4, Spread 100 %, Drift high, Width 100 %. Separate filtering: Upper carries only the oscillators above the root octave; filter it brighter or darker than the main mix. Root is a clean anchor for a sub or for syncing another oscillator. Follow the opening: patch Spread (output) to a filter's cutoff so it opens with the cloud. New variation: press Reshuffle (or send a trigger) for a new random pattern and new glide times. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Swarm does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Swarm under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Swarm: Blooming Pad An LFO on Spread opens the swarm from one note into a Minor 9 chord, and the Spread output opens a filter. Swarm: Dark Cluster The Cluster chord with strong Drift and a little Cross FM : a restless low drone. Swarm: Pentatonic Rain A Major Pentatonic swarm with Reshuffle fired every bar, so the notes rearrange themselves. Swarm: Glitter Fifths Stacked Fifths with Warp and Cross FM on slow LFOs: a glittering bell-like shimmer. title: Modal Voice
text: Modal Voice Modal Voice in the module view Introduction Modal Voice is a complete physical-modelling instrument in one module. An exciter (a bow, breath, a mallet, or any audio) sets a resonant body ringing (a string, a bar, a plate, a bell), and a small room places it in a space. A gate sustains bowed and blown sounds for as long as it is held; a trigger strikes. It is built to sit inside a Voice Cell: one module per voice, with an Active output that tells the cell when the sound has died away. Where the Resonator is an effect that makes other sounds ring, Modal Voice is the instrument that plays itself. How does it work? The body is a bank of 16, 32 or 64 ringing partials. Geometry sets their ratios: string (0 %), stiff string (25 %), bar (50 %), plate (75 %) and a bell-like inharmonic set drawn from Seed (100 %), gliding smoothly in between. Damping sets how long it rings, Brightness how bright it is and how fast the high partials die, and Position where the exciter touches it (50 %, the middle, cancels the even partials). The exciters can all play at once: Bow: a friction model. The bow sticks to the body and slips, again and again, which makes the body sing at its own pitch for as long as the gate is held, even a bar or a bell (bowed metal). Bow Timbre goes from a light, airy bow to a heavy, scratchy one. Blow: breath noise, filtered around the pitch. Up to 60 % Blow Timbre it is a breathy rush that colours the body. Above 60 % the breath starts to couple with the body like the air jet of a flute, and the body sings on its own, with breath noise on top. Strike: a mallet hit on every trigger at Strike (or on every new gate when Strike is unpatched). Strike Timbre goes from soft felt through wood and a hard mallet to a sharp tick, and above 70 % adds a grainy scrape. A strike on a ringing body adds to it. Ext In: any audio, added to the exciters at Ext Level . With the other exciters at 0, the module is a resonator with a room. The bow and the breath follow a gate envelope shaped by Contour : at 0 % a slow swell and a long release, at 100 % a fast attack with a short decay to a lower sustain. Velocity scales every exciter. The space is a small stereo room. Size goes from a booth to a hall, Space is its level. At 0 % it is switched off and costs nothing. How to use it? In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Pitch → Pitch , Gate → Gate , Trigger → Strike , Velocity → Velocity , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . Patch Voice In › Pressure onto Bow or Blow so aftertouch swells the sound. Marimba, vibraphone, bells: Strike only, Geometry 50 – 100 %, Damping 30 – 50 %, Strike Timbre 30 – 60 %. Bowed strings and bowed metal: Strike 0 %, Bow 60 – 90 %, Contour low for a slow swell; Geometry 0 – 25 % for strings, 50 % and up for metal. Flute-like tones: Blow 70 %, Blow Timbre 70 – 90 %, Geometry 0 %. A resonator with a room: any audio → Ext In , all exciters at 0. Many voices: set Space to 0 % inside the cell and put one reverb after it: that saves CPU and gives all voices one shared room. Play button: held, it is a gate (and a strike), for trying sounds without patching. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Modal Voice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Modal Voice under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Modal Voice: Mallet Bars Mallet strikes ( Strike ) on a damped bar-like body; Strike Timbre changes soft to hard mallets. Modal Voice: Bowed Strings Held gates with Bow up make the string sing; an LFO moves Bow Timbre . Modal Voice: Breath Tube Blow excites a tube-like body for an airy melody, with a slowly rising vibrato on Fine . Modal Voice: Metal Plate Groove Rhythmic hits on a large plate while LFOs morph Geometry and Brightness . Modal Voice: Drums Through a Body A drum beat on the Ext input excites the body, tuned by a bass line; Ext Level sets the amount. Reference Knobs and settings Group Control Range Default Exciter Bow 0 – 100 % 0 % Bow Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Blow 0 – 100 % 0 % Blow Timbre 0 – 100 % 40 % Strike 0 – 100 % 80 % Strike Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Contour 0 – 100 % 30 % Ext Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Resonator Coarse −24 … +24 semitones 0 Fine −100 … +100 cents 0 Geometry 0 – 100 % 25 % Brightness 0 – 100 % 55 % Damping 0 – 100 % 40 % Position 0 – 100 % 30 % Space Size 0 – 100 % 40 % Space 0 – 100 % 20 % Partials 16, 32, 64 32 Seed 0 – 999 1 Bow / Blow / Strike: the level of each exciter. Exciters at 0 % cost nothing. Bow Timbre: bow pressure and roughness: airy → scratchy. Blow Timbre: breath colour, dark rush → bright hiss; above 60 % the breath couples with the body and makes it sing. Strike Timbre: soft felt → wood → hard mallet → tick → scrape. Contour: the shape of the bow and breath envelope: attack from 400 ms (0 %) to 2 ms (100 %), release from 1.5 s to 30 ms; from 50 % up the attack overshoots and settles to a lower sustain. Ext Level: the level of Ext In . Coarse / Fine: transposition in semitones and cents; Pitch adds to it. Geometry: the partial ratios: string → stiff string → bar → plate → bell. Brightness: spectral tilt and how fast the high partials decay. Damping: how long the body rings: 0 % = 20 s, 50 % ≈ 1 s, 100 % ≈ 40 ms. Position: where the exciter touches the body and where it is heard. Size: the room, from a small booth to a hall. Space: the room's level. The body itself always stays at full level. Partials: the number of partials of the body: more sounds richer and costs more. Seed: the bell partials (Geometry 100 %) and the scrape of the mallet. The scrapes repeat from the start of the transport. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. title: Perc Voice
text: Perc Voice Perc Voice in the module view Introduction Perc Voice is one percussion voice that covers kicks, toms, hand drums, bells, metal and noisy hits from a single model. Pitch sets the fundamental, Tone walks the spectrum from a pure sine through drum-membrane and bar partials to inharmonic clang, and Click , Decay and Sweep shape the hit. Three engines give three families of sound behind the same knobs, so a sequencer or an LFO can morph a kick into a bell. Put it in a Voice Cell for a polyphonic, pitched percussion instrument. How does it work? Every hit is made of up to eight partials . Tone picks their frequency ratios: Tone Partials 0 % a pure sine 0 – 33 % the drum-membrane partials fade in 33 % membrane: 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65, … 67 % free bar: 1, 2.76, 5.40, 8.93, … 100 % metal: an inharmonic set drawn from Seed Between these points the partials glide smoothly. Each partial rings with its own decay: Decay is the time the fundamental takes to fall by 60 dB, and Damp makes the higher partials die faster. The engine decides how the partials sound: FM: the partials are sine modulators driving one sine carrier at the fundamental. Morph is the modulation index (0 – 8). The index decays twice as fast as the body, so the attack is bright and the tail purer: classic FM toms, kicks and bells. Modal: the partials are eight struck resonators. Morph balances them: at 0 % the fundamental dominates (drums), at 100 % the upper partials (glassy bells). A second hit adds to the ringing like a real body, so rolls build up naturally. Noise Bank: noise rings through eight band-pass filters at the partial frequencies. Morph is their width: narrow sounds almost pitched (steel drums, wood), wide sounds noisy (snares, shakers). With Tone at 100 % it makes cymbals and gongs. Every hit starts with a click (a short burst of filtered noise and a quick upward pitch blip) and a pitch sweep that falls from up to three octaves above to the set pitch. Accent is the hit's strength: a strong hit is louder, has more click, a deeper sweep and, in FM, a higher index. Soft hits are duller as well as quieter, like a real drum. Retriggering never clicks: a new hit starts on a second internal voice while the previous one fades out in 3 ms (in Modal the body is struck again instead). Choke fades everything out in 5 ms. How to use it? Kick: Modal or FM , Pitch around 50 Hz, Tone 0 – 15 %, Sweep 40 – 70 %, Decay 300 – 600 ms. Tom or hand drum: Tone around 30 %, Pitch 80 – 300 Hz, a little Sweep. Bell or glass: Modal , Tone 60 – 100 %, Morph high, Damp low, long Decay. Snare, shaker, cymbal: Noise Bank , Morph high; Tone 100 % for metal. In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Trigger → Trig , Pitch → Pitch , Velocity → Accent , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . Each voice is freed when its hit has died away. Open/closed pairs: patch the trigger of a closed hat into the Choke of an open one. Hit button: plays the voice at accent 70 %, for trying sounds without patching. The Pitch input adds octaves to the Pitch knob (1 V/oct). It is read at each hit unless Track is on. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Perc Voice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Perc Voice under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Perc Voice: FM Kit Three voices make a kit: an FM kick with a long Sweep , a clicky snap and a Noise Bank hat. Perc Voice: Tuned Toms With Track on, a sequencer's pitch tunes the Modal engine: a melody played on toms. Perc Voice: Metal Bells High Tone and the FM engine make long inharmonic bells; try Morph and Spread . Perc Voice: Noise Bank Shakers Noise Bank shakers and ticks with random accents on the Accent input. Perc Voice: Tone Sweep One voice, one rhythm: LFOs walk Tone and Morph from sine to membrane, bar and metal. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Pitch 20 Hz – 4 kHz 55 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 20 % Morph 0 – 100 % 50 % Click 0 – 100 % 30 % Decay 10 ms – 8 s 400 ms Damp 0 – 100 % 40 % Sweep 0 – 100 % 40 % Spread 0 – 100 % 20 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Engine FM, Modal, Noise Bank Modal Track Off, On Off Drive Clean, Warm, Hot Clean Seed 0 – 999 1 Pitch: the fundamental. Tone: the partial ratios, from sine to metal (see above). Morph: per engine: FM index, partial balance (Modal) or band width (Noise Bank). Its name changes with the engine. Click: the attack transient: a 1 – 6 ms noise burst at 2 – 8 kHz (higher with Tone) plus a +2 octave pitch blip during the first 2 ms. In Modal and Noise Bank it also excites the body. Decay: the time the fundamental takes to fall by 60 dB. Damp: how much faster the upper partials decay. At 100 % a partial an octave up decays 8× faster. Sweep: the pitch drop at the start: up to +3 octaves, falling back in about Decay / 8. Spread: the stereo image. Modal and Noise Bank : odd partials lean left, even partials right (the fundamental stays centred). FM : the two sides are detuned by up to ±8 cents. Level: the output level. Engine: FM, Modal or Noise Bank. A stepped knob, so it can be sequenced; it is read at each hit, and a sounding hit finishes with its own engine. Track: off: the Pitch input is read at each hit; on: it is followed live. Drive: soft saturation of the hit: Warm or Hot . It is applied relative to the hit's accent, so soft hits are as warm as loud ones. Seed: the metal partials and the noise. The same seed plays the same sounds; the noise sequence restarts when the transport starts. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Knob changes apply to a sounding hit at once and smoothly. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger plays a hit Accent control, 0 – 1 hit strength, read at each hit; unpatched counts as 70 % Pitch pitch added to Pitch in octaves (1 V/oct); read at each hit unless Track is on Choke trigger fades the sound out in 5 ms Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the voice Env control, 0 – 1 the amplitude envelope of the fundamental, for ducking Active gate high from a hit until the sound has fallen below −80 dB or was choked

title: Noise
text: Noise Noise in the module view Introduction Noise is random audio: every frequency at once, with no pitch. It's the raw material for snares, hi-hats, wind, breath, surf and risers, and a handy random source for modulation. Noise gives you four classic colours on their own outputs, plus a Colour knob that sweeps smoothly from dark to bright. How does it work? All colours come from one white noise source and are filtered from it: White: equal energy at every frequency. Bright and hissy. Pink: falls by 3 dB per octave, so every octave has the same energy. Sounds even and natural, like rain or a waterfall. Brown: falls by 6 dB per octave. Deep and rumbling, like distant thunder or surf. Blue: rises by 3 dB per octave. Thin and fizzy. Every output is about equally loud (around −10 dB RMS), so you can switch colours without jumping in level. Out follows the Colour knob: −100 % is brown, −50 % pink, 0 % white, +50 % blue and +100 % violet (rising by 6 dB per octave, the brightest). Between those points it blends the two neighbours, so turning the knob, or modulating it, sweeps the noise from dark to bright. Level sets the volume of Out only. Each Noise node plays its own noise. Two nodes, or two voices of a Voice Cell, never play the same noise. How to use it? Snare wires or hi-hats: Noise Out → Multi Filter (band-pass or high-pass) → VCA, with a short ADSR on the VCA's Gain . For ready-made drums, the Ring and Punch drum nodes already include their own noise. Wind and surf: brown or pink noise → a resonant low-pass filter, with a slow Function or Random on the cutoff. Risers: patch a long rising envelope onto Colour , so the noise gets brighter as it builds. Breathy oscillator: mix a little pink noise into an oscillator before the filter. Random modulation: brown noise wanders slowly; patched with a small amount onto a pitch or cutoff, it adds unsteady, analog-style drift. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Colour −100 … +100 % 0 % (white) Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Colour: the colour of Out : −100 % brown, −50 % pink, 0 % white, +50 % blue, +100 % violet. Level: the volume of Out . The fixed colour outputs always play at full level. Both knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs None (apart from the knobs). Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio noise in the colour set by Colour , at Level White audio white noise, flat Pink audio pink noise, −3 dB/oct Brown audio brown noise, −6 dB/oct Blue audio blue noise, +3 dB/oct

title: Pulse Generator
text: Pulse Generator Introduction Pulse Generator is a laboratory pulse generator on your board: one precisely timed rectangular pulse per period, with a delay , a width , slewed edges , bursts and double pulses . As a clock it is exact and can lock to the song position. As a sound source its edges excite a ringing resonance, like a badly terminated cable, so the pulses turn into clicks, pings and small drum tones. Its unit is time: set it with the knobs or drag the timing diagram. How does it work? The pulse. Each period starts with a Sync pulse. Delay later the pulse begins: it rises over Rise , stays up, and after Width falls over Fall (both a share of the width; at 0 % the edge is a clean step). The Gate output is the plain logic version: high from the start of the pulse to the start of its fall. Amplitude and Offset set the level of Out . Polarity Complement turns the pulse upside down (Gate too). With Time Units on % of Period , Width and Delay are shares of the period, so they follow it. In Time , a width that would reach the next period is shortened and the Duty lamp lights. Modes. Free Run: a period every Period . With Sync on a note value and the transport playing, periods lock to the song position (stopped, they run at that note length and the current tempo). Reset restarts the period now. Triggered: each Trigger (or the Single button) starts a burst of Burst pulses, one Period apart. A trigger during a burst restarts it; Reset stops it. Gated: while Gate is high, periods run, the first one at the rising edge. After the falling edge no new pulse starts, but the last one plays to its full width. External Width: a gate delay line. Gate 's edges come out Delay later, the pulse as long as the gate was high ( Rise and Fall are still shares of the Width knob). Up to 256 edges can wait; more are dropped and Duty lights. With Gate unpatched, each Trigger becomes a pulse of Width . Sync fires at the input's rising edges. Double gives two pulses per period, at the period start and Delay later. The shortest period is 4 samples (83 µs at 48 kHz). Jitter moves each pulse by a seeded random amount, up to ±25 % of the period (more often small than large). It never moves the period grid, so a synced clock stays on the beat, and Sync is never jittered. The same Seed gives the same jitter every time. Warm-up (Free Run, Sync Free) makes the period settle like a cold instrument: 5 % long at the start (of the transport, or when the module is added), then drifting in. The Warming lamp stays lit until it is within 0.1 %, after about 47 seconds. Ringing. Every edge excites a resonance at Ring Freq (plus Pitch , in octaves). Damping sets how many cycles it lasts: from 200 down to half a cycle. Rising and falling edges ring with opposite sign, so a short pulse gives a two-edge ping whose colour follows the width (half a ring cycle reinforces it, a whole cycle cancels it). Slow edges ring less. Ring mixes it into Out; the Ring output carries it alone, at full strength. A very resonant ring that a pulse train keeps feeding is softly limited. Clean edges. Edges are placed between samples and band-limited, so fast pulse trains don't alias and the ring is clean. All outputs are one sample late for it. How to use it? An exact clock: Sync 1/16, Width 10 %, Gate into a sequencer's clock. Clicks and pings: Period 250 ms, Width 0.2 ms, Ring 100 %, Ring Freq 3 kHz, Damping 60 %. Turn Width to hear the colour change. A small drum: Triggered, Ring output, Ring Freq 180 Hz, Damping 30 %, Width 3 ms: a pitched thump per trigger. One ping per note: in a Voice Cell, Voice In › Trigger into Trigger and pitch into Pitch , Triggered mode. Each voice has its own jitter. Rolls and flams: Triggered, Burst 4, Period 30 ms; or Double with a short Delay for flams. A humanised clock: Sync 1/8, Jitter 15 %. Delay a gate: External Width, Delay 125 ms: the gate comes out late and as long as it went in. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Pulse Generator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Pulse Generator under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Pulse Generator: Humanised Clock Sync 1/8 with some Jitter clocks a melody, while a second generator rings short pulses into hats. Pulse Generator: Ringing Pings Triggered pulses per note excite Ring ; the sequencer's pitch moves Ring Freq for glassy chimes, shaped by Damping and Width . Pulse Generator: Pulse Drums Four generators in Triggered mode, struck by a Drum Grid: Ring Freq and Damping make a thump, a tom, a click and a tick. Pulse Generator: Rolls and Flams Burst gives drum rolls at a 30 ms Period , and Double with a short Delay gives flams. Pulse Generator: Gate Echo External Width mode delays a melody's gate by 330 ms and plays an octave-up echo voice with it. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Period 20 µs – 10 s 100 ms Width 1 µs – 5 s, or 0 – 100 % 10 ms (10 %) Delay 0 – 10 s, or 0 – 100 % 0 Rise 0 – 100 % of Width 0 % Fall 0 – 100 % of Width 0 % Amplitude 0 – 100 % 100 % Offset −1 … +1 0 Jitter 0 – 100 % 0 % Ring 0 – 100 % 0 % Ring Freq 20 Hz – 20 kHz 2 kHz Damping 0 – 100 % 50 % Mode Free Run, Triggered, Gated, External Width Free Run Sync Free, 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 bar, 2 bars, 4 bars, 8 bars Free Time Units Time, % of Period Time Double Off, On Off Burst 1 – 64 1 Polarity Normal, Complement Normal Warm-up Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Period: time from one period start to the next (Free Run with Sync Free, Triggered, Gated). The view's ÷10 / ×10 buttons step it by decades; the knob is the vernier. Width: the pulse length. Time Units picks which of the two Width knobs is shown. Delay: period start to pulse start; with Double , the pair spacing. Rise / Fall: the edge times, as a share of the width. Amplitude / Offset: the pulse height and the baseline of Out. Jitter: random timing, up to ±25 % of the period. Ring / Ring Freq / Damping: how much ringing is mixed into Out, its frequency, and how fast it dies. Burst: pulses per trigger (Triggered). Seed: picks the jitter. Period, Width, Delay, Rise, Fall, Amplitude, Offset, Jitter, Ring, Ring Freq and Damping are modulation destinations. The view The timing diagram shows one period: Sync ticks, the pulse with its ringing, and Period, Delay and Width as dimension lines. Drag an arrow's end to change that value, or drag a slope's dot to change Rise or Fall. When Width or Delay is under 2 % of the period the time axis is compressed, so they stay visible. The Duty lamp lights when a width was shortened or pulses or edges were dropped (at most 32 pulses can wait for their Delay at once); Warming during warm-up. Single starts a burst in Triggered mode (and a pulse in External Width with Gate unpatched). Inputs Input Signal What it does Trigger trigger starts a burst (Triggered), or a pulse (External Width, Gate unpatched) Gate gate runs the generator while high (Gated); the signal delayed (External Width) Reset trigger restarts the period (Free Run unsynced, Gated); stops a burst (Triggered) Pitch pitch added to Ring Freq in octaves Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the pulse plus ringing, band-limited Gate gate a clean logic copy of the pulse Sync trigger one pulse at each period start, before Delay Ring audio only the ringing, at full strength

title: Sweep Generator
text: Sweep Generator Introduction Sweep Generator is a function generator with a built-in frequency sweep, like the bench instruments that measure a circuit across the audio band. It glides from Start to Stop over a set time or a number of bars, and puts out everything other modules need to follow it: the sweep ramp, the frequency as pitch (so a filter can track it), and triggers at markers, at the end of each sweep and on every cycle of the waveform. Musically it is a riser, a siren, a tone-burst source and a tracking test signal for feedback patches. The old benches' character is kept on purpose: a slow Drift , a warm-up that settles after the transport starts, and an audible Retrace as the sweep flies back. How does it work? The sweep. One sweep runs from Start to Stop in Sweep Time , or in the note value set by Sweep Sync . Stop may be below Start for a falling sweep. Direction runs it Up, Down, or Up-Down (up and back within the same length). The Law decides the speed: Log spends the same time on every octave (it sounds even), Lin the same time on every hertz: it rushes through the bass and lingers in the treble. Modes. Continuous: the sweep repeats. Synced to a note value while the transport plays, its position follows the song position, so it stays on the bars after a loop or a jump. Trigger restarts it. Triggered: waits at the beginning until a trigger, runs one sweep, fires End and holds the last frequency. A new trigger starts again from the beginning. Gated: the sweep moves only while Gate is high and pauses while it is low. Trigger restarts it. Burst: the sweep runs as in Continuous, but Out is silent until a trigger. Each trigger plays Burst Count whole cycles of the waveform at the frequency the sweep has reached, with short fades. Bursts step through the band like a stepped response measurement. While Hold is high, the sweep position freezes in every mode; the tone keeps playing. When synced, releasing Hold jumps back onto the grid. The waveform is phase continuous: when the frequency jumps (a new sweep, a trigger, a jump in the song), the wave carries on without a click. Edges and corners are band-limited, so even high sweeps stay clean. Symmetry skews the sine and the triangle, sets the duty of the square and the pulse, and bends the ramps. With Phase Reset on, a trigger also restarts the cycle. FM adds linear (through-zero) frequency modulation from the FM input, with the same depth all along the sweep; AM scales the level. Very low sweeps make Out a sweeping LFO. Retrace. When an Up or Down sweep starts over, Instant jumps back. Glide flies back over 5 % of the sweep (at most a quarter of a second), the way a bench sweeper's flyback can be heard. Sweep follows it, End fires as it starts and the markers stay quiet during it. Markers. Up to three marker frequencies (set by Markers ). Marker fires whenever the sweep crosses one, in either direction, and Marker Gate stays high for Marker Width . Use them to trigger events at points in the band. Drift and warm-up. Drift adds a slow, seeded wander of up to about ±37 cents, plus a warm-up offset of up to ±40 cents that settles over Warm-up after the transport starts (or the module is created), like a cold instrument. With Drift at 0 the frequency is exact. Repeatable. The drift comes from Seed and the song position, and starting the transport restarts the sweep, the waveform and the warm-up, so a render from the same position is always identical. How to use it? Riser: Start 100 Hz, Stop 8 kHz, Sweep Sync 8 bars, Mode Continuous, into a filter or straight into the mix. Patch End to a crash. Filter that follows: Freq into a filter's cutoff pitch input: the filter tracks the tone exactly. Or Sweep into any knob as a ramp. Siren: Direction Up-Down, Sweep Time 1.5 s, Waveform Triangle, Law Lin. Tone bursts: Mode Burst, Burst Count 8, a clock into Trigger : short blips that climb through the band. Events along the sweep: Markers 3, Marker into drum triggers or an envelope: hits at 250 Hz, 1 kHz and 4 kHz. One sweep per note: Mode Triggered, a note's trigger into Trigger , Pitch from the keyboard: each note sweeps from its own key. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Sweep Generator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Sweep Generator under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Sweep Generator: Four-Bar Riser A Ramp Up sweep from Start 100 Hz to Stop 8 kHz over four bars ( Sweep Sync ) opens a filter, and End fires a crash. Sweep Generator: Lab Sirens Two Up-Down sweeps of different Sweep Time wail left and right; Law Lin against Log changes the feel. Sweep Generator: Climbing Bursts Burst mode plays Burst Count cycles at the frequency the slow sweep has reached for each sequencer step. Sweep Generator: Marker Drums Three sweeps each fire Marker when they cross a set frequency and play a kick, a snare and a hat: a drifting polyrhythm. Sweep Generator: Laser Plucks Triggered mode with a falling sweep makes a zap per note, and Pitch from the sequencer moves the sweep.
