Both work in octaves, so modulation sounds even across the range. Res 1 , Res 2 set each filter's resonance (Q 0.5 to 25, the Multi Filter's curve). Mode 1 , Mode 2 morph each response: LP → BP → HP → Notch. Routing decides how the two work together: Serial in ─► F1 ─► F2 ─► out (Balance > 0 lets part of F1 bypass F2) Parallel in ─► F1 + F2 ─► out (Balance: level of F1 vs F2) Parallel (inv.) in ─► F1 − F2 ─► out Stereo in L ─► F1 ─► out L, in R ─► F2 ─► out R Changing the routing crossfades over 10 ms, so it's safe while playing. Link ties the modes together. Same : Mode 2 becomes an offset from Mode 1 (at LP, both filters have the same response), so one cable on Mode 1 morphs both. Mirror : filter 2 moves the opposite way (Mode 1 LP → Notch makes filter 2 go Notch → LP), plus the Mode 2 offset. Character : Clean never self-oscillates; Saturating growls when driven and with high resonance. In Serial, the saturation of filter 1 shapes what filter 2 sees, like an overdriven two-stage filter. Drive saturates the input (tanh) before the filters. Key Track moves both cutoffs with the Pitch input. Mix blends the dry input back in. Two resonant peaks at the same frequency in series could get very loud. In Clean Serial, filter 2's input is turned down while the cutoffs are within a semitone of each other (back to full over the next octave of Spread), and every output passes a soft limiter that is linear up to ±2 and never exceeds ±8. The view draws each filter's response (thin) and the result of the routing (bright; in Stereo, left and right). Drag the centre marker for Cutoff , the f1 and f2 markers for Spread (hold Alt to move only that cutoff), and drag a marker up or down for that filter's resonance. How to use it? Wide band-pass with two edges: Serial, Mode 1 HP, Mode 2 LP, Spread +2 oct. Each edge has its own resonance; Cutoff moves the band, Spread sets its width. Steep low-pass: Serial, both LP, Spread 0: 24 dB/oct with two coinciding resonance peaks. Vowels / formants: Parallel, both BP, Spread around +1.5 oct, Res 60–80 %. Modulate Spread (and Cutoff a little) to change the vowel. Band-reject with steep sides: Parallel (F2 inverted), both BP. Band-pass from two low-passes: Parallel (F2 inverted), both LP: what lies between the two cutoffs. Stereo filter: Stereo routing with a mono source on In L . Spread places the left and right cutoffs apart; an LFO on Spread makes the stereo image breathe. One-knob morph: Serial, Link Mirror, sweep Mode 1 : from two low-passes through band-pass to two notches. Separate processing: take F1 Out and F2 Out to different effects. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Dual Filter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Dual Filter under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Dual Filter: Vowel Pad Parallel band-passes with high Res 1 and Res 2 form a vowel pair; a slow LFO on Spread slides between vowels. Dual Filter: Wide Band Bass Serial with Mode 1 high-pass and Mode 2 low-pass makes a band: Cutoff places it, Spread widens it, Drive with Saturating adds growl. Dual Filter: Stereo Breath Routing on Stereo with a mono source: Spread places the left and right cutoffs apart, and an LFO makes the image breathe. Dual Filter: Notch Sweep Parallel (F2 inverted) turns two band-passes into a steep notch that sweeps through a riff over a beat. Dual Filter: Mirror Morph Link on Mirror and an LFO on Mode 1 morph both filters from low-pass through band-pass to notch, with Character Saturating. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 1 kHz Spread −5 … +5 oct +1 oct Res 1, Res 2 0 – 100 % 20 % Mode 1, Mode 2 LP → BP → HP → Notch LP Balance −100 … +100 % 0 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Key Track 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Routing Serial, Parallel, Parallel (F2 inverted), Stereo Serial Link Off, Same, Mirror Off Character Clean, Saturating Clean Cutoff: the centre, exponential over ten octaves; 10 % of modulation ≈ one octave. f1 = Cutoff × 2^(−Spread/2), f2 = Cutoff × 2^(+Spread/2), each kept between 5 Hz and just below half the sample rate. Spread: distance between the cutoffs in octaves. Res 1 / Res 2: resonance of each filter. Mode 1 / Mode 2: each filter's response. With Link on, Mode 2 is an offset (shown as Mode 2 Offset ). Balance: Serial: the share of filter 1 that bypasses filter 2 (0 to 100 %; negative values do nothing extra). Parallel: the level of filter 1 (negative) vs filter 2 (positive). Stereo: a left/right balance. Drive: tanh saturation before the filters. Key Track: how far Pitch moves both cutoffs (100 % = one octave per octave). Mix: dry/wet. Routing, Link, Character: see above. Not modulatable. Changing Character starts the filters from silence. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct moves both cutoffs, scaled by Key Track Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the routed result, after Balance and Mix F1 Out audio filter 1 alone, mono (Stereo: the left channel's filter) F2 Out audio filter 2 alone, mono (Serial: after filter 1; Stereo: the right channel's filter) Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on Out (5 ms attack, 120 ms release)

title: Filter Bank
text: Filter Bank Filter Bank in the module view Introduction The Filter Bank splits a sound into ten bands with fixed band-pass filters. Each band has its own level, its own audio output and its own envelope output. Shape the spectrum by hand or with modulation (a Tilt knob, an odd/even balance, a window that scans across the bands), send single bands to different effects, or let the envelopes make other sounds follow this one's spectrum. With a voice on the Sidechain input and the Vocode knob up, it's a ten-band vocoder. How does it work? Ten band-pass filters (zero-delay-feedback state-variable filters) sit on fixed frequencies. Each has unit gain at its centre: a sine on a band's frequency comes out of that band at the level it went in. Tuning sets the frequencies: Spectral: spread evenly in octaves from 55 Hz to 14 kHz (55, 102, 188, 349, 645, 1194, 2209, 4088, 7565, 14000 Hz): the classic fixed filter bank. Harmonic: the first ten partials of a note, 65.4 Hz (C2) × 1 … 10, transposed by the Pitch input: a resonant bank that plays in tune. Scale: ten consecutive notes of Scale from Root in octave 2, transposed by Pitch (snapped to the scale): a chord-like resonator. Shift moves all bands together (±2 octaves). Spacing stretches or squeezes them around the middle (between bands 5 and 6). Both work in octaves, so an LFO on Shift sweeps the whole bank like a phaser. Bands pushed above the top of the audio band are muted. Q sets how narrow every band is. The default (2.2) gives an almost flat sum: with all levels at 0 dB the bank sounds like the input. Higher values make the bands ring (great in Harmonic and Scale tuning). Slope 24 dB/oct uses two filter sections per band: steeper bands and an even flatter sum (every other band is polarity-inverted, as in a crossover, so the overlaps add up). Edge Bands Low-pass/High-pass lets band 1 also carry everything below it and band 10 everything above it, so the bank covers the whole spectrum. The gain of each band is the product of: Level (−60 dB = silent … +12 dB; 0 dB at 75 % of the knob), Tilt (dB per octave around 1 kHz: positive is brighter), Odd/Even (−100 %: only odd bands, +100 %: only even bands), the Scan window: a window Width bands wide, centred on band 1 + 9 × Scan , with soft edges. At Width 10 the window is off; with Width 1, sweeping Scan plays one band after the other, Vocode (below). Gains glide over 5 ms, so even fast modulation doesn't click. Envelopes. Each band has an envelope follower ( Attack , Release ) fed by the band's signal before its gain, so the envelopes describe the source and don't change when you turn levels. Env From picks the source: the input, or the Sidechain signal through its own ten filters. A full-scale sine in one band reads about 1. Vocode multiplies each band by its envelope: at 100 % a band is as loud as the matching band of the sidechain (×4, up to +12 dB); lower values blend the unvocoded sound back in. With Env From = Input , it works as a per-band expander (loud bands get louder). Stereo. The filters run per channel. With Stereo = Odd/Even split , Sum L carries the odd bands and Sum R the even bands: a spectral widener for mono sources. The Band , Odd and Even outputs are mono. Jacks chooses which of the many outputs the node shows: just the sums, also the ten band outputs, also the ten envelopes, or the envelopes only. Hidden jacks keep their cables. Bands that are silent and whose outputs are not patched cost nothing. The view shows the ten levels as sliders (drag across them to draw a curve, double-click a band for 0 dB), the effective gain of each band as an outline, the live envelopes below, and the band frequencies (or note names). The Presets menu sets all ten levels at once: Flat , Smile , Telephone , Odd only , Comb . How to use it? Spectral EQ: draw a curve on the sliders, or use Tilt for a quick brighter/darker. Vocoder: a voice (audio input port) into Sidechain , a bright synth (saw chords, noise) into In L , Env From = Sidechain, Vocode 100 %. Attack 2–5 ms, Release 50–150 ms. Try Slope 24 dB/oct for clearer words. Scanning filter: Width 2, an LFO or a sequencer on Scan . Phaser-like sweep: an LFO on Shift , some Q . Resonator: Tuning Harmonic or Scale , Q 15–30, noise or drums in, Voice In Pitch into Pitch : the bank rings in tune. Stereo widening: a mono pad in, Stereo = Odd/Even split. Multiband effects: Jacks = Bands, send Band 1–3 to a distortion and the rest elsewhere. Spectral follower: Jacks = Envs, Env 2 onto a kick-related modulation, Env 8 onto hi-hat-related ones. Vocoder with cables: two banks, Env k of the first into Level k of the second (levels at 0, amount 100 %). Swap cables to shift formants. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Filter Bank does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Filter Bank under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Filter Bank: Rhythm Vocoder A drum beat in the Sidechain with Env From on Sidechain and Vocode at 100 % makes a saw chord speak the rhythm. Filter Bank: Scanning Window A narrow Width with an LFO on Scan sweeps a two-band window across a held chord. Filter Bank: Tuned Resonator Tuning on Harmonic, high Q and a sequencer on Pitch turn noise bursts and drums into pitched hits. Filter Bank: Phaser Sweep An LFO on Shift slides all ten bands together for a vocal, phaser-like sweep on an arpeggio. Filter Bank: Odd-Even Wide Stereo on Odd/Even split puts odd bands left and even bands right for a wide mono-to-stereo pad; Odd/Even and Tilt reshape it. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1 … 10 −60 (silent) … +12 dB 0 dB Q 0.5 – 30 2.2 Tilt −6 … +6 dB/oct 0 Odd/Even −100 … +100 % 0 % Scan 0 – 100 % 50 % Width 1 – 10 bands 10 Shift −2 … +2 oct 0 Spacing 50 – 200 % 100 % Attack 0.5 – 100 ms 3 ms Release 5 ms – 2 s 80 ms Vocode 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Tuning Spectral, Harmonic, Scale Spectral Root C … B C Scale the Step Sequencer's scales Minor Pentatonic Slope 12 dB/oct, 24 dB/oct 12 dB/oct Edge Bands Band-pass, Low-pass/High-pass Low-pass/High-pass Env From Input, Sidechain Input Stereo Normal, Odd/Even split Normal Jacks Sums, Bands, Bands + Envs, Envs Sums Level k: the gain of band k. Q: the sharpness of every band. Low values blur the bands into each other; high values ring. Tilt: spectral slope around 1 kHz. Odd/Even: fades out the even (negative) or odd (positive) bands. Scan / Width: the window over the bands. Shift / Spacing: move and stretch the band frequencies, in octaves. Attack / Release: the envelope followers' times. Vocode: how much the envelopes multiply the band gains. Mix: dry ↔ bank for Sum L/R . Root / Scale: only in Scale tuning. The settings are not modulatable; all knobs are modulation destinations, including the ten levels. Gains and frequencies update every 8 samples and glide in between. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Sidechain audio analysis input for the envelopes when Env From = Sidechain (the voice in a vocoder) Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct transposes the bands in Harmonic and Scale tuning (shown only there) Outputs Output Signal What it does Sum L, Sum R audio all bands after their gains, plus the dry signal per Mix Odd audio bands 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, mono Even audio bands 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, mono Band 1 … 10 audio each band alone, mono, after its gain (shown with Jacks = Bands or Bands + Envs) Env 1 … 10 control, 0 – 1 each band's envelope (shown with Jacks = Bands + Envs or Envs) All audio outputs pass a soft limiter (linear up to ±2, never beyond ±8): +12 dB levels, steep tilt and vocoding can stack up.

title: Low Pass Gate
text: Low Pass Gate Low Pass Gate in the module view Introduction A low pass gate is a filter and an amplifier in one, opened by light. Inside sits a model of a vactrol : a lamp shining on a light-sensitive resistor. When the light comes on, the gate opens almost at once. When it goes out, the gate closes slowly and unevenly, getting darker as it gets quieter. That is how struck and plucked things die away, so one trigger at Ping gives a natural, organic pluck without any envelope. It is stereo and cheap, and its Active output makes it a good last stage in every voice of a Voice Cell. How does it work? The light is Level plus the CV input (together clipped to 0 – 100 %), plus a short flash from every Ping . The cell follows the light: Opening is fast: a few milliseconds. Closing is slow, and it gets slower as the cell darkens. The first half of the decay goes quickly, the quiet tail lingers. Memory: after a long, bright gate the cell closes more slowly than after a short ping, as a real photoresistor does. The cell's openness (shown on the Light output) drives a low-pass filter and a gain together. As the gate closes, the sound gets both quieter and darker. The cutoff rises quickly at the start of a pluck and lingers in the low range as it fades. A Ping is a 2 ms flash of light. A full ping with the Classic cell opens the gate to about half and fades to silence (−60 dB) in about 0.6 s. A ping on a gate that is still open adds to it instead of restarting it, so fast rolls swell like a real struck object. How to use it? Pluck: Oscillator → In L ; a trigger (a sequencer, a clock) → Ping . Out L/R to the output. Turn Response to make the plucks shorter or longer. In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Trigger → Ping , Voice In › Velocity → Velocity , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . The cell then frees each voice exactly when its pluck has faded. Held notes: also patch Voice In › Gate → CV . The gate opens the cell, and the release is the cell's own slow fall. Envelope for other modules: Light is a ready-made pluck envelope: patch it onto a wavefolder's fold or a filter's cutoff so louder plucks are brighter, too. Ping button: fires a manual ping, for trying out Response and Cell . Demo patches Five whole patches show what Low Pass Gate does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Low Pass Gate under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Low Pass Gate: Pentatonic Pings A sequencer's trigger on Ping plucks a saw oscillator through the Classic Cell ; Response and Resonance shape the pluck. Low Pass Gate: Slow Memory Bass The Slow memory cell remembers earlier pings, so fast notes open the bass more; velocity drives the Velocity input. Low Pass Gate: Vactrol Drums Three gates pinged from a Drum Grid turn a sine, noise and a square into kick, snare and ticks. Low Pass Gate: Light Follower The Light output opens a filter on a saw drone so it brightens with each ping. Low Pass Gate: Breathing Chord A slow LFO on CV opens and closes the gate over a held chord, with Cell on Slow memory for a darker-as-it-closes swell. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 0 – 100 % 0 % Response 0 – 100 % 50 % Ping 0 – 100 % 80 % Resonance 0 – 100 % 0 % Brightness 0 – 100 % 75 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Bleed 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode LP, VCA, Both Both Cell Fast, Classic, Slow memory Classic Level: constant light, added to CV . At 0 % the gate is closed until something opens it; at 100 % it is fully open. Response: the speed of the cell. Every time constant is scaled from 0.25× (0 %, snappy) through 1× (50 %) to 4× (100 %, slow and ringing). Ping: the strength of the flash on each Ping pulse (times Velocity ). Resonance: emphasis at the cutoff (Q 0.5 – 6), in LP and Both . Both turns the level down a little as the resonance rises. Brightness: the cutoff when fully open, 1 kHz – 20 kHz. Drive: soft saturation of the input before the gate, for warmth on loud plucks. It is anti-aliased, so it stays clean on high notes. Bleed: how much the closed gate leaks. At 100 % the dark state still passes a muffled −24 dB. Mode: LP: only the filter. Closed, it still passes the lowest bass (30 Hz). VCA: only the amplifier, no change in tone. Both: filter and amplifier together: the classic low pass gate. Cell: the character of the vactrol. Fast is short and snappy, Classic is the familiar bright-then-dark pluck, Slow memory has long, lingering tails that grow after long notes. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is unpatched In R audio right input CV control, 0 – 1 the light driving the cell, added to Level Ping trigger a short flash of light: a pluck Velocity control, 0 – 1 scales the next ping; unpatched counts as 1 Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the gated signal Light control, 0 – 1 the cell's openness: a pluck envelope for other modules Active gate high while the cell is open or the output is still audible; falls 50 ms after it goes quiet

title: Multi Filter
text: Multi Filter Multi Filter in the module view Introduction The Multi Filter shapes the tone of a sound by removing or emphasising frequencies. It's stereo and offers 25 filter algorithms, from clean state-variable and ladder filters to shelves, phasers and a flanger. Most of them have a low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch response that you can morph between continuously. It comes with drive and key tracking. An envelope output tells the rest of the patch how loud the filtered signal is. How does it work? The algorithms follow Vadim Zavalishin's book The Art of VA Filter Design . They are "zero-delay feedback" models of analog circuits: they stay in tune up to high frequencies and stay click-free under fast modulation, even at audio rate. Type picks the algorithm; the dropdown groups them by family. Cutoff sets where the filter acts. The knob is exponential: 20 Hz at the bottom, 20 kHz at the top, about ten octaves in total. Modulation therefore works in octaves: a cable at 10 % moves the cutoff by about one octave, whatever the cutoff is. Resonance boosts the frequencies around the cutoff. On the ladder and allpass types it's the feedback amount; some types self-oscillate near the top (see the table). Drive saturates the input before the filter (a soft tanh curve) for warmth and grit. The saturating types add their own distortion on top. Mode morphs the response on the multimode types: LP (0 %) → BP (33 %) → HP (67 %) → Notch (100 %) On the phasers and the flanger it does something else (see below). Gain sets the boost or cut of the shelving types, in dB. Key Track moves the cutoff with the Pitch input, so high notes are as bright as low ones. Mix blends the dry input with the filtered signal. The algorithms State Variable (12 dB/oct) — the all-round filter: smooth, clean, every response at once. Type What it is Mode Gain SVF Multimode LP / BP / HP / notch morph ✓ SVF Bandpass (unit gain) band-pass with 0 dB at the cutoff, whatever the resonance; resonance makes the band narrower SVF Band Shelf boosts or cuts a band around the cutoff; resonance narrows it ✓ SVF Peaking low-pass minus high-pass: a resonant peak with full bass and treble SVF Allpass flat level, phase turns around the cutoff (resonance makes the turn steeper) 1-Pole (6 dB/oct) — gentle tone shaping. Resonance has no effect. Type What it is Gain 1-Pole Low-pass / High-pass the softest possible slopes 1-Pole Allpass flat level, 180° phase turn 1-Pole Low Shelf / High Shelf tilt the lows or highs by Gain ; Cutoff is the middle of the slope ✓ Transistor Ladder (24 dB/oct) — four low-passes in a feedback loop: the classic fat, steep synth filter. Mode morphs LP → BP → HP → notch, all built from the ladder's taps. In low-pass mode the input is boosted with the resonance, so the bass doesn't thin out. Type What it is Self-oscillates Ladder Linear the clean, ideal ladder no (stops just short) Ladder Feedback HP a high-pass at 250 Hz in the feedback: no resonance below it, full bass at any resonance no Ladder Tanh a tanh saturator at the feedback point: warm overdrive, bounded self-oscillation above ~80 % Ladder Hyperbolic the same with a softer x / (1 + abs x) saturator: rounder, quieter oscillation above ~80 % Ladder Nonlinear Stages every stage saturates, like the real circuit: the cutoff sags on loud signals above ~80 % Diode Ladder (24 dB/oct) — the coupled stages of a diode ladder give a squelchier, less predictable resonance than the transistor ladder. Low-pass only ( Mode has no effect). Type What it is Self-oscillates Diode Ladder Linear the clean model no Diode Ladder Tanh with a saturator at the feedback point above ~80 % Allpass Effects — the dry signal plus allpass-filtered copies: notches and peaks that move with Cutoff . Patch a slow Function onto Cutoff for the classic sweep. Resonance is feedback (sharper peaks). Set Mix to 100 %: the dry signal is already part of the effect. Type What it is Mode Phaser 1-Pole ×4 four 1-pole allpasses: two notches, around 0.4× and 2.4× the cutoff below 50 %: normal; from 50 %: inverted (peaks and notches swap) Phaser 2-Pole ×2 two 2-pole allpasses: two notches whose spacing you set notch spacing: wide at 0 %, close at 100 % Flanger a short delay of 1 / Cutoff (20 Hz = 50 ms, 1 kHz = 1 ms): a comb of evenly spaced notches as the 1-pole phaser Classic Digital — the textbook digital filters the book improves on, kept for comparison and for their sound. Type What it is Naive 1-Pole Low-pass the simplest digital low-pass; above a few kHz the cutoff no longer tracks and it opens fully Biquad (Direct Form I) the classic biquad of the SVF multimode ( Mode works); same sound when static, but fast cutoff modulation at high resonance can make it misbehave (a safety limit keeps it bounded) Nonlinear State Variable (12 dB/oct) — the SVF with saturation inside. Mode morphs LP → BP → HP → notch. Type What it is SVF Atanh Damping the damping grows on loud signals: resonance that compresses itself, bounded self-oscillation at the top SVF Hyperbolic Damping the same with a harder-acting curve: gentler, quieter oscillation SVF Saturating (Rough) saturating integrators: growls when driven, gritty and bounded. Drives harder than the others at the same Drive The Env output follows the level of the filtered signal (fast 5 ms attack, 120 ms release). The view shows the filter's response curve for the selected type. It is drawn from the modulated values, so you can see it move. For the saturating types it shows the quiet-signal (linear) response. How to use it? Subtractive synth: Oscillator Out → Filter In L → VCA. Start with SVF Multimode or Ladder Tanh , Mode at LP, Cutoff around 1 kHz and some Resonance . Self-oscillating sine: pick Ladder Tanh or SVF Atanh Damping , turn Resonance to 100 %, patch Voice In Pitch into Pitch with Key Track at 100 %. The filter rings at the cutoff and plays in tune. Phaser / flanger: pick a type from Allpass Effects , Mix at 100 %, some Resonance , and a slow Function on Cutoff . EQ: a 1-Pole Low Shelf or High Shelf with Gain tilts a track's tone; SVF Band Shelf boosts or cuts a band. Filter envelope: patch an ADSR's Env onto Cutoff . The cable amount sets how many octaves the envelope opens: 30 % ≈ 3 octaves. Key tracking: patch Voice In Pitch into Pitch and set Key Track to 100 %. The cutoff then follows the keyboard one octave per octave. Filter sweeps: patch a slow Function or Random onto Cutoff , or onto Mode for a sweep from low-pass to high-pass. Process a track: route a track's audio onto the board with an input port, through the filter, and back out with an output port. Sidechain-style movement: patch Env onto another module, e.g. a pad's cutoff or a VCA's gain with a negative amount, so it reacts to this signal. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 2 kHz Resonance 0 – 100 % 20 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode LP → BP → HP → Notch LP Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Key Track 0 – 100 % 0 % Gain −24 – +24 dB 0 dB Type 25 algorithms in 7 groups SVF Multimode Cutoff: the corner (LP, HP) or centre (BP, notch) frequency. Exponential over ten octaves; 10 % of modulation ≈ one octave. Resonance: emphasis at the cutoff (Q from 0.5 to 25 on the SVF types, feedback on the ladders, phasers and flanger). Low values are smooth; high values ring and whistle. Self-oscillating types sing on their own near the top. No effect on the 1-pole types. Drive: how hard the input is saturated before filtering. At 0 % the signal is untouched. Turn down the source level if you want drive without much extra loudness. Drive and the filter run at four times the sample rate, so even hard drive and the saturating types stay clean, without the harsh, out-of-tune overtones of aliasing. Mode: the response, morphed continuously: 0 % low-pass (removes highs), 33 % band-pass (keeps a band around the cutoff), 67 % high-pass (removes lows), 100 % notch (removes a band). Applies to SVF Multimode , the transistor ladders, the biquad and the nonlinear SVFs. On Phaser 1-Pole ×4 and Flanger it flips the effect's polarity at 50 %; on Phaser 2-Pole ×2 it sets the notch spacing. Gain: boost or cut of 1-Pole Low Shelf , 1-Pole High Shelf and SVF Band Shelf . No effect on the other types. Mix: dry/wet. 100 % is only the filter; lower values mix the unfiltered input back in. The response curve shows the result. Key Track: how far the cutoff follows the Pitch input. At 100 % the cutoff moves one octave per octave of pitch; at 50 %, half an octave. No effect when Pitch is unpatched. Type: the filter algorithm (see above). Not modulatable. Switching type starts the new algorithm from silence. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct moves the cutoff, scaled by Key Track Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio filtered left channel Out R audio filtered right channel Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on the filtered output The outputs lag the inputs by 71 samples (about 1.5 ms at 48 kHz), the cost of oversampling. The dry signal of Mix lags by the same amount, so the two stay in phase.

title: Wave Analyzer
text: Wave Analyzer Introduction Wave Analyzer is a very narrow band-pass that you tune like an old lab receiver. Turn the big dial and the single partials of a sound come out one by one. Let it sweep and it draws the spectrum on its plotter while it plays a melody of partials. Let it lock and it hunts for the strongest partial in a window and follows it. The imperfections are part of the sound: the filter rings when it moves, the oscillator drifts, and the lock loop springs and wobbles before it settles. How does it work? Tuning. The analyser listens at one frequency, the tuned frequency: the Frequency dial (or the sweep, or the lock loop) with Pitch added in octaves and a little Drift . Bandwidth sets how wide it listens: 3 Hz picks out a single partial even high up, 100 Hz lets neighbours through, 1/3 octave grows with the frequency like a graphic-EQ band. The skirts are steep (24 dB per octave on each side). Band is the isolated partial at its own pitch. Shifted is the same partial moved to the Listen frequency: every partial you tune to is heard at the same pitch, and a partial slightly off the dial is heard slightly off Listen , so vibrato and drift become small bends. At wide bandwidths neighbouring partials beat against each other, and it whistles and talks. Isolated partials are quiet: Gain (+12 dB by default) lifts both outputs, which are softly limited. Ringing. A narrow band needs time: about 1 / bandwidth seconds (a third of a second at 3 Hz). Move the dial faster and the band smears and rings. Level is the loudness of the band on a dB scale, from Floor (0) to 0 dBFS (1), with the ballistics of a moving-coil meter: the needle swings over in about 300 ms and overshoots a hair. Ballistics: Fast follows within milliseconds. Peak fires when Level rises through Threshold ; while sweeping, each loud partial fires once, a rhythm read from the spectrum. Modes Manual: the band sits where the dial is. Sweep: the band moves from Frequency up by Span octaves (or down, or up and down) in Sweep Time , or in a note length when Sync is set and the transport plays (then the sweep follows the song position). Reset restarts a free sweep, Hold pauses it. When the sweep is faster than the band can follow, Too Fast lights: partials then read low and draw late and wide, as on the bench. Lock: the band scans the window Frequency ± Capture once, remembers the loudest place, jumps there and locks on with a phase-locked loop. Locked goes high and Track follows the partial: a crude pitch tracker. If the partial fades by more than 20 dB, or runs out of the window, it hunts again. Reset starts a new hunt, Hold freezes it. Range is the lab range switch: in a decade range the dial covers only 20–200 Hz, 200 Hz–2 kHz or 2–20 kHz, ten times finer. Drift lets the oscillator wander like a warm valve set, up to ±24 cents, slowly. A partial slides out of a 3 Hz band and back; in Lock the loop chases it. The drift follows Seed and the song position, so renders repeat. The view Needle meter: Level on a dB scale from Floor to 0 dB, Threshold as a red tick. Frequency dial: printed with the Range scale. Drag it (Shift for fine, double-click resets); the pointer shows where the band actually is, with Pitch , the sweep, the lock loop and drift. Lights: Locked (blinking while hunting) and Too Fast . Plotter: level against frequency from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Each sweep draws in ink; the previous sweep stays faded, so a spectrum builds up sweep by sweep. In Manual and Lock the pen leaves a trace wherever the band goes. Click the strip to clear it. How to use it? Harmonic melodies: a rich oscillator into In , Mode: Sweep , Frequency at the oscillator's pitch, Span 4, Bandwidth 10 Hz: Band plays the harmonic series. Peak into a drum: the rhythm of the spectrum. One pitch from everything: Shifted with Listen at a note of your track: whatever you tune to sings at that pitch. Pitch tracker: a voice or a bass into In , Mode: Lock , Capture 12 st around its range; Track into an oscillator's pitch, Locked into a VCA. Spectrum on the bench: Sync 4 bars, Bandwidth 30 Hz, Span 10, Frequency 20 Hz: one full spectrum every four bars on the plotter. Frozen partial: Hold from a gate: the band stays put while you play. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Wave Analyzer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Wave Analyzer under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Wave Analyzer: Harmonic Series Sweep mode with a 10 Hz Bandwidth plays the harmonics of a low saw; Peak triggers the hats. Wave Analyzer: One Pitch from Everything The Shifted output moves each partial to the Listen frequency, so a melody becomes changing timbres at one pitch. Wave Analyzer: Pitch Tracker Lock mode follows the loudest partial within Capture ; Track drives a follower voice and Locked gates it. Wave Analyzer: Spectrum Pad A slow synced Sweep with large Span sings through a three-saw chord while the plotter draws the spectrum. Wave Analyzer: Held Partial A square LFO on Hold freezes the sweep, and a 1/3 octave Bandwidth makes it whistle and talk. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Frequency 20 Hz – 20 kHz (or one decade, see Range ) 440 Hz Span 0 – 10 octaves 4 oct Sweep Time 0.1 – 120 s 8 s Capture 0 – 24 semitones 7 st Drift 0 – 100 % 15 % Listen 50 Hz – 4 kHz 800 Hz Threshold 0 – 100 % 60 % Gain −20 … +40 dB +12 dB Mode Manual, Sweep, Lock Manual Bandwidth 3 Hz, 10 Hz, 30 Hz, 100 Hz, 1/3 octave 10 Hz Range Full, 20–200 Hz, 200 Hz–2 kHz, 2–20 kHz Full Sweep Dir Up, Down, Up-Down Up Sync Free, 1/32 … 8 bars, 16, 32, 64 bars Free Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Ballistics Needle, Fast Needle Seed 0 – 999 1 Frequency: the tuning dial; the sweep's start in Sweep , the window's centre in Lock . The small knob text shows the Full scale; the big dial shows the Range scale. Span, Sweep Time, Sweep Dir, Sync: the sweep (shown in Sweep ). Capture: the lock window, ± semitones around Frequency (shown in Lock ). Drift: how far the oscillator wanders. Listen: the pitch of Shifted . Threshold: where Peak fires on the Level scale. Gain: on Band and Shifted . Floor: the bottom of the Level scale. Ballistics: Needle swings like a meter, Fast follows at once. Seed: picks the drift. Frequency , Span , Sweep Time , Capture , Drift , Listen , Threshold and Gain are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the sound to analyse Pitch pitch added to the tuned frequency in octaves (1 V/oct) Reset trigger restarts a free sweep; in Lock starts a new hunt Hold gate while high, the tuned frequency is frozen Outputs Output Signal What it does Thru audio In , unchanged Band audio the isolated band at its own pitch Shifted audio the band moved to Listen Level control the band's level, 0 at Floor … 1 at 0 dBFS, with needle ballistics Track pitch the tuned frequency (0 = C4) Peak trigger a pulse when Level rises through Threshold Locked gate high while the lock loop holds a partial

title: Audio Mixer
text: Audio Mixer Audio Mixer in the module view Introduction A small stereo mixer for the board. It brings up to four sound sources (oscillators, drums, Voice Cells) together into one stereo pair, with a level, a pan, mute and solo for each, and a send for a shared effect. A limiter on the master keeps the sum from clipping. How does it work? Each channel's signal goes through: Level: a fader in dB, from silence to +6 dB. 0 dB (unchanged) sits at about 80 % of the travel. Mute and Solo: a muted channel is silent; when any channel is soloed, only soloed channels reach the master. Changes fade over 5 ms. Pan: a mono channel (only L patched) is placed in the stereo field at even loudness; a stereo channel is balanced (moving right turns the left side down). Send: a copy of the channel goes to the Send outputs at the Send level, after the fader, or before it with Send Point Pre-Fader . The four channels and the Return (at Return Level ) are added, scaled by Master , and pass the limiter . It holds the output below −0.3 dBFS by turning the gain down just before a peak (a 1 ms lookahead) and releasing it over 50 ms. Switching it off leaves the signal untouched. Solo doesn't affect the sends, so a reverb keeps its tail while you solo. Mono sums every channel (and the return) to mono: Pan is ignored and Out L and Out R carry the same signal. The view The view is a horizontal row of channel strips. Each has a Pan dial, a Send dial, M ute and S olo buttons and a Level fader with a level meter beside it (peak, with a hold line and a clip light; click the light to reset). The meter shares the fader's scale, so 0 dB lines up on both. The master strip has the Master fader with a stereo meter, the Limiter and Mono buttons, and the limiter's gain reduction. Double-click a control to reset it. How to use it? Mix a drum kit: each drum into its own channel, Out L/R to an audio output port. A shared reverb or delay: turn up each channel's Send , patch Send L/R into the effect and the effect's output into Return L/R . The return arrives about 0.7 ms late (the board treats the loop as feedback), which is inaudible for reverbs and delays. Rhythmic muting: a clock or a gate pattern into Mute 1 : the channel is silent while the gate is high. Ducking: the Level output follows the master's loudness; patch it with a negative amount onto another VCA's gain. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1–4 −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Pan 1–4 −1 (left) … +1 (right) 0 Send 1–4 −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB silence Return Level −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Master −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Mute 1–4 Off, On Off Solo 1–4 Off, On Off Send Point 1–4 Post-Fader, Pre-Fader Post-Fader Limiter Off, On On Mono Off, On Off Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 L audio Left (or mono) input of each channel In 1–4 R audio Right input; unpatched, the channel is mono Return L, R audio The effect return; Return R unpatched copies L Mute 1–4 gate Mutes the channel while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, R audio The master mix Send L, R audio The send bus Level control The master's loudness, 0 … 1 (10 ms attack, 200 ms release)

title: Crossfader
text: Crossfader Crossfader in the module view Introduction The Crossfader blends between two stereo signals with one knob: dry and wet of an effect, two oscillators, two drum loops, or two modulators. Patch an LFO or an envelope onto Fade and one sound turns into the other. How does it work? Fade at 0 plays only A , at 1 only B ; in between, both are mixed. Curve decides how: Equal Power: the loudness stays even across the fade. Use it for two different sounds. Linear: the gains add up to exactly 1. Use it for dry/wet of the same sound (where equal power would be 3 dB louder in the middle) and for modulation and pitch signals, where the output should be the exact average. If only the left input of a pair is patched, it feeds both sides. How to use it? Dry/wet: the dry signal into A , the effect's output into B , Curve Linear . Morph two oscillators: two different oscillators into A L and B L , a slow LFO onto Fade . Blend two modulators: two LFOs into A L and B L , Curve Linear ; Out L is a modulation source that moves between them. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Fade 0 (A) … 1 (B) 0.5 Curve Equal Power, Linear Equal Power Inputs Input Signal What it does A L, A R audio Source A; A R unpatched copies A L B L, B R audio Source B; B R unpatched copies B L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio The blend

title: VCA
text: VCA VCA in the module view Introduction A VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets the volume of a signal. On its own it's a stereo volume knob. Patch an envelope or an LFO onto its Gain and the volume follows that signal. This is how a note gets its loudness shape, and how tremolo and ducking work. How does it work? Both channels are multiplied by the same gain: Out = In × gain Gain is a 0 – 100 % knob. With the Linear response, gain is the knob value. With Exponential , it is the value cubed: 50 % on the knob is about −18 dB, and the bottom of the range fades smoothly toward silence. This sounds more natural for fades and envelopes. Gain starts at 0 % (closed). Modulation adds to the knob, so an envelope patched at 100 % amount opens the VCA from silence to full volume and closes it again. Range sets how far the amplifier can go: 100 % (the default), 200 % or 400 %. It multiplies the result, so the Gain knob and envelopes keep their meaning (100 % on the knob, or a full envelope, is now 2× or 4× the input, up to +12 dB). Use it to lift a quiet signal; mind the level after it. If only In L is patched, it feeds both channels. A mono oscillator then comes out on both sides. How to use it? Note volume: Oscillator Out → VCA In L ; ADSR Env → VCA Gain knob. VCA Out L/R goes to Voice Out or an output port. Tremolo: turn Gain up to about 50 % and patch a Function (cycling) onto Gain with a small amount. Ducking: set Gain to 100 % and patch an envelope onto Gain with a negative amount: each trigger dips the volume. Plain volume or mute: use the knob without any cable. To shape a control signal instead of audio, use Utility . The VCA is built for audio. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Gain 0 – 100 % 0 % Response Linear, Exponential Exponential Gain: the amplification, from silence (0 %) to unity (100 %). The VCA never boosts. Patch envelopes and LFOs here; the ring around the knob shows the gain really used. Response: how the gain value maps to volume. Linear: volume = gain. Good for amplitude modulation at audio rate and for signals that should stay proportional. Exponential: volume = gain³ (about −60 dB to 0 dB). Fades and envelopes sound even, the way our ears expect. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio left input × gain Out R audio right input × gain

title: Sampler
text: Sampler Sampler in the module view Introduction Sampler plays a WAV file like an instrument. Load a sample, optionally cut it into slices (by hand, at the transients, or into beats), and play it from notes or triggers with up to 16 independent playheads . A play mode decides how each playhead ends, an ADSR envelope and a filter shape it, and Speed, Transpose and Position move it around. Sampler is the module for "play a sample" and "chop a loop and sequence the pieces"; Splice is the one for recording onto a reel, Grains for a moving cloud. How does it work? Loading. Drop a WAV file on the view (or press Import WAV ). The file is stored in the media folder, so the board keeps working on any computer that has it. 8, 16, 24 and 32-bit files, mono or stereo, any sample rate. Slices. Markers cut the sample into slices. Slicing chooses how they are made, and all three write the same markers, so you can start automatically and finish by hand: Manual: double-click the waveform to add a marker, double-click a marker to remove it, drag a marker to move it. Threshold: Detect finds the transients. Sensitivity sets how many (more to the right), Min gap the shortest slice. Beats: Equal cuts Divisions equal slices. On BPM cuts the sample on a grid: Divisions over Bars bars at BPM . Detect BPM estimates the tempo of a loop. Click a slice to select it; its own settings (mode, transpose, level, pan, reverse, choke group) appear below the waveform. Shift-click or Audition plays it. Starting a playhead. With Trigger By = Note , the Notes input plays the sample: in whole-sample mode the note sets the pitch (the sample sounds as recorded at Root Note ); with Slice Mode on, each key plays one slice, slice 1 on the root note and the following slices on the keys above it (keys beyond the last slice do nothing). With Trigger By = CV , a pulse at Trigger starts a playhead: Slice (0 – 100 % picks slice 1 … n) or the selected slice plays, Pitch sets the pitch, Velocity the level. A Gate holds the playhead open; without one, the sample plays to the end of its region. Patch only Gate , without Trigger , and the gate's rising edge starts it. Step moves the selected slice to the next one (and wraps); the Next and Random buttons do the same by hand. Stop releases every playhead. Play modes. Mode decides how a playhead ends; each slice can override it. Gate: plays while the note is held, then fades out over Release . Reaching the end of the sample or slice stops it. To end of sample: plays on to the sample end, whatever the gate does. To end of slice: plays to the next marker, whatever the gate does. Loop: loops the sample (or the slice) until released. Loop Style can be Ping-pong ; Loop Crossfade hides the seam. One-shot: plays the whole slice, ignoring the gate. End fires whenever a playhead reaches its end or wraps its loop. Region. Start and End trim the sample. In slice mode they trim each slice, as a fraction of it, so End at 50 % plays the first half of every slice. Pitch and speed. Transpose (semitones) and Fine (cents) set the pitch; Pitch adds 1 V per octave to CV-triggered playheads. Speed is the playback ratio and negative plays backwards; Speed (input) adds 1 V per octave. In this version pitch and speed are one thing, like tape: playing twice as fast sounds an octave higher. Key Tracking sets how much the note number moves the pitch (100 % is normal; 0 % plays every key at the same pitch). Quality is the interpolation: Linear (cheapest), Cubic , or Sinc (cleanest when pitching down). Moving the playhead. With Position Mode Scrub , turning Position (or modulating it) moves every sounding playhead to that point of its region, with a 3 ms crossfade, so an LFO or a sequencer can scan through the sample. With Offset , Position is read when a playhead starts and sets where in the region it begins (random-access starts). Many playheads. Voices sets how many play at once (1 – 16). Poly gives each note its own playhead; when all are in use the oldest (or the quietest one already releasing) fades out in 5 ms. Mono plays one at a time and goes back to the previous held note when you let go; Legato does the same but changes pitch without restarting the sample. Layers starts several playheads with every note: Layers sets how many, Layer Pitch the interval between them and Layer Offset a delay between starts, for unison, octaves or chords. Choke groups. Slices in the same choke group cut each other off: set a closed and an open hi-hat to the same group. Envelope, filter, level. Every playhead has an ADSR envelope (attack linear, decay and release exponential) and a low-pass filter. Filter Env opens (or closes, when negative) the cutoff with the envelope, up to six octaves. Velocity sets how much a note's velocity changes the level and the brightness. Crush lowers the sample rate and bit depth for a gritty sound. Pan balances a stereo sample, or places a mono one. Outputs. Out L and Out R carry the mix. With Voice Outs on, a jack for each of the 16 voices appears; a voice whose jack is patched is taken out of the mix, so each can have its own effects. Playhead is the position of the newest playhead in the file (0 – 100 %); Active is the share of voices in use; Slice pulses when a playhead starts. How to use it? Play a sample from a keyboard: Mode Gate , Voices 8, a Release of 100 ms. Set Root Note to the note the sample was recorded at. Drum rack from a loop: Slicing Threshold and Detect , then Slice Mode on, Mode To end of slice . A drum sequencer's Notes plays the slices from the root note up. Resequence a break: Beats with 16 divisions, Trigger By CV, a trigger source into Trigger and a control signal (0 – 100 %, from a sequencer or a random source) into Slice . Hi-hats: give the closed and open slices choke group 1. Pad from a one-shot: Mode Loop , Loop Crossfade 20 ms, Attack 300 ms, Release 1 s. Scanning: Mode Loop , a very short region ( Start 40 %, End 41 %) and a slow LFO on Start and End together, or Position Mode Scrub with an LFO on Position . Reverse cymbals: Speed −1 with Mode To end of slice . Chord from one note: Voice Mode Layers , Layers 3, Layer Pitch 4. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Start 0 – 100 % 0 % End 0 – 100 % 100 % Position 0 – 100 % 0 % Transpose −48 … +48 semitones 0 Fine −100 … +100 cents 0 Speed −4 … +4 +1 Attack 0.5 ms – 10 s 1 ms Decay 1 ms – 10 s 100 ms Sustain 0 – 100 % 100 % Release 1 ms – 10 s 50 ms Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Pan −100 … +100 % 0 Velocity 0 – 100 % 50 % Crush 0 – 100 % 0 % Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 20 kHz Resonance 0 – 100 % 0 % Filter Env −100 … +100 % 0 % Layer Pitch −24 … +24 semitones 7 Layer Offset 0 – 200 ms 0 Every knob is a modulation destination. Layer Pitch and Layer Offset show in Layers voice mode. Settings Setting Values Default Trigger By Note, CV Note Slice Mode Off, On Off Mode Gate, To end of sample, To end of slice, Loop, One-shot Gate Loop Style Forward, Ping-pong Forward Loop Crossfade 0 – 50 ms 5 ms Voices 1 – 16 8 Voice Mode Poly, Mono, Legato, Layers Poly Layers 1 – 8 2 Root Note 0 – 127 (MIDI) 60 Key Tracking −100 … +200 % 100 % Quality Linear, Cubic, Sinc Cubic Position Mode Scrub, Offset Scrub Voice Outs Off, On Off Output Stereo, Mono Stereo Per-slice settings Mode (or Inherit ), Transpose (±48 semitones), Level (0 – 200 %), Pan, Reverse and Choke group (none, 1 – 8). They are saved with the markers. Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes plays the sample ( Trigger By Note) Trigger trigger starts a playhead ( Trigger By CV) Gate gate holds CV-triggered playheads open; alone, its rising edge starts one Slice control picks the slice for the next trigger, 0 – 100 % → 1 … n Pitch pitch 1 V/oct for CV-triggered playheads Speed pitch 1 V/oct, added to Speed Velocity control velocity of CV-triggered playheads (full when unpatched) Stop trigger releases every playhead Step trigger moves the selected slice to the next one Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the mix End trigger a pulse when a playhead reaches its end or wraps Slice trigger a pulse when a playhead starts Playhead control the newest playhead's position in the file, 0 – 100 % Active control voices in use ÷ Voices Voice 1 … 16 audio each voice on its own (with Voice Outs on) Not yet Time-stretching (changing the speed without changing the pitch) is planned; for now Speed and pitch go together.

title: Splice
text: Splice Splice in the module view Introduction Splice is a tape-style sampler and looper. You record onto a reel of up to two minutes of stereo, cut it into splices with markers, and play them back at any speed, forwards or backwards. Inside a splice, Window Size , Position and Overlap break playback into small repeating pieces, from micro-loops to a granular cloud. Triggers move between splices, a control signal picks one directly, and WAV files can be dropped onto the reel. Splice is the module for "record something, then play with it"; Grains is the one for a live, moving cloud. How does it work? Recording. Press ● Rec (or send a gate or trigger to Record ) to start and again to stop ( Record Mode Toggle ); with Gate , recording runs while the gate is high. Record Target decides where it goes: New splice (default): the take is appended to the reel as a new splice, which becomes the current one and plays as soon as you stop. Current splice : overdubs into the splice that's playing, at the play head and at its speed (tape style). Overdub sets how much of the old audio stays: 0 % replaces it, 100 % layers on top. Whole reel : clears the reel and records from the start. Reel Length (15 s – 2 min) is how much the reel can hold. Monitor passes the input through: never, while recording, or always. Splices. Mark (button or trigger) cuts: while recording, it splits the take there; while playing, it splits the current splice at the play head. In the view, double-click the reel to add a marker, double-click a marker to remove it (the two splices merge), drag a marker to move it, click a splice to pick it. Playback. Speed is the playback ratio: 1 normal, 2 an octave up, negative backwards, 0 stops the tape. The Speed input adds 1 V per octave, so a sequencer plays the reel melodically. At the end of the splice it loops, or with Loop on One-shot it stops until Play . End fires at the end of each pass. With Sync on 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars, the speed is set so the splice lasts exactly that long at the song's tempo (pitch follows, like tape) and stays locked to the bars, even after a loop jump. Moving between splices. Next steps to the next splice (and wraps). Select (0 … 1, a control input) picks a splice directly; without it, the Pick knob does. Shift decides when the change happens: Immediate (crossfaded over Fade ), End of window , or End of splice . The view shows a pending splice with a dashed outline. Play restarts the current (or pending) splice. Windows. Window Size is the length of a piece of the splice (down to 0.5 ms), Position where in the splice it sits. Overlap decides how the windows play: 0 – 30 %: each window plays once, then a gap: rhythmic stutter (the gap shrinks as Overlap rises). 30 – 50 %: windows repeat back to back with a short crossfade: a clean loop. This is the default; at Window Size 100 % the whole splice loops. 50 – 100 %: 2 to 4 overlapping windows with soft edges: a granular texture. Above 75 % some windows play an octave up or down or a fifth up, spread across the stereo field (from Seed , so it repeats). A slow LFO on Position scrubs through the splice. With End Mode on Window , End fires at every window: a clock taken from the audio. Position and Splice (outputs) report the play head within the splice and which splice is playing. Fade sets the crossfades at window and splice boundaries and the record punch-in and out; at 0 the playback is sample-exact. Level sets the output level. Saving. The reel is stored as a WAV file in the media folder; the view saves it whenever the audio has changed and recording has stopped (the header says "unsaved" until then), and the board keeps its name, markers and current splice. Import WAV : drop a file on the reel or the Import WAV box; it replaces the reel. Clear reel empties it. How to use it? Live looper: Monitor Always , record a phrase, it loops when you stop. Record Target Current splice and Overdub 100 % to layer more. Chopped break: import a drum loop, add markers on the hits, patch a sequencer's trigger into Next (Shift Immediate ), or a stepped random source into Select . Tape tricks: an envelope onto Speed for tape-stop; Speed −1 for reverse. Melodic sampler: a sequencer's Pitch into the Speed input, Window Size 100 %, Loop One-shot , its trigger into Play . Texture: Window Size 3 %, Overlap 90 %, a slow LFO on Position . Phrase in time: Sync 2 bars : whatever you recorded fits two bars. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Splice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Splice under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Splice: Phrase Looper An LFO gate on Record captures one bar of a phrase and Sync locks the splice loop to the bars. Splice: Micro Cloud Window Size of 3 % and high Overlap turn a recorded arpeggio into a cloud that an LFO scrubs through via Position . Splice: Reel Keyboard One recorded note replayed melodically: a sequencer's pitch drives Speed and its trigger restarts the splice ( Loop on One-shot ). Splice: Chopped Break A recorded beat is re-cut with a random Position , short windows with low Overlap and a clock on Mark . Splice: Reverse Tape Drift A slow LFO on Speed sweeps playback from forward through standstill to reverse, like tape dragged by hand. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Speed −4 … +4 (×1 in the middle) +1 Window Size 0.001 – 100 % of the splice 100 % Position 0 – 100 % 0 % Overlap 0 – 100 % 40 % Pick 0 – 100 % 0 % Overdub 0 – 100 % 100 % Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Fade 0 – 50 ms 3 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Reel Length 15 s, 30 s, 60 s, 120 s 60 s Record Mode Gate, Toggle Toggle Record Target New splice, Current splice, Whole reel New splice Shift Immediate, End of window, End of splice End of splice End Mode Splice, Window Splice Loop Loop, One-shot Loop Monitor Off, Input while recording, Always Input while recording Sync Free, 1 bar, 2 bars, 4 bars, 8 bars Free Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the recording source; In L alone feeds both sides Record gate starts/stops recording (per Record Mode ) Mark trigger adds a marker at the record or play head Next trigger moves to the next splice Select control 0 … 1 picks splice 1 … n Play trigger restarts the current splice Speed pitch 1 V/oct on top of Speed Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the playback (and the input, per Monitor ) End trigger the end of each splice pass (or window) Position control the play head within the splice, 0 … 1 Splice control which splice plays, 0 … 1 The reel takes 46 MB at 48 kHz (always sized for two minutes); inside a Voice Cell each voice has its own reel.

title: Bender
text: Bender Bender in the module view Introduction Bender is a glitch effect in the spirit of circuit-bent samplers and skipping CDs. It listens to the input, grabs short pieces of it and, by chance, repeats, re-pitches, reverses, slices and corrupts them. Low settings add the odd stutter to a beat; high settings shred it. Every decision comes from Seed and the song position, so a glitch you like comes back every time you play that section, and the render sounds exactly like what you heard. How does it work? Segments. Bender cuts time into segments. With a note value in Sync and the transport playing, segments sit on the song grid (a 1/16 segment starts on every sixteenth, also after a loop jump). With Sync on Free , or while the transport is stopped, segments follow each other at Time (synced note values keep their length at the last tempo). With a cable in Clock , each pulse starts a segment. Segment fires at every segment start. Decisions. At each segment start Bender decides: pass the input, or glitch . Chance is the probability of a glitch. A glitch repeats the segment that just ended, Repeats segments long, then the input passes again; no new decision is made while a glitch plays. The decisions are drawn from Seed and the segment's number, so turning Chance up only adds glitches (the ones you had stay), and changing Seed gives a different pattern. A pulse at Glitch (or the Glitch button) makes the next segment a glitch; with Now on, it starts one immediately. Random puts out the segment's seeded value (−1 … +1) for modulation that matches the glitches; Active is high while a glitch plays. Bend is the playback speed of the repeats: 1 normal, 0.5 an octave down, 2 an octave up, negative values play backwards, and 0 stops the head on a 2 ms buzz. Bend Steps snaps it to octaves, octaves and fifths, or semitones. Bend Var lets each glitch pick a different speed from a set around Bend (half, double, reversed …). The repeat always lasts its full length: faster speeds loop the source within it. Slice makes each repetition shorter than the last: the accelerating stutter. In sync, the lengths are powers of two of the segment (1/16 → 1/32 → 1/64 …), so the ratchets stay on the grid. Corrupt sets the amount of the damage Mode picks: Mode What Corrupt does Crush lower sample rate (down to 1 kHz) and fewer bits (down to 3), no filter Dropout splits each repetition into 16 cells and silences cells by chance Fold up to +24 dB into a wavefolder, then a hard clip Shuffle cuts the source into 8 slices and plays some of them out of order Smear jitters the read position by up to 20 ms: a scratchy copy With Corrupt When on Always , Crush, Dropout and Fold also act between glitches. At 0 % every mode is exactly transparent. Edge is the crossfade at every switch (pass → glitch, repetition → repetition, glitch → pass, and the loop point of a re-pitched repeat): 100 % is 8 ms, 0 % hard cuts. Bender only clicks when you ask it to. Freeze (the button or the gate) loops the current source for as long as it's held and stops recording; Bend , Slice and Corrupt keep working on it. When you let go, the glitch ends at the next segment start, on the grid. Transport. When the transport stops mid-glitch, the glitch finishes its repeats and the input passes again. Bender has no tail. The view shows the decisions of this bar and the next while the transport plays in sync (the upcoming ones dimmed), otherwise the recent segments; the bar below shows the read head inside the source. How to use it? Occasional stutter on a beat: Sync 1/16, Chance 10 %, Repeats 2. Ratchets: Sync 1/8, Chance 30 %, Repeats 2, Slice 40 %. Tape-stop flavour: Bend 0.5, Bend Steps Octaves, Bend Var 50 %. Shredder: Chance 70 %, Mode Shuffle, Corrupt 80 %, Slice 30 %. Glitch on demand: Chance 0 %, Now on, a sequencer's trigger into Glitch . Matching movement: Random onto a filter's cutoff: it jumps with each decision. In a Voice Cell: each voice glitches on its own; with the same Seed they glitch together unless Voice In › Random moves a knob. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Bender does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Bender under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Bender: Stutter Beat Low Chance at a 1/16 Sync : now and then a slice repeats and stutters before the groove carries on. Bender: Ratchet Arp Slice at 40 % and Chance at 35 % cut an arpeggio into ratchets; Seed picks which beats get them. Bender: Tape-Stop Pad Smear mode with Bend at 0.5 and some Bend Var : pieces of a pad slur downward in octaves. Bender: Shredder Shuffle mode with high Chance and Corrupt rearranges and crumbles a beat and bass line. Bender: Glitch Triggers Chance at zero with a sequencer on the Glitch input: only chosen steps are glitched, and Random moves a filter. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Time 1 ms – 2 s 125 ms Chance 0 – 100 % 25 % Repeats 1 – 16 (stepped) 4 Bend −2 … +2 +1 Bend Var 0 – 100 % 0 % Slice 0 – 100 % 0 % Corrupt 0 – 100 % 0 % Edge 0 – 100 % 70 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Sync Free, 1/1 … 1/64T 1/16 Mode Crush, Dropout, Fold, Shuffle, Smear Crush Corrupt When Glitches only, Always Glitches only Bend Steps Free, Octaves, Fifths + octaves, Semitones Octaves Now Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the input; In L alone feeds both sides Clock trigger each pulse starts a segment Glitch trigger the next segment glitches (with Now : at once) Freeze gate loops the current source while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the processed signal Active gate high while a glitch plays Segment trigger a pulse at each segment start Random control the segment's seeded value, −1 … +1

title: Meta Mod
text: Meta Mod Meta Mod in the module view Introduction The Meta Mod combines two audio signals, a Carrier and a Modulator , into one. A single Algorithm knob sweeps through eight ways of combining them, from a plain crossfade over wavefolding and ring modulation to a vocoder, and Timbre changes the character of whichever algorithm is selected. An internal oscillator stands in for an unpatched input, so the module is a sound source on its own, and a ring modulator or vocoder for any track with one cable. How does it work? Inputs and the oscillator. The internal oscillator is the Oscillator's core (sine → triangle → saw → square with Osc Shape ) at C4 × 2^(Osc Octave + Osc Tune/12 + Pitch). It fills in for one input: Carrier patched Modulator patched Carrier is Modulator is no no oscillator silence no yes oscillator Modulator yes no Carrier oscillator yes yes Carrier Modulator So a synth voice needs only the Modulator cable (the oscillator plays the notes), and a track needs only the Carrier cable (the oscillator is a tunable modulator: a classic ring modulator). Patching or unpatching fades over 5 ms. Carrier Level and Mod Level set the gain into the algorithm (up to 200 %, +6 dB, which drives the nonlinear ones harder). Signals within ±1 pass unchanged; hotter ones are softly limited towards ±4. Algorithms. With carrier a , modulator b and Timbre t : # Algorithm What it does Timbre 0 Crossfade equal-power blend of a and b 0 = carrier, 50 % = both, 100 % = modulator 1 Fold sine-folds the sum a + b fold depth, 1× to 8× 2 Analog ring a diode-ring model: about a × b , saturating at high levels 0 = matched diodes, clean; 100 % = mismatched, carrier bleeds through with odd harmonics 3 Digital ring a × ( b + t ) / (1 + t ) 0 = ring modulation (only sum and difference tones), 100 % = amplitude modulation (carrier audible) 4 Bitwise a and b as integers, combined by Bitwise Op (XOR, AND, OR, wrap-around sum) resolution, 16 bits down to 2 5 Comparator 0–50 %: a square that is +1 where a > b , softening as Timbre rises; 50–100 %: towards max( a , b ) hardness, then the diode maximum 6 Vocoder the carrier through 12 bands, each shaped by the modulator's level in that band formant shift, ±1 octave (50 % = none) 7 Chebyshev the n -th Chebyshev polynomial of a : a full-scale sine becomes its n -th harmonic the order n , 1 to 16; the modulator sweeps it at audio rate Between two whole numbers the neighbours crossfade, so Algorithm 2.5 is half analog, half digital ring; modulating it at audio rate is a sound of its own. Every algorithm is levelled so two full-scale sines come out about equally loud at every position. Vocoder. The modulator is split into 12 bands from 100 Hz to 8 kHz; a follower (2 ms attack, 40 ms release) measures each band. The carrier goes through the same bands (moved by the formant shift), each levelled by its own follower, and each takes the modulator's band level. So the carrier's own spectrum hardly matters, only that it has energy in a band: noise and buzzy waves (saw, square) work best. The modulator's hiss above 8 kHz is added at −6 dB, which keeps consonants intelligible. Anti-aliasing. Fold, both rings, Bitwise, Comparator and Chebyshev create frequencies far above their inputs. Standard runs them at 2× the sample rate, High at 4× (Fold also uses antiderivative anti-aliasing); Eco doesn't oversample, for big Voice Cells. Crossfade, the vocoder and the dry signal are delayed to match, so morphing stays in phase. The outputs are delayed by 1 ms ( Standard , 47 samples) or 1.5 ms ( High , 70.5 samples). Output. A 5 Hz high-pass removes the DC that the comparator, bitwise and ring imbalance produce. Outputs stay within ±4. How to use it? Ring modulator for a track: Audio In → Carrier L/R . Algorithm 2 (default), tune the oscillator with Osc Tune and Osc Octave . Patch an LFO into Osc Tune for sweeping bell tones. Vocoder: a voice or drum loop into Modulator , a saw or noise into Carrier L , Algorithm 6. Patch Pitch from a sequencer for a robot choir with the internal oscillator as the carrier (leave Carrier unpatched and set Osc Shape to saw). Synth voice: Voice In Pitch → Pitch , a second Oscillator into Modulator , sweep Algorithm with an envelope. Harmonic sweeps: Algorithm 7 with a sine carrier; patch an LFO onto Timbre for a harmonic arpeggio. Envelope follower: Env follows the modulator (5 ms attack, 120 ms release); patch it to a filter or VCA for ducking and auto-wah. Dry/wet: Mix blends the carrier (after Carrier Level ) with the result. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Meta Mod does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Meta Mod under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Meta Mod: Ring Bells Algorithm 2 ring-modulates a sine melody with the internal oscillator while a slow LFO sweeps Osc Tune into inharmonic bells. Meta Mod: Robot Choir Algorithm 6 (vocoder): a drum beat in Modulator talks through a buzzy chord in Carrier ; Timbre drifts the formants. Meta Mod: Harmonic Arpeggio Algorithm 7 (Chebyshev) turns a sine into its Nth harmonic, and a stepped Random on Timbre picks N for each sixteenth. Meta Mod: Ring Bass A bass built inside Meta Mod: the internal oscillator is the carrier, a second oscillator the modulator, and an LFO glides Algorithm through ring, crossfade and fold. Meta Mod: Bitwise Machine Algorithm 4 with Bitwise Op XOR combines a saw lead and a square arpeggio into gritty digital chords; Timbre moves the bit depth. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Algorithm 0 – 7 2 (analog ring) Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Carrier Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Mod Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Osc Tune −24 … +24 st 0 st Osc Shape 0 – 100 % 0 % (sine) Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Osc Octave −3 … +3 0 Quality Eco (1×), Standard (2×), High (4×) Standard Bitwise Op XOR, AND, OR, Sum mod XOR All knobs are modulation destinations, evaluated every sample (audio-rate Algorithm and Timbre work). Osc Octave , Quality and Bitwise Op are settings. The view's algorithm strip sets Algorithm with a click. Inputs Input Signal What it does Carrier L audio the carrier; unpatched: the oscillator Carrier R audio right carrier; patched, the module runs in stereo, otherwise Carrier L feeds both sides Modulator audio the modulator (mono, shared); unpatched while the carrier is patched: the oscillator Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the oscillator's pitch, added to Osc Octave and Osc Tune ; 0.0 = C4 Sync trigger restarts the oscillator's cycle (hard sync) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the result after Mix ; Out R equals Out L in mono Osc audio the internal oscillator, whatever it is used for Env control, 0 … 1 envelope of the modulator

title: Delay
text: Delay Delay in the module view Introduction Delay is a simple stereo echo. Each side has its own time, either free in milliseconds or locked to the song's tempo. The echoes return through a low cut and a high cut, so they can get thinner or darker with every repeat, and Ping-Pong bounces them from side to side. Put it after anything that needs echoes: a lead, a drum bus, a vocal. For long, strange or reversed delays use Zone Delay instead. How does it work? The input goes into one delay line per side. What comes out of the line is mixed with the dry signal ( Mix ), and a part of it ( Feedback ) goes back in, after the filters, so every echo is a little quieter than the one before. Free: Time L and Time R in milliseconds. Tempo: Rate L and Rate R are note values (1/32 … 1/1, straight, dotted . and triplet T ) at the song's tempo. Change the tempo and the echoes follow. Stereo: both sides are independent. A mono source patched into In L only is heard in both ears, and with different times on the two sides you get a wide stereo echo. Ping-Pong: the first echo is on the left, the second on the right, the third on the left again. The input is mixed to mono first. Changing a time while the sound plays, by hand, with a modulator or by changing the tempo, makes the echoes slide in pitch like a tape echo. They never click. Turn Time quickly for a classic dub effect. Feedback at 100 % repeats forever without getting louder. Low Cut and High Cut only work on the repeats, so the first sound stays untouched. How to use it? Slapback: Free , both times 80–120 ms, Feedback 0–10 %. Dotted eighth: Tempo , Rate 1/8., Feedback 40 %. The classic rhythm echo that fills the gaps. Wide echo: Tempo with Rate L 1/8 and Rate R 1/8., Mode Stereo . Ping-pong: Mode Ping-Pong , both rates 1/4, High Cut around 4 kHz. Dub: Feedback 70–90 %, Low Cut 200 Hz, High Cut 2 kHz and turn Time . Send effect: Mix 100 % on an effect track or a send; keep the dry signal in the mixer. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Time L 1 … 2000 ms 300 ms Time R 1 … 2000 ms 300 ms Feedback 0 … 100 % 40 % Low Cut 20 … 2000 Hz 20 Hz (off) High Cut 500 … 20000 Hz 20 kHz (off) Mix 0 … 100 % 50 % Sync Free, Tempo Free Rate L 1/32 … 1/1 1/8 Rate R 1/32 … 1/1 1/8 Mode Stereo, Ping-Pong Stereo Time shows with Sync on Free , Rate with Sync on Tempo . The longest time is 4 seconds. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio Left input In R audio Right input; unpatched it follows In L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio Dry and echoes, left Out R audio Dry and echoes, right

title: Delay Net
text: Delay Net Delay Net in the module view Introduction Delay Net is a network of up to eight delay lines whose repeats feed each other. One Time knob sets the span of the network, Taps how many lines take part and Scatter how they're spaced, from even rhythmic echoes to clustered bursts. Some lines can play backwards, every pass through the network can be filtered, saturated or worn down, and Routing decides how the lines feed each other. Small settings give multi-tap rhythms; large ones turn a single hit into an evolving texture. How does it work? Taps. Each tap is its own delay line. The last one sits at Time ; the others are spread before it. With Scatter at 0 they're evenly spaced (4 taps over 1 s: 250, 500, 750, 1000 ms); turning it up bunches them towards the end, down towards the start. Jitter moves every tap away from its place by a seeded random amount (up to half the gap to its neighbours), so the groove is loose but the same every time. Taps is continuous: between two whole numbers the next tap fades in and the others slide to their new places, so modulating it is smooth. Time. In Free , Time is 5 ms – 8 s. With a note value in Sync , the network spans that note at the song's tempo and the Time knob scales it by ¼, ½, 1 or 2 (four zones of the knob): 4 taps over 1/2 give straight eighths. With a cable in Clock , the span is the pulse interval × ¼, ½, 1, 2, 3 or 4. Time Change picks how time changes sound: Crossfade (the default; a second head jumps to the new time and the two crossfade over 40 ms, the pitch stays) or Tape (the heads glide, the repeats bend in pitch). Reverse turns a share of the active taps around: they play the last stretch of audio backwards (windows as long as the tap's own time, up to about 5 s). Which taps turn follows a seeded order, so raising Reverse adds them one at a time. Character processes every repeat before it goes back into the network, so later repeats are darker, dirtier or more worn than early ones: Character Each pass 0 % Clean nothing 20 % Warm 6 kHz low-pass, 60 Hz high-pass, soft saturation 40 % Filter a band-pass per tap, spread over ±1 octave around 1.2 kHz: every echo its own colour 60 % Drive asymmetric saturation (+12 dB), 4 kHz low-pass 80 % Crush 8 kHz sample rate, 8 bits 100 % Wear wow and flutter, a little noise, 3 kHz low-pass, a little level loss: an old tape loop Positions in between blend two neighbours. Tone moves every filter up or down by up to two octaves. Routing decides where each repeat goes: Routing Where Sound Parallel each line into itself independent multi-tap echoes Chain line 1 → 2 → 3 …, the last nowhere a cascade that grows longer, then stops Ring 1 → 2 → … → last → 1 repeats walk around the network Mesh all into all (Hadamard) dense, diffuse, reverb-like build-up Feedback at 100 % is the edge of stability for every routing; above it the loop's soft limiter holds the level. Switching Routing crossfades over 50 ms. Stereo. The taps alternate left and right, spread by Width (0 % is centred). Tap 1 … Tap 4 put out those lines on their own, before panning. Pulse fires at each tap's time after every input onset: a rhythm of the echoes to clock other modules with. Freeze (the button or the gate) fades the input out, sets the feedback to exactly 1 and bypasses the character: the network circulates without loss (Ring and Mesh keep the material moving; Chain loops back to its start while frozen). Clear empties every line with a short fade. Tails and renders. Stopping the transport leaves the network ringing. With Clear on Play the lines are emptied when the transport starts; Jitter, the reverse order and Wear's wow and noise come from Seed , so renders repeat. How to use it? Multi-tap rhythm: Parallel, Sync 1/2, 4 taps, Feedback 30 %, Jitter 20 % for a human feel. Rotating echoes: Ring, Sync 1 bar, 3 taps, Scatter +0.5, Width 100 %. Instant ambience: Mesh, Time 150 ms, 8 taps, Feedback 85 %, Character 20 %. Reverse swells: Reverse 50 %, Time 1.5 s, Feedback 50 %. Lo-fi tape loop: Character 100 %, Feedback 95 %, then Freeze. Echo clock: patch Pulse into a drum's trigger: it plays along with the repeats of whatever you feed in. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Delay Net does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Delay Net under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Delay Net: Ring Pad Six taps in Ring routing with a dark Character and high Feedback smear soft notes into a slowly turning pad. Delay Net: Dotted Pluck Grid Sync on a dotted eighth and Parallel routing place four taps on a rhythmic grid around plucks; Scatter nudges them off it. Delay Net: Reverse Mesh Mesh routing with Reverse and Jitter blooms every note into reversed clouds; a slow LFO drifts Time . Delay Net: Drum Echoes A beat through a synced Chain with Jitter and Scatter : a loose, dubby shadow of the groove. Delay Net: Overdriven Loop Feedback near its limit turns the network into a self-sustaining drone; an LFO on Character moves it from clean to gritty. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Time 5 ms – 8 s 600 ms Taps 1 – 8 (continuous) 4 Scatter −1 … +1 0 Jitter 0 – 100 % 0 % Reverse 0 – 100 % 0 % Feedback 0 – 110 % 45 % Character 0 – 100 % 20 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Width 0 – 100 % 70 % Mix 0 – 100 % 40 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Routing Parallel, Chain, Ring, Mesh Ring Sync Free, 4 bars … 1/16T Free Time Change Tape, Crossfade Crossfade Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the input (mixed to mono into the lines); In L alone feeds both Clock trigger the span is a multiple of the pulse interval Freeze gate the network circulates without loss while high Clear trigger empties all lines Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry and wet mixed by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the network only Tap 1 … Tap 4 audio lines 1 – 4 on their own Pulse trigger each tap's time after an input onset The lines hold 8 seconds each (about 16 MB at 48 kHz), so put Delay Net after a Voice Cell rather than inside one.

title: Verb
text: Verb Verb in the module view Introduction Verb is a stereo reverb built to be played , not just set. Every knob, including Size and Decay , can be modulated, even at audio rate, without zipper noise or clicks. It goes from small rooms through halls to endless, slowly drifting pads, and Freeze holds whatever is in the reverb for as long as you like. Patch an envelope onto Size for swelling spaces, an LFO onto Decay for breathing tails, or a sequencer onto Freeze for rhythmic holds. How does it work? The sound first passes a pre-delay , then four diffusers per channel (allpass filters that smear the onset into a dense wash), then the tank : a feedback delay network of 16 delay lines (8 in Eco quality) whose outputs are mixed and fed back into each other. Every line loses a little level and a little treble on each pass, which sets how long and how dark the tail is. Slow internal modulation of the line lengths keeps the tail from ringing metallically. Size scales every delay in the tank, from a small booth (≈ 3 m) to a huge space (≈ 60 m). Moving it bends the tail in pitch like tape speeding up or slowing down, never a click; very fast modulation turns into a shimmer. Decay is the time the tail takes to fall by 60 dB (T60), 0.1 s to 60 s. Above that the knob enters the infinite zone: between 92 % and 96 % the decay stretches towards endless, and from 96 % up the tail never fades (the view says Infinite ). New sound keeps piling up there, so a soft limiter steps in whenever the tank gets loud. Damping makes the highs die faster than the mids (at 100 % the treble decays ten times faster). Bass stretches (up to 2×) or shortens (down to ½) the lows. Diffusion : low values keep the early echoes audible; high values give a smooth wash.
