Mod Rate and Mod Depth : speed and amount of the internal movement. 0 % depth is static (and can ring); 100 % is a seasick chorus. Tone tilts the reverb around 800 Hz, ±6 dB: dark ↔ bright. Width sets the stereo width of the reverb: 0 % mono, 100 % as the tank makes it, 150 % wider. Mix blends dry and wet with equal power. Wet L/R always carry the reverb alone. Freeze (the gate input, or the latching Freeze button in the view): within 20 ms the input to the tank fades out and the tail stops decaying. The modulation keeps running, so the held sound shimmers instead of freezing solid. Size and Mod Depth still act on it; Decay , Damping and Bass return when you release. The dry path is untouched, so you can play over a frozen pad. Clear (trigger input or button) fades the reverb out over 10 ms, empties it and fades back in. Clear on Play empties it when the transport starts, so two renders of the same section are identical. Otherwise a tail from before keeps ringing, as on a hardware reverb. The internal modulation restarts from Seed on every transport start, so it repeats too. Changing Quality or Seed also goes through a short fade. Pre-delay Sync sets the pre-delay to a note value at the song tempo (1/64 to 1/2, straight, dotted or triplet, at most 1 s); the Pre-delay knob is hidden then. The view shows the decay of the lows, mids and highs from the current (modulated) settings on a log time axis, with the pre-delay as a gap, a Freeze button that lights while frozen (from the button or the gate), and a meter of the wet level. How to use it? Send effect: Mix 100 %, feed it from a send or a mixer's aux, take Out (or Wet ) back in. Insert: Mix 20–40 % directly after a voice or a drum bus. Swelling space: an ADSR onto Size (and a little onto Decay ). Breathing tail: a slow LFO onto Decay or Damping . Endless pad: Decay at the top (Infinite), Mix 100 %, play chords in, then lower Decay to let it go. Or Freeze with a gate from a sequencer for rhythmic holds. Ducked reverb: the Env output of a drum bus onto Mix with a negative amount. Tempo pre-delay: Pre-delay Sync 1/16 or 1/8 keeps the reverb off the transient, in time. Shimmer-ish: Mod Depth high, Mod Rate 2–4 Hz, Tone bright. Spatial effects: an audio-rate oscillator onto Size turns the tail into a frequency-modulated cloud. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Verb does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Verb under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Verb: Cathedral Large Size , a Decay of 14 s, Damping and Pre-delay turn a slow melody into a huge hall. Verb: Tight Room A small Size , short Decay and high Damping glue a drum beat like a booth. Verb: Freeze Pad A square LFO on the Freeze gate holds the tank as an endless chord, then lets it go to catch the next phrase. Verb: Breathing Space Slow LFOs on Size , Decay and Tone plus Mod Depth make the room breathe around an arpeggio. Verb: Pre-delay Echoes Pre-delay Sync on a dotted eighth gives one clear rhythmic echo before a short, diffuse bloom. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Size 0 – 100 % 50 % Decay 0.1 s – 60 s, then ∞ (top 8 % of the knob) 2.5 s Pre-delay 0 – 1000 ms 20 ms Diffusion 0 – 100 % 70 % Damping 0 – 100 % 40 % Bass 0.5× – 2× 1× Mod Rate 0.05 – 8 Hz 0.6 Hz Mod Depth 0 – 100 % 25 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Width 0 – 150 % 100 % Mix 0 – 100 % 35 % Pre-delay Sync Free, 1/64 … 1/2 (triplet, straight, dotted) Free Quality Eco (8 lines), Fine (16 lines) Fine Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Freeze (latch) Off, On Off Decay: the knob reads seconds; past 60 s (92 %) it is the infinite zone, from 96 % fully infinite. Damping: high T60 = Decay × (1 − 0.9 × Damping). Bass: low T60 (below ≈ 250 Hz) = Decay × Bass. Quality: Eco costs about half the CPU; Fine is denser. Seed: the start phases and rates of the internal modulation. Freeze (latch): the view's Freeze button; saved with the board (the reverb itself opens empty). The settings are not modulatable; all knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Freeze gate while high, the reverb holds its contents (ORed with the latch) Clear trigger empties the reverb with a 10 ms fade Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the dry/wet mix set by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the reverb only (after Tone and Width ) Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on the wet signal (5 ms attack, 200 ms release) Verb uses about 2.5 MB of memory per instance at 48 kHz. Inside a Voice Cell every voice gets its own reverb, so it's usually better placed after the cell.

title: Zone Delay
text: Zone Delay Zone Delay in the module view Introduction Zone Delay is one stereo delay for every delay time worth having: tuned combs and flanging, doubling and slapback, rhythmic echoes and loops of up to 20 seconds. Zone picks the time range and Time moves within it. The other knobs shape what happens to the repeats: how they sound, how much they smear into a cloud and how they move across the stereo field. Three switches turn it into a performance instrument: Reverse , Hold and Ping-Pong . How does it work? Zones. Each zone is a time range; Time moves through it exponentially. Zone Name Free range Synced values 1 Comb 0.25 – 12 ms – (follows Pitch ) 2 Short 8 – 120 ms 1/128 … 1/32 3 Echo 80 ms – 1.2 s 1/32 … 1/2 4 Long 0.6 – 5 s 1/4 … 2 bars 5 Vast 3 – 20 s 1 bar … 8 bars The view prints the actual time. With Sync on Transport , Time steps through the zone's note values (straight, dotted and triplet) at the song's tempo. With a cable in Clock , the time is the interval between the last two pulses, and Time picks a ratio of it (¼, ⅓, ½, ⅔, 1, 3/2, 2, 3, 4). In the Comb zone with a cable in Pitch , the delay is tuned to that note ( Time becomes ±12 semitones), so a Voice Cell's pitch plays the comb in tune. Time changes. Time Change decides what happens when the time moves: Tape: the read head glides to the new time ( Glide ), so the repeats bend in pitch like a tape echo. Modulating Time fast gives FM-like wobbles, always without clicks. Crossfade: a second head jumps to the new time and the two crossfade (30 ms in Comb and Short, 60 ms in Echo, 120 ms in Long and Vast). The pitch never changes; fast modulation becomes stepped. The repeats. Feedback sets how much of each repeat comes back; above 100 % the loop grows until the character's saturation holds it, a stable, compressed drone. Character morphs through five loop sounds: Character Sound 0 % Clean flat, only a 20 kHz low-pass 25 % Tape 7 kHz low-pass, 40 Hz high-pass, soft saturation, a little hiss 50 % Dark 2.2 kHz low-pass, 120 Hz high-pass, gentle saturation 75 % Band a band-pass at 1 kHz: telephone repeats 100 % Lo-Fi 12 kHz sample-rate reduction, 10 bits, 5 kHz low-pass Positions in between blend two neighbours. The character colours every pass, so later repeats are darker or dirtier than early ones. Tone moves all its filters up or down by up to two octaves. Diffuse adds allpass diffusion in the feedback path: the first echo stays clear, later ones dissolve into a cloud; at 100 % with high feedback it becomes a reverb with the delay time as its pre-delay. Stereo. Offset makes the right side's time longer (positive) or shorter (negative) than the left's. Wobble adds slow tape wow and a little flutter, chorus-like in the short zones and subtle in the long ones. Ping-Pong crosses the feedback over, and the first repeat starts on the left only, so even a mono source bounces from side to side. Reverse plays the last Time worth of audio backwards in overlapping windows; the reversed sound is fed back, so repeats alternate direction. Hold stops recording and loops what is in the buffer, without any loss; Time then changes the loop's speed (Tape) or its length (Crossfade), and Reverse plays the held loop backwards. Release Hold and the input comes back. The three buttons in the view latch; the gate inputs work while high. Tails and renders. Stopping the transport leaves the echoes ringing. With Clear on Play the buffer is emptied when the transport starts, so renders start from silence and repeat exactly; Wobble restarts from Seed either way. How to use it? Dub echo: Zone 3, Sync on Transport , Time on 1/8., Feedback 70 %, Character 30 %. Ride Tone and Feedback by hand. Karplus pluck in a Voice Cell: Zone 1, Pitch from Voice In › Pitch , a short noise burst into In L , Feedback 95 %, Mix 100 %. Flanger: Zone 1 without Pitch , an LFO on Time , Feedback 60 %. Tape-stop scratches: Tape mode with a short Glide, a stepped random source on Time . Looper: Zone 5, Mix 50 %, press Hold to keep a phrase; Reverse plays it backwards. Ambient wash: Zone 4, Feedback 90 %, Diffuse 80 %, Wobble 40 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Zone Delay does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Zone Delay under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Zone Delay: Dub Echo Zone 3 with Sync on Transport and a tape Character ; a square LFO on the Ping-Pong gate bounces the repeats. Zone Delay: Tuned Combs Zone 1 (Comb) tuned by the Pitch input, with high Feedback : a sequencer plays resonant, string-like rings. Zone Delay: Vast Hold Loop Zone 5 is a multi-bar loop; LFOs on the Hold and Reverse gates freeze and flip what is in the buffer. Zone Delay: Tape Dive Time Change Tape with a long Glide and a stepped random source on Time : every jump bends the echoes. Zone Delay: Diffuse Cloud Full Diffuse and high Feedback in the Long zone melt the repeats of a drum groove into a cloud; Offset widens it. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Zone 1 – 5 (stepped) 3 Time 0 – 100 % of the zone 50 % Feedback 0 – 110 % 40 % Character 0 – 100 % 25 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Diffuse 0 – 100 % 0 % Offset −50 … +50 % 0 % Wobble 0 – 100 % 10 % Mix 0 – 100 % 35 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Sync Free, Transport Free Time Change Tape, Crossfade Tape Glide 5 ms – 2 s (Tape) 150 ms Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the input; In L alone feeds both sides Clock trigger the time is the pulse interval × the ratio Time picks Pitch pitch Comb zone: tunes the delay to the note Reverse gate repeats play backwards while high Hold gate the buffer loops while high Ping-Pong gate repeats bounce between the sides while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry and wet mixed by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the repeats only Tap trigger a pulse each time the delay time elapses The delay holds 30 seconds per side (about 16 MB at 48 kHz), so put it after a Voice Cell rather than inside one.

title: Chorus
text: Chorus Chorus in the module view Introduction The Chorus makes one sound into several: it mixes the input with copies of itself that are delayed by a few milliseconds, with the delay time swinging up and down. The slightly changing delay detunes the copies against the original, which sounds like several players, or a wide, shimmering instrument. Set to a very short delay with feedback it becomes a flanger , with the sweeping comb-filter whoosh of jet planes and tape machines. How does it work? Each channel has a short delay line. A triangle LFO swings its delay time around the centre Delay , with Depth as the share of the centre time it moves. A bit of the delayed signal is fed back into the delay line ( Feedback ). In Chorus mode every channel has two voices, with the LFO half a cycle apart and slightly different delay times, so the sound is thicker. In Flanger mode there is one voice per channel and the feedback is a little more generous. Rate is the LFO speed, 0.02 to 10 Hz. Slow rates (0.2–0.8 Hz) are lush, fast ones become vibrato. Depth is how far the delay time swings. More depth is a stronger detune. Delay is the centre delay time. Chorus likes 7–20 ms; a flanger 0.5–5 ms. Feedback sends the delayed signal back in. Positive feedback emphasises the comb's peaks (metallic ring); negative feedback emphasises the notches (hollow, "inverted" flanging). Chorus uses little or none. Spread moves the right channel's LFO away from the left, up to half a cycle, which makes a wide stereo movement. At 0 both sides move together. Mode is Chorus or Flanger. Mix blends dry and wet. 50 % is the classic setting; the flanger notches are deepest at 50 %. Mix, rate, depth, delay and feedback can all be modulated. Modulating Delay with another LFO is how tape-style wobble is made. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Lush chorus on a pad: Chorus mode, Rate 0.4 Hz, Depth 50 %, Delay 12 ms, Mix 40 %. Jet flanger: Flanger mode, Rate 0.15 Hz, Depth 80 %, Delay 2 ms, Feedback 70 %, Mix 50 %. Hollow flanger: the same with Feedback −70 %. Vibrato: Rate 5 Hz, Depth 20 %, Mix 100 % (no dry signal means no chorus effect, only pitch wobble). Slap thickener on a guitar: Delay 20 ms, Depth 0 %, Mix 30 %. Origin The modulated-delay voice (swinging delay with feedback, and the flanger's extra sample of delay) is from Chorus and Flanger (DaisySP) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version puts both effects in one stereo module, with an LFO phase spread, cubic interpolation, feedback in both polarities and a rate in hertz. The original licence text is in this module's LICENSE file.

title: Freq Shifter
text: Freq Shifter Freq Shifter in the module view Introduction The Freq Shifter moves every frequency of a sound up or down by the same number of hertz. That's different from a pitch shift: a pitch shift keeps the ratios between the partials, a frequency shift breaks them. A few tenths of a hertz give slow phasing and beating; tens or hundreds of hertz turn harmonic sounds into bells, metal and detuned radio. With feedback the shifted signal spirals up or down endlessly (the barber-pole effect). It's stereo, can shift the two channels in opposite directions, locks to the song's tempo, and its quadrature oscillator is available as a two-phase LFO. How does it work? Each channel goes through a Hilbert transformer : two allpass chains whose outputs are 90° apart at every frequency from 15 Hz up. Multiplied with a sine and cosine oscillator at the shift frequency, they give the two sidebands : Up moves every component up by the shift (1 kHz + 100 Hz = 1.1 kHz). Down moves it down (1 kHz − 100 Hz = 900 Hz). The other sideband is suppressed by about 40 dB. A negative shift swaps the two. Components pushed below 0 Hz come back up as positive frequencies (through-zero shifting), which is part of the sound. Shift sets the amount, as a percentage of Range : at ±200 Hz range, 50 % is +100 Hz. The knob is linear and bipolar (centre = no shift), so an LFO or an audio-rate cable on it is through-zero modulation of the shift. Fine adds −10…+10 Hz, for slow phasing at a wide range. Feedback sends the Up signal back into the input, optionally through a delay ( FB Delay ). At 0 ms (one sample) and a small shift you get the barber-pole phaser: a comb of notches that moves endlessly up or down. With 50–500 ms every echo is shifted a little further: rising or falling spirals. Negative values invert the fed-back signal. A soft limiter keeps ±100 % loud but bounded. Spread moves the right channel's shift from the same as the left (0 %) through stopped (50 %) to the opposite (100 %). With a mono input, Spread at 100 % and a 0.3 Hz shift, the phasing turns in opposite directions in the two ears. Mix blends the dry input with the Up signal for Out . The shifted signal is delayed a little by the allpass chains, so 50 % gives some extra phasing of its own. Sync locks the shift rate to the tempo: one cycle per note value, from 1/32 to 8 bars. The direction follows the sign of Shift ; Fine is not used. With the transport playing, the oscillator phase follows the song position, so a barber-pole phaser lands in the same place after a loop jump. Anti-alias filters the input (6-pole low-pass at 0.42 × the sample rate minus the shift) so content shifted past the top of the audio band doesn't fold back as noise. Down loses the same top end. Reset jumps the oscillator to phase 0 (with a 2 ms fade to hide the jump). The Sin and Cos outputs carry the left oscillator: at sub-audio shifts a two-phase LFO, at audio shifts two sines 90° apart. The view shows the spectrum of the input (grey) and of Out (colour): the shift shows up as a translation. The dial shows both oscillators turning. How to use it? Barber-pole phaser: Shift 0, Fine +0.3 Hz, Feedback 70 %, FB Delay 0, Mix 50 %. Negative Fine for a falling phaser. Bells from a pad: Range ±200 Hz, Shift 20–60 %, Mix 100 %. Harmonic sounds become inharmonic and metallic. Spirals: FB Delay 250 ms (or a dotted eighth by ear), Feedback 60 %, Shift ±10 % at ±200 Hz: each echo climbs or falls by 20 Hz. Stereo rotation: a mono source on In L , Spread 100 %, Fine 0.2 Hz. Through-zero FM: an LFO or an audio oscillator onto Shift with Shift at 0. Two-phase LFO: Range ±10 Hz, Shift a few percent, patch Sin and Cos to two destinations (e.g. the pan of two voices) for circular motion. Rhythmic phaser: Sync 1 bar, Shift slightly positive, Feedback 50 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Freq Shifter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Freq Shifter under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Freq Shifter: Barber-Pole Phaser A tiny positive Fine , strong Feedback and half Mix : a phaser sweep that always rises. Freq Shifter: Pad to Bells Shift at about +30 % of ±200 Hz and Mix 100 % make a harmonic pad inharmonic and metallic. Freq Shifter: Spiral Echoes Feedback through FB Delay shifts every repeat up by the same step, so notes spiral upward. Freq Shifter: Stereo Rotation Spread at 100 % shifts left and right in opposite directions so a mono arpeggio rotates. Freq Shifter: Tempo Phaser Sync on one bar locks the shifter to the song for a slow phaser over drums and bass. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Shift −100 … +100 % of Range 0 % Fine −10 … +10 Hz 0 Hz Feedback −100 … +100 % 0 % FB Delay 0 – 1000 ms 0 ms Spread 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Range ±10 Hz, ±200 Hz, ±2 kHz, ±10 kHz ±200 Hz Sync Free, 1/32 … 8 bars Free Anti-alias Off, On On Shift: the shift of the left channel, linear. The view shows it in Hz. Fine: added to Shift . Hidden while Sync is on. Feedback: the delayed Up signal mixed back into the input. A DC blocker in the loop stops offsets from building up. FB Delay: the delay in the feedback loop. 0 is one sample; changes glide like tape (the echoes bend in pitch). Spread: right shift = left shift × (1 − 2 × Spread). Mix: dry ↔ Up for Out . Up and Down are always 100 % wet. Range: the span of Shift . Changing it keeps the knob position, so the shift jumps. Not modulatable. Sync: Free, or one cycle per note value. Not modulatable. Anti-alias: the input low-pass against aliasing. Not modulatable. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Reset trigger sets both oscillators to phase 0 (ignored while synced to a playing transport) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry/wet mix of the Up signal Up L, Up R audio input shifted by +Shift Down L, Down R audio input shifted by −Shift Sin, Cos control, −1 … +1 the left oscillator, 90° apart

title: Phaser
text: Phaser Phaser in the module view Introduction The Phaser makes the slow, swooshing sweep of the 70s: notches that travel up and down through the spectrum. It's best on sustained sounds with a lot of harmonics, like pads, strings, electric piano and guitar, and on drums and noise, where the sweep is easy to hear. How does it work? The sound goes through a chain of allpass filters. An allpass changes only the phase of a signal, not its level, and by a different amount at different frequencies. Mixed with the unprocessed sound, a frequency where the chain has turned the phase by 180° is cancelled: a notch . Every two stages make one notch. An LFO moves the frequency of the allpass filters, so the notches sweep. Rate is the LFO speed, 0.02 to 10 Hz. Depth is how far the notches sweep, up to three octaves up and down from the centre. Centre is the middle of the sweep, 80 Hz to 6 kHz. Low values sound dark and thick, high values thin and airy. Feedback feeds the chain's output back to its input. More feedback makes the notches deeper and the peaks between them sharper and resonant, a more vocal, whistling sweep. Negative feedback gives a hollower sound. It's softly limited, so it can't run away. Stages is how many allpass stages there are: 2 to 12. Two stages give one notch (subtle), four the classic sound, eight or twelve a busy, complex sweep. Spread moves the right channel's LFO away from the left, up to half a cycle, so the sweep rotates across the stereo field. Mix blends dry and wet. At 50 % the notches are deepest. At 100 % you hear only the allpass chain, which has no notches, only changes in phase (and, with feedback, resonant peaks). With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Classic phaser: Rate 0.3 Hz, Depth 60 %, Centre 700 Hz, Feedback 40 %, 4 stages, Mix 50 %. Resonant whistle: Feedback 85 %, 8 stages, Depth 80 %. Slow, wide pad movement: Rate 0.05 Hz, Depth 90 %, Spread 100 %, 6 stages. Envelope phaser: Rate 0, an envelope follower or ADSR onto Centre , for a vocal "wah"-like response. Rhythmic sweep: a clocked LFO onto Centre , with Rate at 0.02 Hz so the internal LFO barely moves. To make the sweep a more sudden swoosh, put a Compressor before it, so the level is constant while notches travel.

title: Pitch Shifter
text: Pitch Shifter Pitch Shifter in the module view Introduction The Pitch Shifter moves a sound up or down by a musical interval and keeps its rhythm: a vocal an octave up, a pad a fifth down, a guitar doubled at +12 and −12. Unlike the Freq Shifter, which adds a fixed number of hertz and breaks harmony, the Pitch Shifter multiplies every frequency by the same ratio, so chords stay chords. Put it in front of a Verb and feed the reverb back into it, and every echo climbs another octave: a shimmer . The factory cell Shimmer Verb is built that way. How does it work? The signal is written into a short delay line. Two read heads sweep through it. A head that moves against the writing point reads faster than real time, so it plays higher; one that moves with it reads slower, so lower. A head can only sweep so far, so each one fades out as it nears the end of the window and jumps back, while the other, half a window behind, fades in. The two fades are sine-shaped, so one head is always loud. This is the simple, cheap way to shift pitch. It has a character: the jump of the heads leaves a faint flutter at the sweep rate (a few Hz to tens of Hz at big intervals), and the sound is a little "grainy", most on sustained tones. Inside a reverb, that is not heard; on a dry vocal it is a voice. A phase-vocoder shifter is cleaner, but it adds a lot of delay and CPU. Pitch is the interval in semitones, −24 to +24. Modulating it with an envelope or LFO gives dive bombs and vibrato. Fine adds ±100 cents for detuned doubling (+7 and −7 cents on two shifters in parallel is a classic widener). Window is the length of the delay the heads sweep through, 20 to 340 ms. Short windows follow fast notes and give a tight, buzzy character; long windows are smoother and stretch into an echo. Around 60–100 ms suits most material; 150 ms or more for pads. The shifter's latency is about half a window. Drift makes the heads wander randomly, slowly: tape-like flutter and a wide, chorused sound. It also works at 0 semitones. Feedback sends the shifted sound back into the input, softly limited. With +12 semitones every repeat is an octave higher than the one before (a rising spiral), with −12 they fall. Mix blends the dry input with the shifted sound. At 100 % you hear only the shifted signal. The left and right sides are separate shifters (with different drift), so the stereo image stays. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Shimmer: Pitch +12, Window 100 ms, Mix 100 %, into a Verb, and the Verb's output back to the shifter's input through a Utility at 30–40 %. Or use the Shimmer Verb preset. Octave down: Pitch −12, Mix 50 %, for a sub-octave under a bass or a lead. Harmoniser: two Pitch Shifters in parallel, +4 and +7 semitones, Mix 40 %, for a major triad on a single note. Wide doubling: Pitch 0, Fine +12 cents, Drift 30 %, Mix 50 %. Dive bomb: an envelope onto Pitch, down 24 semitones, Mix 100 %. Spiral: Pitch +7, Feedback 60 %, Mix 50 %, into a delay: each repeat is a fifth higher. Origin The pitch-shifting algorithm (two crossfading delay-line heads, and the Fun parameter, here called Drift) is from PitchShifter (DaisySP) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version is rewritten for stereo and our delay line, with a smoothed window size, fine tuning, feedback with a soft clip and a seeded random generator, so offline renders repeat. The original licence text is in this module's LICENSE file.

title: Compressor
text: Compressor Compressor in the module view Introduction A compressor turns loud parts of a sound down, so the difference between loud and quiet gets smaller. Used lightly, it makes a bass or a vocal sit evenly in a mix; used hard, it makes drums punch and pumps; with a very high ratio it is a limiter that keeps a signal below a ceiling, for instance inside a feedback loop or on the output of a patch. How does it work? A detector measures how loud the signal is, in decibels. Above the Threshold , the compressor turns the level down so that every Ratio dB over the threshold at the input becomes 1 dB over at the output. At 4:1, a peak 12 dB over comes out 3 dB over. The gain is turned down gradually, over the Attack time, and let go again over the Release time, so the sound doesn't click. Threshold is the level (−60 to 0 dB) where compression starts. Ratio goes from 1:1 (nothing) to 40:1. From 40:1 on the Compressor is a limiter: nothing passes the threshold. Attack (0.1 to 100 ms) is how fast it clamps down. A slow attack lets the start of a note through (punch); a fast one catches every peak. Release (10 ms to 2 s) is how fast it lets go. Short releases pump with the rhythm, long ones are smooth and invisible. Knee (0 to 24 dB) softens the corner at the threshold. A wide knee starts compressing gently before the threshold. Makeup adds gain after compression to bring the level back up. Mix blends the compressed signal with the dry one: parallel compression . 30–50 % keeps the transients and adds weight. Link is how much the two channels follow each other. At 100 % the louder channel controls both, so the stereo image doesn't shift. At 0 they work independently. Detector is Peak (reacts to every peak, fast) or RMS (measures average power over 10 ms, closer to how loud the sound seems and gentler on drums). The Sidechain input lets another signal control the compression: a kick drum pumping the pads (put the kick into Sidechain and a fast attack, release 150–300 ms, ratio 8:1, low threshold). The gain is applied to In L/R . Without a cable there, the detector listens to the input itself. The Reduction output is a control signal from 0 (no compression) to 1 (24 dB of reduction or more). Use it to open a filter when the sound gets squashed or to light a lamp. How to use it? Glue on a mix: threshold −18 dB, ratio 2:1, attack 30 ms, release 200 ms, knee 12 dB. Punchy drums: ratio 6:1, attack 20 ms, release 80 ms, Makeup to taste. Parallel smash: ratio 20:1, threshold −40 dB, attack 1 ms, Mix 30 %. Limiter: ratio 40:1, attack 0.1 ms, release 50 ms, threshold −3 dB. Put one at the end of a feedback loop, like the Shimmer Verb's, to keep it under control. Ducking: a kick on the Sidechain input, ratio 10:1, threshold −35 dB, release 200 ms.

title: EQ
text: EQ EQ in the module view Introduction The EQ turns parts of the spectrum up or down: more bass, less mud around 300 Hz, a cut of harsh 3 kHz, more air above 8 kHz. It has four bands, a low shelf, two bell bands in the middle and a high shelf, in stereo. How does it work? Every band is a biquad filter (the formulas of the well-known "Audio EQ Cookbook"), calculated with the knobs' values and applied one after another. Low shelf : raises or lowers everything below Low Freq (30 Hz–1 kHz) by Low Gain . Mid 1 and Mid 2 : a bell at Freq that boosts or cuts around it by Gain (±15 dB). Q sets the width: 0.3 is very broad (a gentle tonal tilt), 1 is a typical bell, 8 is a narrow notch for a single ringing frequency. High shelf : raises or lowers everything above High Freq (1–18 kHz). Level (−18 to +6 dB) is the gain after the equaliser, to make up for boosts. A band at 0 dB gain is bypassed, so unused bands cost nothing. The frequency and gain of every band can be modulated; the filters are updated every 16 samples, which is smooth for sweeps. Modulating Mid 1 Freq with an LFO or envelope while boosting 10 dB gives a wah-wah. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Clean up mud: Mid 1 at 300 Hz, −4 dB, Q 1. Add presence: Mid 2 at 3 kHz, +3 dB, Q 0.8. Air: High shelf at 10 kHz, +4 dB. Telephone voice: Low shelf at 800 Hz, −15 dB; High shelf at 3 kHz, −15 dB; Mid 2 at 1.5 kHz, +6 dB. Find a resonance: boost Mid 2 +12 dB with Q 6 and sweep its frequency until the problem sticks out, then cut it. Wah: Mid 1 +12 dB, Q 3, an envelope or LFO onto its frequency.

title: Crunch
text: Crunch Crunch in the module view Introduction Crunch dirties up a sound in two ways. Drive is analogue-style overdrive: from a slight warmth through crunchy guitar-amp distortion to a square-wave fuzz. Bits and Rate Red. are digital: they throw away resolution and sample rate until the sound turns into the grit of a 90s sampler, an old game console or a broken phone. Use them separately or together. How does it work? The signal passes through, in this order: Overdrive. A gain stage followed by a soft clipper: the louder the input, the more it is rounded off. Soft clipping creates odd harmonics, which is why overdrive sounds "warm". Drive sets the gain before the clipper. The Drive knob is level-compensated, so more drive changes the colour without getting louder. Sample-rate reduction. Rate Red. holds every sample for several sample periods. This turns the sound into a stair-step wave and folds high frequencies back down as inharmonic, metallic aliasing. At 100 % the signal is held for 96 samples. Bit crushing. Bits rounds the level to a coarse grid of 2^(bits−1) steps per unit. At 16 bits nothing happens; at 8 bits you hear a faint hiss on quiet parts; at 4 bits the sound is rough; at 1 bit it's a square wave. The knob is continuous, so you can sweep it. Tone. A low-pass filter at the end, from 500 Hz to 20 kHz (20 kHz is off) takes the harshest top off the digital sound. Level sets the processed signal's volume, Mix blends it with the dry input (parallel distortion keeps the transients). With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Warm saturation on a bus: Drive 20 %, Mix 50 %. Crunchy bass: Drive 60 %, Tone 4 kHz, Mix 70 %. Fuzz lead: Drive 100 %, Tone 3 kHz. Lo-fi drums: Bits 8, Rate Red. 25 %, Tone 8 kHz. Broken radio: Bits 4, Rate Red. 60 %, Tone 2 kHz. Sweep: an LFO or envelope onto Bits or Rate Red. for sounds that dissolve and rebuild. Origin The overdrive curve and its gain structure are Émilie Gillet's (Mutable Instruments, Plaits , 2014), the sample-rate reduction is from DaisySP's Decimator , both through Overdrive and Decimator (DaisySP, from Plaits) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version has both in one stereo module; the Drive knob covers the useful part of Plaits' curve with level compensation, the bit crusher rounds (and takes fractional bit depths) instead of truncating, and a tone filter and output level were added. The original licence texts are in this module's LICENSE file.

title: Folder
text: Folder Folder in the module view Introduction The Folder is a stereo wavefolder: six folding stages in a row turn a simple waveform into a rich, bright, vocal tone. Its Fold knob sweeps through the harmonics the way a filter sweeps through a spectrum, only upwards. Symmetry adds even harmonics, Tap chooses how many stages you hear. It is anti-aliased, so deep folds on high notes stay clean. With a cable in Pitch it plays its own sine/triangle oscillator, which makes it a complete "west coast" voice on its own. How does it work? Folding. When a signal goes past ±1, a folder reflects it back instead of clipping it: a sine driven twice as hard comes back with a dip at each peak, driven harder it folds again and again. Every fold adds harmonics. Shape chooses the fold curve: at 0 % a soft fold (a sine curve, which already rounds a full-scale signal a little), at 100 % a hard, mirror-like fold that leaves signals within ±1 untouched. Stages. The signal runs through six folders in a row. Each multiplies it by the Fold gain (1× at 0 %, 4× at 100 %) before folding, so the folds multiply from stage to stage. Symmetry adds an offset before the first stage (and half of it before the second): the folds become lopsided and even harmonics appear. Tap picks the stage you hear, 1 to 6; between two whole numbers it crossfades the neighbouring stages, so modulating Tap opens the sound from a gentle fold to a dense one without changing the level. Stages after the tapped one are not computed. Anti-aliasing. Folding creates harmonics far above the audible range; without care they fold back down as inharmonic noise. The Folder runs the stages at 4× the sample rate ( Normal ) or 2× ( Eco ), and each stage uses antiderivative anti-aliasing, which smooths the corners. At Normal a C5 sine folded with Fold 100 % at Tap 2 keeps aliases about 84 dB below the fundamental; very deep settings (high Fold at Tap 4–6) are meant to sound like dense noise and do. Dry and DC. Mix blends the dry signal back in; the dry signal is delayed by the same 1.5 ms as the folded one, so the two stay in phase. A 5 Hz high-pass on the outputs removes the offset that Symmetry creates. Symmetry and Level changes are smoothed over 2 ms; Fold and Tap follow audio-rate modulation. Internal oscillator. With Source on Auto , a cable in Pitch and none in In L turns on the oscillator: a sine (or, with Wave , a triangle) at C4 × 2^(Octave + Pitch + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200), at ±1 into both channels. Internal always uses the oscillator; In L then becomes its FM input. Input always folds the inputs. Switching fades over 5 ms. Stereo. In R unpatched: In L feeds both channels. Spread offsets Symmetry (by ±Spread/2) and Fold (±10 %) between left and right, which makes a mono source wide. A mono source with Spread at 0 is computed once. How to use it? Complex oscillator voice: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; an envelope onto Fold ; Out L → VCA. Wave 0 % (sine) gives the classic sound. Moving timbre: a slow LFO onto Symmetry and another onto Tap . FM plus folding: set Source to Internal , patch another Oscillator into In L and raise FM Depth . Brighten anything: put it after an oscillator or a filter and use low Fold with Mix at 50 %. Stereo width: Spread 30–60 % on a mono source. Tame hot sources: lower Level rather than Fold : it changes how far the signal reaches into the folds. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Folder does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Folder under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Folder: Complex Voice The internal sine played from a sequencer, with an envelope on Fold : each note starts bright and relaxes. Folder: Moving Bass Slow LFOs on Symmetry and Tap turn a low sine from hollow to buzzy and back. Folder: Fold Bells An Oscillator into In L with FM Depth up, then folded: bright, bell-like tones. Folder: Stereo Brightener A plucked saw on the input with low Fold , Mix at half and Spread open: harmonics and width added to a dry sound. Folder: Folded Beat A whole drum loop through the Folder with Fold moved by a slow LFO and Mix for parallel crunch. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Fold 0 – 100 % 0 % Symmetry −100 … +100 % 0 % Tap 1 – 6 6 Shape 0 – 100 % 50 % Spread 0 – 100 % 0 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Wave 0 – 100 % 0 % (sine) Coarse −24 … +24 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Source Auto, Input, Internal Auto Octave −3 … +3 0 Quality Eco (2×), Normal (4×) Normal Fold: the gain into each stage, 4^Fold (1× … 4×). Symmetry: offset before the folds: even harmonics, a reedy sound. Tap: which stage is heard; fractions crossfade two stages. Halfway between stages whose outputs are opposite, the sound can thin briefly. Shape: soft (0 %) to hard (100 %) fold curve. Level: input gain before folding (cubic curve, silent at 0 %). Wave, Coarse, Fine, FM Depth: the internal oscillator: sine → triangle, transposition, and through-zero FM from In L (±4× the frequency at 100 %). Quality: Normal (4×) is clean for almost any setting; Eco (2×) costs half and suits moderate folds or many voices. All knobs are modulation destinations; Source , Octave and Quality are settings. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio the signal to fold; also feeds the right channel when In R is unpatched. FM input while the oscillator runs on Internal In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the internal oscillator's pitch; 0.0 = C4. On Auto , patching it (without In L ) switches the oscillator on Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the folded signal after Tap , Mix and DC blocking. Within ±1, up to about ±2 with strong Symmetry Osc audio the internal oscillator before folding; silent while it is off The folded path (and the dry path with it) is delayed by about 1.5 ms (70.5 samples plus a fraction at 48 kHz in Normal , 47 in Eco ); patch parallel paths around the Folder with that in mind.

title: Saturator
text: Saturator Introduction Saturator adds warmth and harmonics without the brittle, fizzy edge that digital distortion usually has. It is a small model of an analogue gain stage: a smooth curve, a frequency-dependent drive, a power supply that gives way under load and parts that slowly drift. Use it from a hint of warmth on a bus to a thick amp-like crunch. For deliberately digital grit (bit crushing, sample-rate reduction) use Crunch . For metallic, folded harmonics use Folder . How does it work? The signal passes through, in this order: Colour (pre-emphasis). Before the curve, the highs (or lows) are boosted by up to 12 dB. The stage then distorts those frequencies harder. After the curve the boost is undone exactly, so Colour changes what gets distorted , not the overall tone. Bias and Drive. Drive is gain into the curve (0 to 36 dB). Bias moves the signal off the curve's centre, so the top and bottom of the wave are rounded differently. That makes even harmonics (the octave, warm and full) next to the odd ones a symmetrical curve makes. The curve (Character). Tube : a smooth tanh curve. Reacts most to Bias and Sag. Warm, round. Tape : a softer knee and a little memory: the stage hears a lagged copy of its own output, like the magnetic lag of tape. Gentle and glued. Diode : soft on top, harder at the bottom. Asymmetric by itself, even without Bias. Edgier and more vocal. Sag. A model of a power supply: loud signals lower the stage's gain and push its bias, then it recovers over about 150 ms. The result is compression and a "bloom" after hard hits. Quiet signals are left alone. Age. Slow random drift of bias and gain (a few seconds per cycle), different on the left and the right. Nothing ever sounds exactly the same twice, as with real hardware. Clean-up. DC from the bias is removed, then Tone (a 12 dB/oct low-pass, 500 Hz to 20 kHz; 20 kHz is off) rolls off the top, the way analogue stages do. Why it does not sound digital. The curve runs at 2× or 4× the sample rate with first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing, so the harmonics it creates do not fold back down as inharmonic noise. Quality chooses 2× (Eco) or 4× (Normal). Level sets the output. Drive is level-compensated: a signal at 0.5 comes out near 0.5 at any drive, so more drive changes the colour without getting much louder. Mix blends with the dry input; the dry path is delayed to match the oversampling, so parallel use stays in phase. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Warmth on a bus: Tube, Drive 25 %, Bias 20 %, Sag 30 %, Mix 100 %. Tape glue on drums: Tape, Drive 45 %, Sag 50 %, Colour −20 %. Amp-like crunch: Tube, Drive 70 %, Colour +40 %, Tone 5 kHz. Fat bass without fizz: Tube, Drive 55 %, Colour −60 %, Tone 3 kHz, Mix 70 %. Edgy vocal: Diode, Drive 40 %, Colour +30 %. Alive pads: Age 80 % and a little Drive: the harmonics breathe slowly. Dynamic saturation: an envelope or LFO on Drive or Bias .

title: Grains
text: Grains Grains in the module view Introduction Grains records its input into a buffer of a few seconds and plays it back as many short, overlapping grains . Where the grains read, how long they are, how high they play and how many there are turn any sound into shimmering textures, stretched pads or stuttering rhythms. Freeze holds the buffer, so the cloud plays on after the input has stopped. Every grain's random choices come from Seed , so a texture renders the same way every time. How does it work? The buffer. The input is recorded continuously into a stereo buffer of Buffer seconds. Position says where grains read: 0 % is the newest audio, 100 % the oldest. Freeze (the setting or the gate) stops recording; Position then counts from the moment of the freeze, so the frozen sound stays put. The seam where recording stopped is crossfaded, so a frozen buffer loops cleanly. A grain is a short piece of the buffer under a window. Size is its length (5 ms – 2 s), Texture its window shape: 0 % nearly square, 25 % trapezoid, 50 % smooth bell, 75 % narrow bell, 100 % percussive (a fast attack and a decay). Pitch transposes every grain (−24 … +24 semitones); the Pitch input adds 1 V per octave, so a sequencer plays the cloud melodically. Pitch Quant snaps the result to semitones, octaves, or octaves and fifths. Reverse is the chance that a grain plays backwards. How many. In Continuous mode, Density sets the number of grains per second, from one every two seconds to 200. Below 50 % they also come irregularly; the middle of the knob is a smooth cloud. With a note value in Sync , grains start on the song's grid instead: above 50 % Density adds subdivisions, below it skips grid points. In Triggered mode each pulse at Trigger starts a grain (above 50 % Density, a burst of up to 8); in Continuous mode a pulse adds an extra grain. When the grains run into Max Grains , the oldest one fades out quickly to make room. The level is normalised to the overlap, so turning up Density or Size doesn't get louder. Scatter. Spread gives every grain a random offset from Position (up to ±25 % of the buffer) and a random place in the stereo field. Pitch Jitter detunes each grain randomly by up to that many semitones (before quantizing). Space. Feedback writes the output back into the buffer with the input (soft-clipped), building dense, evolving textures. Blur smears the grains into a reverb-like wash; it sets both its level and its length (0.3 – 8 s). With Feedback, the blur's tail goes back into the buffer, so frozen pads never end. Mix blends the dry input with the result. Grain fires at each grain start; Grain Env follows the window of the latest grain, to move something else along with the cloud. The view shows the buffer (oldest on the left, the write head on the right), the area grains read from, and each grain as a dot. Drag on it: left/right sets Position, up/down sets Size. While frozen, Keep frozen buffer saves the buffer to the media folder, so it comes back with the board (the module then starts frozen on it); unfreezing lets it go. How to use it? Pad from anything: Size 400 ms, Density 60 %, Texture 50 %, Spread 40 %, Blur 40 %. Freeze when you hear something you like. Shimmer: Pitch +12, Pitch Jitter 7 with Octaves + fifths , Feedback 30 %, Blur 50 %. Rhythmic stutter: Sync 1/16, Size 60 ms, Texture 100 %, Density 50 %. Melodic cloud: a Step Sequencer's Pitch into Pitch , Pitch Quant Semitones. Granular delay: Position 30 %, Spread 5 %, Mix 40 %. Scrubbing: a slow LFO on Position while frozen. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Grains does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Grains under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Grains: Frozen Cloud A slow square LFO on Freeze holds the buffer for a few bars at a time: one moment of a phrase becomes an endless pad. Grains: Stutter Rhythm Triggered mode synced to 1/16 chops a bass loop into a reversing, stuttering rhythm; Position jumps with a Random. Grains: Shimmer Leaps Pitch Quant on octaves and fifths, a little Pitch Jitter and Feedback make a halo around a slow melody. Grains: Melodic Cloud A sequencer drives the Pitch input of a noise cloud: the grains themselves play the tune. Grains: Backwards Garden Long, mostly reversed grains scattered by Spread and Blur into a swelling reverse wash. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Position 0 – 100 % 0 % Size 5 ms – 2 s 120 ms Pitch −24 … +24 semitones 0 Density 0 – 100 % 50 % Texture 0 – 100 % 40 % Spread 0 – 100 % 30 % Pitch Jitter 0 – 12 semitones 0 Feedback 0 – 100 % 0 % Blur 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Reverse 0 – 100 % 0 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Mode Continuous, Triggered Continuous Sync Free, 1/4 … 1/64T Free Buffer 2, 4, 8, 16 s 8 s Pitch Quant Off, Semitones, Octaves, Octaves + fifths Semitones Max Grains 16, 32, 64 32 Freeze Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio recorded into the buffer; In L alone feeds both sides Trigger trigger starts a grain (Triggered) or adds one (Continuous) Freeze gate stops recording while high Pitch pitch 1 V/oct, added to Pitch Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry and grains mixed by Mix Grain trigger a pulse at each grain start Grain Env control the window of the latest grain, 0 … 1 The buffer always holds 16 seconds (about 6 MB at 48 kHz, plus 2 MB for Blur), so in a Voice Cell every voice has its own.

title: Resonator
text: Resonator Resonator in the module view Introduction The Resonator is a tuned body that rings when something hits it. Feed it any audio (a drum loop, noise bursts, a voice, a sequenced click) and it answers with pitched, physical-sounding tone: a struck bar, a plate, a bell, a plucked string, or a set of strings ringing in sympathy. Without input it is an instrument of its own: every trigger at Strum fires a small internal exciter. Up to four voices take turns on the strums, so chords and overlapping notes ring out naturally, and the Odd and Even outputs give a wide stereo image from a mono source. How does it work? Three models of the body: Modal: a bank of 16, 32 or 64 ringing partials. Structure sets their ratios: harmonic string (0 %), stiff string (25 %), free bar (50 %), membrane/plate (75 %) and a bell-like inharmonic set drawn from Seed (100 %), gliding smoothly in between. Sympathetic: eight strings with no excitation of their own. They pick up whatever matches their tuning in the input, like the sympathetic strings of a sitar. Structure chooses the tuning of the set: octaves, fifths, major, minor, sus, add9, detuned unisons, inharmonic. String: one plucked string (a waveguide), tuned exactly. Structure is its stiffness, from a soft nylon string to a metal bar. In every model Damping sets how long the fundamental rings, Brightness how much high content there is and how fast it dies, and Position where the body is struck and heard (50 % is the middle, which cancels the even partials). Voices and strums. With Polyphony 1 there is one voice: Strum fires the exciter and takes the current Pitch . With 2 or 4, each strum moves on to the next voice. That voice gets the input and follows Pitch ; the earlier ones ring out at the pitch they were strummed at. A strum on a voice that is still ringing adds to it, like hitting a string again. The internal exciter is a 3 ms burst of noise with a click, darker or brighter with Brightness , at the level of Exciter . With Strum Source › Input onsets , the Resonator listens to its input and strums on every hit it hears. A drum loop played into a four-voice Resonator then spreads its hits over the voices, and each hit takes the current Pitch . A body fed with a loud input in tune with its partials can build up far above the input level, so both outputs pass a soft limiter. How to use it? Tuned percussion from a drum loop: drum loop → In , Model Modal , Structure 50 – 100 %. Sequence Pitch , or use Input onsets with Polyphony 4 for overlapping notes. Plucked instrument: a sequencer's gate → Strum , its pitch → Pitch , Model String . Raise Damping for short plucks, Brightness for twang. Sympathetic shimmer: any melodic sound → In , Model Sympathetic , Structure at the tuning you like, Dry up to hear the source too. Stereo: Odd → left, Even → right. Width 0 % makes both the same. In a Voice Cell: keep Polyphony at 1 and let the cell provide the voices: Voice In › Trigger → Strum , Pitch → Pitch . Strum button: fires the exciter, for trying sounds without patching. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Resonator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Resonator under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Resonator: Struck Bells The Modal model strummed by a sequencer, with Structure drifting between string, bar and bell. Resonator: Plucked Strings The String model with four voices turns an arpeggio into a harp; try Brightness , Damping and Position . Resonator: Sympathetic Drone A melody fed into the Sympathetic model makes its strings ring along; Frequency retunes them. Resonator: Drum Body With Strum Source on Input onsets every drum hit rings the body, and a random source on Frequency walks its pitch. Resonator: Noise Plate Noise bursts excite a Modal plate while LFOs move Structure and Brightness , from glass to gong. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Frequency −48 … +48 semitones around C4 0 (C4) Structure 0 – 100 % 25 % Brightness 0 – 100 % 60 % Damping 0 – 100 % 45 % Position 0 – 100 % 30 % Input Gain −24 … +24 dB 0 dB Exciter 0 – 100 % 50 % Width 0 – 100 % 100 % Dry 0 – 100 % 0 % Model Modal, Sympathetic, String Modal Polyphony 1, 2, 4 1 Modes 16, 32, 64 (Modal) 32 Strum Source Jack, Input onsets Jack Seed 0 – 999 1 Frequency: the fundamental; Pitch adds to it. Modulation moves it in semitones. Structure: the partial ratios (Modal), the tuning of the set (Sympathetic) or the stiffness (String). Its name follows the model. Brightness: the high-frequency content: tilts the partials and makes the high ones decay faster; also colours the exciter. Damping: how long the fundamental rings: 0 % = 30 s, 50 % ≈ 1.2 s, 100 % ≈ 50 ms. Position: where the body is excited and heard. 0 % and 100 % are the ends; 50 % is the middle and cancels the even partials. Input Gain: the level of In into the body. Exciter: the level of the internal exciter on each strum. 0 % switches it off. Width: 0 % gives both outputs the mono sum; 100 % fully separates odd and even. Dry: the input (after Input Gain ) mixed into both outputs. Model: Modal, Sympathetic or String (see above). Switching fades the sound out and in again. Polyphony: how many voices take turns on the strums. Modes: the number of partials of the Modal body: more sounds richer and costs more. Strum Source: Jack strums only from the Strum input; Input onsets also strums on every hit detected in In . Seed: the bell partials (Modal, Structure 100 %), the inharmonic tuning (Sympathetic) and the exciter's noise. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the excitation; feeds the most recently strummed voice Strum trigger starts the next voice, takes Pitch for it and fires the exciter Pitch pitch 1 V/oct, 0 V = C4, added to Frequency ; the newest voice follows it Outputs Output Signal What it does Odd audio odd partials / odd strings / the first pickup: the left channel Even audio even partials / even strings / the second pickup: the right channel Mix audio Odd + Even, mono

title: Attenuverter
text: Attenuverter Attenuverter in the module view Introduction Four rows that make a signal smaller, bigger, upside down or shifted. In the module view each row is a column of two knobs: Scale on top, Offset below. With nothing patched, a row is a knob you set by hand, so the Attenuverter is also four macro controls: one row can feed many destinations with the same value. How does it work? Each row computes Out = In × Scale + Offset Scale runs from −2 to +2: +1 passes the signal unchanged, 0 mutes it, −1 turns it upside down, and values beyond ±1 boost a weak signal. Offset shifts the result up or down. An unpatched In counts as a constant +1 , so an empty row outputs Scale + Offset . Sum adds the four rows. Every cable already has its own amount at the destination. The Attenuverter is for scaling once, at the source: one knob changes the depth for every destination, and that knob can itself be modulated. How to use it? One depth for many destinations: LFO → In 1 , Out 1 to several knobs at full amount. Scale 1 now sets all depths at once. Macro knobs: leave a row unpatched, set Scale to 0 and use Offset as a manual control. Patch Out to several knobs and move them together. Unipolar from bipolar: an LFO (−1 … +1) with Scale 0.5 and Offset 0.5 runs from 0 to 1. Invert: Scale −1 makes an envelope fall instead of rise. Mix four rows: use Sum as a small four-input mixer. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Scale 1–4 −2 … +2 +1 Offset 1–4 −1 … +1 0 Clip Off, Soft, Hard Off Scale: the gain of the row. Negative values invert. Offset: added after scaling. Clip: limits every output, including Sum , to ±1. Soft leaves values up to ±0.8 untouched and bends smoothly into ±1; Hard cuts off at ±1. Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 control The signal of each row. Unpatched: a constant +1. Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1–4 control In × Scale + Offset, per row Sum control Out 1 + Out 2 + Out 3 + Out 4

title: CV Mixer
text: CV Mixer CV Mixer in the module view Introduction The CV Mixer combines up to four modulation signals into one. Adding them up is only one way: it can also average them, follow whichever is highest or lowest, or scan across them with one knob. Simple shapes combined like this become complex, living modulation. How does it work? Each channel's input is multiplied by its Level (−1 … +1, so it can also invert). Then Mode decides how the four channels combine: Sum: all channels added. Average: the sum divided by the number of channels in use. Max: the highest channel at every moment. Min: the lowest channel at every moment. Scan: a crossfade from channel 1 to channel 4, set by the Scan knob. The result is multiplied by Master , Offset is added, and Clip keeps it in range. Inv is the same signal upside down; Abs is its absolute value. A channel counts as "in use" when its input is patched. Channel 1 also counts when unpatched with a Level other than 0: its input then reads +1, so Level 1 works as a manual offset. Max , Min and Average ignore unused channels. How to use it? Blend two LFOs: a slow and a fast LFO into In 1 and In 2 , mixed by their levels. Two simple waves give a much less predictable shape. A floor for an envelope: envelope and a slow LFO into two channels, Mode Max . The output follows the envelope, but never falls below the LFO. Pick a modulator with one knob: four different sources, Mode Scan , and patch an LFO or a macro onto Scan to move between them. Bipolar to unipolar: Abs turns a −1 … +1 LFO into a 0 … 1 shape at twice the rate. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1–4 −1 … +1 +1 (channel 1), 0 (others) Scan 0 … 1 0 Master 0 … 2 1 Offset −1 … +1 0 Mode Sum, Average, Max, Min, Scan Sum Clip Off, Soft, Hard Soft Level: each channel's level; negative values invert it. Scan: only used in Scan mode. 0 is channel 1, 1/3 channel 2, 2/3 channel 3, 1 channel 4; in between, the two neighbours crossfade. Master: gain on the combined signal. Offset: added after Master . Clip: Soft leaves values up to ±0.8 untouched and bends smoothly into ±1; Hard cuts off at ±1; Off doesn't limit. Soft is the default because four full-scale signals added up easily leave the range. Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 control The channels. In 1 unpatched reads +1; In 2–4 read 0. Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control The mix Inv control −Out Abs control the absolute value of Out

title: Matrix Mixer
text: Matrix Mixer Matrix Mixer in the module view Introduction A grid of up to 8 inputs by 8 outputs . Every crosspoint is a gain from −1 to +1, so each output is its own mix of all the inputs. It mixes audio (send and return busses, feedback networks, spreading one sound to several effects) and control signals (blending LFOs into many related movements). Every crosspoint is a knob you can modulate, and whole matrices can be stored as snapshots and morphed . How does it work? The mix. Out j = Level j × Σ (gain i→j × In i) . Inputs and Outputs set how many rows and columns are in use; jacks beyond them are hidden (their cables stay) and carry nothing. An unpatched input is 0, or 1 with Unpatched = 1, so its row becomes a set of fixed offsets. Crosspoints. In the grid a circle's size is the gain, warm colours are positive, cool ones negative. Click an empty crosspoint for +1, a set one for 0; Alt-click for −1; drag up and down to set it (Shift: fine); double-click to type a value. Every crosspoint is also a knob: cables can modulate it, even at audio rate (ring modulation). Changes ramp over 20 ms, so recalling a snapshot doesn't click. Mutes silence a row with a 5 ms ramp. Level sets each output from silent to +6 dB. Output Stage. Clean passes everything (limited to ±10). Soft clip rounds peaks above 0.9 smoothly towards ±1. Normalize divides each output by the sum of its gains when that is above 1, so a column never gets louder than its loudest input: feedback patches stay tame. Snapshots. The eight buttons below the grid hold whole matrices (gains, levels, mutes). Click recalls one, Shift-click stores the current matrix, right-click renames, clears or makes it morph end A or B. Morph. With Morph on, the gains blend from snapshot A to snapshot B as the Morph knob turns ( Morph Curve : Linear, Smooth, Equal power); levels blend too, mutes switch halfway. Cables on crosspoints still add on top. Editing a crosspoint then edits the snapshot nearest the Morph position, so move Morph to 0 % or 100 % to shape either end. Feedback. Patching an output back into an input works (one 32-sample delay); with Normalize such loops stay stable. How to use it? Effect sends: inputs are sounds, outputs go to a delay and a reverb; each crosspoint is a send amount. A feedback network: outputs through delays or filters back into the inputs, Normalize on, gains around ±0.5. Modulation blender: four LFOs in, eight related modulations out. Scene changes: store snapshots, patch a slow LFO into Morph . Demo patches Five whole patches show what Matrix Mixer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Matrix Mixer under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Matrix Mixer: Send Matrix Eight inputs, four outputs: a lead, bass and drums, two outputs as sends to an echo and a reverb, and the returns mixed back in by crosspoints. Matrix Mixer: Scene Morph Two snapshots (a sparse scene and a full groove) blended by a slow LFO on Morph with Morph Curve on Equal power . Matrix Mixer: Crosspoint Ring An oscillator patched into the 1 → 1 crosspoint ring-modulates the melody at audio rate; the 1 → 2 crosspoint keeps the dry sound. Matrix Mixer: Feedback Web Two echo networks feed back into the matrix with Output Stage on Normalize : loops of repeats that stay stable. Matrix Mixer: Modulation Blender Four Quad LFO waves go in, four blended (some inverted) mixes come out to move the filters of a chord. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default i → j (64) −1 … +1 1 on the diagonal, else 0 Level 1 … 8 0 – 200 % 100 % Morph 0 – 100 % 0 % Every knob is a modulation destination. The knob list shows only the rows and columns in use. Settings Setting Values Default Inputs 1 – 8 4 Outputs 1 – 8 4 Mute 1 … 8 on / off off Output Stage Clean, Soft clip, Normalize Clean Unpatched 0, 1 0 Morph Off, On Off Morph Curve Linear, Smooth, Equal power Linear Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1 … In 8 audio (any signal) the sources Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1 … Out 8 audio Level × the weighted sum of the inputs, after the output stage

title: Multiplier
text: Multiplier Multiplier in the module view Introduction Two multipliers that compute X × Y, with both signals allowed to be negative. With audio it's a ring modulator: metallic, bell-like tones from two oscillators. With modulation it lets one signal control the depth of another, for example an LFO whose depth follows an envelope. How does it work? Each section computes Out = (X + Bias X) × (Y + Bias Y) × Gain An unpatched Y reads +1, so the section simply passes X at Gain . An unpatched X2 takes Out 1 . Patch three signals into X1, Y1 and Y2 to multiply all three together. Bias adds a constant before multiplying. With Bias Y at 1, a bipolar Y gives amplitude modulation (the original tone stays); at 0 it's ring modulation (the original tone disappears, only sum and difference tones remain). Unlike the VCA, the Multiplier treats both inputs the same, has no response curve, and lets the gain go negative. Multiplying two audio signals creates new frequencies, which can fold back as aliasing. Oversampling computes the product at 2× or 4× the sample rate and filters it. This adds a short latency, so leave it off for modulation. How to use it? Ring modulator: two oscillators into X1 and Y1 , Out 1 to an output. Detune one oscillator for bell tones; set Oversampling to 4× for high notes. Tremolo with character: audio into X1 , an LFO into Y1 , Bias Y1 at 1. Depth from an envelope: LFO into X1 , envelope into Y1 : the LFO only moves while the envelope is open. Squaring: the same signal into X and Y. A sine becomes a sine at twice the frequency, an LFO gets a rounder, always-positive shape. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Bias X1, Bias X2 −1 … +1 0 Bias Y1, Bias Y2 −1 … +1 0 Gain 1, Gain 2 −2 … +2 +1 Oversampling Off, 2x, 4x Off Inputs Input Signal What it does X1, Y1 control First multiplier. Y1 unpatched reads +1. X2, Y2 control Second multiplier. X2 unpatched takes Out 1; Y2 unpatched reads +1. The inputs accept audio and pitch signals too. Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1 control (X1 + Bias X1) × (Y1 + Bias Y1) × Gain 1 Out 2 control the same for the second section

title: Utility
text: Utility Utility in the module view Introduction Utility is the glue between modules. It scales, inverts, offsets and mixes control signals, then shapes the result: rectify, fold, quantize to semitones or sample and hold. It can smooth the result with a slew and turn it into a gate with a comparator. Whenever a signal is almost what you need, put a Utility in between. How does it work? The signal passes through four stages, in this order: Mix: X × Scale X + Y × Scale Y + Offset . The scales are attenuverters: +1 passes the input unchanged, 0 mutes it, −1 inverts it. Mode: one shaping function (see Mode below). Slew: a smoothing filter that limits how fast the value can change. Outputs: Out is the result, Inv is the same value inverted, and Gate is high while Out is above Threshold . With nothing patched, Out is simply the Offset : a constant you can set by hand or modulate. How to use it? Attenuate or invert: patch a signal into X and set Scale X . At −1 an LFO runs the other way. Unipolar from bipolar: an LFO running −1 … +1 into X , Scale X 0.5, Offset 0.5 gives 0 … 1. Mix two modulators: one into X , one into Y , and balance them with the two scales. Quantized melodies: feed a slow random or LFO into X , choose Quantize , and patch Out into an oscillator's Pitch . Sample and hold: patch noise or an LFO into X , a clock into Clock , and choose Sample & Hold for stepped values on each clock. Portamento and smoothing: raise Slew to round off steps from a sequencer or Random. For pitch that gives glide. Wavefolding: choose Fold and push the level with Scale X or Offset beyond ±1. Folding turns a simple LFO into a complex shape. Gates from control signals: use Gate with a Threshold . An LFO into X becomes a square gate; an envelope follower becomes a trigger when a sound gets loud. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Scale X −1 … +1 +1 Scale Y −1 … +1 0 Offset −1 … +1 0 Slew 0 – 5 s 0 s Threshold −1 … +1 0 Mode Through, Rectify, Fold, Quantize, Sample & Hold Through Scale X: gain for the X input. Negative values invert it. Scale Y: gain for the Y input. It starts at 0, so Y does nothing until you turn it. Offset: a constant added to the mix. Shifts a signal up or down, or acts as a manual control on its own. Slew: smoothing time (a one-pole lag). The output covers about two thirds of a jump in this time. 0 is instant. The knob's centre is 100 ms. Threshold: the level Out must exceed for Gate to go high. Mode: how the mixed signal is shaped before the slew: Through: unchanged. Rectify: the absolute value; negative parts flip up. An LFO becomes a bouncing shape at twice the rate. Fold: anything beyond ±1 is reflected back inside, again and again. More input level means more folds. Quantize: rounded to steps of 1/12: semitones at 1 V/oct. Sample & Hold: the value is taken on each rising edge at Clock and held until the next. Scale X , Scale Y , Offset , Slew and Threshold are modulation destinations. Modulating Scale X from an envelope makes a simple VCA for control signals. Inputs Input Signal What it does X control first input, scaled by Scale X Y control second input, scaled by Scale Y Clock gate rising edges sample the signal in Sample & Hold mode X and Y take audio, pitch and control signals alike; they are just numbers. Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control the result (limited to ±10) Gate gate high while Out > Threshold Inv control − Out

title: Coin Toss
text: Coin Toss Coin Toss in the module view Introduction Coin Toss is a probability router. Every gate or trigger that arrives at its input is sent to output A or to output B , decided by a weighted coin. There are two channels, so one clock becomes two complementary rhythms that keep changing. Every toss comes from a seed, so a rendered song sounds exactly like the live playback. How does it work? Tosses. Each rising edge at In tosses the coin. Probability is the chance that it lands on B : 0 % always A, 100 % always B, 50 % a fair coin. In 2 listens to In 1 while nothing is patched into it, so channel 2 makes its own decision on the same events. Memory. With Memory above 0 % a toss sometimes simply repeats the last result instead of flipping a new coin. You get runs of A and runs of B, while the long-term balance stays the same. At 50 % the runs are about twice as long. Modes. Trigger: the chosen output copies the input gate (same length); the other stays low. A trigger in gives a trigger out. Latch: the chosen output goes high and stays high until a toss chooses the other side. A and B are always opposite: a random switch. Toggle: a toss that lands on B swaps which output is high; one that lands on A changes nothing. Probability becomes the chance of a change. Link. Independent: each channel tosses its own coin. Shared: one coin for both, compared against each channel's own Probability . If channel 1's probability is lower, channel 2 always goes B when channel 1 does: nested probability, e.g. hats at 70 % and an open hat at 20 %, never one without the other. Opposed: one coin, but channel 2 reads it from the other end, so the channels avoid each other: B on both never happens as long as the two probabilities add up to 100 % or less. In Shared and Opposed the tosses happen on channel 1's edges; In 2 only sets channel 2's gate lengths. Repeatable. Each channel counts its tosses. Reset (or a transport start) sets the count to 0, so the same decisions follow again. Loop makes the count wrap after 2 … 32 tosses: a fixed random rhythm that repeats. Change Seed for another one. How to use it? Two rhythms from one clock: patch a clock or a sequencer's gate into In 1 , A 1 to one drum, B 1 to another. Ghost notes: Probability 15 %, B 1 into a quieter second voice. Fills that build up: an LFO or a slow envelope on Probability 1 . A random switch: Mode 1 on Latch , Coin 1 into a crossfader or a sequential switch's address. Nested hats: Link on Shared , Probability 1 20 % (open hat on B 1 ), Probability 2 70 % (closed hat on B 2 ). A fixed random pattern: Loop on 8 or 16, and a Reset from the bar (e.g. the Step Sequencer's End ) so it stays on the bar. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Coin Toss does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Coin Toss under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Coin Toss: Heads or Tails Drums Probability 1 and 2 send each sixteenth to a hat, a ghost snare or an open hat (with Memory 2 for runs) over a fixed backbeat. Coin Toss: Trading Voices One melody dealt note by note to a low pluck on A 1 and a bright one on B 1 ; Memory 1 makes them trade in runs. Coin Toss: Latch Layers Mode Latch on both channels: A and B are always opposite, switching the pad, arpeggio and drums on and off by bar. Coin Toss: Looped Groove Link Shared with Loop at 16 tosses: nested clap and hat figures that repeat every bar. Coin Toss: Coin on the Pitch The Coin outputs as control voltages: Toggle lifts a bell melody by a fifth, Latch opens and closes a drone's filter. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Probability 1, 2 0 – 100 % 50 % Memory 1, 2 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode 1, 2 Trigger, Latch, Toggle Trigger Link Independent, Shared, Opposed Independent Loop Off, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 32 tosses Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Probability: the chance that a toss chooses B. Read at the moment of the edge, so modulating it never cuts a gate. Memory: the chance that a toss repeats the last result. Mode: see above. Changing it while a gate is high sets the outputs low until the next toss. Link: how the two channels' coins relate. Loop: the number of tosses before the decisions repeat. Seed: picks the sequence of tosses. Probability and Memory are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1 gate each rising edge tosses channel 1's coin; the gate is routed to A 1 or B 1 In 2 gate the same for channel 2; unpatched it listens to In 1 Reset trigger both toss counters back to 0; Latch and Toggle back to A Outputs Output Signal What it does A 1, B 1, A 2, B 2 gate the routed gates (see Mode ) Coin 1, Coin 2 control, 0 … 1 1 while the last toss chose A, 0 after B

title: Logic
text: Logic Logic in the module view Introduction Logic combines gates and triggers the way digital circuits do: AND, OR, XOR and their inverses, a flip-flop, and edge detectors. Two rhythms become a third, a clock is divided by two, and a gate turns into triggers at its start and end. How does it work? Every input is either high or low . It goes high when the signal rises above Threshold , and low again when it falls below Threshold minus Hysteresis . The hysteresis keeps slow or noisy signals from flickering around the threshold. The logic outputs combine A and B , plus C when it is patched: AND: high when all are high. OR: high when any is high. XOR: high when an odd number are high (for two inputs: when they differ). NAND , NOR: AND and OR inverted. NOT A: A inverted. An unpatched A or B counts as low, so AND needs both patched. That makes B an enable: AND of a clock and a gate passes the clock only while the gate is high. The flip-flop ( FF ) changes state on each trigger at Flip (or on each rising edge of A, see Flip Source ). Reset sets it low. Rise and Fall fire a trigger when A goes high and low. Change fires whenever AND, OR or XOR changes. How to use it? Rhythm from rhythms: two clocks or patterns into A and B. AND plays where they meet, XOR where they differ, OR everything. Mute a clock: clock into A, a gate into B, use AND . Clock ÷ 2: clock into A, Flip Source on A Rising Edge , use FF . Chain more Logic modules for ÷ 4, ÷ 8. Gate to triggers: a gate into A; Rise fires at the start, Fall at the end. Patch Fall into an envelope for a sound on note release. Pulses from an LFO: an LFO into A, Threshold 0.8; NOT A is low only near the LFO's peaks. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Threshold −1 … +1 0.5 Hysteresis 0 … 0.5 0.02 Flip Source Flip Jack, A Rising Edge Flip Jack Threshold: the level at which an input counts as high. Applies to every input, including Flip and Reset . Hysteresis: how far below Threshold an input must fall to count as low again. Flip Source: what toggles the flip-flop. Inputs Input Signal What it does A, B gate The main operands. Unpatched: low. C gate Optional third operand for AND, OR, XOR. Unpatched: ignored. Flip trigger Toggles FF Reset trigger Sets FF low; wins over a toggle on the same sample Outputs Output Signal What it does AND, OR, XOR gate The logic of A, B (and C) NAND, NOR gate AND and OR inverted NOT A gate A inverted FF gate The flip-flop Rise, Fall trigger When A goes high, when A goes low Change trigger When AND, OR or XOR changes

title: Patch Bay In
text: Patch Bay In Introduction The Patch Bay In collects signals into one bundle cable. Patch any signal into its free input and it becomes a channel, named after what you patched; a new free input appears. Take the Bundle output to a Patch Bay Out, here or on the other side of a cell. How does it work? A Patch Bay In and a Patch Bay Out are a pair. They stay in step by themselves: the Patch Bay Out always shows the channels of the Patch Bay In its bundle comes from. Nothing is processed: the engine turns every channel into a plain cable, so a patch bay costs nothing while it plays. How to use it? A panel for a module: put the dials that control a module in a cell, collect them in a Patch Bay In, send the bundle out of the cell, and put a Patch Bay Out next to the module. One bundle replaces a cable per dial. The Warm Saws preset is built this way. A long way across the board: one bundle cable instead of several parallel ones. Reference The jacks, the signal types and how the bundle is resolved are in the design, doc/specs/modules/patchbay.md . A bundle carries any signal except notes.

title: Patch Bay Out
text: Patch Bay Out Introduction The Patch Bay Out gives you the channels of a bundle back as separate outputs, named like the signals that went into the Patch Bay In at the other end. Cable them to knobs or inputs as you would any other output. How does it work? A Patch Bay In and a Patch Bay Out are a pair. They stay in step by themselves: the Patch Bay Out always shows the channels of the Patch Bay In its bundle comes from. Nothing is processed: the engine turns every channel into a plain cable, so a patch bay costs nothing while it plays. How to use it? A panel for a module: put the dials that control a module in a cell, collect them in a Patch Bay In, send the bundle out of the cell, and put a Patch Bay Out next to the module. One bundle replaces a cable per dial. The Warm Saws preset is built this way. A long way across the board: one bundle cable instead of several parallel ones. Reference The jacks, the signal types and how the bundle is resolved are in the design, doc/specs/modules/patchbay.md . A bundle carries any signal except notes.

title: Switch
text: Switch Switch in the module view Introduction The Switch is a sequential switch with up to 8 steps. It picks one of eight inputs for its Out , and at the same time sends its In to one of eight outputs. The step moves on each trigger, follows the song, or is chosen with the Select knob. It can cycle through melodies, pick a sound source, send one sequence to several voices in turn, or, with nothing patched, be an 8-step sequencer of knob values. How does it work? One step, two sections. The current step chooses: 8 → 1: which of In 1 … In 8 plays at Out . Each input is multiplied by its Level . An unpatched input plays its Level as a constant, so the eight Level knobs are eight steps of a value sequencer. 1 → 8: which of Out 1 … Out 8 gets In . The other outputs are silent ( Idle Outputs Zero ) or keep their last value ( Hold ). Moving the step. Length sets how many steps are used (2 … 8). A trigger at Step moves one step in Direction : Forward , Backward , Ping-Pong , Random (never the same step twice) or Random Walk (one step up or down at random). Reset goes back to the first step. With Step unpatched and a Rate set, the switch steps with the song, locked to the bars: after a loop it is at the same step again. Select adds an offset: with Length 4, 0 … 0.25 is no offset, 0.25 … 0.5 one step, and so on. With nothing stepping, Select chooses the step; patch an LFO onto it to sweep through the steps. Changing smoothly. Each change fades over Fade . Short fades (the default 2 ms) remove clicks from audio; 0 switches instantly, right for gates and stepped values. A change in the middle of a fade continues from what's playing, so fast switching never jumps. Fade Curve Equal Power keeps the loudness even between two different sounds; Linear is right for modulation and for two versions of the same sound. With Mode Glide , Out doesn't crossfade but slides from the old value to the new one over Fade : portamento for a value sequencer driving a pitch. Gate drops for one sample at every step change (to restart envelopes), Changed fires a trigger, End fires when the steps start a new round, and Position tells where the switch is. How to use it? Source selector: four oscillators into In 1–4 , Out to the filter. Turn Select , or patch a slow random onto it. 8-step sequencer from knobs: leave the inputs unpatched, set the Levels , a clock into Step (or set Rate ), Out to an oscillator's pitch through a Quantizer. Gate plays an envelope on each step; Mode Glide adds slides. Alternating melodies: two sequencers' Pitch into In 1–2 , Length 2, one sequencer's End into Step . Spread notes over voices: one random source into In , Idle Outputs Hold , a clock into Step : eight outputs, each with its own held value. Rhythmic routing: a drum into In , Out 1–4 to four different effects, Rate 1/16, Direction Random .
