Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1–8 −1 … +1 +1 Select 0 … 1 0 Fade 0 … 2 s 2 ms Length 2 … 8 4 Direction Forward, Backward, Ping-Pong, Random, Random Walk Forward Rate Off, 1/32 … 8 bars Off Fade Curve Equal Power, Linear Equal Power Mode Crossfade, Glide Crossfade Idle Outputs Zero, Hold Zero Seed 0 … 999 1 Rate: only used while Step is unpatched. One step per this length, locked to the song position. Seed: chooses the sequence of the random directions. Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–8 audio The sources for Out . Unpatched: the Level as a constant. Any signal type passes. In audio The source for Out 1–8 Step trigger Moves one step Reset trigger Back to the first step Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio The selected input Out 1–8 audio In at the selected output Gate gate Low for one sample at each step change, high otherwise End trigger When the steps start a new round Position control The current step, 0 (first) … 1 (last) Changed trigger A pulse at each step change

title: Chord Quantizer
text: Chord Quantizer Chord Quantizer in the module view Introduction One pitch in, a chord out. The input picks the chord's root, the module builds a chord on it, inverts and voices it, and plays it on four pitch outputs and a Notes output. Patch a melody in and get a chord that moves with it; switch on Voice Leading and each new chord picks the inversion that moves the voices least, so a jumpy sequence turns into smooth changes. How does it work? Mode decides how the root and the chord are found: Chromatic: the root is the input rounded to the nearest semitone and Chord chooses the chord (Major, Minor, Dominant 7, … Quartal). Diatonic: the input snaps to Root + Scale , and Chord chooses a stack of scale steps (Triad, Seventh, Sus4, Ninth, …). The chord quality follows the key: in C major a Triad on D is D minor. With Harmony on a bus, key and scale come from the Harmony Master. Follow: the chord is the Harmony Master's current chord (slash bass included); the input only moves it up and down. Without a Harmony Master on the bus it acts as Diatonic and says "no harmony". Voices sets how many notes the chord has (1–4). With fewer than the chord has, the fifth goes first, then extensions, the seventh, the third; with more, the root, fifth and third are doubled an octave up. Inversion moves the lowest voice up an octave (or the highest down, for negative values). Voicing spreads the chord: Drop 2 and Drop 3 move the 2nd or 3rd voice from the top down an octave, Spread opens it into a wide pad (bass down, the rest at least a fourth apart), Open moves every second voice up an octave. A voicing that needs more voices plays Close. Register. The chord is moved by octaves so its lowest voice ( Anchor = Bass ), its middle ( Centre ) or its top voice ( Top ) is as close to the input as possible. Range folds voices more than that many octaves above the bass back down. Voice Leading. Smooth tries every inversion of the next chord in a few octaves and plays the one whose voices move least (and that stays near the input). Smooth + Top also keeps the top voice still where it can, like a held melody note. Inversion is ignored then. Trig. Unpatched, the chord follows the input all the time; Hysteresis keeps a slightly noisy input from flickering between roots. Patch a trigger and the input is read only on each pulse, then held. A pulse that gives the same chord plays it again. Strum. With Strum above 0 a new chord reaches the voices one after the other ( Strum Order Up: bass first), spread over the Strum time. How to use it? Chords from a melody: a Step Sequencer's Pitch into Pitch , its Trigger into Trig , Notes into a Voice Cell. Smooth pads: Voice Leading Smooth , Voicing Spread , a slow sequence of roots. Follow the song's chords: Mode Follow , Harmony = the Harmony Master's bus; patch an LFO into Pitch to move the chord's register. Four oscillators: Voice 1 … 4 into four oscillators instead of a Voice Cell; Change retriggers their envelopes. Gated chords: patch a gate into Gate : notes sound only while it is high. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Chord Quantizer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Chord Quantizer under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Chord Quantizer: Strummed Dorian Strum rolls open-voiced ninth chords across the four voices, with a dotted echo. Chord Quantizer: Offbeat Stabs Chromatic Mode with Chord Minor 7 and a Drop 2 voicing for syncopated stabs; Root feeds a sine bass. Chord Quantizer: Follow the Changes Mode Follow takes the chord from a Harmony Master progression; an LFO into Pitch moves the register. Chord Quantizer: Whole-tone Pulse A Random walks Pitch through a Whole Tone scale, so every chord is augmented; an LFO gate pulses them in eighths. title: Harmony Master
text: Harmony Master Harmony Master in the module view Introduction Harmony Master says what key and chord the music is in right now, for the whole board. Modules that follow harmony (the Quantizer Suite and the Chord Quantizer, set to the same Bus ) quantize to it instead of their own Root and Scale: change the chord here and every follower changes with it, on every track of the Live set. The chord comes from the knobs, from a progression that runs with the song, or from chords you play into its Notes input. Its own outputs carry the key, the root, the bass and the chord tones as pitches, and the chord as notes. How does it work? Key and scale. Key and Scale set the key. Every chord is built in it. Source chooses where the chord comes from: Manual: the chord on scale degree Degree (1–7) with Quality . Diatonic Triad and Diatonic Seventh stack every other scale note, so degree 2 in C major is D minor, degree 5 with a seventh is G7. Any other quality (Sus4, Major 7, …) is built on the degree's note as it is. Patch a sequencer or a slow Random into Degree to walk through the key's chords. Progression: up to 16 slots, drawn in the view. Each slot has a root (a degree, or a fixed note C … B), a quality, an optional bass note (for slash chords) and a length in beats. Advance decides how it moves: Transport follows the song position, so loop jumps and renders always land on the right chord; Trigger moves one slot per pulse at Next ( Reset goes back to slot 1); Select plays the slot the Slot knob points at. When the transport stops, the chord holds. Detect: the chord is recognised from the notes held at Notes . Notes must be stable for 30 ms, so a strummed chord counts once. The lowest note is the bass, so C E G A is A minor 7 over A and C6 over C. With Latch on the last chord stays when you let go; off, it falls back to the Manual chord. Scale Policy. Keep publishes the scale as set. Adapt bends it to contain the chord: in A minor, an E major chord turns the scale into A harmonic minor while it lasts, so followers play the G♯. Transpose shifts key and chord by the input, in semitones. In Progression it takes effect at the next chord change (or Next/Reset), so a sequencer on it changes key in time with the progression; otherwise at once. Bus. The context goes to bus A, B, C or D. Followers pick the same bus. If two Harmony Masters share a bus, the first one wins and the other shows a warning and publishes nothing. How to use it? One key for the whole set: put a Harmony Master on the board, set the key, switch the followers' Harmony to Bus A . A progression: choose Progression . Click a slot to edit it, drag its right edge to change its length, + adds a slot. Play the changes: choose Detect , patch a MIDI input's Notes into Notes and play chords; the arpeggios and bass lines follow. A pad that plays the chord: patch Notes into a Voice Cell. Notes that stay in the next chord keep sounding. A bass line: Root or Bass into an oscillator; Change restarts its envelope at every chord change. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Harmony Master does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Harmony Master under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Harmony Master: Rhythmic Changes Advance Trigger: a sequencer pulses Next , so the chords change in a syncopated rhythm, with the Root as bass. Harmony Master: Adapting Scale Scale Policy Adapt bends A minor to harmonic minor on the E major chord; a Quantizer Suite follower plays the G♯. Harmony Master: Wandering Key Manual source with a Random on Degree and a sequencer on Transpose that moves the key every two bars. Slot: the slot that plays in Progression with Advance = Select ; wraps round the number of slots. Velocity: the velocity of the Notes output. title: Quantizer
text: Quantizer Quantizer in the module view Introduction The Quantizer snaps a pitch to the nearest note of a scale. Feed it an LFO, a random voltage or an envelope, and an oscillator plays a melody that always fits the key. A trigger on every note change lets the melody play envelopes too. How does it work? The signal goes through these steps: Range: In is scaled, so a full-scale LFO (−1 … +1) spans ± Range octaves. Transpose is added. Because this happens before quantizing, the result stays in the scale. Clock (optional): when patched, the value is only taken on each clock pulse and held until the next. Quantize to the scale chosen by Root and Scale . Rounding picks the nearest note, the one below, or the one above. Shift is added after quantizing: a chromatic transposition that may leave the scale. Glide smooths the jumps between notes. Hysteresis stops flicker: the input has to move a bit past the halfway point between two notes before the output changes. Trigger fires and Gate drops for one millisecond each time the note changes, so an envelope or CV to Notes can start a new note. To build your own scale, click keys on the keyboard. Clicking a key while another scale is selected copies that scale and switches Scale to Custom , so any scale is a starting point. How to use it? Melodies from an LFO: a slow LFO into In , Out into an oscillator's Pitch . Try Minor Pentatonic : no wrong notes. Random melodies: Random into In , a clock into Clock , Trigger into an ADSR's gate. Key changes: a sequencer or another quantizer into Root In sets the key; everything stays in the new scale. Arpeggios: a sawtooth LFO into In plays the scale upwards. Portamento: raise Glide for slides between notes. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Range 0 … 4 octaves 1 octave Hysteresis 0 … 50 % of a semitone 10 % Glide 0 … 2 s 0 s Root C … B C Scale the Step Sequencer's 17 scales, plus Custom Major Rounding Nearest, Down, Up Nearest Range: how many octaves a full-scale input covers in each direction. It applies to In only. Hysteresis: how far past the midpoint between two notes the input must move before the note changes. 0 is plain quantizing. Glide: a smoothing time on Out . Trigger still fires at the change. Root , Scale: the key. Custom uses the keys set in the keyboard. Rounding: Nearest rounds to the closest scale note (an exact tie goes down), Down to the one at or below, Up to the one at or above. Inputs Input Signal What it does In pitch The signal to quantize, 1 V/oct (0 = C4) Clock trigger Optional: the output changes only on a clock Transpose pitch Added before quantizing (stays in the scale) Shift pitch Added after quantizing (chromatic) Root In pitch Optional: overrides Root with this note's pitch class Outputs Output Signal What it does Out pitch The quantized pitch, plus Shift , after Glide Trigger trigger A pulse at each note change Gate gate Low for 1 ms at each note change, high otherwise

title: Quantizer Suite
text: Quantizer Suite Quantizer Suite in the module view Introduction Four quantizers in one module. Each channel snaps a pitch to a scale, and can also transpose it in scale steps, arpeggiate a chord on it, or follow the board's Harmony Master. Unpatched inputs take the previous channel's signal, so one melody into In A gives a four-voice diatonic harmony on Out A … D without another cable. How does it work? Allowed notes. Each channel quantizes to its Root and Scale , minus the notes you switch off on its keyboard in the view (the mask). With Link on, channels B – D use channel A's Root, Scale and Harmony. Halfway between two notes the lower wins; Hysteresis keeps a note until the input is clearly in the next one's range. Modes (per channel): Quantize: the nearest allowed note. Transpose: the nearest allowed note, moved by Steps allowed notes. +2 in C major turns C into E and A into the C above. The defaults (A 0, B +2, C +4, D +6) turn one melody into seventh chords moving with it. Arp: at each Trig a chord is built on the input's note from scale steps ( Chord : Triad, Seventh, …) over Span octaves, and the channel plays its next tone in Order (Up, Down, Up-Down, Converge, Random). Steps shifts the starting tone. With no trigger patched on this or an earlier channel, it steps in 1/16 notes with the song. Follow: needs Harmony on a bus with a Harmony Master (otherwise it quantizes and says "no harmony"). Target chooses what it lands on: Scale (the Harmony Master's scale), Chord (the nearest chord tone, then Steps chord tones up or down), Chord + Scale (scale notes, but a chord tone within a semitone wins), or Root (the chord's root in the nearest octave: a bass line from any contour). A continuous channel changes on the chord change itself. Sample. Continuous follows the input. Trigger reads it on each pulse at Trig and holds it (a pulse on the same note plays it again). Track & Hold follows while Trig is high and holds while it is low. Unpatched Trigs take the previous channel's, so one clock on Trig A samples all four. Octave shifts the result, Slew glides to each new note in the same time however far it jumps. Notes. Each channel with Notes on plays its note on note channel 1 – 4 (A – D) at Velocity ; a new note starts before the old one ends (legato). How to use it? Instant harmony: a sequence into In A , Notes into a Voice Cell. Pentatonic only: click notes off on the keyboard. An arpeggiator: channel A Mode Arp , a clock into Trig A . A bass that follows the chords: Mode Follow , Target Root , any melody or LFO into the input. Harmoniser: Mode Follow , Target Chord , Steps 1 and 2 on B and C. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Quantizer Suite does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Quantizer Suite under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Quantizer Suite: Pentatonic Mask The note mask keeps five notes of D major, so a random line always sounds right; channel B plays the same notes an octave down. Quantizer Suite: Four-voice Harmony One melody into In A ; Transpose Steps 2, 4 and 7 on B, C and D make a moving four-part chord. Quantizer Suite: Arp Machine Channels A and B in Arp Mode : a seventh chord played Up-Down over two octaves and a shuffled triad. Quantizer Suite: Chord Followers Follow Mode on a Harmony Master bus: Target Chord for a lead and a harmony voice, Root for a bass line. Quantizer Suite: Gliding Lines Track & Hold Sample with Slew turns a smooth random curve into two sliding F Lydian lines. Steps means scale steps (Transpose, Follow · Scale), chord tones (Follow · Chord) or the arpeggio's start (Arp). title: CV to MIDI
text: CV to MIDI CV to MIDI in the module view Introduction CV to MIDI turns control signals into MIDI control changes (CC). Patch an LFO, an envelope or an Envelope Follower into one of its four lanes, and the value goes out as a CC message that other modules, plugins in Live or outside hardware can use to move a parameter. Its Notes output carries the messages, as any notes cable does: patch it into a MIDI output, a Voice Cell's neighbour or the Monitor to see what is sent. How does it work? Each lane has an input and its own CC number (0–127) and Channel (1–16). Only patched lanes send anything. The signal is read as 0 … +1 (or −1 … +1, see Input Range ) and mapped onto the lane's Min … Max data range, which you can use to limit a parameter's travel or, with Min above Max, to invert it. A message is sent only when the 7-bit value changes , so a still input is silent and a slow LFO sends a handful of messages per second, not thousands. Max Rate caps how often one lane may send. When the signal moves faster than that, in-between values are skipped, but the latest one always arrives. When a lane is patched, or when you press Resend , its current value is sent at once, so the receiver starts in sync. With Resolution set to 14 bit , lanes on CC 0–31 send the high part on the CC number and the low part on CC + 32, the MIDI standard for fine control. Lanes on higher CCs stay 7 bit. How to use it? Filter sweep in Live: an LFO into In 1 , CC 74 on the channel your instrument listens to, then map CC 74 to the cutoff. Loudness to a parameter: Envelope Follower 's Env into a lane: the audio moves a MIDI-mapped control. Bipolar sources: set Input Range to −1 … +1 so an LFO's centre sends Smooth controls: use 14 bit on CC 0–31 for receivers that support it. Reference Settings Setting Values Default CC 1–4 0 – 127 1, 74, 71, 91 Channel 1–4 1 – 16 1 Min 1–4, Max 1–4 0 – 127 0, 127 Input Range 0 … +1, −1 … +1 0 … +1 Resolution 7 bit, 14 bit (CC 0–31) 7 bit Max Rate 10 – 1000 per second per lane 200 Buttons Button What it does Resend sends every patched lane's value again Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 control the value for each lane Outputs Output Signal What it carries Notes notes the control change messages

title: CV to Notes
text: CV to Notes CV to Notes in the module view Introduction CV to Notes turns a pitch and a gate into notes . Voice Cells and note outputs take notes, while sequencers, Random and other mono sources make pitch and gate signals. Put CV to Notes in between, and any mono source can play a polyphonic synth or a MIDI instrument. How does it work? The module watches the Gate and the Pitch inputs: Gate goes high: a note-on is sent. The note number is the pitch rounded to the nearest semitone (0.0 = C4 = MIDI note 60). The exact pitch, including any fraction of a semitone, travels with the note. Velocity comes from the Velocity knob. Gate goes low: a note-off for that note. Pitch moves to another semitone while the gate is high: a legato change. The new note starts first and the old one is released right after. A mono or legato Voice Cell glides without restarting its envelopes; a poly cell plays the new note on another voice. Pitch changes smaller than a semitone don't start a new note. Only one note sounds at a time. How to use it? Sequencer into a synth: patch the sequencer's Pitch and Gate here, and Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes input. Generative melodies: Random Out (with Semitones on) → Pitch , and a Function's A (or Random Trig through a short envelope) → Gate . Accent and dynamics: patch a control signal onto the Velocity knob to vary the velocity of each note. Legato lines: keep the gate high and move the pitch. Set the Voice Cell's Mode to Legato and add some Glide for slides. Need a gate from a trigger? A short ADSR or a Function in envelope mode turns a trigger into a gate. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Velocity 0 – 100 % 80 % Velocity: the velocity of each new note, read at the moment the note starts. It's a modulation destination: patch a Random or an LFO onto it for changing dynamics. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the note's pitch; 0.0 = C4, +1.0 = one octave up; notes are limited to MIDI 0 – 127 Gate gate high (≥ 0.5) plays a note, low releases it Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes note-on and note-off events; connects to any notes input

title: Drum Notes
text: Drum Notes Introduction Drum Notes turns the General MIDI drum notes of a MIDI track into triggers: one output per drum. Patch Kick into a kick drum's trigger, Closed Hat into a hat voice, and the keys of a drum pad or a MIDI clip play your kit. It is how the drum machines in Bleep Instrument take MIDI from Live while their own pattern keeps playing. How does it work? Notes in, triggers out. Each note-on whose note belongs to a drum sends a one-sample pulse to that drum's output. Note-offs are ignored: a drum is a hit, not a held note. Notes that are not on the table below do nothing. Velocity. Velocity carries the velocity of the last hit (0 … 1) for a moment (about a millisecond) around the trigger, and is 0 the rest of the time. Patch it into the Velocity (or Accent ) input of a drum voice that also gets a velocity from a sequencer: the voice then plays a key's hit at the key's velocity and the sequencer's hits unchanged. Several drums on one voice. An output can go to any number of inputs, and an input takes any number of cables, so two drums can share one voice, for example Closed Hat and Open Hat into one hat. How to use it? Play a kit from the keys: a Notes source (a MIDI input, or a drum machine cell's Notes input) into Notes ; each drum output into one voice's trigger. Add MIDI to a pattern: keep the sequencer's cables and add Drum Notes next to them. Triggers merge, so the pattern and the keys both play. Fewer voices than drums: send Closed Hat and Open Hat , or the three toms, to the same voice. Reference Notes Output Drum General MIDI notes Kick Bass drum 35, 36 Snare Snare 38, 40 Rim Side stick 37 Clap Hand clap 39 Closed Hat Closed and pedal hi-hat 42, 44 Open Hat Open hi-hat 46 Tom Low to high toms 41, 43, 45, 47, 48, 50 Cowbell Cowbell 56 Ride Ride cymbals 51, 53, 59 Crash Crash cymbals 49, 52, 55, 57 Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes the MIDI notes to listen to, all channels Outputs Output Signal What it does Kick, Snare, Rim, Clap, Closed Hat, Open Hat, Tom, Cowbell, Ride, Crash trigger a one-sample pulse for each note-on of that drum Velocity control, 0 … 1 the hit's velocity for about a millisecond, then 0 The module has no knobs.

title: Notes to CV
text: Notes to CV Notes to CV in the module view Introduction Notes to CV turns notes into pitch , gate and friends. Notes come from a MIDI port, a MIDI Device or the Step Sequencer's Notes output; this module lets them play an oscillator, open an envelope or move a filter outside a Voice Cell. It is the opposite of CV to Notes . How does it work? The module remembers which notes are held. One of them is the active note , chosen by Priority : Last: the most recent note. Releasing it goes back to the note held before, like a classic mono synth. Lowest / Highest: the lowest or highest held note. First: the oldest held note; others take over only when it is released. Pitch and Velocity follow the active note and hold their values after release. Gate is high while any note is held. Trigger fires each time the active note changes. With Retrigger On , the gate drops for one sample when the active note changes while another is held, so envelopes restart. With Off (Legato) , the gate stays high and only Trigger marks the change. Glide smooths Pitch . With Glide Mode Legato Only , it only glides between overlapping notes; detached notes jump. All held notes are released when the transport stops or the Notes cable is removed, so the gate never hangs. How to use it? A mono synth from MIDI: MIDI port Notes → Notes to CV; Pitch → Oscillator Pitch ; Gate → ADSR gate; ADSR → VCA. Acid lines: Retrigger off, Glide Mode Legato Only , some Glide : overlapping notes slide, others don't. Velocity to the filter: Velocity onto the filter's cutoff knob. Key tracking for modulation: Pitch onto an LFO's rate, so higher notes move faster. Bass from chords: Priority Lowest always plays the lowest held note. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Glide 0 … 2 s 0 s Priority Last, Lowest, Highest, First Last Retrigger Off (Legato), On On Glide Mode Always, Legato Only Always Channel All, 1 … 16 All Channel: only notes on this MIDI channel are used. Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes The note stream Outputs Output Signal What it does Pitch pitch The active note, 1 V/oct (0 = C4); holds after release Gate gate High while any note is held Trigger trigger A pulse at each new active note Velocity control The active note's velocity, 0 … 1; holds after release Release control The last note-off's release velocity, 0 … 1 Pressure control The active note's pressure, 0 … 1; 0 after release Count control Held notes ÷ 16

title: Level Meter
text: Level Meter Level Meter in the module view Introduction The Level Meter shows how loud a signal is : a bar per channel for the peak and the average (RMS) level, a peak-hold line and a clip light. Put it anywhere in an audio path: the audio passes through unchanged, so it can sit between a mixer and an output, or hang off a cable on the side. Its Level output turns the loudness into a control signal, so a sound can move other things: an envelope follower. How does it work? Open the meter's view to see the bars. The bright part of each bar is the RMS level (roughly how loud it sounds), the pale part above it the peak level (the highest sample). The thin line is the peak hold ; the numbers below show the held peak and the RMS level in dB. The clip light turns red when a sample goes over 0 dBFS, the point where the signal would distort on its way out of the computer, and stays red until you click it (or the meter). With only In L patched, the meter shows one mono bar. Response sets how quickly the RMS level and the Level output follow the signal: short for punchy drums, long for a smooth average. Floor is the bottom of the scale: everything quieter shows as empty and gives 0 on Level . Level Follows picks what Level tracks: RMS (smooth) or Peak (fast attack, falling over Response ). Peak Hold is how long the hold line stays up. How to use it? Check the mix: put it before an Audio Out and keep the RMS around −18 dB to −12 dB with the peaks below 0. Ducking: a kick's Out into the meter, Level into a VCA's Gain with a negative cable amount: the pad ducks under the kick. Loudness to brightness: Level into a Multi Filter's Cutoff , so louder playing opens the filter. Watch the output: leave one before the last Audio Out with Peak Hold at Until Reset : the hold line and the clip light tell you afterwards if anything overloaded while you weren't looking. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Response 10 ms – 2 s 300 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Level Follows RMS, Peak RMS Peak Hold Off, 1 s, 3 s, Until Reset 3 s Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left channel, or mono In R audio right channel; unpatched, it follows In L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the inputs, unchanged Level control 0 at Floor and below, 1 at 0 dBFS, on a dB scale; the louder channel Clip gate high while a sample goes over 0 dBFS, and 50 ms after

title: Monitor
text: Monitor Monitor in the module view Introduction The Monitor shows what is on a cable . Patch a Notes cable into it to see every note, controller, program change and bend in a table; patch audio for a level meter, a control signal for a readout and a gate or trigger for a pulse meter. Everything passes through: each input comes out of the output with the same name, so the Monitor can sit in the middle of a patch or hang off a cable on the side. Use as many of the inputs as you need; the others stay dim. How does it work? Open the Monitor's view. MIDI. Every event that arrives on Notes becomes a row, newest on top: the time since you opened the window, the MIDI channel (1–16), the kind of event, its number and its value. A note shows its name and number (60 is C4), a controller its number and, where it has a standard name, the name (74 is Cutoff ). The small bar under a value shows it from 0 to 127; for a bend it shows the position of the wheel. Under the table, a keyboard lights the notes that are on right now. A note that stays lit after you let go is a stuck note : its note-off never arrived. All Notes Off (controller 123) clears them. The chips above the table choose what you see: Notes , CC , Program , Bend , Pressure and Clock . Clock is off at first, since it sends 24 events per quarter note and would bury everything else. Pause stops adding rows (the events still pass through); Clear empties the table. If more events arrive than the window can follow between two updates (a knob sweeping a controller), the count says how many were missed . The cables are not affected. Audio. A bar per channel: the solid part is the RMS level (about how loud it sounds), the pale part the peak, and the thin line the held peak. The numbers show both in dB, and the lamp turns red when a sample goes over 0 dB. With only Audio L patched you get one mono bar. Click the bars to reset the hold and the lamps. Response is how quickly the RMS level follows, Floor the bottom of the scale. CV. The value as a number, the note name it would play if you read it as 1 V per octave with 0 as C4 (0.25 reads D♯4 ), a history graph with a band for the lowest and highest value of each update, and the lowest and highest value since you last clicked the graph. A short spike is never missed. The graph's scale follows the signal. Gate. A lamp and HIGH or LOW , a strip of the recent gate history, and numbers: Pulses counted since you last clicked the strip, the Rate of the pulses in Hz and in BPM (taken from the last two; it shows a dash when the pulses stop), the Length of the last gate and the Duty , the share of the last second the gate was high. A one-sample trigger lights the lamp for a moment, so even the shortest pulse shows. How to use it? What does my controller send? MIDI In or MIDI Device into Notes ; turn the knob you are interested in and read its controller number. Give one of the MIDI In 's CC settings that number to get it as a control signal. Find a stuck note: keep an eye on the keyboard under the table; a lit key with no note-off row means the sender missed one. Check a clock: a clock or sequencer Gate into Gate ; the BPM is the pulse rate × 60, so a clock with four pulses per beat shows four times the tempo. Check an envelope or LFO: into CV . The graph shows its shape, the numbers its range. Set a level: a source into Audio L and R , with the RMS around −18 dB and the peaks below 0. Chain it: the outputs follow the inputs, so a Monitor can sit between a MIDI In and a Voice Cell without changing anything. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Response 10 ms – 2 s 300 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes the MIDI events for the table and the keyboard Audio L audio left channel, or mono Audio R audio right channel; unpatched, it follows Audio L CV control the signal for the CV readout Gate gate the gate or trigger for the gate meter (high at 0.5 and above) Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes the input's events, unchanged Audio L, Audio R audio the inputs, unchanged CV control the input, unchanged Gate gate the input, unchanged

title: XY Scope
text: XY Scope XY Scope in the module view Introduction XY Scope is an oscilloscope with a green phosphor screen, made for the old bench trick of comparing two oscillators by eye. Patch one into X and one into Y : the beam draws a Lissajous figure. It stands still when the two are in a simple ratio and turns slowly when they are slightly off. A Y-T mode shows ordinary waveforms. It also turns what you see into signals: Phase , Correlation , Ratio and a Still gate. Patch Still into a sequencer's clock and the music moves on whenever two drifting oscillators happen to lock. How does it work? The screen. X moves the beam left and right, Y up and down; at 1 × gain ±1 reaches the edge of the graticule. The beam glows where it moves slowly and is faint where it moves fast, as on a real tube, and the trace fades over Persistence . Focus sets how sharp the line is, Intensity how bright, and the Z input modulates the brightness (−1 blanks the beam, +1 doubles it). Character Vintage adds the tube's flaws: a slightly bulging picture, softer corners, a trace of mains hum and a short warm-up when the view opens. None of this reaches the outputs. Frequencies. Both inputs are measured by timing their rising zero crossings, from about 0.2 Hz to 10 kHz. A channel counts as valid while it is patched, louder than −60 dBFS and crossing zero at least every 5 s. The readout shows both frequencies, or a dash while a channel is not valid. Ratio is fy / fx as an interval: 1.0 is an octave, 0.585 a fifth, −1 an octave down. From it the scope picks the figure ratio p:q, the simplest fraction (up to 8:8) within 3 % of it; it shows in the readout and decides what Phase compares. A new figure ratio takes over after 200 ms, so it doesn't flicker between neighbours. Phase is the phase of the figure, −1 … +1 for −180° … +180°. At 1:1 it is the plain phase difference: 0 for a diagonal line, +0.5 for a circle with Y leading, ±1 for the other diagonal. At other ratios it is constant as long as Y is exactly p/q times X. When the oscillators drift apart, Phase becomes a sawtooth at the rate the figure turns: two detuned oscillators make a slow LFO from their own beating. Correlation is +1 when X and Y move together, −1 when they move opposite, and near 0 when they are unrelated or a quarter cycle apart. Still goes high once the figure has stood still for 100 ms: both channels valid, the ratio within 0.25 % of p/q and the figure turning slower than the Still Tolerance (Tight 0.05, Normal 0.2, Loose 1 turn per second). It goes low 50 ms after that stops being true. While a channel isn't valid, Ratio and Phase hold their last value and Still is low. Y-T mode draws Y over time, one sweep per Timebase . Trigger Y Rising starts each sweep at a rising zero crossing of Y, so a steady wave stands still; Auto does the same but sweeps anyway when no crossing comes; Beat starts a sweep on every beat while the transport plays. X, when patched, is drawn as a second, dimmer trace. Out X and Out Y pass the inputs on unchanged, so the scope can sit in a signal path. The scope has no random parts: the same input always gives the same outputs. How to use it? Tune by eye: two oscillators into X and Y, tune one until the figure stands still. A circle or line is unison, a figure-eight an octave. Beating as an LFO: two oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, Phase into a filter's cutoff: a slow sweep that speeds up as they drift apart. Music that waits for a lock: two free-running oscillators slightly detuned (or slowly modulated), Still into a sequencer's clock. Stereo width: a stereo signal's left and right into X and Y. A line at 45° is mono, a round cloud is wide; Correlation below 0 warns of phase problems. Interval follower: Ratio into an oscillator's pitch makes it follow the interval between two others. Classic scope: Mode Y-T, any signal into Y. Demo patches Five whole patches show what XY Scope does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick XY Scope under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows XY Scope: Beating Lissajous Two detuned sines turn the figure slowly; Phase becomes a sawtooth LFO for a pad's filter. XY Scope: Interval Figures A sequenced sine against a fixed one draws each interval; Ratio steers a voice that follows the interval. XY Scope: Waiting for Lock The Still gate opens a melody only while two wandering oscillators agree; try Still Tolerance . XY Scope: Stereo Width A detuned pad's left and right on X and Y; Correlation darkens an arpeggio as the pad widens. XY Scope: Drum Scope Mode Y-T with Trigger Beat draws a drum loop as a waveform, with the bass as a second trace. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default X Gain 0.1 – 10 × 1 × Y Gain 0.1 – 10 × 1 × Timebase 1 ms – 2 s 20 ms Persistence 10 ms – 5 s 150 ms Focus 0 – 100 % 80 % Intensity 0 – 100 % 60 % Mode X-Y, Y-T X-Y Trigger Y Rising, Auto, Beat Y Rising Phosphor Green, Amber, Blue-White Green Character Clean, Vintage Vintage Still Tolerance Tight, Normal, Loose Normal X Gain, Y Gain: the size of the picture across and up. Timebase: the length of one sweep (Y-T mode only). Persistence: how long the trace glows: the time it takes to fade by 40 dB. Focus: 100 % is a fine line, 0 % a soft, wide glow. Intensity: the beam's brightness. Trigger: what starts a sweep (Y-T mode only). Phosphor: the screen colour. Character: Vintage adds the tube's flaws, Clean draws none. Still Tolerance: how slowly the figure must turn for Still . The six knobs are modulation destinations. Only Timebase (in Y-T mode) changes anything but the picture; the others never touch the outputs. Inputs Input Signal What it does X audio horizontal deflection; the reference for Phase and Ratio Y audio vertical deflection; the signal compared with X Z control beam brightness: 0 normal, −1 off, +1 double Outputs Output Signal What it does Out X audio X, unchanged Out Y audio Y, unchanged Phase control the figure's phase, −1 … +1 = −180° … +180° Correlation control how alike X and Y are, −1 … +1 Ratio pitch fy / fx as an interval (1.0 = an octave) Still gate high while the figure stands still

title: Button
text: Button Button in the module view Introduction The Button is a pad to press while the patch plays. Click it, tap it or press Space: it opens a gate, fires triggers, or switches something on and off. Use it to start an envelope by hand, reset a sequencer, fire a drum or mute a part. How does it work? In Momentary mode, Gate is high for as long as you hold the pad. In Toggle mode, each press switches Gate on or off, and it stays there. Whatever the mode: Trigger fires a short pulse each time you press, Release fires one each time you let go, Toggle switches on or off with every press. Once you've clicked the pad, Space and Enter press it too. The toggle's state is saved with the set, so a part you switched off stays off when you open it again. How to use it? Play an envelope by hand: Gate into an ADSR's Gate , the ADSR into a VCA. Restart the music: Trigger into a Step Sequencer's or an LFO's Reset . Fire a drum: Trigger into a drum's Trig . Mute a part: Toggle mode, Gate onto a VCA's Gain (or into a Switch to choose between two sources). Reference Settings Setting Values Default Mode Momentary, Toggle Momentary Outputs Output Signal What it does Gate gate high while held (Momentary) or while toggled on (Toggle) Trigger trigger a pulse on every press Release trigger a pulse on every release Toggle gate switches on or off with every press

title: Dial
text: Dial Dial in the module view Introduction The Dial is one big knob whose position comes out of a jack as a control signal. Patch Out onto several knobs at once, at different cable amounts, and one turn moves them all together: a macro for the filter, the mix and the decay of a sound. How does it work? Turn the dial (drag up and down, Shift for fine, or use the wheel; double-click resets it). Out goes from Min with the dial fully left to Max fully right. Set Max below Min to turn the dial around, or Min to −1 for a bipolar dial that moves its destinations both ways. Steps gives the dial detents: with 4, it only stops at four positions, evenly spaced, and each wheel notch moves one step. Handy for choosing between a few settings, or for octave jumps on a pitch. Smooth glides Out to a new position instead of jumping, so fast turns don't click. At 0 it follows the dial exactly. A cable into Value moves the dial like a hand would: the big dial shows the modulation as a ring. How to use it? Macro: Out onto a Multi Filter's Cutoff , a VCA's Gain and an LFO's Rate ; set each cable's amount for how far each one moves. Morph between two sounds: Out onto a Crossfader's Mix . Octave switch: Min −1, Max +1 and Steps 3 into an Oscillator's Pitch input: an octave down, unchanged, an octave up. Slow manual sweep: Smooth at 1 s turns any quick move into a sweep. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Value 0 – 100 % 50 % Min −1 – +1 0 Max −1 – +1 +1 Smooth 0 – 2 s 20 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Steps 0 (continuous), 2 – 24 0 Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control the dial's position, scaled from Min to Max

title: XY Pad
text: XY Pad XY Pad in the module view Introduction The XY Pad gives you two control signals from one touch . Drag a point over the pad: its horizontal position comes out of X , its vertical position out of Y . Patch the two onto a filter's cutoff and resonance, or a pair of mix knobs, and one finger plays both. How does it work? X and Y go from Min at the left and bottom edges to Max at the right and top edges; both axes share the range. The default is 0 to 1; set Min to −1 for a pad that moves its destinations both ways from the centre. Smooth glides both outputs to a new position instead of jumping. A cable into the X or Y knob moves the point like a hand would. In a panel, an XY pad control drives this module. How to use it? Filter sweep: X onto a Multi Filter's Cutoff , Y onto its Resonance . Morph: X and Y onto two Crossfader mixes for a four-way blend. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default X 0 – 100 % 50 % Y 0 – 100 % 50 % Min −1 – +1 0 Max −1 – +1 +1 Smooth 0 – 2 s 20 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Outputs Output Signal What it does X control horizontal position, scaled from Min to Max Y control vertical position, scaled from Min to Max

title: Keyboard
text: Keyboard Keyboard in the module view Introduction The Keyboard is a piano keyboard on the board . Play it with the mouse, a finger or your computer keyboard to try a sound without reaching for a MIDI controller. Its Notes output plays a Voice Cell directly; Pitch and Gate play a single oscillator and envelope. How does it work? Mouse and touch. Press a key to play it; drag across the keys for a glissando. Computer keyboard. Click the keys once, then play: the row A S D F G H J K L holds the white keys from C, the row above ( W E T Y U O P ) the black ones, like a piano. Z and X move down and up an octave. It goes by the keys' positions, so any keyboard layout works. Octave (or the ‹ › buttons) chooses which three octaves the keys show. Velocity sets how hard every key is played. Hold latches keys: a click starts a note and it keeps playing until you click it again. Switch Hold off, or press All off , to end them. Notes sends every key you play, so a Voice Cell plays chords. Pitch , Gate , Velocity and Trigger follow one note at a time, chosen by Priority (the last key pressed, the lowest, the highest or the first), and fall back to a key still held when you let go. Glide slides Pitch from note to note. How to use it? Try a synth: Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes ; the cell's output to Audio Out. Hold a few keys for a chord. A mono synth without a cell: Pitch into an Oscillator's Pitch , Gate into an ADSR, the ADSR onto a VCA. Raise Glide for slides. A drone: switch on Hold and click a few keys. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Velocity 1 – 100 % 80 % Glide 0 – 2 s 0 s Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Octave −3 – +3 0 (C3 – C6) Priority Last, Lowest, Highest, First Last Hold Off, On Off Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes every key played Pitch pitch the active key, 1 V/oct Gate gate high while any key is held Velocity control the active key's velocity Trigger trigger a pulse each time the active key changes

title: Wheel
text: Wheel Wheel in the module view Introduction The Wheel is a pitch or mod wheel as a control signal. Drag it up and down and Out follows; with Spring on it returns to the middle when you let go, like the wheel on a keyboard. Patch Out onto an Oscillator's Pitch for a pitch bend, or onto a filter's cutoff for a mod wheel. How does it work? Out goes from Min at the bottom of the wheel to Max at the top. The default range is −1 to +1 with the wheel centred, so at rest Out is 0. For a mod wheel that rests at the bottom, set Min to 0 and turn Spring off. Spring (on by default) moves the wheel back to the middle when you let go. Off, it stays where you leave it. Smooth glides Out to a new position instead of jumping. A cable into Value moves the wheel like a hand would. In a panel, a Wheel control drives this module. How to use it? Pitch bend: Out onto an Oscillator's Pitch , cable amount ±2 semitones. Mod wheel: Min 0, Max 1, Spring off, Out onto a filter's Cutoff . Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Value 0 – 100 % 50 % Min −1 – +1 −1 Max −1 – +1 +1 Smooth 0 – 2 s 20 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Spring off, on on Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control the wheel's position, scaled from Min to Max

title: Arpeggiator
text: Arpeggiator Arpeggiator in the module view Introduction The Arpeggiator plays the notes you hold one at a time , in a pattern, in time with the transport or a clock. Hold a chord and it becomes a running line. Its Notes output plays a Voice Cell directly; Pitch , Gate , Velocity and Trigger drive modules outside one. How does it work? The held notes form a pool, lowest first. Octaves repeats the pool one octave higher per copy (up to four), and Pattern chooses the order: Up / Down: lowest to highest, or the other way. Up-Down / Down-Up: there and back; the top and bottom notes are played once per cycle. Up & Down: there and back; the top and bottom notes are played twice. Played: in the order you pressed the keys. Random: any note, chosen with Seed . The same seed gives the same line every time, also in a render. Converge: lowest, highest, second lowest, second highest, and so on towards the middle. Diverge: from the middle outwards. One step lasts one Rate (1/1 … 1/32T). Gate Length sets how much of the step the note sounds, Swing delays every second step. With nothing patched into Clock , the steps lock to the song position, so the transport has to be running. Patch a trigger into Clock and every pulse is one step, whatever the transport does. A pulse into Reset ends the note and the next step starts the pattern again. With Latch on, the notes keep playing after you let go. The next key you press starts a new chord. Switch Latch off to stop. Adding or releasing keys while it plays changes the pool from the next step on; the pattern keeps its place. How to use it? Classic arpeggio: MIDI port Notes → Arpeggiator Notes ; Notes out → Voice Cell. Start the transport and hold a chord. Hands-free: Latch on, play a chord, take your hands off. Chord Quantizer as the source: its Notes output into the Arpeggiator for an arpeggio that follows a chord progression. Rhythmic gates: Gate Length around 25 % with Rate 1/16 for staccato; 100 % for a legato line. Mono synth voice: Pitch → Oscillator, Gate → ADSR. Wider range: Octaves 3 or 4 with Up-Down . Generative lines: Random plus a clock from a Pulse Generator or a Rotating Divider. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Gate Length 1 … 100 % 50 % Swing 50 … 75 % 50 % Rate 1/1 … 1/32T 1/16 Pattern Up, Down, Up-Down, Down-Up, Up & Down, Played, Random, Converge, Diverge Up Octaves 1 … 4 1 Latch Off, On Off Seed 0 … 999 1 Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Sync To: what steps the module. Auto : the clock pulses while Clock is patched, otherwise the transport. Clock : only the pulses step it. Transport : the song position steps it, and a patched Clock is ignored. Seed: only used by Random . Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes The keys to arpeggiate Clock trigger One step per pulse; unpatched, the transport sets the steps Reset trigger Ends the note; the next step is step 0 Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes The arpeggio, one note at a time Pitch pitch The playing note, 1 V/oct (0 = C4); holds Gate gate High while a note sounds Velocity control The note's velocity, 0 … 1; holds Trigger trigger A pulse at each new note

title: Cartesian Seq
text: Cartesian Seq Cartesian Seq in the module view Introduction The Cartesian Seq is a sequencer on a grid : up to 8 × 8 cells, each with a gate (off, on or tied), a pitch , a velocity , a mod value and an access switch that takes it out of the path. Two playheads walk the grid, one across the columns ( X ) and one down the rows ( Y ), each with its own rate or clock and direction. The same handful of cells plays very different melodies depending on how the playheads move. In Cartesian mode the playheads stop walking and the X and Y knobs pick the cell instead: patch an LFO, an XY gesture or another sequencer onto them and the grid becomes a map you travel through. Patch Notes into a Voice Cell and press play: a new module plays a rising figure on the 4 × 4 corner of the grid right away. How does it work? The grid. The module always keeps all 64 cells. Columns and Rows set the playing area; cells outside it keep what you drew. Clocks mode (the default). The X playhead follows the transport at X Rate (or one column per pulse on X Clock ). What Y does depends on Y Rate : Wrap: Y moves one row each time X has crossed its row. That's a raster scan: row by row through the grid, like reading a page. A note value: Y moves on its own grid, independent of X. With 4 columns at 1/16 and Y at 1/4., X repeats every quarter note but Y every dotted quarter, so the 16 cells play a line that only repeats after 3 bars. Off: Y stays on the row chosen by the Y knob. With a cable in Y Clock , each pulse moves Y one row, whatever Y Rate says. When both playheads move on the same sample the cell plays once. Each axis has a Direction : forward, backward, back and forth ( Ping-Pong , ends not repeated) or a seeded random order that never repeats a cell twice in a row. The X and Y knobs shift the playheads: X at 50 % on a 4-column grid starts every row two columns later. Modulate them to rotate the pattern while it plays. Skipped cells. A cell with access Skip is taken out of the path; its notes stay. In a raster scan the path just gets shorter (skip 3 of 16 cells and the pattern repeats every 13 steps). With independent axes a skipped cell lends its turn to the next playing cell in the row; a row with every cell skipped stays silent. Cartesian mode. X and Y (knob plus cables) choose the column and the row directly. With Sample = Clock the position is read at every X step and that cell plays. With Change a cell plays as soon as the position moves into a new cell — no clock needed, and it keeps playing when the transport stops, which makes it a performance instrument. A little hysteresis stops a position sitting on a border from chattering. Skipped cells can't be reached; the nearest playing cell plays instead. Gates and ties. On plays for Gate Length of an X step. Tie holds the note into the next cell; a different pitch there starts before the old note ends, so a Voice Cell in Legato mode glides. Off plays nothing, but the playhead still visits the cell and Mod still moves. No note is ever left hanging: stopping, Reset, changing the size or mode, and skipping or silencing the sounding cell all end it. Pitch. A cell's pitch counts semitones above Root + Octave ; with the Transpose input it snaps to the nearest note of the Scale . Mod. Each cell carries a value from −100 % to +100 % that appears on the Mod output when the playhead arrives, gliding there over Mod Slew . Use it for a filter, a wavefold amount, a pan — a second melody for anything. How to use it? A melody right away: Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes input, press play. Drawing: pick a layer at the top. Gate : click cycles Off → On → Tie, drag paints. Pitch , Vel and Mod : drag up and down on a cell (Shift for fine steps; pitch snaps to the scale unless Shift is held); double-click resets. Access : click to skip a cell or bring it back. Alt-drag paints the first cell's value of the layer across others. Rotating: ◀ ▶ beside each row and ▲ ▼ under each column rotate that row or column by one cell. Right-click a cell to copy, paste or reset it. Randomize rewrites the shown layer inside the playing area; ▾ sets the density, pitch range, velocity range and how many cells to skip. Long phrases from short loops: set Y Rate to a dotted or triplet value against X Rate . XY performance: Mode = Cartesian, Sample = Change, and patch two slow LFOs (or a Random) onto X and Y . The crosshair shows where they go. Shuffling the order: X Direction = Random with a slow Function on Y . Chaining: Row End and Grid End make good clocks or resets for other modules; X Pos and Y Pos are handy modulation sources. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Cartesian Seq does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Cartesian Seq under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Cartesian Seq: Lattice Pluck A 4 × 3 corner of the grid in F Lydian: X Rate 1/16 and Y Rate Wrap turn a twelve-step figure against the bar. Cartesian Seq: Bass Raster Eight columns by two rows of bass; each cell's Mod value opens the filter, and a beat plays underneath. Cartesian Seq: Crosshair Drift Mode Cartesian: two slow LFOs on X and Y steer the crosshair over a full 8 × 8 grid, with Sample set to Change. Cartesian Seq: Two Clocks Independent X Rate and Y Rate with X Direction Ping-Pong; Row End and Grid End play a hat and a kick. Cartesian Seq: Random Walk Arp Random X Direction and Y Direction with a fixed Seed hop around the grid in Hirajoshi. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Gate Length 1 – 100 % of an X step 50 % Swing 50 – 75 % 50 % X 0 – 100 % 0 % Y 0 – 100 % 0 % Mod Slew 0 – 1 s 0 s Gate Length: how long each On cell sounds. Ties ignore it. Swing: delays every second X step. X / Y: Clocks mode: shift the playheads by whole cells. Cartesian mode: the position on the grid. Mod Slew: how long the Mod output takes to reach a new cell's value. Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Columns 1 – 8 4 Rows 1 – 8 4 Mode Clocks, Cartesian Clocks X Rate 1/1 … 1/32, dotted (.) and triplet (T) 1/16 Y Rate Wrap, Off, 1/1 … 1/32T Wrap X Direction, Y Direction Forward, Backward, Ping-Pong, Random Forward Sample Clock, Change (Cartesian mode) Clock Root C … B C Scale the Step Sequencer's scales Major Octave −3 … +3 0 Seed 0 – 999 1 Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Sync To: what steps the module. Auto : the clock pulses while X Clock / Y Clock is patched, otherwise the transport. Clock : only the pulses step it. Transport : the song position steps it, and a patched X Clock / Y Clock is ignored. Inputs Input Signal What it does X Clock trigger each pulse moves X one column; unpatched, the transport drives X Y Clock trigger each pulse moves Y one row (Clocks mode) Reset trigger both playheads start again at the first cell Transpose pitch added before quantizing (1 V/oct) Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes one note per played cell, ties as legato Pitch pitch the cell's quantized pitch, held between notes Gate gate high while a cell sounds, across ties Velocity control, 0 – 1 the cell's velocity, held Mod control, −1 – +1 the cell's mod value, through Mod Slew Trigger trigger a pulse when a cell starts a new note X Pos, Y Pos control, 0 – 1 the playing column and row Row End trigger a pulse when X starts a new row (raster) or wraps Grid End trigger a pulse when the whole path starts over

title: Polymeter Seq
text: Polymeter Seq Polymeter Seq in the module view Introduction The Polymeter Seq takes what a step usually holds — does it play, which note, which octave, how long, how likely, how many repeats — and gives each its own track : Trigger , Note , Octave , Gate , Probability and Ratchet . Every track has its own length , loop window , clock division and direction , so they drift against each other. A 16-step rhythm over a 7-step melody and a 5-step octave pattern takes 560 steps to repeat — and it still lands on the song's grid and renders the same every time. Patch Notes into a Voice Cell and press play: a new module plays exactly that drifting line. How does it work? Base ticks. With nothing in Clock , ticks follow the transport at Rate ; with a trigger in Clock , each trigger is one tick. Each track runs at its division of the tick: ×2, ×3, ×4 step two to four times per tick, /2 … /16 every 2 to 16 ticks. Its position is worked out from the tick count, so after a loop jump, or starting in the middle of the song, every track is exactly where it would have been. Loops and directions. A track plays the steps between its loop start and end: forward, backward, back and forth (ends not repeated) or at random (seeded). Hits. A note happens when the Trigger track steps onto an On or Accent step and the Probability step wins the dice (plus Prob. Bias ). The other tracks are read at that moment: Note holds a scale degree (0 = the root, 1 = the next note of the scale, −1 the one below …), so changing Scale keeps the melody's shape and every note stays in key. Octave shifts by −3 … +3 octaves. Gate is the share of the hit the note lasts (times Gate Scale ), or Tie : the note holds into the next hit. Above 100 % notes overlap, and a Voice Cell in Legato mode glides. Ratchet splits the hit into 1–8 quick repeats, evenly spaced, accelerating or decelerating; each repeat is 8 % softer. Accent steps play 20 % louder than Velocity . Spread adds seeded human feel: a little velocity variation and a slight delay. A track's skipped values are simply never heard: a Note track at ×2 under a Trigger track at 1 plays every other note. That's part of the fun. Mute makes a track give its neutral value (Trigger: always on; Note, Octave: 0; Gate: 50 %; Probability: 100 %; Ratchet: 1). Bar and Track Ends. Bar fires when every unmuted track is back at its loop start on the same tick — the full cycle, shown at the top of the view. Track Ends fires whenever any track wraps. Pattern slots. Up to 8 slots, each a complete set of six tracks. Choose one with the slot buttons, or patch the Pattern input (0 … 1 across Slots used ). Pattern Change decides when a new slot takes over: immediately, at the next track end, at the next full cycle or at the next bar. The tick count isn't reset, so the new slot comes in in time. Hold stops every track from advancing while it's high. No note is left hanging: stop, Reset, slot changes, edits and releasing Hold all end the sounding note. How to use it? A generative line: Notes into a Voice Cell. Change the Note track's length to 5 or 9 and hear the phrase change. Editing: each row is a track. Trigger : click cycles Off → On → Accent, drag paints. Note , Octave , Gate , Probability , Ratchet : drag up and down (Note shows the note name on hover). Shift-click a Gate step for Tie, a Ratchet step for its shape (» accelerate, « decelerate). Double-click resets a step. Drag the bracket under a row to set the loop window. Row controls: length, division, direction (→ ← ↔ ?), M mute and ⟳ randomize that track. Randomize all rewrites every track; ▾ sets the trigger density, the degree range, step-wise melodies and the ratchet chance. Slots: build variations in slots 2–8 (Copy / Paste), set Slots used and sequence them with a slow ramp into Pattern . Thinning out: a slow LFO on Prob. Bias thins the line and fills it up. title: Stage Seq
text: Stage Seq Stage Seq in the module view Introduction The Stage Seq plays stages instead of steps. Each of up to 16 stages has a pitch and a length in pulses (1–8), and a gate mode that decides what those pulses sound like: one long note, a note on every pulse, only the first pulse, silence, or fast ratchets . Slides glide into a stage, accents make it louder. Because every stage has its own length, a few stages make long, uneven phrases: the factory pattern is 8 stages and 12 pulses, so it shifts against the bar every time round. It's a natural bass-line and lead sequencer. Patch Notes into a Voice Cell and press play. How does it work? Pulses. With nothing in Clock , pulses follow the transport at Rate ; with a trigger in Clock , each trigger is one pulse. A stage of 3 pulses lasts three pulses, then the next stage starts. Order. Mode chooses how the stages follow each other: Forward 1 … S, Reverse S … 1, Pendulum 1 … S … 2 (the end stages once per turn). Random jumps to a random stage, never the same one twice in a row. Brownian walks: one stage on (50 %), one back (25 %) or stays (25 %), wrapping around at the ends. The fixed orders are worked out from the song position, so a loop jump lands on the right stage and pulse. Random and Brownian start a new walk at every Phrase (1–16 bars): the walk depends only on Seed and the phrase, so it plays the same in every render, and after a jump the module replays the walk from the phrase start and lands where it should. A stage that would cross the end of a phrase is cut short there. Gate modes. Mode Gate Notes Rest low none; Pitch and Velocity hold First Gate Length of the first pulse one Every Gate Length of each pulse one per pulse Hold the whole stage one long note Ratchet each pulse split into 2–4 fast gates pulses × ratchets Slide. A stage with slide is entered legato : the previous note keeps sounding into it (its gate is stretched to the stage boundary), the new note-on comes before the old note-off, and Pitch glides there over Slide Time . A Voice Cell in Legato mode glides with it. A slide into a Rest stage does nothing. Accent. An accented stage plays louder — by how much is set with the Accent knob — and holds the Accent gate high while its notes sound. Hold. While the Hold input is high, a stage that ends starts again. With a clock, the order carries on where it stopped when Hold falls. With the transport, the module rejoins the song position at the next pulse, so it's never out of time. No hanging notes. Stopping, Reset, changing Stages , Mode or Phrase , and changing the sounding stage's gate mode or pulses all end the note. How to use it? A bass line: Notes into a Voice Cell with a low Octave . Use Hold stages for long notes and a slide or two for the squelch. Editing: the timeline shows each stage as wide as its pulses. Drag in the Pitch lane (it snaps to the scale; Shift for semitones; double-click resets). Drag sideways in Pulses to set the length, or scroll on the dots. Click Gate to cycle Rest → First → Every → Hold → Ratchet; scroll (or Shift-click) a Ratchet stage to set 2–4. Click Slide and Accent to toggle them; drag Vel . Randomize rewrites the lanes you tick in ▾ (pitch, pulses, gate, slide, accent, velocity), with the pitch range, the longest stage and the slide and accent chances. ◀ ▶ rotate the stages; Clear starts over. Generative lines: Mode = Brownian, Phrase = 4 bars. Change Seed until you like the walk; it stays the same every time you play. Breaks: patch a gate from another sequencer into Hold to stutter the current stage. Chaining: Stage Start fires on every stage, End when the cycle (or phrase) starts over. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Stage Seq does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Stage Seq under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Stage Seq: Brownian Bells Mode Brownian takes one stage up or down at a time over 16 stages of bells. title: Step Sequencer
text: Step Sequencer Step Sequencer in the module view Introduction The Step Sequencer plays a melody of up to 32 steps . Each step has a gate (off, on or tied to the next step), a pitch and a velocity , drawn in three lanes. Pitches snap to a scale , so every pattern stays in key. Randomize buttons write new gates, pitches or velocities in one click, and the Variation knob adds seeded variation while the pattern plays, without changing it. Patch Notes into a Voice Cell and you have a polyphonic synth playing a sequence. The Pitch , Gate and Velocity outputs drive everything else. How does it work? Timing. With nothing in Clock , the sequencer follows the transport: the step is worked out from the song position at the chosen Rate , so it's always in time with the bars and lands on the right step after a loop jump. When the transport stops, the note ends. Patch a trigger into Clock and each pulse moves one step instead. Reset makes the next step step 1. Steps. Length sets how many steps play (1–32). Steps beyond it keep what you drew, so shortening a pattern loses nothing. Direction plays the steps forward, backward, back and forth ( Ping-Pong ) or in a seeded random order that never repeats a step twice in a row. Gates and ties. On plays a note for Gate Length of the step. Tie holds the note into the next step. If the next step has another pitch, the new note starts before the old one ends, so a Voice Cell in Legato mode glides instead of retriggering. With the same pitch, the note just continues. Off plays nothing; Pitch and Velocity keep their last values. Pitch. A step's pitch counts semitones above Root + Octave . The result (plus the Transpose input) snaps to the nearest note of the Scale ; halfway between two notes it goes down. Transpose is applied before snapping, so a transposed melody stays in the scale. Variation. At each step, with the chance set by Variation , the step plays a random scale note within Var. Range of its own pitch, and a velocity up to 25 % louder or softer. Gates never change. The choices come from Seed and the step's place in the song, so the same Seed plays the same variations every time. How to use it? A sequenced synth: patch Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes input. Press play. Drawing: click a gate to cycle Off → On → Tie; drag across gates to paint them. Drag in the pitch lane to draw a melody; it snaps to the scale (hold Shift for single semitones outside it). Double-click a pitch to reset it to the root. Drag in the velocity lane to draw accents. New ideas: each lane has its own dice button (⚄) next to its name: new gates and ties, new pitches from the scale, or new velocities, leaving the other lanes alone. Randomize all rewrites all three. The ▾ button sets how many steps get a gate ( Density ), the pitch range in octaves and the velocity range. Each click is one undo step. Moving patterns: ◀ and ▶ rotate the steps; Clear turns all gates off. Evolving lines: patch a slow Function or Random onto Variation . The melody wanders off and comes back. Key changes: patch another sequencer's Pitch , or a MIDI Device's Pitch , into Transpose . Without Voice Cells: Gate into an ADSR, Pitch into an Oscillator. Chaining: End fires when the pattern starts over; use it to reset or advance other modules. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Gate Length 1 – 100 % of a step 50 % Swing 50 – 75 % 50 % Variation 0 – 100 % 0 % Var. Range 0 – 24 semitones 12 Gate Length: how long each On step sounds. Ties ignore it. Swing: delays every second step; 50 % is straight, 75 % a heavy shuffle. Variation: the chance per step of playing a varied note. Var. Range: how far a varied note may move from the step's own pitch. Every knob is a modulation destination. title: Drum Grid
text: Drum Grid Drum Grid in the module view Introduction The Drum Grid is a drum machine's step sequencer: 8 tracks by up to 32 steps , and each step is off, on or accented . Every track has its own Gate , Accent and Velocity outputs, so each row plays one drum module. The module holds 16 pattern slots that you can switch while it plays, and single patterns can be saved to a pattern library shared by all your sets. A set of factory patterns gets you started. How does it work? Timing. The grid plays steps of Rate . Time comes from one of three places: Transport (the default): the step is worked out from the song position, so the grid stays in time with the bars and after loop jumps. It stops with the transport. Tempo: set Source to Tempo and the grid runs from its own Tempo knob, transport or not. Tempo is a knob, so you can modulate it. Clock: patch a clock into Clock and it takes over. Clock PPQN says how many pulses make a quarter note (24 and 48 are common), or 1 per step for one pulse per step whatever the Rate. If the pulses don't divide the Rate evenly, the view shows ⚠ PPQN and steps are rounded to whole pulses. Run and Reset. A gate into Run starts and stops the grid: a rising edge starts again at step 1, low stops it. Without a cable the grid just runs. Reset jumps to step 1 without stopping. Steps. On steps open the track's gate for Gate Length . Accent steps do too and also open the track's Accent gate. Velocity is 100 % on an accented step and the Velocity knob on a normal one, and holds until the track plays again, so a drum's Velocity input reads the right value at the hit. Two steps in a row always make two separate hits, even at 100 % Gate Length. Patterns. Each slot has its own pattern and Length . Choosing another slot switches at the end of the current pattern ( Switch: At End ) or at the next step ( Immediate ). A cable into Pattern chooses the slot instead (0 … 1 covers slots 1 … 16). An empty slot plays silence: a break. How to use it? A drum kit: patch Gate 1 into a kick's Trig and Velocity 1 into its Velocity ; the same for the other tracks. Press play. Drawing: click a step to cycle off → on → accent; Shift-click toggles accent directly. Drag across steps to paint. Drag the marker on the ruler, or type in Length , to set the pattern's length. Tracks: click a name to rename it. M mutes, S solos. Hover a row for ‹ › to rotate just that row; ◀ ▶ rotate them all. Slots: click a number to play it (it blinks until it starts) and edit it. Alt-click edits a slot without playing it. Copy and Paste move a pattern between slots; Clear empties one. Presets: Presets ▾ loads a factory or saved pattern into the slot you're editing. Save Pattern… stores the slot in your library. Loading a pattern only renames tracks that still have their default names. Accents elsewhere: Accent n or the shared Accent output can open a filter, push a VCA or switch a drum's tone on the accented hits. Chaining: Step Clock clocks other sequencers in step with the grid; End fires when a pattern starts over. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Tempo 20 – 300 BPM 120 Gate Length 1 – 100 % of a step 25 % Swing 50 – 75 % 50 % Velocity 0 – 100 % 70 % Tempo: the speed when Source is Tempo . Gate Length: how long each hit's gate stays high. Swing: delays every second step; 50 % is straight, 75 % a heavy shuffle. Velocity: the velocity of normal steps; accented steps are always 100 %. Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Source Transport, Tempo Transport Rate 1/4 … 1/32, dotted (.) and triplet (T) 1/16 Clock PPQN 1 per step, 2, 4, 24, 48 1 per step Switch At End, Immediate At End Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Sync To: what steps the module. Auto : the clock pulses while Clock is patched, otherwise the transport. Clock : only the pulses step it. Transport : the song position steps it, and a patched Clock is ignored. With Transport , the Source setting still picks the song position or the internal tempo. title: Drum Map
text: Drum Map Drum Map in the module view Introduction The Drum Map plays kick , snare and hats from a map of patterns . Move X and Y and the beat travels smoothly between rhythms: from straight to broken along X, from sparse to busy along Y. One Density knob per voice thins a part out or fills it up, and Chaos adds seeded variation that comes back the same in every render. There's nothing to draw. Patch its triggers into drum modules ( Trig and Velocity ), or Notes into a drum rack in Live, press play, and perform the beat — by hand on the map, or with an LFO or a Random on X and Y. How does it work? The map. The map is a 5 × 5 grid of nodes . Each node holds, for each voice, 32 levels (two bars of 16ths). A level says how much a step wants to be a hit: the backbone is high, ghost notes and fills are low. X and Y pick a point between four nodes and mix their levels. They're read once per step, so a fast LFO changes the pattern step by step, never mid-step. The factory map is built from rhythmic rules, not taken from any machine: Kick: on every beat at the straight edge; toward broken it moves off beats 2 and 4 to pushed 16ths and a 3 + 3 + 2 feel. Busier rows add pickups. Snare: a backbeat on 2 and 4, turning into a half-time snare on 3 and then a displaced backbeat toward the broken edge. Busier rows add ghost notes. Hats: quarters at the sparse edge, 8ths in the middle, 16ths at the busy edge; toward broken the strong hats move to the off-beats. The last beat of every second bar is lighter, with rising kick and snare pickups, so raising Density or Fill reveals a fill. Density. A step plays when its level is above (1 − Density) · 255 . At 0 % nothing plays, at 100 % everything above zero. Because the important steps have the highest levels, turning Density up adds hits from the backbone outward and never takes one away. Accent and velocity. Louder levels play louder ( Vel = 30 % … 100 %); a level above Accent also fires the voice's Acc output. Fill. While the Fill gate is high, Fill Amount is added to every Density. Chaos nudges every step's level up or down by a seeded amount, so weak hits come and go while the backbone stays. The nudges change every bar (or every 2, 4, 8 bars — Chaos Rate — or never: Frozen ), counted from the song position, and they're the same every time you play that bar. Timing. With nothing in Clock , steps follow the transport at Rate and land on the right step after a loop jump; with a trigger in Clock , each pulse is a step. At 1/8 the two-bar map becomes four bars, at 1/32 it's double time. Length shortens the pattern; End fires when it starts over. Every hit is also a note at the voice's note number, ending after Note Length ; no note is left hanging on stop, Reset or a note change. How to use it? Drums on the board: Kick into a kick's Trig and Kick Vel into its Velocity ; the same for snare and hats. Drums in Live: Notes into a MIDI Out port with a drum rack (36, 38 and 42 are kick, snare and closed hat). Performing: drag the puck on the map. The ring is where the knobs are; the dot (with its trail) is where X and Y really are, cables included. Evolving beats: a slow LFO on X and a Random on Y: the groove wanders through the map and stays musical. Fills: a gate from a clock divider or another sequencer's End into Fill gives a fill every 4 or 8 bars. Your own map: press Edit node , click a node on the map and draw its levels in the lanes. Edited nodes show as larger dots; Reset node brings back the factory node. The lanes show what plays right now: level bars, a threshold line per voice and the hits (accents bolder). Demo patches Five whole patches show what Drum Map does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Drum Map under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Drum Map: Straight Four The straight corner of the map: kick on every beat, backbeat snare and eighth hats; move X and Y or the Density knobs. Drum Map: Wandering Groove A slow LFO on X and a Random on Y walk the beat over the whole map, with Chaos adding ghost notes. Drum Map: Fill Every Four A square LFO on the Fill gate adds Fill Amount to every density for one bar in four. Drum Map: Half-Time Dub Rate 1/8 stretches the map into a sparse half-time beat; the snare and hats feed a delay through the mixer sends. Drum Map: Chaos Shuffle Rate 1/16T, Swing and Chaos at 60 % make a rolling shuffle whose ghost notes change every bar.
