title: Gate Sequencer
text: Gate Sequencer Gate Sequencer in the module view Introduction The Gate Sequencer is a rhythm sequencer with deep steps : four tracks of up to 32 gates, where every step has its own probability , gate length (or a tie), ratchets (fast repeats inside the step), nudge (playing a little early or late) and a condition (every Nth loop, only the first time, only during a fill …). Each track has its own length and rate , so tracks drift against each other and still land on the bars. It has no pitches: it's about how hits happen. Patch its gates and triggers into drum modules or envelopes, or Notes into a drum rack. The chances are seeded, so a pattern that "breathes" plays the same in every render. A new module plays a small beat on tracks 1–3 straight away. How does it work? Timing. With nothing in Clock , every track follows the transport on its own grid (its Rate ), worked out from the song position, so a loop jump lands each track on the right step. A 16-step track against a 12-step track lines up again every 3 bars; the Cycle output fires when all four are back on step 1 together. With a cable in Clock , each pulse is a 1/16 tick and the tracks run at their rates relative to it (a 1/32 track plays twice per tick, spaced by the measured tick length). Whether a step plays. A step that is On plays when: its condition is true: A:B — on the A-th of every B loops (2:4 = the second of every four); First / Not First — on the first loop since the transport started (or since Reset), or on every other loop; Fill / Not Fill — while the Fill input is high, or while it isn't; Prev / Not Prev — when the last earlier chance-or-condition step on the track played (or didn't). Chain them for "if this, then that". its probability wins the dice: 100 % always plays; below that the chance is scaled by the track's Chance knob (0 % leaves only the certain steps, 200 % doubles every chance). The dice come from Seed , the track, the step and the loop, so renders repeat and a jump replays the same choices. Dice decides how often they change: every loop, every 2/4/8 loops, or never ( Fixed ). the track isn't muted (the M button or the Mute input). Inside a step. Length is the gate as a share of the step; Tie keeps the gate up until the next step on the track that doesn't play. Ratchet splits the step into 1–8 hits: Even , Faster (gaps shrink) or Slower (gaps grow). Ratchet Decay makes each repeat softer. Nudge moves the whole step up to half a step early or late, scaled by Nudge Depth . Early hits really are early: the module looks ahead. Velocity goes to the Vel output and the notes. Two gates that touch drop for 1 ms, so the next one starts with a clean edge. Notes. Each hit is a note at the track's Note number, ending with its gate. No note is left hanging: stopping, Reset, Mute, changing a track's length, rate or note, and editing the step that's sounding all end it. How to use it? Drums on the board: Trig 1 into a kick's Trig , Vel 1 into its Velocity ; the same for tracks 2–4. Drums in Live: Notes into a MIDI Out port with a drum rack; Note 1–4 default to kick, snare, closed and open hat. Editing: choose what a click edits with On / Prob / Len / Ratch / Nudge / Cond / Vel . On : click toggles, drag paints. Prob , Len , Vel , Ratch : drag up and down. Nudge : drag sideways. Cond : click cycles the condition. Click a step to select it (Shift: several) and set every field in the inspector line below. Steps drawn hollow won't play on this pass. Length and rate: at the start of each row, or drag the marker at the end of the row. Track tools act on the track you last clicked: Randomize (density, probability range, ratchet chance and nudge in ▾), Euclid (k hits spread evenly, with a rotation), ◀ ▶ rotate, Copy / Paste . Fills: patch a gate into Fill (every 4th bar from a Clock divider or another sequencer's End ) and mark some steps Fill or Not Fill . Thinning and filling: a slow LFO on Chance 3 makes the hats breathe. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Gate Sequencer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Gate Sequencer under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Gate Sequencer: Broken Beat Ghost notes, coin-flip hits, ratchets, Swing and Ratchet Decay make a loose beat that changes every few loops ( Dice ). Gate Sequencer: Bell Cycles Four tracks with Length 1–4 of 5, 7, 9 and 11 steps each strike a bell: a slowly rearranging weave. Gate Sequencer: Four-Note Bass Each track's Note setting and rhythm are merged on the Notes output into one mono bass line. Gate Sequencer: Chance Rain Slow LFOs on Chance 1–4 make the density of glassy drops rise and fall on four separate cycles. Gate Sequencer: Fill and Drop A square LFO holds Fill for the last bar of four, and another on Mute 4 drops the percussion. Nudge Depth: scales every step's nudge; 0 % plays straight. Ratchet Decay: repeat i of r plays at 1 − Decay · i / r of the velocity. Swing: delays every second step of each track, on its own grid. Every knob is a modulation destination. title: Rhythm Bank
text: Rhythm Bank Rhythm Bank in the module view Introduction Four related rhythms from one number. Choose a Family (how the rhythms are made) and turn Pattern (0 – 127) to browse grooves: all four outputs change together, as parts of one beat. Out 1 is the strongest part (think kick), Out 4 the busiest. Modulate Pattern with something slow and the drum part develops over the song, the same in every render. How does it work? Families. In most families the lower bits of Pattern set the density and the higher ones how the four parts relate. Even: evenly spread hits ("Euclidean"); the parts are copies in canon, a ladder of densities, halves and doubles, mirror images, off-beats, … Prime: each part repeats every 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13 steps; with Length Open the parts drift against each other. Metric: hits by metric weight: Pattern 0 is kick on 1, snare on 1 and 3, quarters and eighths; higher numbers move parts to the off-beats (backbeat). Poly: each part plays 2 – 9 hits per cycle, not tied to the steps (polyrhythms); Grid = Free plays them at their exact time. Interlock: parts that never hit on the same step. Seeded: random grooves weighted towards strong beats; every number is its own groove. Steps. With nothing in Clock , one step is Rate at the song tempo, locked to the song position. Patch a trigger into Clock and every pulse is a step. Reset makes the next step the first. Length sets the cycle (2 – 32 steps, or Open : no cycle). Shaping. Rotate 1 … 4 delay or advance each part. Mute 1 … 4 silence a part. Complement makes the parts work together: Avoid (a part only plays where no lower part plays), Fill (the same, and the last part fills every empty step), Pairs (Out 2 plays where Out 1 doesn't, Out 4 where Out 3 doesn't). Changes. With Change = Cycle a new Pattern (or Family, Length, Complement) starts at the next step 1; with Step at the next step. Outputs. Gates last Width of a step (or one-sample triggers with Output = Trigger ). Any is high while any part plays, Accent where two or more parts hit together (before Complement), Cycle fires at step 1. How to use it? A drum part: Out 1 – 4 into a drum kit's triggers; turn Pattern . A part that develops: a slow LFO or Random into Pattern , Change = Cycle . Accents: Accent into a drum's level or a VCA. Choke groups: Complement = Avoid : hi-hat and snare never collide. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Rhythm Bank does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Rhythm Bank under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Rhythm Bank: Euclid Kit The Even family spreads hits evenly for kick, snare, hats and rim; turn Pattern and Rotate 1 … 4 . Rhythm Bank: Prime Marimba Prime with Length Open: four plucked notes repeat every few steps and drift against each other. Rhythm Bank: Metric Backbeat The Metric family with Complement on Avoid; a Random moves Pattern once per bar. Rhythm Bank: Cross-Rhythms The Poly family with Grid on Free plays hand drums and a bell at their exact cross-rhythm positions. Rhythm Bank: Interlocking Hats Interlock never doubles a hit, and Complement on Fill puts hats on every step the others leave empty. title: Recall
text: Recall Recall in the module view Introduction Recall generates random rhythms and melodies in two sections that share one clock. T makes random gates: coin tosses between two outputs, random divisions and ratchets, or drum-like patterns weighted by the bar. X makes three random voltages whose distribution you shape and whose steps go from smooth glides to notes of a scale. Each section has a Recall knob that makes it repeat its own recent past: from always new, through variations on what just happened, to a locked loop you can capture into the board. How does it work? Clock. Each tick comes from Clock if patched, else from the song position when Sync is on a note value and the transport plays, else from Rate (or the synced length while the transport is stopped). Clock out fires on every tick. Reset makes the next tick tick 0: the loops start again at their first slot, and the memory stays. T section. On every tick the section takes a decision from four random numbers. T Mode turns it into gates: Coin: exactly one of T1 and T2 fires; T Bias is the chance of T1. Chance: T1 and T2 fire independently, each with the chance T Bias . Ratchet: each output picks a rate: ÷4, ÷3, ÷2 (fires on the first tick of its group), ×1, or ×2, ×3, ×4 (two to four evenly spaced pulses in one tick). T Bias left of the middle prefers divisions, right of it multiplications. Drums: T1 is a kick, strong on beats 1 and 3 of a 16-tick bar; T2 a snare, strong on 2 and 4. At T Bias 50 % you get a plain backbeat with occasional ghost notes; more fills in, less thins out. T Jitter delays each gate by up to half a tick (never early). Gate Length sets the gate length as a share of a tick (of a sub-pulse when ratcheting). X section. On each X event (every tick, every T1 or T2 gate, or each pulse at X Clock , chosen with X Source ) the section draws three values: X Spread is the width: 0 % is a constant; up to 50 % a bell around the middle; up to 85 % it widens to even; above that values are pushed to the edges. X Bias pulls values down (left) or up (right). X Steps: below 45 % the outputs glide to each new value (at 0 % over the whole time to the next one, a smooth random curve); 45 – 55 % plain steps; above 55 % the values snap to Scale from Root . From 70 % on, scale notes drop out (for seven-note scales the 2nd, 6th, 4th, 7th, 3rd and 5th degree) until at 100 % only the root is left, in octaves. X Range: −1 … +1, 0 … 1 or −2 … +2 (±2 octaves into a pitch input). X Mode Sorted sorts the three so X1 ≤ X2 ≤ X3: low, middle, high. Recall. Each section remembers its last Loop decisions. With Recall at 0 % every decision is new; at 50 % about half of them repeat the decision from one loop ago, so the pattern keeps its shape while it changes; at 100 % the loop is locked: exactly what was playing when the knob reached the top. The memory holds the raw random numbers, not the gates and voltages, so Bias , Spread , Steps , Scale and T Mode still reshape a locked loop: lock a melody, then change the scale, and it keeps its contour. Capture. Capture T and Capture X store a section's loop in the board and switch on Use for it: the section then plays the stored loop on every tick, whatever the Recall knob, the seed or the song position. Use T / Use X in the view switch back to the live memory and forth again. Repeatable. New decisions come from Seed and the tick number. On a transport start or a loop jump the memory is rebuilt by replaying the ticks before it, so a render from the same position always sounds the same. How to use it? Two drum voices: T Mode Drums, T1 to a kick, T2 to a snare, Clock out to a hi-hat. A melody that stays itself: X Steps 65 %, X1 into an oscillator's pitch, T1 into its envelope, X Source T1. Raise X Recall until you like the phrase, then Capture X . Chords: X Mode Sorted, X Steps 60 %, X1 … X3 into three oscillators. Smooth random modulation: X Steps 0 %, X Spread 40 % into a filter. Human timing: T Jitter 15 %. Rolls: T Mode Ratchet, T Bias 75 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Recall does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Recall under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Recall: Locked Melody T Recall and X Recall at 100 % lock an eight-step loop; change Scale or X Spread to reshape the same contour. title: Shift Register
text: Shift Register Shift Register in the module view Introduction Shift Register is a looping row of 16 bits. On every step the bits move one place along and the bit at Length comes back in at the front, sometimes flipped. Everything it outputs is read from those bits: a stepped voltage, a quantized pitch, eight gates, a combined gate and a weighted mix. Because only one bit is new on each step, consecutive values are related, and the gates are delayed copies of each other: rhythms and melodies that echo through the register like a canon. One knob, Lock , moves the pattern from frozen through slowly changing to fully random. How does it work? The register. Bit 1 is the newest bit, bit 16 the oldest. On each step: The bit at position Length is read: that's the bit that comes back. Every bit moves one place along. The bit comes back in at position 1, flipped or not, depending on Lock . Lock is the chance that the returning bit stays as it is. At +100 % nothing ever flips: the pattern repeats every Length steps. Between +100 % and 0 % it changes now and then and stays recognisable; at 0 % every bit is a coin toss. At −100 % every returning bit is flipped: the pattern repeats every 2 × Length steps, with the second half the inverse of the first. Source chooses what comes back: Loop (the register's own bit), Data (the Data input, so the register delays an incoming rhythm, corrupted by Lock below +100 %) or Data ⊕ Loop (the input scrambles the loop). Voltage and Pitch read the first eight bits as a number from 0 to 255, with bit 1 counting most. Each step roughly halves the previous value and adds the new bit on top, which gives melodies from the register a recognisable contour. Voltage is that number scaled to 0 … 1 (times Level ); Pitch spreads it over Octaves , adds Transpose and snaps it to Scale . Bit 1 … Bit 8 are high for Gate Length of a step while their bit is 1. At 100 % consecutive 1s merge into one long gate. Bit 2 is Bit 1 one step later, Bit 3 two steps later, and so on. Bits beyond Length keep shifting, so with Length 4, Bit 5 … 8 are older copies of the same pattern. Combo combines the bits chosen with the toggles in the view: Any (one of them is 1), All (all of them are 1) or Odd (an odd number of them is 1). Mix is a weighted sum of bits 1 … 6, using the six Weight knobs, scaled so it stays within −1 … +1. The defaults (1, ½, ¼, ⅛) make a 4-bit version of Voltage ; other weights give stepped patterns that don't follow the register's number. Steps come from Clock if patched, else from the song position when Sync is on a note value and the transport plays, else from Rate (or the synced length while the transport is stopped). Reset reloads the start pattern on the next step. Repeatable. The flips come from Seed and the step number. The register also has a start pattern : a transport start loads it and replays the steps up to the song position, so a render from the same position always sounds the same, wherever you start. The view The top row shows the live register (newest left; bits beyond Length dim; ▲ marks the bit that comes back; a ring flashes when the entering bit was flipped). Click a bit to flip it in the running register. The row below is the start pattern. Click to edit it. Capture copies the live register into the start pattern, so a pattern you like comes back on every play. Load loads the start pattern now. Combo toggles choose the bits for Combo . The strip shows the last 32 values of Voltage ; × marks steps where the entering bit was flipped. How to use it? Canon rhythms: Bit 1 , Bit 3 and Bit 6 to three drums, Lock 90 %. A melody that evolves: Pitch into an oscillator, Step into its envelope, Lock 80 %. Raise Lock to 100 % to keep a phrase, then Capture it. Stepped modulation: Mix to a filter, an LFO on Weight 2 morphs between two stepped patterns. Delay a rhythm: Source on Data , a gate pattern into Data : the bit outputs play it back delayed by 0 … 7 steps. Accents: Combo on All with two bits chosen, into a velocity or a VCA. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Shift Register does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Shift Register under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Shift Register: Locked Loop Lock just below 100 % with a slow LFO: a repeating pentatonic melody that occasionally slips. Shift Register: Canon Beat A 16-step pattern read at Bit 1 , Bit 3 , Bit 4 and Bit 6 drives kick, clap, hat and rim as a rhythmic canon. Shift Register: Rhythm Echo Source Data: a drum pattern into Data returns as echoes that trigger chimes. Shift Register: Mirror Flip Lock at −100 % inverts the pattern on every pass; Combine Odd rings a bell and Voltage opens the filter. Shift Register: Drifting Free Run Sync Free with an LFO on Rate and another on Lock , in a whole-tone scale. Auto : the clock pulses while Clock is patched, otherwise the transport. Clock : only the pulses step it. Transport : the song position steps it, and a patched Clock is ignored. With Transport (or Auto and nothing patched), the Sync setting still picks a note value or free running. Lock: the chance the returning bit is kept: flip chance = (1 − Lock) / 2. Rate: steps per second when Sync is Free and Clock is unpatched. Level: scales Voltage . Gate Length: length of the bit gates and Combo , as a share of a step. Weight 1 … 6: the mixer's weights for bits 1 … 6. Length: which bit comes back. Changing it never clears bits. Sync: one step per note value at the song tempo. Source, Combine, Octaves, Root, Scale: see above. Seed: picks the sequence of flips. Lock , Rate , Level , Gate Length , the weights and Length are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Clock trigger each pulse is a step; overrides Rate and Sync Reset trigger the next step reloads the start pattern and counts as step 0 Data gate the bit to write with Source on Data or Data ⊕ Loop Transpose pitch added to Pitch before quantizing, read at each step Outputs Output Signal What it does Voltage control, 0 … 1 the first eight bits as a number, times Level Pitch pitch the same number over Octaves , quantized to Scale Bit 1 … Bit 8 gate high while that bit is 1 Combo gate the chosen bits combined Mix control, −1 … +1 weighted sum of bits 1 … 6 Step trigger a pulse on every step Loop trigger a pulse every Length steps

title: Clock Div
text: Clock Div Introduction Eight clock dividers on one clock, each with its own division. Set Div 1 to 2 and Out 1 fires every second step; set Div 4 to 7 and Out 4 fires every seventh. Patch a clock in, or leave Clock empty and it follows the song: everything is worked out from the song position, so it stays on the bars, after loop jumps and in renders. For eight divisions that are a family and move together with one knob, see Rotating Div. How does it work? The base step. Unpatched, one step is Base (1/16 by default) at the song's tempo. Patch a trigger into Clock and every pulse is a step instead. Divisions. Div 1 … Div 8 are whole numbers from 1 to 64. Output k fires on step 0 and then every Div k steps. The defaults are the classic /2 /3 /4 /5 /6 /8 /16 /32. A new division takes effect at that output's next cycle; a gate that is already high always finishes its length. Realign. Odd divisions drift against the bar: /3 of 1/16 notes repeats only every 3 bars. Realign restarts every output every 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars; the last cycle before the restart is shortened, and its gate ends at least 1 ms before the next one starts. With a patched clock there is no bar, so Realign has no effect: patch a bar-rate trigger into Reset instead. Gates. In Gate output, an output is high for Width of its own period ( Gate Length = Division ) or of one base step ( Base Step ). Trigger output sends a one-sample pulse instead. Reset makes the next base step the start of every output's cycle (with a clock: the next pulse). When the transport stops, every output goes low; on play, nothing fires until the next due step. How to use it? Drum rhythms from one clock: Out 1 … 8 into drum triggers, set to /2, /3, /4 and /16 for a hat, a clap, a kick and a crash. Phrases: /16 or /32 into a sequencer's Reset , or into a Harmony Master to change chord every two bars. Odd against even: /3 and /4 together, Realign 1 bar so they meet on every downbeat. Slow modulation: Trigger output of a long division into a Random or a Shift Register. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Clock Div does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Clock Div under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Clock Div: Basic Kit Six divisions of a 16th clock drive a small kit; Realign every bar keeps the odd ones landing on the downbeat. Clock Div: Three Against Four Four toms on /3, /4, /5 and /7 with Realign off drift against each other for 420 steps. Clock Div: Slow Chimes Divisions with no common factors (/5 … /29) strike six bells in a pattern that takes minutes to repeat. Clock Div: Gate Pad Gate output with long divisions swells six chord notes in and out at different rates. Clock Div: Half-Time Melody Out 1 (/2) clocks a step sequencer in half time while Out 2 (/32) resets it every two bars. title: Rotating Div
text: Rotating Div Rotating Div in the module view Introduction Eight clock dividers on one clock. Out 1 fires every step, Out 2 every second step, Out 3 every third, and so on, and the Rotate knob shifts the whole set across the outputs: one turn (or an LFO on Rotate ) turns a steady hi-hat into half time, odd meters or sparse accents. Everything is worked out from the song position, so it stays on the bars, after loop jumps and in renders. How does it work? The base step. Unpatched, one step is Base (1/16 by default) at the song's tempo. Patch a trigger into Clock and every pulse is a step instead. Sets. Set chooses the eight divisions: Integers (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8), Odds (1 3 5 …), Evens (2 4 6 …), Primes (1 2 3 5 7 11 13 17), Powers of 2 (1 2 4 … 128), Fibonacci (1 2 3 5 8 13 21 34), or Custom (your eight values, typed in the view). Rotate. Wrap cycles the eight values round the outputs: Rotate 1 on Integers gives 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 1. Extend keeps going along the series, so the outputs get slower: Rotate 4 gives 5 … 12. Custom always wraps. Rotate Sync. A new Rotate (or Set) waits for the next base step ( Next Step ), the next bar ( Next Bar ; with a clock: the next step where all outputs line up), or applies at once ( Immediate ). A gate that is already high always finishes its length. Realign. Odd divisions drift against the bar: /3 of 1/16 notes repeats only every 3 bars. Realign restarts every output every 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars; the last cycle before the restart is shortened, and its gate ends at least 1 ms before the next one starts. Gates. In Gate output, an output is high for Width of its own period ( Gate Length = Division ) or of one base step ( Base Step ). Trigger output sends a one-sample pulse instead. Stair reads the eight outputs as a binary number (Out 1 the highest bit), so it is a stepped shape that repeats with the pattern; into a quantizer it makes a melody. Align fires when all eight outputs start together. Reset makes the next base step the start of every output's cycle. When the transport stops, every output goes low; on play, nothing fires until the next due step. How to use it? Drum variations: Out 1 … 8 into drum triggers; an LFO or a Random on Rotate . Odd meters that still land on the one: Set Odds , Realign 1 bar. A melody from rhythm: Stair into a Quantizer Suite. Phrase starts: Align resets a sequencer or advances a Harmony Master. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Rotating Div does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Rotating Div under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Rotating Div: Integer Gears The Integers Set on a 16th clock drives a drum kit; a slow ramp on Rotate changes the gearing, Realign every 4 bars. Rotating Div: Prime Chimes The Primes Set on 8ths strikes six chimes, with Rotate reassigning the fast and slow divisions. Rotating Div: Fibonacci Pad Output Gate with the Fibonacci Set opens six notes of a chord and Width sets how long each is held. Rotating Div: Powers Groove Powers of 2 make a techno grid, and the Stair output, quantised, plays the bass. Rotating Div: Odd Meters Set Custom (4, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12) drives a tuned drum ensemble that Realign resets every 8 bars. title: Transport
text: Transport Transport in the module view Introduction Transport is the control panel for the song's clock. Set the tempo, switch Ableton Link on or off, send MIDI clock to a drum machine, follow the MIDI clock of another device, and start and stop the song from the module's buttons, from cables or from incoming MIDI. Everything on the board that keeps time (sequencers, delays, LFOs) follows what Transport sets. Transport changes the clock in the standalone app . In Live the host's own transport leads, and in the browser there is none: there it still sends MIDI clock and shows the tempo, but cannot change it. How does it work? Tempo. Move Tempo to set it. With Tap , tap a few times in the beat you want. The tempo stays what you set; loading a board does not change it, so a project keeps its own tempo. With Link on, the tempo is shared with the other Link apps and devices, and they can change it too. Link. Link turns Ableton Link on or off. With Link Start/Stop on, playing and stopping is shared as well. Link needs an app built with it; without, the switch has no effect and the app runs on its own clock. MIDI clock out. With MIDI Clock Out on, Transport sends 24 pulses per beat while the song plays, plus Start when it begins at the beginning, Continue when it resumes anywhere else, and Stop. Patch MIDI Out into a MIDI Out module. MIDI clock in. With MIDI Clock In on, patch a MIDI In or MIDI Device module's Notes into MIDI In . Transport measures the incoming clock and sets the tempo from it; it settles after about a beat and follows changes within a bar. Start, Continue and Stop from the device start and stop your song. This sets the tempo, but does not line up the beats exactly: for that, use Link. Play and Stop. The Play / Stop button toggles. A trigger in Play starts a stopped song from the beginning, a trigger in Stop stops it. Patch a Button or a pad to either. How to use it? Tempo on a knob: put a Dial on the Tempo knob's input (or play with the knob itself). Drum machine follows you: MIDI Clock Out on, MIDI Out → MIDI Out (the drum machine's port). Start your song and the machine starts with it. You follow the drum machine: MIDI Clock In on, its MIDI Device's Notes → MIDI In . Press play on the machine. Tap tempo: press Tap to the beat, four times or more. Footswitch: a MIDI Device's gate or a Button into Play and Stop . A lamp that shows the song runs: Playing into a Level Meter or a light. Tempo-linked effects: Tempo into a control input (BPM / 100: 120 BPM is 1.2). Do not connect the module's MIDI Out back into its own MIDI In with both clock settings on: that makes a loop. Reference Knobs, settings and buttons Control Range Default Tempo 20 … 400 BPM 120 Link Off, On On Link Start/Stop Off, On On MIDI Clock In Off, On Off MIDI Clock Out Off, On Off Play / Stop button Tap button If the board also has a Link node, its Start/Stop Sync setting decides. Inputs Input Signal What it does Play trigger Starts the song from the beginning Stop trigger Stops the song MIDI In notes The MIDI clock to follow (MIDI Clock In) Outputs Output Signal What it does MIDI Out notes MIDI clock, Start, Continue and Stop (MIDI Clock Out) Playing gate High while the song runs Tempo control The tempo in BPM divided by 100 (120 BPM is 1.2)

title: Ring Clap
text: Ring Clap Ring Clap in the module view Introduction A hand clap: band-passed noise opened by a few quick bursts, as if several people clapped a few milliseconds apart, then a short diffuse tail like a small room. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Each hit fires Bursts short bursts of noise, Spread apart. Every burst snaps open and fades before the next one. The last burst also starts the tail, which fades over Decay . The noise passes through a band-pass filter centred on Tone , which gives the clap its pitch. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds starts the bursts again. How to use it? Clap on the backbeat: with or instead of a snare, on beats 2 and 4. Tighter clap: fewer Bursts , smaller Spread . Big, loose clap: 5 or 6 Bursts , Spread around 20 ms, longer Decay . Snap: 1 burst, Tone around 2.5 kHz, short Decay . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tone 500 Hz – 4 kHz 1.1 kHz Decay 50 ms – 1.5 s 300 ms Spread 3 – 30 ms 11 ms Bursts 1 – 6 4 Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tone: the centre of the band-pass: the clap's pitch. title: Ring Cowbell
text: Ring Cowbell Ring Cowbell in the module view Introduction A cowbell: two square waves, a fifth-ish apart, through a band-pass filter, with a sharp initial hit and a softer tail. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Two square-wave oscillators run at an inharmonic interval. A band-pass filter, set by Tone , picks out the clang. The envelope has two parts: a loud hit that fades in a few tens of milliseconds, and a quieter tail that lasts Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts both parts of the envelope. How to use it? Accent pattern: a few syncopated hits per bar. Darker bell: Tone low, Tune down a few semitones. Melodic cowbell: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune at 50 % amount. Tune spans 24 semitones, so the bell follows the notes in tune. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 50 ms – 2 s 400 ms Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: how long the tail lasts. Tone: the band-pass centre: dark … bright. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Cymbal
text: Ring Cymbal Ring Cymbal in the module view Introduction A cymbal from the same six square waves as Ring Hats, split into two bands: a low clang that fades first and a long, high sizzle. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? The metallic source is split by a band-pass (the low clang) and a high-pass (the sizzle). The sizzle lasts Decay ; the clang lasts less than half of that. Tone balances the two bands. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts both bands. How to use it? Crash on the one: the first beat of a new section, Decay 2 – 4 s. Ride-like pattern: quarter notes, Decay around 1 s, Tone high. Gong-ish: Tune down 12 semitones, Tone low, Decay at maximum. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 300 ms – 8 s 2 s Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: how long the sizzle lasts; the clang dies sooner. Tone: the balance of the two bands: clang … sizzle. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Drums
text: Ring Drums Introduction The Ring drums are a drum kit, one node per instrument. They are built the way the classic analog drum machines of the early eighties built their sounds: resonators that are struck and ring away, band-passed noise, and six detuned square waves for everything metallic. The result is deep, round and a little soft: long booming kicks, ringing toms, gentle hats. For a tighter, harder kit, see the Punch drums. The voices Node What it is Main controls Ring Kick a struck resonator, from tight to booming Tune, Decay, Sweep, Tone, Drive Ring Snare two ringing heads and a burst of noise Tune, Tone, Snappy, Decay Ring Clap quick bursts of noise and a short tail Tone, Decay, Spread, Bursts Ring Tom a ringing tone that falls in pitch; also hand drums Tune, Decay, Bend, Noise Ring Rim rim shot or clave Voice, Tune, Decay Ring Cowbell two squares through a band-pass Tune, Decay, Tone Ring Hats closed and open hats; closed cuts open Tune, Closed Decay, Open Decay, Tone Ring Cymbal a low clang and a long sizzle Tune, Decay, Tone Each node has its own manual behind the ? button in its window. How does it work? Every Ring drum works the same from the outside: A rising edge at Trig plays it (Ring Hats has two inputs, Closed and Open ). Triggers and gates both work. Velocity , when patched, sets the loudness of each hit, read at the moment of the trigger. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes the loudness only, not the sound. Level sets the output volume. It starts at 80 %, so a few drums mixed together leave some headroom. Out is mono audio. Every knob is a modulation destination, as everywhere on the board. How to use it? A basic beat: a Step Sequencer per drum, each one's Trigger into a drum's Trig and its Velocity into the drum's Velocity . Patch every drum's Out into the same Audio Out port: cables into one jack add up. Hats with a choke: two sequencer patterns into Ring Hats' Closed and Open ; the closed hits cut the open ones. A drum kit as one node: select the drums and their sequencers and group them into a cell, with a single audio output. Bass kick: a long Ring Kick, with a sequencer's Pitch on Tune at 50 % amount. Effects: run a drum through a Multi Filter, or patch a Random onto a knob, for drums that change on every hit. Reference Inputs (every Ring drum) Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the drum (Ring Hats: Closed and Open ) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs (every Ring drum) Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum, mono

title: Ring Hats
text: Ring Hats Ring Hats in the module view Introduction Closed and open hi-hats in one node. The sound comes from six square waves at inharmonic frequencies, a dense metallic clang, filtered down to its top. A closed hit cuts a ringing open hat short, like a real hi-hat pedal. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Six square-wave oscillators sum to a metallic tone. A band-pass and a high-pass keep only its bright top; Tone moves the high-pass up for a thinner, crisper hat. Closed and Open share one envelope: each hit starts it with its own decay ( Closed Decay or Open Decay ), so a closed hit chokes an open one. Playing it. A rising edge at Closed or Open plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts the envelope with the decay of the input that was hit. How to use it? Eighth-note hats: a sequencer's Trigger into Closed . Open hat on the offbeat: a second pattern into Open ; the next closed hit cuts it. Shaker: short Closed Decay (around 20 ms), Tone high, sixteenth notes with varied velocity. Trashy hats: Tune down 5 – 12 semitones. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Closed Decay 10 – 300 ms 60 ms Open Decay 50 ms – 3 s 500 ms Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Closed Decay: how long a closed hit lasts. Open Decay: how long an open hit lasts. Tone: the high-pass: full … thin. Level: the output volume. Tune , Closed Decay , Open Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Closed trigger plays the closed hat Open trigger plays the open hat; a closed hit cuts it short Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Kick
text: Ring Kick Ring Kick in the module view Introduction A deep, round bass drum. A resonator is struck and rings at Tune , dying away over Decay : short and tight, or a long booming tone you can play bass lines with. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? The body is a resonator, a circuit that rings like a bell when struck. Each hit starts the ring with a soft, rounded attack. Sweep starts the pitch higher and lets it settle onto Tune within the first few tens of milliseconds, for more punch. Tone adds the click of the strike itself, a short thump on top of the body; higher values make it louder and brighter. Drive saturates the whole sound, from warm to distorted. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing, like hitting a real drum twice. How to use it? Classic kick: the defaults on every beat (a Step Sequencer's Trigger into Trig ). Long bass kick: Decay at 1.5 s or more, Drive around 30 %. To play bass lines, patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune at 50 % amount: Tune spans two octaves, so the kick then follows the notes in tune. Tight kick: Decay around 200 ms, Tone up for more click. Accents: patch the sequencer's Velocity into Velocity . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 30 – 120 Hz 50 Hz Decay 50 ms – 3 s 800 ms Sweep 0 – 100 % 30 % Tone 0 – 100 % 30 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the body rings at. Decay: how long the body rings (until it has fallen by 60 dB). Sweep: how far above Tune the pitch starts. At 100 % it starts 2.5 times higher. Tone: the click of the strike: louder and brighter as you turn it up. Drive: saturation, from clean to heavily distorted. The peak level stays the same. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Sweep , Tone , Drive and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Rim
text: Ring Rim Ring Rim in the module view Introduction Short, high, woody clicks: a rim shot (the stick hitting the rim of a snare) or a clave (two hardwood sticks). It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Rim strikes two high resonators at once and passes them through a high-pass and a little saturation, for a sharp crack. Clave is one resonator, higher and purer, that rings a little longer. Decay multiplies each voice's own ringing time, from a quarter to four times as long. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Rim on the offbeats: a light, ticking pulse that leaves room for a snare. Clave pattern: Voice Clave, on a syncopated pattern. Wood block: Clave tuned down 7 – 12 semitones, Decay around 2×. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Voice Rim, Clave Rim Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 0.25 – 4 × 1 × Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Voice: which sound plays. A setting, not a knob. Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: multiplies how long the voice rings. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Snare
text: Ring Snare Ring Snare in the module view Introduction A snare drum: two ringing drum heads for the body, and a burst of bright noise for the snare wires. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Two resonators ring at Tune and a little below twice Tune , like the low and high modes of a drum head. Tone blends between them: low and full, or high and ringing. White noise, high-passed so it doesn't muddy the body, plays at the same time; Snappy sets its level and Decay how long it lasts. The body rings for about half of Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts the noise and adds to the ringing heads. How to use it? Backbeat: the defaults on beats 2 and 4. Tight, dry snare: Decay around 120 ms, Snappy 40 %. Rattly, bright snare: Snappy at 100 %, Tone high. Ghost notes: low velocities between the main hits. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 100 – 400 Hz 180 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Snappy 0 – 100 % 60 % Decay 50 ms – 1 s 250 ms Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch of the lower head; the higher one follows. Tone: the balance of the two heads, low … high. Snappy: the level of the noise (the snare wires). Decay: how long the noise lasts; the body rings for about half as long. Level: the output volume. Tune , Tone , Snappy , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Tom
text: Ring Tom Ring Tom in the module view Introduction A tom or hand drum: a ringing tone that falls slightly in pitch as it dies away, with a little noise for the skin. With Noise at 0 it becomes a pure, conga-like tone. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? A resonator rings at Tune . Bend starts the pitch above Tune and lets it fall back over the whole note, the way a drum head's pitch falls as it loses tension. Low-passed noise adds the sound of the stick on the skin; it fades in less than half the time of the tone. Use several Ring Tom nodes, tuned apart, for a set of toms. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Tom fills: three Ring Toms at about 100, 140 and 200 Hz, played by the last steps of a sequence. Hand drums: Noise at 0, Decay around 200 ms, Tune 200 – 400 Hz. Melodic toms: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune and adjust the cable's amount until the intervals sound right. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 50 – 600 Hz 140 Hz Decay 50 ms – 2 s 400 ms Bend 0 – 100 % 30 % Noise 0 – 100 % 30 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the tom settles on. Decay: how long the tom rings. Bend: how far above Tune the pitch starts; at 100 % it starts 50 % higher. Noise: the level of the skin noise. 0 % is a pure tone. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Bend , Noise and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Clap
text: Punch Clap Punch Clap in the module view Introduction A bright, roomy hand clap: tight bursts of noise and a louder tail than Ring Clap. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit fires Bursts short bursts of noise, Spread apart; the last one starts the tail, which fades over Decay . The noise passes through a wide band-pass centred on Tone and a high-pass, for a bright, open clap. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds starts the bursts again. How to use it? Clap on the backbeat: layered with Punch Snare, or on its own. Big room clap: Decay 600 ms or more. Tight clap: 2 – 3 Bursts , Spread around 5 ms. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tone 500 Hz – 4 kHz 1.5 kHz Decay 50 ms – 1.5 s 350 ms Spread 3 – 30 ms 8 ms Bursts 1 – 6 4 Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tone: the centre of the band-pass. Decay: how long the tail lasts. Spread: the time between bursts. Bursts: how many bursts play before the tail. A setting, not a knob. Level: the output volume. Tone , Decay , Spread and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Cymbal
text: Punch Cymbal Punch Cymbal in the module view Introduction A crash or a ride cymbal: bright, slightly crunchy metal with a long decay. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Crash mixes six square waves with plenty of noise, high-passed, with an extra burst of energy at the start that settles into a wash lasting Decay . Ride uses a different set of square waves, less noise, and a band-passed bell tone on top, for a ping you can play in patterns; it rings 1.5 × Decay . Tone moves the high-pass, Crunch adds grit as in Punch Hats. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Crash on the one: Voice Crash on the first beat of a section. Ride pattern: Voice Ride, quarter or eighth notes, varied velocity. Reverse-style swell: patch a rising envelope onto Level . Crunch: bit and sample-rate reduction: clean … gritty. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone , Crunch and Level are modulation destinations. title: Punch Drums
text: Punch Drums Introduction The Punch drums are a drum kit, one node per instrument. They are built the way the drum machines of the mid eighties built their sounds: sine waves that restart on every hit and sweep down fast, with a click of noise on top, and bright metal for the hats and cymbals, with an optional crunch like the early samplers those machines used. The result is tight, hard and forward: a kick that punches through, a snappy snare, crisp hats. For a deeper, rounder kit, see the Ring drums. Crunch (hats and cymbals) lowers the bit depth and sample rate of the metal, for the gritty sheen of an early sampler. At 0 % it's clean. title: Punch Hats

title: Punch Kick
text: Punch Kick Punch Kick in the module view Introduction A hard, tight bass drum: a sine wave that starts high and sweeps down fast onto Tune , with a click of noise on top. It cuts through a busy mix. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit restarts a sine oscillator at the top of its cycle and drops its pitch from far above Tune : a very fast fall in the first few milliseconds, then a slower settle. Sweep sets how far it falls. Attack adds a short burst of noise and a thump, the beater hitting the skin. The body fades over Decay . Drive saturates the sound, rounding the sine toward a square for a harder, louder kick. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it; the previous hit is cut off. How to use it? Four on the floor: the defaults on every beat. Long, booming kick: Decay 1 s or more, Drive up. Soft, round kick: Sweep and Attack low, Drive 0. title: Punch Rim

It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Three high resonators are struck at once, together with a tiny burst of noise. A high-pass and saturation turn them into a sharp crack. Decay multiplies how long they ring. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Rim accents: sparse hits between snare and hats. Stick click: Decay at 0.25 ×, Tune up. title: Punch Snare
text: Punch Snare Punch Snare in the module view Introduction A snare with a hard, forward body: two sine waves that drop slightly in pitch, and filtered noise for the snare wires. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Two sine oscillators, at Tune and about 1.6 × Tune , restart on each hit and fall a little in pitch, then fade quickly. White noise passes through a low-pass, set by Tone , and a high-pass that keeps it out of the body; Snappy sets its level and Decay its length. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Backbeat: the defaults on beats 2 and 4. Crisp snare: Tone high, Snappy 80 %, Decay around 200 ms. Fat snare: Tune low, Decay 500 ms. Rolls: fast hits with rising velocity. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 120 – 400 Hz 200 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Snappy 0 – 100 % 60 % Decay 50 ms – 1 s 300 ms Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch of the body. Tone: the brightness of the noise (its low-pass). Snappy: the level of the noise. Decay: how long the noise lasts. Level: the output volume. Tune , Tone , Snappy , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Tom
text: Punch Tom Punch Tom in the module view Introduction A tom: a sine wave that starts above its pitch and drops onto it, with a touch of noise. Punchier than Ring Tom, with a clear pitch drop. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit restarts a sine oscillator. Its pitch starts above Tune and falls: quickly at first, then slowly over the whole note. Bend sets how far. A short burst of low-passed noise adds the stick; Noise sets its level. The tone fades over Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Tom fills: three Punch Toms at about 90, 120 and 170 Hz. Electronic toms: Bend at 100 %, Decay long, Noise 0. Melodic toms: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune and adjust the cable's amount until the intervals sound right. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 50 – 500 Hz 110 Hz Decay 50 ms – 2 s 450 ms Bend 0 – 100 % 50 % Noise 0 – 100 % 20 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the tom settles on. Decay: how long the tom lasts. Bend: how far the pitch drops; at 100 % it starts about twice as high. Noise: the level of the stick noise. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Bend , Noise and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum
